profile.overview: The Highland Tinamou, also called Bonaparte’s Tinamou or Tinamú Serrano, is a secretive, ground-dwelling bird of humid mountain forests. It belongs to an ancient South American bird group that can fly but usually moves quietly through dense vegetation. The species is most often detected by its repeated whistle rather than seen. In Costa Rica, it is associated with highland and montane forests, including protected areas in the Cordillera de Guanacaste and other mountain ranges.
profile.classification: The Highland Tinamou is a member of the tinamou family, Tinamidae, in the order Tinamiformes. The Costa Rican population is generally assigned to the subspecies Nothocercus bonapartei frantzii.
profile.identification: This medium-sized tinamou measures about 38–41 cm long. It has a rounded body, short tail, gray legs, and a relatively small head. The back and wings are dark, mottled, or barred, with pale cream spotting. The breast is distinctly rufous or tawny, which helps separate it from the similar Great Tinamou. It is usually encountered walking on the forest floor, and its shy behavior, dark plumage, and dense habitat make visual identification difficult.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama south through the Andes of Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, and northern Peru. In Costa Rica it is a resident of montane and humid highland forest, ranging from roughly 1,200 m to at least 2,500 m in suitable areas. Records include the Cacao sector of Área de Conservación Guanacaste. It favors wet, dense forest with a shaded, relatively open floor, thick undergrowth, and sometimes bamboo or other ground cover.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and not considered a regular long-distance migrant. It is expected to remain in suitable highland forest throughout the year, although local movements may occur with food availability or weather.
profile.breeding: Highland Tinamou breeding information is limited, but tinamous commonly nest on or very near the ground in sheltered vegetation or beside tree buttresses. The male generally incubates the eggs and cares for the young, while females may mate with more than one male. Reports for this species describe small clutches of glossy turquoise to violet eggs. Exact breeding dates in Costa Rica are not well documented, so the local nesting season should be treated as uncertain.
profile.dietFeeding: It forages mainly on the forest floor, taking fallen fruits, seeds, and other plant material, along with insects and other small invertebrates. Feeding usually involves quiet walking and probing among leaf litter and low vegetation. Its diet may vary with seasonal fruiting and local forest conditions. Because it spends much of the day in dense cover, feeding activity is often heard or inferred from tracks and brief sightings rather than observed closely.
profile.behavior: The Highland Tinamou is generally shy and difficult to observe. It usually walks rather than flies, but can make a rapid, explosive flight when startled. Individuals may forage alone or in loose association, and they retreat quickly when approached. Males give repeated, musical or tremulous whistles from their forest territories, especially during breeding activity. At night, the bird may roost on a low or moderate forest perch rather than sleeping on the ground.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not reliably quantified in commonly available summaries.

profile.overview: The Great Tinamou is a large, ground-dwelling forest bird of the tinamou family. It has a plump body, small head, very short tail, and cryptic brown plumage that blends with leaf litter. Usually heard rather than seen, it gives a distinctive, low, whistled song from dense forest. The species is native to Central and South America and is an important consumer and disperser of fallen fruits and seeds in tropical forests.
profile.classification: The Great Tinamou belongs to the family Tinamidae and the order Tinamiformes. Its scientific name is Tinamus major.
profile.identification: This tinamou is about 43 centimeters long and has a heavy, rounded body with a thin neck, small head, and short tail. Adults are generally olive-brown or grayish brown above, with dark barring and spotting; the underparts are paler and also barred. The legs are grayish. Both sexes look similar, although females are often somewhat heavier and may show brighter coloration. Its secretive behavior and repeated whistle are often more useful for identification than direct views.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Great Tinamou ranges from southern Mexico through Central America into northern and western South America. In Costa Rica, it is a resident species in suitable forest, especially in lowlands and foothills across the Caribbean slope, generally up to about 1,000–1,500 meters. It also occurs on the southern Pacific slope, reaching higher elevations locally, including the Coto Brus Valley, and is found in parts of the Guanacaste volcanoes. It favors humid and very humid tropical forest, particularly mature forest and dense understory.
profile.migrationStatus: Non-migratory and resident in Costa Rica. Individuals remain in forested areas throughout the year rather than undertaking regular seasonal migration.
profile.breeding: Great Tinamous place their eggs directly on the forest floor, usually in a shallow scrape among leaf litter near a tree base, buttress root, log, or other cover. The clutch commonly contains three to five glossy blue or blue-green eggs. Breeding in Costa Rica has been reported mainly from December through August. The male incubates the eggs and cares for the chicks, which are able to walk soon after hatching and become independent relatively quickly.
profile.dietFeeding: The species forages mainly by walking slowly through the forest understory and leaf litter. Its diet consists chiefly of fallen fruits and seeds, with additional plant material and animal prey such as insects, spiders, other arthropods, frogs, and small lizards. It often searches beneath vegetation and among decomposing leaves, swallowing food from the ground. This feeding behavior may help move seeds through forest habitats.
profile.behavior: Great Tinamous are secretive, mostly solitary birds that spend much of their time walking or running through shaded forest. They may occur in pairs during courtship or breeding but are difficult to observe because their plumage provides excellent camouflage. Their clear whistles are frequently heard in the morning and afternoon, and sometimes at night. When alarmed, they generally run into cover, although they can make short, explosive flights when necessary.

conservation.populationTrend: No strong global population trend is reliably established; the species remains widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Little Tinamou (Crypturellus soui) is a small, secretive ground-dwelling bird of tropical America. It is usually detected by its distinctive, repeated whistle rather than seen. Its compact body is nearly tailless, with generally dark brown plumage, a grayer head, pale throat, and buffy underparts. In Costa Rica it is a resident tinamou associated especially with humid lowland and foothill habitats, forest edges, and dense secondary vegetation.
profile.classification: The Little Tinamou belongs to the tinamou family, Tinamidae, in the order Tinamiformes. It is one of several small forest tinamous in the genus Crypturellus.
profile.identification: This tinamou is about 23 centimeters long and has a rounded, compact body with a very short tail. The upperparts are mostly plain sooty or dark brown, while the head is somewhat gray and the throat is whitish. The underparts are usually cinnamon-buff to brownish. Legs may be yellowish, olive, or gray. It normally runs through dense cover when disturbed and seldom flies, making its clear, tremulous whistle an important identification clue.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Little Tinamou ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and widely across northern and central South America. In Costa Rica it is a native resident, occurring mainly from sea level to about 1,500 meters on the Caribbean slope, in humid areas of the southern and western Nicoya Peninsula, and generally southward from the Orotina region on the Pacific slope. It is absent or scarce in the dry northwest. Typical habitats include lowland evergreen forest, river-edge forest, forest margins, plantations, and dense secondary growth.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout its range; it does not undertake regular long-distance migration. Individuals generally remain within or near suitable local forest and dense-cover habitats.
profile.breeding: The Little Tinamou lays its eggs in a simple nest or shallow depression on the ground, often beneath dense vegetation or other cover. The clutch is small, and the eggs are typically glossy and strongly colored. As in other tinamous, the male takes primary responsibility for incubation and care of the young. Chicks are precocial: they are downy, mobile soon after hatching, and follow the attending male while feeding on the forest floor.
profile.dietFeeding: It feeds mainly on seeds, fruits, berries, and other plant material collected from the ground, while also taking small invertebrates such as insects and other arthropods. It forages quietly in leaf litter and dense undergrowth, using its bill to pick up food. Feeding activity is often greatest during the cooler parts of the day, especially morning and late afternoon.
profile.behavior: The Little Tinamou is highly secretive and usually travels alone or in pairs through thick vegetation. It spends most of its time walking or running on the forest floor and may cross narrow trails or quiet roads, but it flies only when strongly pressured. Its repeated whistle may be heard at dawn or dusk and is often the best evidence of its presence. Dense secondary growth provides important concealment and foraging cover in Costa Rica.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not considered to be declining at a rate that currently qualifies the species for a threatened category.

profile.overview: The Thicket Tinamou (Crypturellus cinnamomeus) is a shy, ground-dwelling bird of tropical and subtropical forests from Mexico through Central America. It is recognized by its warm brown plumage, dark barring, cinnamon-colored breast, reddish legs, and distinctive repetitive whistle. It usually walks quietly through dense vegetation rather than flying, and is more often heard than seen. In Costa Rica, it is especially associated with dry forests, gallery forests, and regenerating woodland in the northwestern Pacific region.
profile.classification: The Thicket Tinamou belongs to the order Tinamiformes and family Tinamidae. The Costa Rican population is generally treated as the subspecies Crypturellus cinnamomeus praepes.
profile.identification: About 28 centimeters long, the Thicket Tinamou has brown upperparts marked with strong blackish barring across the back, rump, and wings. The underparts are paler, with a noticeable cinnamon wash on the breast and darker lower tail feathers. Its head and bill are brown, while the legs are reddish or pinkish. It can resemble other Costa Rican tinamous, especially the Slaty-breasted Tinamou, but its more obvious barring, habitat, distribution, and distinctive voice help separate it.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from western and eastern Mexico south through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly in the northwestern lowlands, particularly Guanacaste and northern Puntarenas, and is a resident rather than a seasonal visitor. It is common locally in dry forest, deciduous woodland, gallery forest, forest edge, dense scrub, and regenerating vegetation. It may occur to about 1,000 meters in wetter areas, but is most characteristic of lowland Pacific habitats.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica, with no regular long-distance migration documented. Individuals remain in suitable local habitats throughout the year, including dry forest and regenerating woodland in the northwestern Pacific region.
profile.breeding: Breeding occurs in the wet-season period in parts of Costa Rica, although timing can vary locally. Like other tinamous, the species nests on the ground, often beside raised roots, a small bank, or dense vegetation. The nest is a shallow depression in leaf litter and may contain several glossy pinkish or purplish eggs. Males maintain nesting territories, incubate the eggs, and provide the main parental care after hatching, while females may mate with more than one male.
profile.dietFeeding: The Thicket Tinamou forages mainly on the forest floor, walking through leaf litter and low vegetation. Its diet includes fallen fruits, seeds, insects, other small invertebrates, and occasionally small frogs. It may feed beneath shrubs or along forest edges, where cover provides protection from predators. Its feeding activities can also help disperse seeds within forest and woodland habitats.
profile.behavior: This tinamou is secretive and strongly terrestrial, usually walking or running through dense cover and flying only when startled. It may occur alone, in pairs, or in small family groups. Its repeated, plaintive whistle is often the best way to detect it. Birds in areas with little human disturbance are particularly wary, so observers usually have the best chance of seeing one by remaining still and listening carefully near suitable ground cover.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not considered to meet the thresholds for a threatened category, although the species may be declining locally where forest is cleared or degraded.

profile.overview: The Slaty-breasted Tinamou is a secretive, ground-dwelling bird of humid tropical forests in Middle America. It spends most of its time walking through leaf litter and dense understory rather than flying. Its low, repeated calls are often the best way to detect it. The species occurs from southern Mexico through Central America to northern Costa Rica, where it is a local resident of suitable lowland and foothill forest.
profile.classification: The Slaty-breasted Tinamou belongs to the tinamou family, Tinamidae, in the order Tinamiformes. Its scientific name is Crypturellus boucardi.
profile.identification: This medium-sized tinamou is about 28 cm long and has a stocky body, short tail, and reddish legs. Adults are generally dark brown above, with black barring on the back and flanks, a gray to slaty-gray head, neck, and upper breast, and warmer buff or rufous lower underparts. The throat is pale. Females may show more extensive buff barring on the upperparts. It is usually seen briefly on the forest floor or detected by its distinctive low call.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is a locally resident bird, most associated with the northern Caribbean lowlands and extending south toward Limón. It can occur in foothills to about 700 m and may reach the Pacific slope through mountain passes in the Guanacaste region. Preferred habitat is humid primary or mature secondary forest with dense understory, leaf litter, and moist ground, although it may tolerate some disturbed forest and regenerating plantations.
profile.migrationStatus: Slaty-breasted Tinamous are considered resident rather than migratory. In Costa Rica, the species remains year-round in suitable forest, including parts of the Caribbean lowlands and nearby foothills; seasonal movements are not known to be significant.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited, but the species nests on the forest floor in a shallow depression lined with leaves, often among low dense vegetation or near roots. The eggs are typically glossy lavender or purplish. A nest may contain about two eggs, with larger clutches possibly resulting when more than one female lays in the same nest. Males incubate the eggs and care for the chicks. In Costa Rica, nesting has been reported mainly from May through June, possibly continuing into October.
profile.dietFeeding: The Slaty-breasted Tinamou forages by walking slowly and irregularly through the leaf litter. Its diet includes fallen fruits, seeds, ants, termites, and other small invertebrates. It may also take small frogs or lizards. Rather than scratching vigorously like domestic poultry, it uses its bill to toss aside leaves and small twigs while searching for food on the forest floor.
profile.behavior: This tinamou is mainly solitary and terrestrial. It is most active on the ground and usually relies on camouflage and dense cover. Males defend small territories with repeated calls and may confront rivals. Calling is especially common in the morning and evening, and courtship can involve vocal exchanges between males and females. When alarmed, the bird may freeze or walk away quietly; if closely threatened, it runs through cover and makes a short, noisy flight only as a last resort.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing. Abundance varies locally: the species may remain common in well-protected forest but become scarce where forest is heavily cleared or hunting is intensive.
conservation.threats: Major threats include conversion and degradation of humid forest for agriculture, plantations, pasture, and infrastructure. Fragmentation reduces suitable understory habitat, while hunting can cause local declines because the species is a terrestrial game bird. Continued loss of mature and regenerating forest in Central America is an additional concern.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore humid lowland and foothill forest, especially in the Caribbean region of Costa Rica. Support protected areas, forest corridors, and shade-grown or wildlife-friendly farming that retains dense native vegetation. Avoid hunting tinamous and discourage the purchase or consumption of wild-caught game birds. Birdwatchers can contribute well-documented sightings to conservation databases and follow quiet, low-impact practices in forest habitat.

profile.overview: The Black-bellied Whistling-Duck is a long-legged, long-necked waterfowl species with a distinctive whistling call. It combines duck-like feeding habits with some goose-like features, including an upright posture and frequent use of land and elevated perches. Adults are boldly colored, with a chestnut breast, black belly, grayish face, pink bill and legs, and a broad white wing stripe. It is social, often traveling and resting in noisy groups.
profile.classification: The Black-bellied Whistling-Duck belongs to the whistling-duck family Anatidae and the genus Dendrocygna. It is divided into northern and southern geographic forms, including the subspecies autumnalis found in much of South America and Central America.
profile.identification: This large, slim waterfowl measures about 47–51 centimeters long. Adults have a chestnut-brown breast and neck, a gray face, a prominent black belly and lower flanks, a pink to orange bill, and long pink legs. A broad white stripe is visible along the folded wing and becomes especially obvious in flight. Juveniles are duller, with browner plumage, a darker bill, paler legs, and little or no black on the belly. Its high-pitched, whistling calls are distinctive.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from the southern United States through Mexico and Central America to northern and central South America. In Costa Rica it is a regular resident, especially on the lowlands and Pacific slope, where it is locally common rather than uniformly abundant. It uses shallow freshwater ponds, marshes, lagoons, rice fields, flooded agricultural land, river edges, mangroves, and wet grassy areas. It may also rest in trees, on fence posts, wires, rooftops, and other structures near feeding or roosting sites.
profile.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Black-bellied Whistling-Duck is generally regarded as a resident species, not mainly a Nearctic migrant. Local movements may occur between wetlands, agricultural fields, and roosting areas, and numbers can vary seasonally. Northern populations may migrate south in winter, but Costa Rican birds are part of the established Central American population.
profile.breeding: Breeding can occur in tree cavities, natural hollows, nest boxes, dense vegetation, or occasionally on the ground. The species usually places eggs directly on accumulated debris inside a cavity rather than constructing a substantial nest. Both adults participate in selecting a nest site and caring for the young. Clutches commonly contain about 9–18 white eggs, which hatch after roughly 25–30 days. Ducklings are mobile soon after hatching and are covered in strongly patterned black-and-yellow down.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet is mainly plant-based and includes grasses, sedges, seeds, aquatic vegetation, grains, and agricultural crops such as rice, corn, sorghum, and millet. Small amounts of animal food, including insects, snails, spiders, and other aquatic invertebrates, are also eaten. Birds forage by dabbling in shallow water and grazing on land. They often feed at dusk or during the night, traveling between daytime roosts and feeding sites.
profile.behavior: Black-bellied Whistling-Ducks are highly social and commonly occur in pairs, family groups, or large flocks. They walk readily on land and perch more often than most typical ducks, using trees, posts, wires, and logs. Their repeated, high-pitched whistles help maintain contact within a flock. Pairs often remain together for many years. Courtship includes synchronized movements, bill dipping, and water-flicking displays, while aggressive encounters may involve chasing, nipping, and forward-stretched neck postures.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered stable to increasing. In parts of the southern United States, the species has expanded its range and increased in abundance, although regional trends may differ.

profile.overview: The Fulvous Whistling-Duck is a long-necked, long-legged waterfowl of tropical wetlands. Its rich cinnamon-brown plumage, pale facial markings, dark wings, and white side stripes make it distinctive among whistling-ducks. It often gathers in flocks and produces clear, whistled calls while flying or resting. The species occurs across tropical regions of the Americas, Africa, and South Asia, usually where shallow freshwater, marsh vegetation, and abundant seeds or aquatic invertebrates are available.
profile.classification: The Fulvous Whistling-Duck belongs to the order Anseriformes and the duck family Anatidae. Its scientific name is Dendrocygna bicolor; it is one of the whistling-ducks, a group distinct from typical dabbling ducks in body shape, behavior, and vocalizations.
profile.identification: Adults are mainly warm fulvous or cinnamon-brown, with a darker back and crown, a grayish bill, and bluish-gray legs. A conspicuous pale or white stripe runs along each side of the body, contrasting with the dark wings. The neck and legs are unusually long for a duck. In flight, the wings appear mostly dark, helping distinguish it from the Black-bellied Whistling-Duck, which shows a contrasting pale wing patch. Juveniles are duller and less strongly marked.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species has a broad tropical distribution in the Americas, including parts of Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and South America. In Costa Rica it is a localized species, associated especially with lowland wetlands in the Tempisque Basin and other suitable sites in the northwest, where it may breed. It uses freshwater marshes, shallow lakes, seasonally flooded savannas, ponds, rice fields, and other wetlands with emergent or floating vegetation. Occurrence can vary with water levels and wetland conditions.
profile.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Fulvous Whistling-Duck is generally considered a localized resident or seasonal resident rather than a regular long-distance migrant. Birds may make local or regional movements as wetlands flood or dry, and records can be irregular outside favored lowland areas. Some populations elsewhere are partly migratory or nomadic.
profile.breeding: Breeding takes place in wetlands with dense emergent vegetation, floating plants, or nearby flooded grassland. The species usually nests on or close to water, sometimes among reeds or grasses, and may nest in loose colonies. Both adults participate in caring for the brood. Clutches commonly contain several pale eggs, and the ducklings leave the nest soon after hatching. In Costa Rica, breeding is particularly associated with suitable wetlands of the Tempisque lowlands, although breeding evidence may be local and seasonal.
profile.dietFeeding: The Fulvous Whistling-Duck feeds mainly on seeds, grasses, aquatic plants, and other plant material, supplemented by aquatic invertebrates. It forages in shallow water, wet mud, flooded fields, and marsh vegetation. Unlike many ducks, it can filter fine material from the water and mud with its bill, straining out small seeds and invertebrates. Feeding commonly occurs during daylight, but the species may also forage around dawn, dusk, or at night.
profile.behavior: This social duck is usually seen in pairs, family groups, or flocks. It swims well but also walks readily through shallow marshes and flooded grassland. Birds often rest on open water, low banks, or vegetation and may fly between feeding and roosting sites at dusk. Its repeated whistled calls are an important feature of its behavior. Fulvous Whistling-Ducks are alert and readily take flight when disturbed, often forming coordinated flocks.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered decreasing, but the decline is not currently judged severe enough for a threatened category. Trends are uneven among regions, and local populations may fluctuate with wetland conditions.
conservation.threats: Wetland drainage, conversion of marshes and seasonally flooded areas, agricultural expansion, altered water management, pollution, and disturbance can reduce available habitat. In Costa Rica, the species depends on a limited network of lowland wetlands, making local populations sensitive to changes in water levels and loss of wetland vegetation.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore freshwater marshes, seasonal wetlands, flooded savannas, and rice-field habitats that retain suitable shallow-water conditions. Support wetland reserves and responsible water management, reduce pollution and unnecessary disturbance, and report sightings through reputable bird-monitoring programs to improve knowledge of the species in Costa Rica.

profile.overview: The Swan Goose is a large, long-necked goose native to eastern Asia. It breeds in Mongolia, northeastern China, and the Russian Far East, then migrates south to winter mainly in central and eastern China. The wild species is distinct from domesticated Chinese Geese, which are widely kept and may appear far outside the natural range. Swan Geese are strongly associated with wetlands, grasslands, lakes, rivers, floodplains, and agricultural areas near water.
profile.classification: The Swan Goose belongs to the family Anatidae and genus Anser. Its scientific name is Anser cygnoides.
profile.identification: A wild Swan Goose is a tall, slim-bodied goose with a long neck, a dark brown crown and hindneck, a pale or buff face and fore-neck, and a long, mostly dark bill. The body is generally gray-brown, with pale underparts and darker flight feathers. Its upright posture and distinctive two-toned head help separate it from other geese. Domestic forms vary greatly, including white and mottled birds, and often have a prominent knob at the bill base.
profile.rangeHabitat: The wild Swan Goose breeds across inland Mongolia, northeastern China, and the Russian Far East, especially around steppe lakes, river valleys, marshes, and wet grasslands. It winters mainly in floodplains and wetlands of central and eastern China, including areas around the Yangtze River. Costa Rica lies far outside the species' natural range and is not part of its regular wild distribution. Records there, when present, are most plausibly escaped, released, or captive-origin birds rather than wild migrants.
profile.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant in Asia, moving between northern breeding grounds and Chinese wintering wetlands. It is not a regular migratory species in Costa Rica; Costa Rican occurrences should be treated as exceptional and potentially involving domestic or captive-origin birds.
profile.breeding: Swan Geese usually form long-term pair bonds and breed during the northern spring and summer. Nests are placed on or near the ground in grassy vegetation close to lakes, rivers, marshes, or other wetlands. The female incubates a clutch of several eggs while the male remains nearby and helps defend the nesting area. Young leave the nest soon after hatching and remain with their parents, often forming family groups before migration.
profile.dietFeeding: The species is primarily herbivorous. It grazes on grasses and other terrestrial plants and also eats aquatic vegetation, roots, rhizomes, seeds, and grains. Swan Geese commonly feed in wet grasslands, lake margins, floodplains, riverbanks, and agricultural fields near wetlands. Wintering birds may rely heavily on submerged plants and managed or natural grasslands, while domestic birds are often fed grain and other farm foods.
profile.behavior: Swan Geese are social and often gather in family groups or large flocks, especially during migration, molting, and winter. They spend time both swimming and grazing on land. The species is generally wary and may take flight when approached or disturbed. Calls are loud, goose-like honks. During the nesting season, pairs become more closely associated, but outside breeding they commonly mix with other waterfowl in suitable wetlands.

conservation.populationTrend: Decreasing.
conservation.threats: Major threats include the loss and degradation of wetlands and floodplains, conversion of grasslands and marshes for agriculture, disturbance, hunting, and the collection of eggs. Problems are especially serious at migration stopover sites and wintering areas in eastern Asia, where much of the wild population gathers.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore wetlands, floodplains, steppe lakes, and wet grasslands along the species' Asian migration route. Support responsible management of important waterbird sites, reduce disturbance during migration and winter, and discourage illegal hunting and egg collection. In Costa Rica, do not release domestic geese into natural wetlands, and report unusual birds with documentation so captive-origin individuals are not confused with wild records.

profile.overview: The Greater White-fronted Goose is a medium-sized, stocky goose of the Northern Hemisphere. Adults are brown overall, with a white feathered area around the bill, orange legs, and usually black markings across the belly. It breeds mainly in Arctic tundra and migrates south to wetlands, grasslands, agricultural fields, and shallow-water habitats. In Costa Rica it is an exceptionally rare visitor rather than a regular wintering species, with accepted records from the country.
profile.classification: The Greater White-fronted Goose belongs to the order Anseriformes and family Anatidae. Its scientific name is Anser albifrons, and several geographic forms or subspecies are recognized across North America, Greenland, Europe, and Asia.
profile.identification: Adults have a brown head and neck, a pale brown body, orange legs, and a pinkish, orange, or yellow-orange bill bordered by a conspicuous white forehead patch. Black belly bars vary among individuals and may be absent or faint in juveniles. Immatures lack the strong white facial patch and extensive belly markings. The species is smaller and less pot-bellied than many domestic geese. In Costa Rica, any identification should be documented carefully because it is an accidental or very rare species there.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species has a broad Holarctic range, breeding in Arctic and subarctic tundra, wet meadows, river margins, and lake edges. During migration and winter it uses freshwater marshes, shallow lakes, coastal wetlands, grasslands, and croplands where it feeds on grasses, grains, and other vegetation. In Costa Rica, the Greater White-fronted Goose is listed as rare or accidental. The first accepted national record was observed at Las Trancas, Guanacaste, on November 29, 2021; it is not considered a regular component of the country's waterfowl community.
profile.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. North American birds generally breed in Alaska and Arctic Canada and winter mainly in the United States and Mexico. Costa Rica lies well south of the species' normal wintering range, so occurrences there are exceptional vagrants rather than predictable seasonal migrants.
profile.breeding: Breeding begins after arrival on Arctic nesting grounds in late spring or early summer. The nest is a shallow ground depression, usually near water and lined with down and plant material. A female commonly lays several eggs and incubates them while the male remains nearby to defend the territory. Young leave the nest soon after hatching and are raised by both parents. Family groups often remain together during migration and winter.
profile.dietFeeding: The Greater White-fronted Goose is primarily herbivorous. It grazes on grasses, sedges, roots, shoots, leaves, and other green vegetation, and it consumes grains and waste crops in agricultural areas. It may feed both by grazing on land and by dabbling in shallow water. In winter, flocks often move between feeding fields and nearby wetlands used for drinking, resting, and avoiding predators.
profile.behavior: This social goose usually occurs in flocks, sometimes mixed with Snow Geese, Canada Geese, or other waterfowl. It is alert and wary, often giving loud calls while feeding or moving between sites. Flight is strong and direct, with family groups maintaining contact by voice. Like other geese, it forms durable pair bonds, and young birds may remain associated with their parents beyond the first migration cycle.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered broadly stable, although trends differ among regional populations and some localized groups may be increasing or declining.

profile.overview: The Comb Duck, also called the American Comb Duck, is a large, distinctive waterfowl species of tropical South America. It belongs to the duck family Anatidae and is named for the fleshy knob or comb on the male’s bill. It uses freshwater wetlands, flooded grasslands, marshes, lakes, rivers, and nearby agricultural areas. Although its normal range is South American, it is recorded only rarely in Costa Rica, where it is treated as an accidental or very rare visitor.
profile.classification: The Comb Duck is an anseriform waterfowl in the family Anatidae. Its scientific name is Sarkidiornis sylvicola; it is separate from the closely related African and Asian Knob-billed Duck, Sarkidiornis melanotos.
profile.identification: This is a large duck with a white head and neck marked by dark spots, glossy blue-black upperparts, and dark flanks. The male is considerably larger than the female and develops a prominent black, fleshy knob on the upper bill during the breeding season. Females have a smaller or poorly developed knob. In flight, the contrasting white body and dark wings are noticeable. Immature birds are duller and may lack the strongly developed bill knob.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Comb Duck’s regular range extends across tropical South America, from Colombia and Venezuela south through the Amazon and eastern lowlands to Paraguay, southeastern Brazil, and northeastern Argentina. It occupies freshwater marshes, seasonally flooded savannas, quiet lakes, slow rivers, ponds, flooded grassland, and sometimes rice fields or other agricultural wetlands. In Costa Rica it is not a regular resident or breeder. The species is listed as accidental or very rare, with records mainly involving lowland wetlands, including Guanacaste.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is largely resident, but it can make local or seasonal movements in response to rainfall, flooding, and water availability. In Costa Rica it is an accidental or very rare visitor, not a regular migrant.
profile.breeding: Comb Ducks usually breed near still or slow-moving freshwater. They commonly nest in tree cavities, but may also use tree stumps, abandoned nests, tall grass, or other sheltered sites close to water. The female lays a clutch of pale eggs and normally performs incubation. Nesting behavior can include more than one female laying in a shared nest. Males defend females and young, while nest-site defense is less pronounced. There is no reliable evidence that the species regularly breeds in Costa Rica.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet is mainly plant-based. Comb Ducks graze or dabble for grasses, sedges, seeds, grains, and soft parts of aquatic plants. They also take aquatic insect larvae, other invertebrates, and occasionally small aquatic animals. Feeding occurs in shallow water, wet grassland, muddy margins, and cultivated fields such as rice-growing areas. The species may feed by day and often rests or perches in trees near wetlands.
profile.behavior: Comb Ducks are strong swimmers and can also walk and graze on land. They often occur singly, in pairs, or in small groups, although larger concentrations may form where food and water are abundant. They regularly perch in trees and roost near wetlands. Their movements are influenced by seasonal flooding and drying. Males are conspicuous because of their large size and bill knob, while females and immature birds can appear less boldly patterned.

conservation.populationTrend: A precise global population trend is not well established. The species is not currently considered globally threatened, although it is locally uncommon and has a scattered distribution in parts of its range.

profile.overview: The Orinoco Goose is a large, distinctive sheldgoose of tropical South America. It is strongly associated with rivers, oxbow lakes, marshes, sandy banks, and nearby savanna or open woodland. Unlike many geese, it spends much time walking and grazing on land and often perches in trees. The species is usually seen in pairs or small family groups and is generally quiet and wary. In Costa Rica, it is an exceptionally rare accidental visitor rather than a regular native species.
profile.classification: The Orinoco Goose belongs to the duck and goose family Anatidae and the order Anseriformes. It is often placed in the genus Oressochen, although some taxonomic authorities use Neochen jubata. It is considered monotypic, with no widely recognized subspecies.
profile.identification: This is a medium-large goose, about 56–66 cm long, with a heavy body, long legs, and a relatively short bill. Adults have a dark head and upperparts, a contrasting pale or whitish throat and lower face, rich chestnut-brown coloration across the breast and flanks, and darker wings and tail. The sexes look alike, although females are slightly smaller. It usually walks upright on riverbanks and grasslands and may sit in trees. Costa Rican records require careful documentation because confusion with escaped waterfowl is possible.
profile.rangeHabitat: The normal range extends across tropical South America east of the Andes, including parts of Venezuela, Colombia, Brazil, Bolivia, Peru, Paraguay, and northern Argentina. It uses broad rivers, river islands, sandy beaches, marshes, forest lakes, oxbows, gallery forest, savanna, and open woodland, generally in lowland or foothill settings. Costa Rica lies outside its established native range. The species is listed there as rare or accidental, so records represent exceptional vagrancy or possible escape or release, not a resident population.
profile.migrationStatus: Mostly resident, but some populations make local or regional seasonal movements, especially after breeding or in response to changing water levels. There is no reliable evidence that Costa Rica forms part of a regular migration route; occurrences there are accidental and highly unusual.
profile.breeding: Orinoco Geese usually breed as territorial pairs during a season influenced by rainfall and local hydrology. They commonly nest in cavities in large trees, including hollow trunks or branches, but may occasionally nest on the ground. The female generally lays about 7–10 eggs, and incubation lasts roughly four weeks. Adults remain protective around the nest and lead their precocial young to nearby water and feeding areas. No established breeding population is known from Costa Rica.
profile.dietFeeding: The species is primarily herbivorous. It grazes on grasses, sedges, leaves, shoots, seeds, and other tender vegetation in open areas beside water. It may also take aquatic plants and algae, particularly around stagnant water, oxbows, and river margins. Feeding is mainly terrestrial and often occurs during the day, with movements between resting and feeding sites around dawn and dusk. Small invertebrates may be taken occasionally, but they are not the main food.
profile.behavior: Orinoco Geese are generally terrestrial, walking and grazing more often than swimming. They frequently occur in pairs or small family groups and may rest or roost in trees, on exposed riverbanks, or on sandy islands. Breeding pairs defend territories and can become aggressive toward intruders. The birds are wary and usually fly only when disturbed or traveling between sites. Some populations make seasonal movements along river systems, and individuals may travel at night during these movements.

conservation.populationTrend: The global trend is not fully resolved. Declines have been reported in parts of the range, while some populations, particularly in Brazil, appear stable or increasing; the overall population is therefore best described as locally declining or uncertain rather than clearly stable.
conservation.threats: Important pressures include conversion and degradation of river margins, sandy breeding and roosting beaches, wetlands, gallery forest, and adjacent grasslands. Hunting and local collection for meat can affect some populations, while disturbance near nesting areas and disruption of seasonal movements may also reduce breeding success. Because Costa Rica supports no known established population, local conservation concerns there mainly involve accurate documentation and preventing the release of captive or non-native waterfowl.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect rivers, wetlands, oxbow lakes, sandy banks, gallery forest, and nearby natural grasslands across the species’ South American range. Support protected areas and management that limits hunting and disturbance at nesting and roosting sites. In Costa Rica, report any suspected Orinoco Goose to a recognized bird-records committee or conservation organization with photographs, location, date, and notes on origin; do not release captive waterfowl into the wild.

profile.overview: The Egyptian Goose (Alopochen aegyptiaca) is a distinctive African waterfowl that is more closely related to shelducks than to true geese. It has a pale gray-brown body, a prominent dark eye patch, pinkish legs, and bold white markings on the wings. It is adaptable and often lives near lakes, rivers, marshes, farmland, grasslands, and urban ponds. In Costa Rica, it is not recognized as a regular native or established wild species.
profile.classification: The Egyptian Goose belongs to the family Anatidae, which includes ducks, geese, and swans. It is the only living species in the genus Alopochen.
profile.identification: This medium-large waterfowl has a buff, gray-brown body, a pale head, and a conspicuous dark patch around the eye. The breast and upperparts may show warm chestnut tones, while the wings display contrasting white, dark, and metallic markings in flight. The bill is pinkish to reddish, and the legs are pink. Males and females look similar, although males are often larger and may have different vocal qualities. Juveniles are duller and lack the full adult pattern.
profile.rangeHabitat: Egyptian Geese are native mainly to sub-Saharan Africa and the Nile Valley, with especially broad distributions in eastern and southern Africa. They use freshwater lakes, rivers, marshes, floodplains, reservoirs, farm dams, grasslands, agricultural areas, and city parks. They have also established introduced populations in parts of Europe and elsewhere. In Costa Rica, the species is not a regular component of the native avifauna or a known established population; an apparent sighting would most plausibly involve a captive or ornamental bird, an escapee, or an exceptional vagrant.
profile.migrationStatus: Mostly resident or locally dispersive across its African range, moving in response to rainfall, water levels, and food availability rather than following a fixed long-distance migration. It is not a regular migrant in Costa Rica, where reliable evidence for a wild, established occurrence is lacking.
profile.breeding: Egyptian Geese commonly form pairs, and breeding may occur during different seasons depending on local rainfall and water conditions. Nests are placed in tree hollows, on cliffs, among reeds, in dense vegetation, or on the ground near water; they may also use abandoned nests of other birds. The female usually lays a clutch of several eggs and performs most incubation. Both adults care for the goslings, which can swim and feed soon after hatching.
profile.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on grasses, aquatic plants, seeds, grains, and other vegetable matter. It grazes on land, crops, lawns, and riverbanks, and also feeds in shallow water. Small quantities of insects and other invertebrates may be taken, especially by young birds. Egyptian Geese often feed during the day, resting near water between grazing periods and moving between wetlands and nearby open habitats.
profile.behavior: Egyptian Geese are vocal, alert, and strongly territorial, particularly around nest sites and broods. They are usually seen in pairs, family groups, or small flocks, although larger congregations can form at productive wetlands. Adults graze, swim, walk readily on land, and fly strongly when disturbed. They may defend feeding or nesting areas aggressively against other waterfowl. Their loud calls and conspicuous eye patches make them easy to notice.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered decreasing overall, but the species remains widespread and secure. Some regional populations, particularly in southern Africa, are stable or increasing, and introduced populations in parts of Europe have expanded.

profile.overview: The Muscovy Duck is a large tropical duck native to Mexico, Central America, and South America. It is the only living species in the genus Cairina and has been domesticated widely for meat and eggs. Wild birds are associated with forested wetlands, rivers, lagoons, marshes, and estuaries, while domestic and feral birds may occur around farms, gardens, and urban ponds. The species is generally quiet compared with many other ducks.
profile.classification: The Muscovy Duck belongs to the duck, goose, and swan family Anatidae. Its scientific name is Cairina moschata. Wild and domestic forms are commonly treated as the same species, although domestic birds show substantial variation in size and appearance.
profile.identification: This is a large, heavy-bodied duck with a long tail, broad wings, and relatively long claws. Wild birds are mostly blackish with bold white wing patches, while females are smaller and duller. Both sexes have bare red or pink skin around the eyes and bill; males usually have larger facial caruncles. Domestic birds can be white, pied, brown, or highly variable and may look unlike wild individuals.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Muscovy Duck occurs naturally from Mexico through Central America and across much of tropical South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, recorded locally in suitable lowland and foothill wetlands rather than as a regular migrant. It uses wooded streams, rivers, swamps, lagoons, estuaries, marshes, and small forest pools. In the country, sightings may involve wild birds as well as domestic or feral individuals near farms and settlements.
profile.migrationStatus: Non-migratory. In Costa Rica, Muscovy Ducks are generally present year-round, with local movements between feeding, roosting, and breeding wetlands. Domestic and feral birds may also appear in places outside the species’ usual wild habitat.
profile.breeding: Muscovy Ducks nest in tree cavities, hollow trunks, dense vegetation, or other sheltered sites close to water. The female usually lays a large clutch of pale eggs and incubates them alone, while the male may remain nearby. Ducklings are precocial and leave the nest soon after hatching. In tropical regions, breeding can occur during different parts of the year, often influenced by rainfall and local water conditions.
profile.dietFeeding: The species has a varied diet that includes aquatic plants, seeds, fruits, grasses, grain, insects, small crustaceans, and other invertebrates. It feeds by grazing on land, dabbling in shallow water, and probing mud or vegetation. Muscovy Ducks often forage along stream edges and wet forest margins, and domestic or feral birds readily exploit food provided around farms, parks, and residences.
profile.behavior: Muscovy Ducks are usually quiet and spend time resting on banks, low branches, fallen logs, or vegetation near water. They are strong fliers and can perch in trees, unlike many heavier domestic ducks. Birds may occur singly, in pairs, or in small groups. Males commonly defend space around females, while females lead ducklings between nesting, feeding, and shelter areas. They may become accustomed to people where domesticated.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, but the species remains widespread and relatively abundant across much of its range.

profile.overview: The Wood Duck (Aix sponsa) is a colorful, medium-sized perching duck associated with wooded freshwater habitats. It has a compact body, broad tail, and strong claws that help it perch in trees. Adult males are especially striking, with a glossy green and purple head, white facial markings, a red eye, and a chestnut breast. Females are gray-brown with a noticeable white eye-ring. The species is native mainly to North America.
profile.classification: The Wood Duck belongs to the order Anseriformes and the family Anatidae, which includes ducks, geese, and swans. Its scientific name is Aix sponsa.
profile.identification: The male has an iridescent green-and-purple crested head, white lines around the face, a red eye, a reddish bill, a chestnut breast, and patterned flanks. The female is mostly gray-brown, with a rounded crest, a white eye-ring, and a pale throat. Both sexes have a long, squared tail and a relatively large head. In flight, dark upperparts contrast with a pale belly and light wing markings. Its habit of resting on branches can also be distinctive.
profile.rangeHabitat: Wood Ducks breed across much of eastern and central North America, along the Pacific coast, and in parts of southern Canada and western Mexico. They favor wooded swamps, bottomland forests, freshwater marshes, ponds, beaver wetlands, and slow-moving streams with dense shoreline vegetation and nearby tree cavities. In Costa Rica, the species is not a regular resident or breeding duck. It has been recorded there as a very uncommon visitor or vagrant, mainly at suitable freshwater wetlands, ponds, and forest-edged waterways; sightings are unusual and localized.
profile.migrationStatus: The Wood Duck is partly migratory. Northern birds move south in autumn, while many birds in the southern part of the range remain year-round. Costa Rica lies well south of the principal regular range, so occurrences there are best treated as rare, irregular records rather than a predictable migration passage or wintering population.
profile.breeding: Wood Ducks nest in natural tree cavities, often near or above water, and readily use nest boxes. The female lines the cavity with down and usually lays 6–16 creamy white to tan eggs. Incubation lasts about 28–37 days. Ducklings leave the cavity soon after hatching by climbing or jumping to the ground and following the female to water. Most pairs raise one brood, although two broods can occur, especially in southern parts of the range. There is no reliable evidence of regular breeding in Costa Rica.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of plant material, including seeds, acorns, fruits, aquatic vegetation, and agricultural grains. Wood Ducks also eat insects, beetles, caterpillars, flies, snails, isopods, and other small invertebrates, with animal foods often more important during breeding. They feed by dabbling in shallow water, picking food from vegetation or the surface, and walking on land beneath trees to gather fallen nuts and fruit.
profile.behavior: Wood Ducks are agile fliers and usually remain close to cover rather than spending long periods on open water. They perch on branches and logs, swim quietly through vegetation, and forage in shallow water. Pairs form during the winter and display with head movements, raised wings, and mutual preening. Females sometimes lay eggs in the nests of other Wood Ducks. After hatching, ducklings leave the cavity together, while the female calls them toward nearby water.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is considered stable to increasing overall, with substantial recovery after severe declines caused by overhunting and loss of nesting habitat in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

profile.overview: The Mandarin Duck (Aix galericulata) is a small, striking perching duck native to eastern Asia. Males are famous for their multicolored breeding plumage, while females are mainly gray-brown with a prominent pale eye-ring. The species usually lives around wooded rivers, streams, ponds, and lakes. It nests in tree cavities and is closely related to North America's Wood Duck. Outside its native range, introduced and escaped populations are established in parts of Europe and occur locally elsewhere.
profile.classification: The Mandarin Duck belongs to the order Anseriformes and family Anatidae, the duck, goose, and swan family. It is one of two living species in the genus Aix, the other being the Wood Duck (Aix sponsa).
profile.identification: The male has a purplish-green head, white facial markings, orange cheek feathers, a reddish bill, a purple breast, pale flanks, and distinctive upright orange feathers on the back that resemble sails. The female is less colorful, with a gray head, brown body, pale eye-ring, and pale spotting on the sides. Mandarin Ducks are compact, broad-bodied ducks that often perch in trees and usually occur singly, in pairs, or in small groups.
profile.rangeHabitat: Mandarin Ducks are native to eastern Siberia, northeastern China, Korea, and Japan, with populations associated with forested wetlands and slow-moving water. They favor wooded river valleys, streams, ponds, and lakes with dense bankside vegetation and nearby mature trees containing nesting cavities. In Costa Rica, the species is not native and is not a regular component of the country's wild waterfowl community. Occasional records may represent escaped or released captive birds, and there is no reliable evidence of an established breeding population.
profile.migrationStatus: Native Asian populations make seasonal movements between breeding and wintering areas, while many introduced European populations are largely resident or make short-distance movements. In Costa Rica, it should be treated as an exceptional non-native or captive-origin occurrence rather than a regular migrant.
profile.breeding: Breeding takes place in spring in the northern part of the range. Pairs form before or during the breeding season, and the female selects a cavity in a mature tree, sometimes well above the ground or far from water. She lays about 9–12 eggs and incubates them alone. After hatching, the ducklings leave the cavity by jumping to the ground, then follow the female to water. Nest boxes may also be used where natural cavities are scarce.
profile.dietFeeding: The Mandarin Duck feeds on seeds, acorns, grains, aquatic plants, fruits, insects, snails, small crustaceans, and other invertebrates. Its diet changes with season and local food availability. It commonly forages by dabbling in shallow water, grazing along muddy or vegetated margins, and feeding on land beneath trees. Acorns and other fallen plant foods can be especially important during autumn and winter.
profile.behavior: Mandarin Ducks are generally shy and alert, often keeping close to overhanging vegetation or wooded shorelines. They swim well, fly strongly, and readily perch on branches. Pairs may remain together during much of the breeding season, while nonbreeding birds can gather in small flocks. Males give soft whistles and other calls, whereas females produce quieter clucks and alarm notes. Ducklings leave the nest soon after hatching and are guided to water by the female.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered broadly stable, with regional differences. Some introduced European populations have increased, while habitat loss and degradation have affected parts of the native Asian range.

profile.overview: The Blue-winged Teal is a small dabbling duck that breeds mainly in shallow wetlands across North America and migrates south for winter. It is named for the powder-blue wing coverts visible in flight, especially on adult males. Males have a dark head with a broad white crescent in front of the eye, while females are mostly mottled brown. In Costa Rica, it is a seasonal migrant and winter visitor rather than a breeding resident.
profile.classification: The Blue-winged Teal belongs to the duck family Anatidae and the order Anseriformes. Its scientific name is Spatula discors.
profile.identification: This small, slim duck has a short bill and a relatively compact body. The adult male has a slate-blue head, a bold white facial crescent, a blackish back, and pale blue shoulder patches. The female is mottled brown and can resemble other small dabbling ducks, but its dark bill, compact shape, and pale blue wing patch help with identification. In flight, both sexes show a distinctive blue forewing and green speculum.
profile.rangeHabitat: Blue-winged Teal breeds across much of Canada and the northern and central United States, especially in prairie potholes, shallow ponds, marshes, and wet grasslands. It winters from the southern United States through Mexico, Central America, and northern South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs as a regular migrant and winter visitor, using shallow freshwater wetlands, marshes, flooded fields, rice fields, ponds, lake margins, and sometimes brackish coastal wetlands. It is not known as a regular breeding species there.
profile.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Birds generally arrive in Costa Rica during the northern autumn and remain through the boreal winter, with most departing northward in spring. Costa Rica records classify it as a migrant rather than a resident.
profile.breeding: Blue-winged Teal usually form pairs during migration or before reaching the breeding grounds. The female selects a concealed nest site in grass or other low vegetation near shallow water, often some distance from the wetland edge. She lays a clutch of several pale eggs and incubates them alone. The ducklings leave the nest soon after hatching and feed themselves, while the female leads them to nearby shallow wetlands. Breeding does not normally occur in Costa Rica.
profile.dietFeeding: Blue-winged Teal feed by dabbling, tipping forward, and straining food from shallow water rather than routinely diving. Their diet includes aquatic insects, insect larvae, small crustaceans, mollusks, seeds, aquatic plants, and grains. Animal foods are especially important during breeding, while seeds and plant material become more prominent during migration and winter. In Costa Rica, they forage in shallow marshes, flooded fields, pond margins, and other productive wetlands.
profile.behavior: This species is active, social, and often gathers in flocks with other dabbling ducks. It spends much of the day feeding, resting, and preening in open shallow wetlands. Blue-winged Teal usually flush readily when disturbed and can maneuver quickly in flight. Males give short whistles during the breeding season, while females produce a deeper quack. During migration and winter, birds may form mixed-species groups and move among wetlands as water conditions change.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered broadly stable to declining, with numbers strongly influenced by annual wetland conditions and the availability of breeding habitat.
conservation.threats: Loss and degradation of shallow wetlands, conversion of native grasslands to agriculture, drought, changing water conditions, and reduced nesting cover can affect the species. Migratory birds in Central America may also be exposed to disturbance and the loss of suitable wintering wetlands.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore shallow wetlands, marshes, flooded fields, and wet grasslands along migration routes. Support conservation of prairie pothole breeding habitat, reduce disturbance around wintering ducks, maintain clean water, and participate in responsible bird monitoring that helps track migration and population changes.

profile.overview: The Cinnamon Teal is a small dabbling duck of the Americas, named for the rich cinnamon-red plumage of the adult male. Females are mottled brown and resemble female Blue-winged Teals, but usually have a longer, broader bill and warmer overall coloration. The species uses shallow wetlands, marshes, ponds, flooded fields, and slow-moving waters, where it feeds mainly by dabbling and filtering food from the water’s surface.
profile.classification: Cinnamon Teal belongs to the duck family Anatidae and the dabbling-duck group. Its scientific name is Spatula cyanoptera.
profile.identification: The adult male has a bright cinnamon or reddish-brown head and body, a darker back, a red eye, and a dark bill. The female is mottled brown with a grayish bill and is easily confused with female Blue-winged Teal. Cinnamon Teal generally shows a larger, more spatulate bill, warmer brown coloration, and less sharply defined facial markings. In flight, both sexes may show a pale blue forewing patch and a green speculum, although these can be difficult to see.
profile.rangeHabitat: Cinnamon Teal occurs in western North America, parts of Mexico, Central America, and South America. Northern populations breed mainly in shallow freshwater marshes and ponds and migrate south, while South American populations are more resident. In Costa Rica it is a rare or irregular visitor, mainly associated with wintering or passage records rather than a regular breeding population. Documented observations have included wetlands such as Palo Verde, and suitable habitat includes freshwater marshes, lagoons, flooded fields, reservoirs, and shallow ponds with emergent vegetation.
profile.migrationStatus: Northern Cinnamon Teal are migratory, moving south after breeding and returning in spring. In Costa Rica the species is considered an uncommon to rare winter visitor or migrant, with irregular records; there is no reliable evidence that it regularly breeds there.
profile.breeding: Breeding usually takes place in shallow marshes and ponds with dense emergent or nearby grassland vegetation. The female selects a concealed site close to water, often among sedges, grasses, or other low plants, and makes a shallow nest lined with vegetation and down. Clutches commonly contain several pale eggs. The female performs most incubation and care of the ducklings, while the male generally remains nearby during the early nesting period.
profile.dietFeeding: Cinnamon Teal feed mostly on seeds and other plant material, including sedges, grasses, smartweeds, and aquatic vegetation. They also take aquatic insects, insect larvae, snails, small crustaceans, and other small invertebrates. The duck commonly dabbles with its bill at the surface, strains food from shallow water, and grazes in wet vegetation or along muddy margins.
profile.behavior: This active duck usually swims, dabbles, and rests in shallow wetlands. It often occurs in small groups, with larger flocks forming outside the breeding season. Males defend females and nesting areas during breeding. Cinnamon Teal can take flight quickly from marshes and usually flies low over wetlands. Courtship includes head movements, mock feeding, preening displays, and short pursuit flights. Calls include a soft whistle from the male and a lower quack from the female.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered large, but precise demographic information is limited, especially for some regional populations. Long-term trends are not well documented.

profile.overview: The Northern Shoveler (Spatula clypeata) is a medium-sized dabbling duck named for its broad, spoon-shaped bill. This specialized bill has fine comb-like edges that help filter small aquatic animals, seeds, and plant material from shallow water. Males have a dark green head, white breast, chestnut sides, and black back, while females are mottled brown. The species breeds across northern parts of North America, Europe, and Asia and winters farther south, including Central America.
profile.classification: The Northern Shoveler belongs to the duck family Anatidae and the order Anseriformes. It is one of the dabbling ducks, and its current scientific name is Spatula clypeata.
profile.identification: The large spatulate bill is the most distinctive feature in both sexes. The adult male has a glossy dark green head, white breast, chestnut flanks, blackish back, and a dark bill. The female is mainly mottled brown with an orange-and-dark bill. In flight, both sexes can show pale bluish forewing coverts, a green speculum, and contrasting white wing markings. The species is generally about 48 to 50 centimeters long.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Northern Shoveler has a broad breeding range across northern North America and Eurasia, with wintering areas extending through southern North America, Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America. In Costa Rica it is a winter visitor, most regular from about October through March or early April. It is relatively common in Guanacaste and occurs locally elsewhere in lowlands and middle elevations. It uses open freshwater marshes, shallow lakes, ponds, lagoons, flooded fields, and occasionally brackish or saltwater wetlands.
profile.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, it is primarily a nonbreeding winter visitor from approximately October to March or early April, with numbers and records varying by region and wetland conditions. It does not normally breed in Costa Rica.
profile.breeding: Breeding occurs in shallow freshwater wetlands, including prairie ponds, marshes, sloughs, and small lakes, usually where dense grass or other vegetation provides cover. The nest is a ground scrape lined with plant material and down, generally placed near water but concealed in surrounding vegetation. Northern Shovelers commonly form pairs during the breeding season. The female incubates the eggs and leads the ducklings to shallow feeding areas after they hatch.
profile.dietFeeding: The Northern Shoveler feeds mainly in shallow water by sweeping its bill from side to side or holding it near the surface while swimming. Comb-like structures along the bill filter small crustaceans, aquatic insects, mollusks, algae, and other tiny organisms. Seeds and other plant material are also important, especially at some times of year. It usually forages by dabbling rather than diving and may feed in flocks.
profile.behavior: Northern Shovelers are generally social outside the breeding season and may gather in small or large flocks on suitable wetlands. They are active swimmers and often forage with the bill immersed while filtering food. Migrating flocks may circle on rising air currents before continuing their journey. When disturbed, they can take flight quickly from open water. In Costa Rica, wintering birds may occur alone, in small groups, or among mixed gatherings of waterfowl.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall global population trend is considered decreasing, with regional differences and some populations stable or increasing.

profile.overview: The American Wigeon is a medium-sized dabbling duck of North America. It breeds mainly across Alaska, Canada, and the northern United States, then migrates south for winter. Males are known for a white forehead and crown, green eye patch, and pinkish-brown body, while females are more subdued brown and gray. The species often gathers in flocks on wetlands, lakes, flooded fields, and coastal habitats, where it feeds largely on vegetation.
profile.classification: The American Wigeon belongs to the duck family Anatidae and the order Anseriformes. Its scientific name is Mareca americana; older references may place it in the genus Anas.
profile.identification: Adults have a compact body, rounded head, short bluish-gray bill with a black tip, and a broad white wing patch visible in flight. The breeding male has a white forehead and crown, green around the eye and rear of the head, a pink-brown breast and sides, and a white belly. The female is gray-brown overall, with a paler head and a darker smudge around the eye. Both sexes commonly show a dark rear end and white underparts in flight.
profile.rangeHabitat: The American Wigeon breeds across much of Alaska, Canada, and parts of the northern United States. It winters through the United States and south into Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and northwestern South America. In Costa Rica it is a regular winter resident, usually present from about October through March. It is most often reported in relatively small numbers around the Tempisque River basin and elsewhere in Guanacaste. Typical habitats include marshes, pond margins, shallow lakes, lagoons, mudflats, and wet grasslands.
profile.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly during the northern winter, generally from October to March, and does not normally breed there. Its local movements can follow changing water levels; in unusually dry years, some may leave as early as January.
profile.breeding: Breeding takes place in northern wetlands, including tundra ponds, boreal forest wetlands, prairie parklands, and shallow lakes. The female selects a concealed ground site near water, often among grass or other dense vegetation, and lines the nest with down. She usually lays a clutch of several eggs and performs most incubation and brood care. The male remains nearby for part of incubation and helps guard the female and nesting area. There are no reliable records of regular breeding in Costa Rica.
profile.dietFeeding: The American Wigeon eats more plant material than most dabbling ducks. It grazes on grasses and other terrestrial vegetation and plucks aquatic plants such as wigeon grass, sedges, duckweed, pondweed, and cattails. It also feeds on seeds and may take insects and other small aquatic invertebrates, especially during breeding. Its short, strong bill helps it crop vegetation efficiently. It sometimes takes food disturbed or exposed by diving ducks.
profile.behavior: This species is social outside the breeding season and often forms mixed flocks with other ducks. It feeds by dabbling in shallow water, grazing on land, and occasionally tipping forward to reach submerged plants. American Wigeons are alert and frequently flush when approached, especially where hunted or disturbed. Males give a clear, breezy whistle, while females produce lower growling calls. Flocks may rest on open water during the day and feed in nearby fields or marshes.

conservation.populationTrend: Available large-scale monitoring indicates an overall long-term decline in relative abundance, with regional variation and fluctuations linked partly to wet and dry conditions. Recent continental surveys have shown periods of stability or recovery, so the trend is not uniform across the range.
conservation.threats: Important conservation concerns include the loss and degradation of breeding and wintering wetlands, altered water levels, drought, agricultural conversion, pollution, disturbance, and hunting pressure. Climate change may further affect wetland availability and migration conditions, particularly in dry regions such as parts of northwestern Costa Rica.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore wetlands, marshes, shallow lakes, flooded fields, and connected riparian habitats used during migration and winter. In Costa Rica, conserving wetlands in the Tempisque basin and Guanacaste is especially valuable. Reduce disturbance at important waterbird sites, support responsible water management, prevent pollution and pesticide runoff, and follow legal hunting regulations and seasonal limits.

profile.overview: The Mallard is a widespread dabbling duck found across much of the Northern Hemisphere. It is adaptable and uses natural wetlands, ponds, lakes, slow-moving rivers, reservoirs, estuaries, and urban park waters. Males have a glossy green head, narrow white neck ring, chestnut breast, gray body, and yellow bill. Females are mottled brown with an orange-and-dark bill. The species is also the main wild ancestor of most domestic ducks.
profile.classification: The Mallard belongs to the family Anatidae and order Anseriformes. Its scientific name is Anas platyrhynchos. Several regional forms are recognized, and domestic ducks are largely descended from this species.
profile.identification: This is a fairly large, heavy-bodied duck with a relatively broad bill and a blue or purple wing speculum bordered by white. The adult male is distinctive: the head and upper neck are iridescent green, separated from the chestnut breast by a white collar. The female is mottled buff and brown, with an orange bill marked by darker areas. In Costa Rica, unusual ducks should be compared carefully with native and more regularly occurring species, as Mallards are exceptionally uncommon there.
profile.rangeHabitat: Mallards have a very broad native range across North America, Europe, Asia, and parts of North Africa. They occupy freshwater marshes, shallow lakes, ponds, flooded fields, quiet rivers, reservoirs, and occasionally brackish coastal wetlands. In Costa Rica, the species is not a regular or common component of the avifauna. It has been regarded as a rare to casual visitor, with historical records from Guanacaste and the Central Valley, including wintering birds near Turrialba. There is no reliable evidence of an established breeding population.
profile.migrationStatus: Northern populations are often migratory, while many birds in milder regions remain year-round. In Costa Rica, the Mallard is best treated as an exceptionally rare or casual migrant and winter visitor rather than a regular seasonal species. Historical Costa Rican records are sparse, and recent occurrence appears very limited or undocumented.
profile.breeding: Mallards usually breed near shallow freshwater, including marshes, lake margins, ponds, and slow streams. The female selects a concealed nest on the ground among grasses or other vegetation, sometimes at a considerable distance from water. She commonly lays a large clutch and alone incubates the eggs and leads the ducklings. Mallards can breed successfully in human-modified landscapes, but there are no reliable records indicating regular breeding by wild Mallards in Costa Rica.
profile.dietFeeding: Mallards are opportunistic feeders. They eat seeds, aquatic plants, grasses, grains, and other plant material, along with insects, insect larvae, small mollusks, crustaceans, worms, and other small aquatic animals. They commonly feed by dabbling, tipping forward in shallow water while keeping the body afloat, and they also graze on land. Food availability and local habitat strongly influence their diet.
profile.behavior: Mallards are generally social outside the breeding season and may gather in flocks or mix with other waterfowl. They spend much time resting on banks, mudflats, or floating vegetation and are strong, capable fliers. Pairs often form before the breeding season. Males give relatively quiet calls compared with females, whose familiar loud quacks are especially noticeable. They readily use artificial ponds and urban wetlands where suitable food and cover are available.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable overall, although trends vary among geographic populations and some regional populations may be declining.

profile.overview: The White-cheeked Pintail (Anas bahamensis) is a medium-sized dabbling duck of tropical and subtropical wetlands. It is named for its clean white cheeks and throat, which contrast with a dark crown and warm brown body. The species is patchily distributed across the Caribbean, northern South America, the Galápagos Islands, and some coastal areas farther south. It usually remains in suitable areas year-round rather than undertaking long-distance seasonal migration.
profile.classification: The White-cheeked Pintail belongs to the duck family Anatidae and the order Anseriformes. Three commonly recognized subspecies occur across the Caribbean, South America, and the Galápagos region.
profile.identification: This pintail has a warm brown body marked with darker spotting, a dark brown crown, and prominent white cheeks and throat. The grayish bill has a reddish or pinkish patch near its base. Its tail is pointed, and a green wing speculum may be visible in flight or when the bird stretches. Males and females are broadly similar, although females may be slightly duller and larger. Juveniles generally show less sharply defined facial markings.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs patchily in the Caribbean, northern and western South America, the Galápagos Islands, and locally in other coastal regions. It favors shallow saline or brackish lagoons, tidal wetlands, mangrove margins, coastal ponds, marshes, and quiet freshwater wetlands. In Costa Rica, it is a rare or accidental visitor rather than a regular resident or widespread migrant. Verified or reported individuals have occurred at wetlands and coastal sites, and the species is regarded as a vagrant in the Central American region.
profile.migrationStatus: Generally resident or locally dispersive across its main range. It is not a regular long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, White-cheeked Pintails are rare, irregular vagrants, with records not indicating a predictable seasonal migration pattern.
profile.breeding: Breeding commonly takes place near quiet coastal or inland wetlands, including mangrove areas, lagoons, marshes, and ponds.
