profile.overview: The Plain-breasted Ground Dove (Columbina minuta) is a very small dove that spends much of its time walking or feeding on the ground. It has plain, warm brown plumage and lacks the strongly scaled breast pattern of the Common Ground Dove. The species inhabits open, often seasonally dry country rather than dense forest. Its broad distribution extends from southern Mexico through Central America and across parts of northern and eastern South America.
profile.classification: The Plain-breasted Ground Dove belongs to the dove and pigeon family Columbidae. It is one of several small ground doves in the genus Columbina.
profile.identification: This is a tiny, compact ground dove with a short bill, short tail, and rounded wings. Adults are generally warm brown above and paler below, with relatively plain breast and belly plumage. The wings may show richer rufous or cinnamon tones in flight. Compared with the Common Ground Dove, it is smaller-looking and lacks the latter's obvious dark, scaled breast pattern. Sexes are similar, although males may appear slightly richer or more contrasting.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southern Mexico and Belize through Central America, then in separated regions of northern and eastern South America. In Costa Rica it is a local native bird, recorded mainly in open habitats of the drier northwest, especially Guanacaste, but it also occurs locally in parts of the central highlands and has been recorded near Turrialba. It uses dry or seasonally wet grassland, scrub, brushy second growth, agricultural edges, and other open lowland or lower-elevation habitats, generally avoiding dense forest.
profile.migrationStatus: Generally resident in Costa Rica. Local or seasonal movements may occur, but it is not normally treated as a regular long-distance migrant there.
profile.breeding: The Plain-breasted Ground Dove is believed to breed in suitable parts of its range, including Central America and Costa Rica, although detailed information on its breeding biology is limited. Like other small Columbina doves, it is expected to place a simple platform nest of twigs in low vegetation, shrubs, or similar cover. Clutches are usually small, and both adults typically share incubation and care of the young. Breeding timing may vary with rainfall and local food availability.
profile.dietFeeding: It feeds mainly on small seeds and other plant material collected from the ground. Foraging usually takes place in open areas, where the dove walks quietly through short grass, bare soil, scrub margins, fields, and disturbed ground. It may forage alone, in pairs, or in small groups. Grain-producing plants and naturally available seeds become especially important in seasonally dry landscapes.
profile.behavior: This discreet ground dove usually walks rather than flies while searching for food and may remain concealed in grass or low cover. When disturbed, it makes a quick, direct flight and often drops back into vegetation nearby. It is generally unobtrusive and may be overlooked among other small doves. Courtship and social behavior are likely most noticeable during the breeding season, when pairs defend small areas and perform display flights or postures.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well documented, but the species is not currently considered to be undergoing a major global decline.

profile.overview: The Ruddy Ground Dove (Columbina talpacoti) is a small, compact dove of open and disturbed landscapes in tropical and subtropical America. Males are warm reddish-brown, while females are generally duller brown. It often walks on the ground in pairs or small groups, feeding on fallen seeds. The species adapts well to farmland, pastures, roadsides, gardens, and towns, and is a familiar resident bird in suitable parts of Costa Rica.
profile.classification: The Ruddy Ground Dove belongs to the dove and pigeon family Columbidae. Its scientific name is Columbina talpacoti.
profile.identification: This small dove has a short tail, rounded body, and pinkish to reddish legs. Adult males are rich cinnamon or rufous on the head, neck, breast, and upperparts, with darker wings marked by black spots. Females and immature birds are more uniformly brown and less reddish. Both sexes may show pale or whitish edges on the outer tail feathers. Its steady, rapid wingbeats and low, direct flight are typical when it leaves the ground.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Ruddy Ground Dove ranges from Mexico through Central America and much of South America, including parts of Brazil, Peru, Paraguay, and northern Argentina. In Costa Rica it is a native resident, reported as common to abundant in deforested lowlands, especially on the Caribbean side. It uses open and semi-open habitats such as pastures, cultivated areas, scrub, roadsides, gardens, and settlements. It can occur at higher elevations locally, reaching approximately 1,400 meters around Cartago.
profile.migrationStatus: The Ruddy Ground Dove is generally a year-round resident in Costa Rica rather than a regular long-distance migrant. Local movements may occur in response to food availability, weather, or changes in land use, but Costa Rican birds are not normally considered seasonal passage migrants.
profile.breeding: It breeds in suitable open habitats in Costa Rica and elsewhere across its range. The nest is a small, loosely built platform of twigs, usually placed in a shrub, tree, or other vegetation above the ground. Two white eggs are normally laid. Incubation lasts about 12–13 days, and the young usually leave the nest roughly 12–14 days after hatching. Pairs may nest near human habitation where food and vegetation are available.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small seeds and other plant material collected from the ground. It commonly feeds in bare soil, grassy areas, crop fields, roadsides, yards, and beneath bird-feeding areas. The dove usually walks or makes short hops while searching, and may forage alone, in pairs, or in small groups. It can take advantage of seeds in disturbed landscapes and agricultural settings.
profile.behavior: Ruddy Ground Doves are usually terrestrial and spend much of their time walking through open ground. They often occur singly, in pairs, or in loose groups, becoming more social where food is concentrated. When disturbed, they make a quick, low flight to nearby cover or a perch. Their calls are soft and repetitive. They frequently use low branches, fences, wires, and buildings as resting or display sites.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered increasing.

profile.overview: The Blue Ground Dove (Claravis pretiosa) is a small tropical dove of humid forest edges, clearings, secondary woodland, and riverine vegetation. It is notable for strong sexual differences: males are powder blue-gray with dark wings, while females are mainly warm brown and rusty. The species ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and much of northern and central South America. In Costa Rica, it is a resident but generally localized and uncommon bird, especially on the Pacific side.
profile.classification: The Blue Ground Dove belongs to the dove and pigeon family Columbidae and the order Columbiformes. Its scientific name is Claravis pretiosa.
profile.identification: This small, slim dove is about 20 centimeters long. The male is distinctive, with powder-blue or blue-gray upperparts and underparts, dark wings, a dark face, and a rusty-brown rump and tail. The female is browner overall, with warm cinnamon or rufous plumage, a rusty rump, and a relatively long rusty tail. Birds are often detected as singles or pairs flying quickly and directly, or moving quietly through low vegetation. Females can be difficult to identify without a male nearby.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Blue Ground Dove occurs from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and central South America, including Trinidad. In Costa Rica it is a resident species recorded mainly in humid lowlands and foothills, particularly along the Caribbean side and in suitable forest-edge habitats; it is generally less abundant on the Pacific side. It uses forest edges, clearings, low second-growth forest, river-edge and gallery forest, roadsides, and rural areas with nearby cover, usually from sea level to about 1,200 meters.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered a resident species in Costa Rica and does not undertake a regular long-distance migration. Local movements may occur between forest, edge, and feeding areas, but seasonal migration is not well established.
profile.breeding: The Blue Ground Dove builds a flimsy platform nest of twigs in a tree, commonly several meters above the ground. The clutch normally contains two white eggs. Breeding takes place in wooded habitats and forest edges, where the nest may be concealed among branches or foliage. Detailed information on nesting dates and breeding behavior in Costa Rica is limited, but the species is regarded as a resident breeder in suitable parts of the country.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of seeds and other small plant foods collected on or near the ground. It typically forages quietly in clearings, forest margins, second-growth vegetation, and areas with sparse ground cover. The Blue Ground Dove may feed alone or in pairs and can visit rural landscapes when adequate shelter and seed-producing vegetation are available. Specific feeding records for Costa Rica are limited.
profile.behavior: The Blue Ground Dove is usually wary and unobtrusive. It is most often seen in rapid, direct flight, either alone or as a pair, rather than remaining conspicuously in the open. On the ground it moves through low vegetation and forest edges while searching for food. Its quiet habits and preference for dense cover can make it easy to overlook, even where it is regularly present.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly established in readily available assessments.

profile.overview: The Maroon-chested Ground Dove is a small, secretive dove of humid mountain forests in Central and South America. It is strongly associated with bamboo, especially when bamboo plants flower and produce abundant seed. The species may be present at a site for only a short period, making it difficult to find even where suitable habitat remains. Its irregular appearances and preference for dense vegetation have contributed to limited knowledge of its population and breeding biology.
profile.classification: The Maroon-chested Ground Dove belongs to the pigeon and dove family, Columbidae. It was formerly widely treated in the genus Claravis but is now generally placed in Paraclaravis.
profile.identification: This dove is about 20–22 cm long and has a compact, rounded shape with a relatively short tail. The adult male is mainly dark blue-gray, with a distinctive maroon or purplish chest and broad dark wing markings. The female is duller, with brownish-gray upperparts, a warmer cinnamon-brown face, and less vivid underparts. Broad pale tips on the outer tail feathers can be useful in identification. It is usually seen walking or feeding quietly in dense ground vegetation.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southern Mexico through the highlands of Central America and south along the Andes to Bolivia. In Costa Rica it is a rare, local bird of humid montane and cloud-forest regions, generally recorded from roughly 900 to 3,000 meters elevation, including highland areas such as the Cordillera de Talamanca and volcanic ranges. It uses dense forest understory, forest edges, second growth, and bamboo or chusque thickets. Costa Rican sightings are often associated with local bamboo-seeding events rather than regular year-round abundance.
profile.migrationStatus: It is not considered a regular long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, its occurrence is highly irregular and probably reflects nomadic movements between flowering or seeding bamboo patches. Birds may appear suddenly in suitable highland habitat and leave when the seed supply is exhausted.
profile.breeding: The breeding biology of the Maroon-chested Ground Dove remains poorly documented, including in Costa Rica. Available observations suggest that breeding may coincide with bamboo flowering and seed production, and birds may nest in loose groups or colonies near suitable bamboo. The known nest is a simple, shallow platform of sticks, leaf stems, and grass fibers placed in bamboo. One documented nest contained two eggs. Both adults participate in parental care, but nesting dates and success vary across the range.
profile.dietFeeding: The dove feeds mainly on seeds and fallen fruit collected on the ground beneath dense vegetation. Bamboo seeds, especially those of montane Chusquea and related bamboos, can be an important food source. It usually forages alone or in pairs, although small flocks have been reported where food is concentrated. In Costa Rica, its presence may be especially likely during major bamboo-seeding events, when abundant seed temporarily supports several uncommon mountain birds.
profile.behavior: This is a quiet, ground-foraging dove that often remains concealed in thick understory. It typically walks beneath bamboo, shrubs, or forest-edge vegetation while searching among leaf litter for seeds and fruit. Individuals may occur singly, in pairs, or in small groups. Its low, slightly rising two-syllable coo can help reveal its presence. Because it follows unpredictable food resources and is difficult to observe in dense cover, it may be overlooked during periods when it is not concentrated at seeding bamboo.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified. Its numbers and local distribution may fluctuate greatly because the species tracks irregular bamboo flowering and seeding events.

profile.overview: The Ruddy Quail-Dove (Geotrygon montana) is a compact, shy dove of tropical forests in the Americas. It spends much of its time walking quietly on the forest floor, where its rounded body and short tail give it a quail-like appearance. The species occurs from the Caribbean and southern Florida as a rare visitor through Central America and into northern and central South America. It is usually detected by movement, soft calls, or brief flights rather than by prolonged open views.
profile.classification: The Ruddy Quail-Dove belongs to the pigeon and dove family Columbidae and the genus Geotrygon. It is one of several forest-floor quail-doves found in the Neotropics.
profile.identification: This stout, short-tailed dove is about 21–28 cm long. Adults are mainly rich reddish or chestnut brown above, with paler buff or cinnamon-brown underparts. A pale buff or whitish stripe below the eye is an important field mark, although it can be subtle in poor light. Males are generally more strongly colored, while females tend to be duller and less distinctly patterned. It often walks with a deliberate, quail-like gait on the ground.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Ruddy Quail-Dove ranges through the West Indies, Central America, and much of tropical South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, occurring mainly in lowland and foothill forests, especially in humid regions, but also locally in drier woodland and forest edges. It may use primary forest, secondary growth, dense scrub, shaded plantations, and other habitats with substantial ground cover. Costa Rican records extend from the lowlands into foothill zones, locally reaching approximately 1,200–1,400 m.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally resident in Costa Rica and is not considered a regular long-distance migrant there. Local movements may occur in response to food availability, weather, or changes in habitat conditions.
profile.breeding: Breeding information varies across its broad range. The species usually builds a loose, flimsy platform of twigs in low vegetation, although nests may sometimes be placed on the ground or on a low stump. Two buff-colored eggs are typically laid. In Costa Rica, breeding activity has been reported during the wetter part of the year, with observations concentrated in spring and early summer in some regions. Nest placement in dense cover helps conceal the adults and young from predators.
profile.dietFeeding: The Ruddy Quail-Dove forages mainly on the ground, where it searches through leaf litter for fallen fruits, seeds, and other plant material. It may also take small invertebrates such as insects and worms. Individuals are often encountered alone or in pairs, moving quietly beneath forest vegetation. Fruit-bearing trees, undisturbed litter, and moist shaded ground can provide important feeding opportunities.
profile.behavior: This is a secretive, ground-oriented dove that commonly walks or runs away when disturbed rather than flying immediately. If flushed, it usually makes a short, direct flight into nearby vegetation. Its plumage blends well with shadowed leaf litter and reddish-brown forest debris. The species is most active in quiet forest understory and may be easier to detect by its low, prolonged cooing calls than by sight.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified. The species remains widespread, but local abundance can vary with the condition and continuity of forest habitat.

profile.overview: The Violaceous Quail-Dove (Geotrygon violacea) is a small, secretive dove of tropical forests in Central and South America. It is named for the violet or purplish sheen on the hindneck and upper back, especially in males. Unlike many doves, it spends much of its time in dense understory and may be difficult to detect. The species occurs in Costa Rica, where it is generally uncommon and local but resident in suitable forest habitats.
profile.classification: The Violaceous Quail-Dove belongs to the dove and pigeon family Columbidae and the genus Geotrygon. Two subspecies are generally recognized, including the Central American form Geotrygon violacea albiventer.
profile.identification: This quail-dove is about 20–23 cm long and has a compact body, short legs, a small head, and a slightly down-curved bill. Males show a grayish or purplish head, a violet to amethyst sheen on the hindneck and shoulders, brown wings, and a pale to whitish underside. Females are duller and browner, with less iridescence. Juveniles are darker and more heavily scaled, lacking the adult’s glossy purple tones.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species has a discontinuous range from Nicaragua and Costa Rica through Panama and northern South America, extending east of the Andes into parts of the Amazon and Atlantic forests. In Costa Rica it is a resident, uncommon and local species. It occurs mainly in humid Caribbean lowlands and foothills, reaching at least about 600 m, and is also recorded on the Nicoya Peninsula. It can be locally more numerous in humid forests on the Pacific slopes of the Guanacaste Cordillera, roughly from 600 to 1,200 m. Habitat includes dense, shaded understory in primary and secondary evergreen forest and cacao plantations.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica. Seasonal movements have been suggested elsewhere, but regular migration has not been documented.
profile.breeding: Available information on breeding is limited. The breeding period across the range appears to extend approximately from March to November, based on records of birds in breeding condition, a nest, and juveniles. A documented nest was a small stick structure placed low above the ground, about 1–3 m high, and contained two eggs. Nesting details in Costa Rica are poorly known, so the timing and frequency of breeding there remain uncertain.
profile.dietFeeding: The Violaceous Quail-Dove forages mainly on or near the forest floor, taking seeds and fallen fruits and probably small invertebrates. Its feeding activity is concentrated in shaded, leafy understory and on the ground beneath forest vegetation. Although it is more arboreal than several other Geotrygon quail-doves and sometimes perches high in the understory, it is still primarily associated with low-level forest foraging.
profile.behavior: This is a shy, inconspicuous bird that usually remains in dense, dark understory and may be detected more readily by movement or soft calls than by prolonged views. It is more arboreal than some related quail-doves and occasionally perches well above the ground, but it commonly searches through leaf litter and low vegetation. Its quiet habits and preference for thick cover make it easy to overlook, even where it is regularly present.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified. The species is generally uncommon or locally rare in parts of its range, but its broad distribution does not currently meet global threatened-species thresholds.

profile.overview: The Olive-backed Quail-Dove is a secretive, ground-feeding dove of humid forests in Central America and northwestern South America. It usually stays in dense understory, where its dark olive-brown back and contrasting pale facial markings provide camouflage. The species is most often encountered alone or in pairs, walking quietly along shaded forest floors. In Costa Rica, it is a resident bird of lowland Caribbean forests and is locally fairly common where suitable dense habitat remains.
profile.classification: The Olive-backed Quail-Dove belongs to the pigeon and dove family Columbidae. It is the only species in the genus Leptotrygon; it was formerly placed in the genus Geotrygon.
profile.identification: This medium-sized quail-dove is about 21.5 cm long. Adults have dark olive-brown upperparts, a pale to whitish forehead, a grayish or purplish crown and hindneck, and a broad white stripe beneath the eye bordered by darker markings. The throat is pale, while the breast is dark gray-brown with a greenish sheen and the belly is whitish. The wings and lower body may show subdued cinnamon tones. Juveniles are duller and more heavily scaled with rusty-brown markings.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from the Caribbean slope of southern Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama, and along the Pacific slope from eastern Panama through western Colombia to northwestern Ecuador. It favors dense, humid lowland forest, wet ravines, heavy understory, and occasionally shaded second growth, generally from sea level to about 900 m. In Costa Rica, it is a resident and fairly common species in forested Caribbean lowlands, extending at least north to the Tortuguero region. Records away from these habitats, including the Pacific slope, are local or unusual.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident throughout its range, including Costa Rica. It is not regarded as a regular long-distance migrant, although individuals may occasionally appear outside the species' usual Costa Rican lowland forest range.
profile.breeding: Breeding has been recorded mainly from January through July in Costa Rica and during comparable periods elsewhere in its range. The species builds a relatively bulky nest from twigs and rootlets, usually in low vegetation about 1–2 m above the ground. The clutch generally contains two eggs. Detailed information on incubation, chick development, and parental care is limited, and breeding activity may vary with local rainfall and food availability.
profile.dietFeeding: The Olive-backed Quail-Dove searches on the forest floor and in low understory for fallen seeds, small fruits, and other plant material. Small invertebrates may also be taken. It normally forages alone or in pairs, walking slowly through leaf litter and dense vegetation. Its unobtrusive behavior and dark plumage make it easy to overlook, especially in dim forest interiors. It may occasionally use shaded trails or nearby regenerating woodland.
profile.behavior: This species is quiet and secretive, spending much of its time walking or running through dense understory rather than flying. When disturbed, it commonly slips away on foot and may flush only for a short distance. It is usually seen singly or in pairs. The bird's low, subdued call can be difficult to detect, and its cryptic plumage helps it remain concealed in shadowy forest habitats.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly quantified in readily available sources, but the species remains locally common in parts of its range.

profile.overview: The White-tipped Dove is a medium-sized tropical dove found from southern Texas and Mexico through Central and South America. It is usually secretive, spending much of its time walking on the ground beneath trees and shrubs. Its soft, repeated calls are often easier to detect than the bird itself. The species tolerates a range of wooded environments and is a familiar resident of many lowland and foothill habitats in Costa Rica.
profile.classification: The White-tipped Dove belongs to the dove and pigeon family Columbidae. It is one of several ground-feeding doves in the genus Leptotila.
profile.identification: This dove is about 27 centimeters long, with a warm gray-brown back, a gray head, and a pinkish or vinaceous chest. The neck and upper breast may show subtle green or purple iridescence. Its most distinctive feature is the white outer tail feathers, visible when the tail is spread or the bird flies. It has a slender dark bill, reddish legs, and a relatively long, rounded tail. It is generally less boldly marked than related quail-doves.
profile.rangeHabitat: The White-tipped Dove ranges from southern Texas and Mexico south through Central America to much of South America. In Costa Rica it is a common to abundant resident, especially in the lowlands along the Pacific slope. It also occurs in suitable foothill habitats, reaching roughly 800 meters in northern mountain areas and about 1,500 meters or higher in parts of central and southern Costa Rica. Habitats include forest edges, secondary woodland, plantations, gardens, scrub, and other areas with dense ground cover.
profile.migrationStatus: The White-tipped Dove is generally resident and does not undertake regular long-distance migration. In Costa Rica it is present throughout the year, although local movements may occur as birds respond to food availability, rainfall, and habitat conditions.
profile.breeding: Breeding may occur during different parts of the year across its broad range, often coinciding with favorable rainfall and food conditions. The nest is a simple, loosely built platform of twigs placed in a shrub, small tree, or other vegetation. The clutch usually contains two white eggs. Both parents participate in incubation and care of the young. In Costa Rica, breeding can occur in lowland and foothill woodland, forest margins, plantations, and well-vegetated gardens.
profile.dietFeeding: The White-tipped Dove feeds mainly on seeds, fallen fruits, berries, and other plant material collected on or near the ground. It may also take small quantities of invertebrate food. The bird commonly forages alone or in pairs beneath trees, along forest paths, and at woodland edges, using its bill to search through leaf litter and low vegetation. It often visits areas where fruiting plants or spilled grain provide concentrated food.
profile.behavior: This dove is usually quiet and cautious, walking slowly through shaded vegetation and remaining difficult to see. When disturbed, it may flush suddenly with rapid wingbeats and reveal its white-tipped tail. Its low, rhythmic call is frequently heard from dense cover, particularly in the early morning. White-tipped Doves are commonly solitary or found in pairs, although several may gather where food is abundant. They often use the same sheltered feeding areas repeatedly.

conservation.populationTrend: No major global decline is currently recognized for the species.

profile.overview: The Gray-chested Dove is a medium-sized forest dove of Middle America and northern South America. It is usually encountered alone or in pairs, often walking quietly on the ground beneath trees and dense vegetation. Its understated brown, gray, and white plumage provides effective camouflage. In Costa Rica, it is a native resident associated mainly with humid lowland and foothill habitats, especially on the Pacific side and in the southern part of the country.
profile.classification: The Gray-chested Dove belongs to the dove and pigeon family Columbidae and the genus Leptotila. Several geographic forms are recognized across its range, and the Costa Rican population is generally associated with the form Leptotila cassinii cerviniventris.
profile.identification: This dove is about 25 centimeters long, with a warm brown crown and hindneck, grayish upperparts, a dusky gray or gray-brown chest, and paler underparts. The wings and back are subdued olive-brown to brown, while the tail commonly shows pale edging or tips. The bill is dark, the eye is reddish to orange-red, and the legs are pinkish. It can be confused with White-tipped Dove and Gray-headed Dove, but its brown crown and distinctly grayish chest are useful field marks.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Gray-chested Dove occurs from southeastern Mexico through Central America to western Colombia. In Costa Rica it is a regularly occurring native bird, especially on the Pacific slope and in the southern lowlands, including the Puntarenas region; it is less characteristic of the Caribbean lowlands. It uses humid evergreen and semi-evergreen forest, forest edges, second growth, shrubby clearings, plantations, and other areas with dense cover. It is generally a lowland and foothill species, although it may occur at moderate elevations.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered resident in Costa Rica, with no well-established long-distance migration. Individuals may make local movements in response to food availability, rainfall, or changes in vegetation, but the species is not treated as a regular seasonal migrant in the country.
profile.breeding: The species builds a relatively flimsy platform nest from twigs, usually in a shrub, vine tangle, or low tree within dense vegetation. Like other Leptotila doves, it normally lays two plain white eggs, and both adults are expected to share incubation and care of the young. Breeding information is less completely documented than for some widespread doves, but nesting has been recorded during several months in Central America, including Costa Rica, rather than being restricted to one short season.
profile.dietFeeding: The Gray-chested Dove feeds mainly on seeds, fallen fruits, berries, and other plant material. It usually forages on the ground beneath forest or dense secondary vegetation, walking slowly and pausing to pick up food from leaf litter or bare soil. It may also use gardens, plantations, and disturbed habitats when suitable cover and food are available. Its quiet, terrestrial feeding habits can make it easy to overlook.
profile.behavior: This is a shy, inconspicuous dove that often stays beneath vegetation and flushes only when approached closely. It is usually seen singly or in pairs rather than in large flocks. Its flight is direct and rapid, with strong wingbeats followed by brief gliding. The species spends much time on the ground but retreats into shrubs or low trees when alarmed. Its soft calls may be heard more often than the bird is seen.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is not known to be undergoing a sufficiently rapid decline to qualify for a threatened category, although local populations may be affected by habitat loss.

profile.overview: The Gray-headed Dove (Leptotila plumbeiceps) is a secretive, forest-dwelling dove of Middle America and northwestern South America. It usually stays on or near the ground, where it walks quietly through leaf litter and dense vegetation. Its soft, mournful call is often easier to detect than the bird itself. The species is locally distributed and can be overlooked because it spends much of its time in shaded forest interiors and edges.
profile.classification: The Gray-headed Dove belongs to the dove and pigeon family Columbidae and the genus Leptotila. It is closely related to several other forest doves, including the Gray-chested Dove and Gray-fronted Dove.
profile.identification: This is a medium-sized, long-tailed dove with a gray to bluish-gray head and neck, a pale throat, warm pinkish or vinaceous tones on the breast, and brownish-olive upperparts. The belly is paler, and the bill is dark while the legs and feet are pink. Bare reddish skin around the eye can be visible at close range. It is distinguished from the similar Gray-chested Dove by its head pattern and generally more restricted range in Costa Rica.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Gray-headed Dove occurs from eastern Mexico through Central America to Colombia, with a discontinuous distribution in parts of the southern range. In Costa Rica it is a local resident, especially in lowland forest on the Pacific slope and in northwestern areas, including the Nicoya region; it may reach about 1,000 meters there. It uses humid primary and secondary forest, forest edges, thick understory, and other well-wooded habitats, and is also recorded locally in northern lowlands.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and generally regarded as nonmigratory. It remains in suitable areas year-round, although local movements may occur in response to food or habitat conditions.
profile.breeding: The breeding biology of the Gray-headed Dove is poorly documented. Like other Leptotila doves, it is believed to build a simple platform nest of twigs in low or moderate vegetation, usually in sheltered forest habitat. Available records indicate that breeding can occur during the regional dry or early wet season, but the timing may vary across the range. Detailed information on clutch size, incubation, and parental care remains limited.
profile.dietFeeding: The species forages mainly on the ground beneath forest cover. Its diet is thought to include fallen seeds, small fruits, berries, and other plant material collected from leaf litter or low vegetation. It commonly walks rather than flies while searching for food and may visit openings, forest edges, or lightly disturbed woodland when cover remains available. Specific dietary studies are limited, so the relative importance of different food items is not well established.
profile.behavior: The Gray-headed Dove is shy, quiet, and usually solitary or found in pairs. It moves slowly through shaded understory and leaf litter, where its subdued brown and gray plumage provides effective camouflage. When disturbed, it may freeze, walk into dense cover, or make a short, rapid flight. Its repeated call is a low, mournful, somewhat rising and falling note, and vocal activity may reveal birds that are difficult to see.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered broadly stable, although exact numbers are poorly known and local populations may fluctuate or decline where forest is lost.

profile.overview: The Buff-fronted Quail-Dove, also called the Costa Rican Quail-Dove, is a secretive ground-dwelling dove of Central American mountain forests. It is especially associated with humid montane and cloud forests in Costa Rica and western Panama. Its rich rufous-brown back, gray head and breast, buff forehead, dark facial lines, red eye-ring, and coral-red legs provide useful identification marks. Most sightings are brief because the bird usually moves quietly through dense understory.
profile.classification: The Buff-fronted Quail-Dove belongs to the pigeon and dove family, Columbidae, in the order Columbiformes. It is the monotypic species Zentrygon costaricensis; no subspecies are generally recognized.
profile.identification: This medium-sized quail-dove is about 24–28 cm long, with sexes appearing similar. Adults have a gray head, neck, and breast, a distinct buff forehead, and pale gray cheeks bordered by narrow black lines around the eye. The upperparts, wings, and tail are rich maroon or rufous-brown, while the lower belly is browner and sometimes buff-tinged. A thin red eye-ring, reddish-based bill, and bright coral-red legs are notable field marks. Juveniles are duller and more barred.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from northern Costa Rica through the Talamancan highlands into western Panama, reaching roughly as far east as Veraguas. In Costa Rica it is a resident of mountainous regions, including the Cordillera de Guanacaste, Cordillera de Tilarán, Central Volcanic Cordillera, and Talamanca range. It inhabits humid lower montane, montane evergreen, and cloud forests, generally from about 1,000 to 3,000 m. It may use forest edges, trails, and other lightly disturbed places where dense cover remains available.
profile.migrationStatus: The Buff-fronted Quail-Dove is considered resident in Costa Rica and is not known for regular long-distance migration. It may make local movements along elevation gradients or in response to food and weather conditions.
profile.breeding: Reliable information on the species’ breeding biology is limited. Like related forest quail-doves, it is believed to nest in dense vegetation, with the nest placed above the ground and the young receiving crop milk from the adults. Breeding records are reported from the broader range, but the timing and details of nesting in Costa Rica are not sufficiently documented for a precise account.
profile.dietFeeding: The Buff-fronted Quail-Dove forages mainly on the forest floor, where it searches through leaf litter for fallen fruits, seeds, and other plant material. It may also take small invertebrates opportunistically. The bird usually feeds quietly beneath dense vegetation, walking or making short movements rather than spending much time in the canopy. Its dependence on intact, humid forest understory makes ground cover and undisturbed leaf litter important feeding resources.
profile.behavior: This quail-dove is shy, quiet, and difficult to detect despite its attractive plumage. It usually travels alone or in pairs through shadowed understory and may freeze or slip away when approached. When flushed, it typically makes a rapid, low flight into nearby cover. Calls are often more useful for detection than visual searching. Individuals may use trails and forest edges but generally remain closely associated with dense vegetation and mountainous forest.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend has not been precisely quantified, but the species is not currently recognized as undergoing a sufficiently rapid decline to qualify for a threatened category.

profile.overview: The Purplish-backed Quail-Dove is a secretive, ground-feeding dove of wet mountain forests in Costa Rica and western Panama. It is recognized by its purplish mantle, bluish-gray head and breast, white face and throat, dark facial markings, and warm brown wings. Usually seen alone or in pairs, it often walks or runs through dense vegetation rather than flying when disturbed. Its soft, distinctive song may be heard more often than the bird is seen.
profile.classification: The Purplish-backed Quail-Dove belongs to the dove and pigeon family Columbidae and the genus Zentrygon. It is generally treated as a monotypic species.
profile.identification: This medium-sized quail-dove is about 25–27 cm long. Adults have a grayish-white forehead, bluish-gray to greenish tones on the crown and neck, and a dull purplish back. The remaining upperparts are olive-brown with some reddish tones, while the wings become dark brown. The face and throat are white, marked by a black line through the eye and a dark malar stripe. The breast is slate-gray, the belly is pale buff to cinnamon, and the flanks are chocolate brown. The eye and surrounding bare skin are reddish or magenta.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species is a resident of the mountains from Costa Rica into western and central Panama. In Costa Rica, it occurs from the Cordillera de Guanacaste in the north through suitable wet montane forests in the central and southeastern highlands. It inhabits cool, humid, dense forest, especially areas with thick understory and undisturbed ground cover. It is reported from roughly 400–800 m on some Caribbean slopes, at higher elevations in southeastern areas, and locally up to about 2,600 m.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and Panama; no regular long-distance migration is known. Individuals may make local movements within mountain forests, but seasonal patterns are poorly documented.
profile.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported mainly from June through October. The nest is a loose, bulky cup or shallow bowl made from sticks and finer plant material, usually positioned in dense vegetation close to the ground. The species generally lays a single egg. Available information on incubation, parental care, and fledging is limited, and breeding behavior may vary between Costa Rica and Panama.
profile.dietFeeding: The Purplish-backed Quail-Dove forages mainly on the forest floor, usually alone or in pairs. Its diet includes fallen fruit, seeds, insects, and worms. It searches through leaf litter and low vegetation, taking food from the ground. Dense, moist forest with a well-developed understory and abundant leaf litter provides important feeding habitat.
profile.behavior: This quail-dove is shy and difficult to observe in dense forest. When alarmed, it commonly walks or runs away rather than immediately taking flight. If it does flush, it may fly to a higher perch or into nearby cover. Birds are usually encountered singly or in pairs. Its song is a soft, three-part phrase with the strongest emphasis on the final note, which can reveal its presence in thick vegetation.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified, but the species is described as locally fairly common in parts of its range.

profile.overview: The Chiriqui Quail-Dove, also called the Rufous-breasted Quail-Dove, is a secretive, ground-feeding dove of Central American mountain forests. It belongs to a group of forest quail-doves noted for compact bodies, rounded wings, and quiet habits. The species is found in Costa Rica and western Panama, where it occupies forest understory and is more often detected by its low, repeated song or brief movements along shaded trails than by prolonged views.
profile.classification: The Chiriqui Quail-Dove is a member of the dove family Columbidae and the order Columbiformes. Its scientific name is Zentrygon chiriquensis, and it is generally treated as a monotypic species.
profile.identification: This medium-sized quail-dove is about 27–30 cm long. Adults have a gray crown and head, a buffy forehead and face, a narrow black stripe through the eye and along the cheek, and reddish bare skin around the eye. The breast and sides are rich rufous or cinnamon, contrasting with darker, subtly glossy brown, chestnut, and olive upperparts. The legs are reddish. Females resemble males but may have a darker breast; juveniles are duller and more barred below.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Chiriqui Quail-Dove occurs from the Cordillera de Guanacaste in northern Costa Rica south through the Talamancan highlands and into western Panama, including Chiriquí and Veraguas. In Costa Rica it is a native resident of suitable montane forest, with records from protected highland areas such as the Talamanca region and Cloudbridge Nature Reserve. It favors dense understory in humid or seasonally drier montane forest, generally from about 600 to 2,000 m, but locally occurring higher, especially on Pacific slopes.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident and non-migratory. In Costa Rica, it is present year-round in suitable montane forests, although local movements may follow food availability or elevation.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited. Nesting has been reported during at least August and September, but the full breeding season is not well established. The nest is described as a shallow cup made from twigs and leaves, placed on a branch. A clutch of two eggs has been reported. Both parents are expected to contribute to care of the young, as in other columbids, but detailed information on incubation, nest placement, and fledging is scarce.
profile.dietFeeding: The Chiriqui Quail-Dove forages mainly on the forest floor, usually under dense cover. Its documented food includes seeds, fallen fruit, and small invertebrates. It walks quietly through leaf litter, singly or in pairs, searching beneath vegetation and picking up food from the ground. Individuals may occasionally use shaded roads, trails, or other open patches within forest, particularly during the early morning.
profile.behavior: This is a shy, largely terrestrial dove that is usually encountered alone or in pairs. It moves quietly through the understory and often remains concealed, making its vocalizations especially useful for detection. The song is a low, monotonous note that gradually swells in volume, and calling activity may increase during the breeding period. Courtship includes head-bobbing while the tail is raised. When disturbed, it typically makes a short, direct flight into cover.

conservation.populationTrend: The population trend is not well documented. Available assessments indicate that the species is relatively poorly known, with a possible decline, but there is insufficient reliable information to quantify the trend.

profile.overview: The White-winged Dove (Zenaida asiatica) is a medium-sized, warm gray-brown dove named for the broad white wing patch visible in flight. It is native to the southern United States, Mexico, Central America, and parts of the Caribbean. The species commonly uses open, warm landscapes rather than dense forest and can adapt to farms, towns, gardens, and dry woodland. In Costa Rica, it is especially associated with the dry Pacific lowlands and is locally common to abundant there.
profile.classification: The White-winged Dove belongs to the dove and pigeon family Columbidae and the order Columbiformes. Its scientific name is Zenaida asiatica.
profile.identification: This dove has a bulky body, rounded head, short tail, and mostly grayish-brown plumage. The most distinctive feature is the conspicuous white patch along the wing, especially obvious during flight, together with broad white tips on the outer tail feathers. Adults usually show orange to reddish eyes, a bluish bare eye-ring, a black bill, and pinkish-red legs. A dark cheek mark and subtle purplish or bronze iridescence on the neck may be visible, particularly in males. It is heavier and shorter-tailed than a Mourning Dove.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from the southwestern and southern United States through Mexico and Central America, with additional populations in the Caribbean. In Costa Rica, it is a permanent resident mainly in the northwestern Pacific dry zone, extending south approximately to Jacó and usually occurring below about 500 meters, though it is occasionally found higher. It also sometimes reaches the Central Valley and San José. Typical habitats include savannas, dry woodland edges, thorn scrub, cactus areas, agricultural land, villages, and suburbs, especially where scattered trees and nearby feeding areas occur.
profile.migrationStatus: White-winged Doves are resident in southern parts of their range, including much of Costa Rica, while northern populations make seasonal movements. Costa Rica supports both resident birds and wintering migrants from North America, with larger numbers reported in Guanacaste roughly from November through May. Movements within Costa Rica may also be local or elevation-related.
profile.breeding: White-winged Doves usually build a simple, shallow platform of coarse sticks. In Costa Rica, nests may be placed about 2 to 8 meters above the ground in thorn trees, shrubs, cacti, mangroves, or other suitable vegetation. The usual clutch is one or two white eggs. In the Costa Rican dry Pacific region, breeding has been reported mainly from January through March, although timing can vary with local rainfall, food availability, and habitat conditions. Both parents participate in incubation and care of the young.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of seeds and other plant material, including grains, fruits, berries, and seeds from grasses and dry-zone plants. White-winged Doves commonly forage on the ground in open areas, agricultural fields, gardens, and around settlements. They may also visit elevated feeders. Feeding sites are often close to trees or other cover used for perching and roosting, and the birds may gather in groups where food is plentiful.
profile.behavior: This is a social dove that often travels and roosts in flocks, sometimes numbering many individuals. It spends much of the day perched in trees or searching the ground for food, and it commonly visits water sources in warm, dry landscapes. Its flight is direct and fast, with the white wing patches becoming highly conspicuous. The species has a distinctive repetitive cooing song and may become accustomed to human-modified environments, including towns and suburban neighborhoods.

conservation.populationTrend: Broad-scale North American monitoring has indicated an increasing population in recent decades, although trends may differ among regions and subspecies. A reliable long-term population trend specifically for Costa Rica is not established.

profile.overview: The Eared Dove is a medium-sized, adaptable dove native mainly to South America. It commonly occupies open country, scrub, farmland, towns, and city parks, where it may gather in large flocks. Its plumage is grayish-brown, with dark marks around the ear, black spots on the wings, reddish legs, and a small iridescent patch on the neck. In Costa Rica it is a rare or accidental species rather than a regular resident.
profile.classification: The Eared Dove belongs to the dove and pigeon family Columbidae. It is placed in the genus Zenaida, which also includes the Mourning Dove and White-winged Dove.
profile.identification: The Eared Dove is about 22 to 28 centimeters long and has a slender, long-tailed shape. Adults are generally pale gray-brown, with a gray crown, pinkish or reddish legs, and dark spots on the wing coverts and behind the eye. A dark line and small black marks near the ear are characteristic. In good light, the sides of the neck may show a subtle iridescent sheen. It is more slender than many Leptotila doves and usually lacks a bold white wing patch.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species is widespread through much of South America, from lowlands to high elevations, and uses dry scrub, grassland, savanna, agricultural land, plantations, open woodland, and urban areas. It generally avoids dense, unbroken tropical forest. In Costa Rica, the Eared Dove is included on national bird lists but is regarded as rare or accidental, with scattered records rather than an established widespread population. Sightings are most likely in open or disturbed habitats, including urban and agricultural landscapes.
profile.migrationStatus: The Eared Dove is partly migratory and movements vary among populations; some undertake seasonal or nomadic journeys in response to food and water. In Costa Rica it is not considered a regular resident or predictable seasonal migrant. Records there are best treated as occasional, unusual occurrences, probably involving wandering or dispersing birds.
profile.breeding: Breeding behavior varies across its broad range, and the species can reproduce during much of the year where food is plentiful. It usually nests in trees, shrubs, dense vegetation, or other sheltered sites, sometimes in colonies when resources are concentrated. The nest is a relatively flimsy platform of twigs, and a typical clutch contains two white eggs. Both adults participate in incubation and care for the young. Reliable evidence of regular breeding in Costa Rica is lacking.
profile.dietFeeding: Eared Doves feed mainly on seeds and other plant material, including grains and seeds from grasses, weeds, and cultivated crops. They usually forage on the ground in open areas, walking through fields, roadsides, bare soil, and urban spaces. Birds may gather in large flocks at productive feeding sites and commonly drink at water sources. Their ability to exploit agricultural land and human settlements has helped the species become abundant in many parts of its range.
profile.behavior: This is a social dove that often travels, feeds, and roosts in groups. It has a steady, direct flight and may form conspicuous flocks when moving between feeding and roosting areas. The usual call is a repeated, soft, mournful coo. Eared Doves are strongly associated with open landscapes and tolerate substantial human disturbance. Some populations make extensive movements, while others remain relatively local or shift irregularly as food conditions change.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered increasing.

profile.overview: The Mourning Dove is a slender, long-tailed dove widely distributed across North America and parts of Central America. It is named for its soft, repeated cooing call, which can sound mournful. Usually seen on the ground or perched on wires and tree branches, it feeds mainly on seeds and often visits farmland, gardens, roadsides, and open woodland. In Costa Rica, it is a relatively local species rather than one of the country’s most widespread common doves.
profile.classification: The Mourning Dove belongs to the dove and pigeon family Columbidae. Its scientific name is Zenaida macroura.
profile.identification: This medium-sized dove is generally gray-brown above and pinkish or buff below, with a small head, pointed wings, and a long, tapered tail edged in white. Adults usually show black spots on the upperwing and a dark mark behind the eye. In flight, the white outer tail feathers contrast with the darker central feathers. It can be confused with other small Costa Rican doves, but its long pointed tail, streamlined shape, and distinctive mournful coo are useful clues.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Mourning Dove ranges across much of North America and extends south through Mexico and Central America to Panama. In Costa Rica, it occurs locally and is recorded as both a resident and a migrant, with observations associated mainly with open, dry, or disturbed areas rather than dense humid forest. Suitable habitats include agricultural land, pasture, savanna, scrub, gardens, towns, roadsides, and woodland edges. It may be especially noticeable in the Central Valley and other open upland or lowland landscapes.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is partly migratory overall. In Costa Rica, it includes resident birds as well as migrants or seasonal visitors from farther north; its occurrence is local and it is not uniformly distributed throughout the country.
profile.breeding: Mourning Doves usually build a flimsy platform nest of twigs in trees, shrubs, vines, or on building ledges. The female generally lays two white eggs, and both parents produce a nutritious secretion called crop milk for the young. The species can raise several broods in a favorable season. Breeding is documented in parts of its range, but detailed information on its breeding distribution and timing specifically in Costa Rica is limited.
profile.dietFeeding: Seeds make up most of the Mourning Dove’s diet. It commonly eats grains, grass seeds, weed seeds, and other small seeds collected from bare ground or short vegetation. The bird often forages in pairs or small groups in fields, gardens, roadsides, and beneath bird feeders. It usually swallows seeds whole and then drinks by drawing water continuously rather than taking separate small sips.
profile.behavior: Mourning Doves are generally calm, wary birds that spend considerable time walking on the ground while feeding. They often perch conspicuously on wires, fence posts, and exposed branches. Their flight is rapid and direct, with whistling wing sounds during takeoff. The repeated, low-pitched coo is most often given from a perch. Outside the breeding season, individuals may gather in small flocks around reliable feeding and drinking sites.

conservation.populationTrend: Globally decreasing, but the species remains widespread and abundant enough that it does not currently meet the criteria for a threatened category.

profile.overview: The Greater Ani (Crotophaga major) is a large, glossy black member of the cuckoo family. It is strongly associated with water and usually lives in small, noisy social groups. Unlike the more familiar Smooth-billed and Groove-billed Anis, it favors wooded riverbanks, lake margins, flooded forest, mangroves, and other forested habitats close to wetlands. Its long rounded tail, broad bill, pale eye, and blue-green sheen make it distinctive where it occurs.
profile.classification: The Greater Ani belongs to the cuckoo family, Cuculidae, in the order Cuculiformes. It is one of four highly social ani species in the subfamily Crotophaginae.
profile.identification: This is the largest ani, measuring roughly 45–50 cm including its long tail. Adults are entirely dark, with glossy black plumage that may show blue, green, or purple reflections on the wings and tail. The bill is large, deep, and laterally broad, while the iris is pale yellow to whitish. The long tail is rounded rather than sharply pointed. Greater Anis are commonly encountered in groups and often remain near water or forest edges.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Greater Ani ranges from eastern Panama and Trinidad through much of tropical South America to northern Argentina. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly as a localized and uncommon species in suitable lowland habitat, especially toward the southwestern Pacific region near rivers, lakes, wetlands, and forest margins; it is not widespread throughout the country. Preferred sites include mangrove edges, flooded woodland, gallery forest, riverbanks, and semi-open forest bordering slow-moving water. It generally avoids dry, open agricultural landscapes favored by some other anis.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is generally resident or locally mobile, although seasonal movements are reported in parts of its broad range. In Costa Rica, it is best treated as an uncommon local resident or irregularly recorded species rather than a regular long-distance migrant; reliable evidence for a consistent Costa Rican migration pattern is limited.
profile.breeding: Greater Anis breed cooperatively in groups, commonly involving several pairs and sometimes additional helpers. The group builds a large, deep cup-shaped nest from sticks and leaves, usually in a tree near or overhanging water, or in vegetation beside wetlands. Several females may lay in the same communal nest. Group members share nest construction, incubation, defense, and feeding of the young. Nesting success depends strongly on maintaining trees, shrubs, and emergent vegetation along quiet waterways.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of large insects, including beetles, grasshoppers, caterpillars, dragonflies, and other arthropods. Greater Anis also take spiders and may eat small lizards, frogs, other small vertebrates, fruits, berries, and seeds. They usually forage in loose groups along forest edges and watercourses, searching foliage, branches, bark, and the ground. Their social foraging and conspicuous movements can make a group easier to detect than a single bird.
profile.behavior: Greater Anis are highly social and typically travel in groups that may include several adults and young birds. They produce deep, resonant, sometimes mechanical-sounding calls and often vocalize together. Groups move through low and middle vegetation, especially beside rivers and lakes, and may rest communally. Cooperative breeding, joint territory defense, and shared care of nestlings are prominent features of their behavior. Birds can be secretive in dense riverside vegetation despite their loud calls and dark plumage.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not known with confidence. Available assessments do not indicate a decline severe enough to qualify the species for a threatened category. In Costa Rica, its limited and localized occurrence may partly reflect specialized habitat requirements and incomplete documentation.

profile.overview: The Smooth-billed Ani (Crotophaga ani) is a large, glossy-black cuckoo with a long tail and a distinctive heavy, arched bill. It usually lives in small, noisy family groups and searches for prey in low vegetation, pastures, scrub, and open woodland. Unlike many cuckoos, it does not normally lay its eggs in other birds’ nests. Several females may lay in one communal nest, which is built, incubated, and defended by the whole group.
profile.classification: The Smooth-billed Ani belongs to the cuckoo family, Cuculidae, in the order Cuculiformes. It is one of three closely related ani species in the genus Crotophaga.
profile.identification: Adults are entirely black, often showing a subtle greenish or bronze gloss in good light. They have a bulky, slightly flattened body, short rounded wings, a long tapering tail, and a large laterally compressed bill with a noticeable raised ridge or hump on the upper mandible. The bill lacks the grooves characteristic of the similar Groove-billed Ani. Smooth-billed Anis are often detected in pairs or groups, moving clumsily through shrubs or hopping along the ground.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species is widespread from the Caribbean and southern Florida through Central America and much of South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident, especially common on the southern Pacific slope, from near sea level to at least about 1,200 meters, and it occurs around the Osa Peninsula and other suitable lowland areas; it is less frequent farther north. It favors pastures, savannas, second-growth scrub, overgrown fields, plantations, gardens, roadsides, wetlands, and other open or disturbed habitats, usually near water.
profile.migrationStatus: The Smooth-billed Ani is generally non-migratory. In Costa Rica it is present year-round rather than being a seasonal migrant, although groups may wander locally or gather near wetter areas during dry periods.
profile.breeding: Smooth-billed Anis breed cooperatively in groups that may contain several pairs and their offspring. Group members build a large, bulky cup nest of twigs and green leaves, usually in a tree or shrub, often between about 0.5 and 15 meters above the ground. Several females lay pale blue eggs in the same nest. The adults share incubation, nest defense, and feeding of the young; later-laid eggs may be placed over earlier eggs, forming layers.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects and other invertebrates, including grasshoppers, katydids, beetles, caterpillars, ants, wasps, flies, dragonflies, and ticks. The birds also take small lizards, frogs, snails, and other small vertebrates, and eat berries and fruit, especially during dry periods. They forage by walking or hopping through grass, shrubs, vine tangles, and low trees, sometimes following cattle or army-ant swarms to capture prey flushed into view.
profile.behavior: Smooth-billed Anis are highly social and commonly feed, travel, roost, preen, and defend territories as a group. While some birds forage, another may perch above the group as a lookout for predators. They often sit close together and use a range of harsh, whining, and conversational calls. Groups can be territorial during breeding, but birds may become less settled after breeding and form larger flocks around dependable food or water sources.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified; some assessment sources describe it as decreasing, but the species remains widespread and common across much of its range.

profile.overview: The Groove-billed Ani is a social, long-tailed cuckoo of open tropical and subtropical landscapes. Its entirely black plumage, bulky curved bill, and distinctive bill grooves make it recognizable at close range. It often travels in small groups and feeds mainly on insects captured on the ground or in low vegetation. Unlike many cuckoos, it commonly breeds cooperatively, with several adults sharing nest construction, incubation, and care of young.
profile.classification: The Groove-billed Ani belongs to the cuckoo family, Cuculidae, and the order Cuculiformes. Its scientific name is Crotophaga sulcirostris.
profile.identification: This is a slender, black bird measuring about 30–38 cm long, with a very long tail and a large, laterally compressed bill. The bill is strongly curved and marked by conspicuous longitudinal grooves, the feature that gives the species its name. The plumage may show subtle greenish or purplish gloss in good light. The sexes look alike. Its loose, somewhat hunched posture and group behavior are also useful field clues, especially in open country.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Groove-billed Ani ranges from southern Texas and Mexico through Central America and into northern South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, occurring widely in suitable open and semi-open habitats on both the Pacific and Caribbean slopes, especially in lowlands and lower foothills. It uses pastures, savannas, agricultural areas, field edges, scrub, roadsides, clearings, and riparian or wetland margins with scattered trees and dense bushes for roosting. It generally avoids extensive closed-canopy forest.
profile.migrationStatus: Mostly resident across Central America, including Costa Rica. Costa Rican birds may make local or seasonal movements between drier open habitats and wetter marsh or riverside areas, but there is no evidence of regular long-distance migration there. Northern populations in Texas and parts of Mexico are more migratory.
profile.breeding: Groove-billed Anis commonly breed cooperatively. Several adults, often including more than one pair, may build and use a single bulky stick nest placed in a shrub or small tree. Multiple females can lay in the same nest, and group members share incubation and feeding of the young. Breeding timing varies geographically and is linked to local rains and food availability. In Costa Rica, nesting is associated with open habitats containing shrubs or small trees near productive foraging areas.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects and other small invertebrates, including grasshoppers, beetles, caterpillars, and spiders. The birds also eat small fruits, seeds, and occasionally other small animals. They usually forage on the ground or in short grass, hopping along and making quick pounces at prey. They may follow grazing mammals, which disturb insects, and can gather in larger groups around wetlands or river margins when food is concentrated.
profile.behavior: Groove-billed Anis are highly social and are usually seen in pairs, family groups, or small flocks. They perch together in bushes, thorny vegetation, or small trees and often roost communally. Their flight is direct but relatively weak, with rapid wingbeats and brief glides. Vocal groups produce harsh, squeaky, or nasal calls. Cooperative breeding and shared territorial behavior are notable features of their social system, and groups may shift locally in response to food and moisture conditions.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered increasing in some major conservation summaries, although local trends may differ and comprehensive monitoring is limited.

profile.overview: The Striped Cuckoo (Tapera naevia) is a slender Neotropical cuckoo recognized by its strongly streaked upperparts, long tail, and distinctive whistled song. Unlike most North American cuckoos, it is an obligate brood parasite: it lays its eggs in the nests of other birds, especially species that build covered stick nests. It usually inhabits open or partly wooded landscapes rather than deep forest and is often easier to detect by voice than by sight.
profile.classification: The Striped Cuckoo is the only species in the genus Tapera and belongs to the cuckoo family, Cuculidae. It is one of the few obligate brood-parasitic cuckoos in the Americas.
profile.identification: Adults are medium-sized, slim cuckoos with brown upperparts marked by conspicuous pale or whitish streaks, a pale eyebrow, buffy or whitish underparts, and a long, graduated tail with darker central feathers. The wings are rounded, and the bill is slightly curved. Its repeated, clear whistle is often the best way to locate it. When alarmed, it may raise or flash the small feathers near the wing bend, creating a noticeable pale-wing display.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and much of northern and central South America. In Costa Rica it is a native lowland bird, recorded especially in open country, pastures, agricultural landscapes, scrub, second growth, woodland edges, and areas with scattered trees. It also occurs around mangroves and other semi-open habitats, generally from sea level into the foothills. Historical observations from southwestern Costa Rica found it locally common in disturbed second-growth areas, including around Sierpe.
profile.migrationStatus: The Striped Cuckoo is generally considered a year-round resident, not a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica it occurs as a resident or regular local species, although numbers and detectability may vary seasonally and some individuals may make short local movements.
profile.breeding: The Striped Cuckoo is an obligate brood parasite and does not build a nest, incubate its eggs, or raise its young. Females place an egg in the nest of another bird, commonly in the large covered or domed stick nests of spinetails, wrens, and related species. Confirmed Costa Rican host records include the Pale-breasted Spinetail, while local sources also report hosts among wrens and sparrow-like birds. Breeding records span much of the year, with activity documented from January through October.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of insects and other small invertebrates, including caterpillars, grasshoppers, beetles, and similar prey. It forages in low vegetation, shrubs, tangled growth, and along woodland edges, usually moving deliberately while searching among leaves and branches. It may also take small vertebrates or other foods opportunistically, but detailed information on the diet in Costa Rica is limited.
profile.behavior: The Striped Cuckoo is secretive and often remains hidden in dense shrubs, vines, tall grass, or low woodland. It frequently gives its distinctive repeated whistle from a concealed perch. Individuals may sit quietly for long periods before moving through vegetation or flying between scattered trees. Females inspect potential host nests, and the cuckoo chick is dependent on the foster parents after hatching; in some cases the young cuckoo eliminates competing host nestlings.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not precisely quantified, but the species is widespread and has no reliable evidence of a major worldwide decline.

profile.overview: The Pheasant Cuckoo is a large, secretive Neotropical cuckoo named for its exceptionally long, graduated tail. It spends much of its time walking quietly through dense ground vegetation and leaf litter, so it is usually heard rather than seen. Its distinctive song consists of clear whistles followed by a trill. Unlike many familiar cuckoos, it is strongly associated with forest understory and thick secondary growth across Central and South America.
profile.classification: The Pheasant Cuckoo belongs to the cuckoo family, Cuculidae, and the ground-cuckoo subfamily Neomorphinae. Its scientific name is Dromococcyx phasianellus.
profile.identification: This cuckoo has dark brown to sooty upperparts, pale buff underparts, and a long, broad, pheasant-like tail with graduated feathers. The head is relatively small and bears a short rusty-tipped crest that may be raised when the bird is alert. The breast is finely streaked or spotted with dark markings. The iris and bare eye-ring are yellowish to greenish yellow. It is difficult to observe because it moves stealthily through dense vegetation and often remains concealed.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Pheasant Cuckoo occurs from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and central South America. In Costa Rica it is regarded as a resident, with a broad but very local and apparently rare distribution, especially in lowlands along the Pacific slope; it has been recorded locally up to about 800 meters. It uses dense forest understory, riverine forest, forest edges, secondary growth, scrubby woodland, and other areas with thick ground cover.
profile.migrationStatus: Generally resident rather than migratory. In Costa Rica, it is present year-round, although its unobtrusive habits and seasonal singing may make it seem absent outside the main vocal period.
profile.breeding: The Pheasant Cuckoo is a brood parasite and lays its egg in the nest of another bird, leaving the host to provide parental care. Reported or suspected hosts include several small flycatchers, such as Myiozetetes species, Rhynchocyclus flycatchers, and the Pied Water-Tyrant, as well as the Barred Antshrike. Details of its breeding cycle remain poorly known. In Costa Rica, parasitism has been associated with nests of broad-billed or related flycatchers.
profile.dietFeeding: It feeds mainly on insects and other small animals found on or near the ground. Recorded prey includes grasshoppers, cicadas, beetles, and other arthropods; small lizards and nestlings may also be taken occasionally. While foraging, it walks through leaf litter and low vegetation, sometimes vibrating its plumage, clapping its bill, or bobbing its body and tail before making a short rush to seize prey.
profile.behavior: The species is usually solitary or found in pairs and is notably elusive. It forages terrestrially in dense cover but often sings from a low or middle-height perch in the understory or from the ground. Its loud, distinctive song is more frequently detected than the bird itself, especially during the breeding season. The rusty crest may be raised during excitement, and the long tail is often conspicuous when the bird crosses an opening.

conservation.populationTrend: A precise global population estimate and well-supported population trend are not available. The species remains widespread, although it is locally uncommon and difficult to detect.

profile.overview: The Lesser Ground-Cuckoo (Morococcyx erythropygus) is a secretive, mostly terrestrial cuckoo of dry Central American habitats. It spends much of its time walking or hopping through dense low vegetation, where its brown upperparts and warm rufous underparts provide camouflage. Bright yellow and blue skin around the eye creates a striking facial pattern. Unlike many cuckoos, it builds its own nest rather than regularly laying eggs in the nests of other bird species.
profile.classification: The Lesser Ground-Cuckoo belongs to the cuckoo family, Cuculidae, and the order Cuculiformes. It is the only species in the genus Morococcyx.
profile.identification: This slender, long-tailed cuckoo is about 25 cm long. Adults have brown upperparts with subtle bronze or greenish reflections, warm cinnamon-rufous underparts, and a dark tail with pale tips on the outer feathers. The bill is yellow with a dark upper ridge, and the legs are yellowish or orange-brown. The eye is surrounded by a yellow orbital ring, with bright blue bare skin behind it bordered by black markings. It is usually detected by its loud, rolling or trilling calls.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from western and southern Mexico through Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is a resident, especially on the Pacific slope, where it is associated with the dry lowlands of Guanacaste, the Gulf of Nicoya, and areas around the Tárcoles River. It also occurs locally in the western Central Valley. Typical habitat includes thorn scrub, tropical deciduous woodland, savanna, forest edges, abandoned fields, dense secondary growth, and semi-open woodland, generally from sea level to about 1,200 m.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident, not a regular long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, individuals are present throughout the year in suitable Pacific-slope and western Central Valley habitats, although local detectability may vary with season and rainfall.
profile.breeding: Breeding in Costa Rica generally occurs from February through May. The Lesser Ground-Cuckoo builds a shallow, loosely formed bowl from small sticks, leaf stems, and dry leaves. The nest is placed on the ground, usually behind concealing vegetation in dense scrub or low woodland. A typical clutch contains two chalk-white eggs, and both adults are believed to participate in incubation. Details of incubation length, chick development, and parental care remain incompletely documented.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of insects and other small invertebrates. It searches on the ground beneath scrub and woodland, walking, hopping, and making short leaps to seize prey from the leaf litter or low vegetation. Likely prey includes grasshoppers, crickets, caterpillars, beetles, and other arthropods. Because it forages close to cover and is reluctant to fly, it can be difficult to observe even where it is locally common.
profile.behavior: The Lesser Ground-Cuckoo is secretive and usually solitary or found in pairs. It moves quietly through dense undergrowth, often pausing before making a short dash or hop to capture prey. When disturbed, it may run or fly only a short distance into cover. Its loud, rolling calls are more conspicuous than the bird itself and may be given from concealed positions. It is primarily active during the day and maintains close contact with dry, brushy ground habitats.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is thought to be decreasing, but the species remains widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Rufous-vented Ground-Cuckoo is a large, secretive, ground-dwelling cuckoo of tropical forests. It spends much of its time walking or running through dense understory rather than flying in open areas. Its dark brown body, long tail, cinnamon face, irregular black breast band, and rufous lower belly help identify it. The species is especially difficult to observe because it is shy, occurs at low densities, and depends on extensive, mature forest with little disturbance.
profile.classification: The Rufous-vented Ground-Cuckoo belongs to the cuckoo family, Cuculidae, and the ground-cuckoo genus Neomorphus. The Costa Rican population is generally assigned to the subspecies Neomorphus geoffroyi salvini.
profile.identification: This ground-cuckoo is about 48 cm long and has a long tail, long neck, shaggy crest, and strong legs. Adults are mainly dark brown above, with subtle green or purple gloss on the wings, tail, and crest. The face is cinnamon, the underparts are grayish brown becoming warmer and more rufous toward the belly and undertail, and an irregular black band crosses the breast. Juveniles are duller and usually lack the distinct breast band.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama into western Colombia, with other populations extending through parts of the Amazon Basin and eastern Brazil.
