profile.behavior: This hummingbird is usually inconspicuous and spends much of its time perched quietly in shaded forest. Males may gather in loose groups or defend territories around flowering plants, sometimes giving characteristic songs from exposed perches. Females tend to forage and travel more along ravines and streams. Young birds may descend into shrubs, clearings, and forest edges to use shorter-tubed flowers. Flight is rapid and maneuverable, especially around streamside vegetation and waterfalls.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified, but the species is generally regarded as broadly distributed with no confirmed rapid decline.

profile.overview: The Brown Violetear (Colibri delphinae) is a medium-sized hummingbird of humid mountain forests and woodland edges in Central and South America. It is named for the broad violet patch behind the eye, which is especially noticeable when the bird turns its head in sunlight. Although often associated with forested uplands, it may also visit plantations, gardens, clearings, and flowering trees. Costa Rica lies near the northern part of its range and supports local populations in suitable highland habitats.
profile.classification: The Brown Violetear belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the genus Colibri. It is one of the four recognized violetears.
profile.identification: This hummingbird is about 11 to 12 centimeters long. Adults are mainly olive-green to bronzy green above, with a grayish or brownish breast and belly. The most distinctive feature is the large violet patch on the sides of the head behind the eyes. The bill is fairly straight and dark, and the tail is dusky bronze or greenish. Its appearance can vary with lighting, and the violet ear patch may be difficult to see when the bird is facing away.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Brown Violetear occurs from southern Mexico through Central America and into northern and western South America, including parts of the Andes. In Costa Rica, it is a local bird of humid and wet highlands, especially in forested mountain regions and adjacent foothills. It uses montane evergreen forest, forest borders, second growth, shaded coffee plantations, gardens, and other areas with abundant flowers. Records are generally associated with middle and upper elevations, although its local distribution can vary with season and food availability.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally regarded as a resident or partly resident species in Costa Rica. Individuals may make local or elevational movements, following flowering plants and changing food supplies, but it is not known as a long-distance migrant there.
profile.breeding: The breeding season varies across its broad range and may be influenced by rainfall and local flowering conditions. Like other hummingbirds, the female builds a small cup-shaped nest, usually from plant fibers, moss, and other soft material, often on a slender branch. She incubates the eggs and raises the young without assistance from the male. Nest placement and timing in Costa Rica can vary among elevations and habitats.
profile.dietFeeding: The Brown Violetear feeds mainly on nectar from flowering trees, shrubs, vines, and epiphytes. It also captures small insects and other arthropods, which provide important protein, especially during breeding. It may defend productive flowers or feeding areas from other hummingbirds, but it can also forage widely through forest edges and gardens. Flowers with tubular or exposed nectar are commonly used, and the species may visit feeders where these are available.
profile.behavior: This species is active and agile, moving rapidly between flowers and often hovering briefly while feeding. It commonly perches on exposed twigs or branches between feeding bouts. Brown Violetears can be territorial around rich flower sources and may chase other hummingbirds, although several individuals may occur in the same general area when food is plentiful. Their calls are sharp, high-pitched notes, and their plumage can appear quite different depending on light and viewing angle.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly established, although habitat loss may be causing local declines in parts of its range.
conservation.threats: Potential threats include clearing and fragmentation of humid montane forest, loss of flowering plants, agricultural expansion, and degradation of forest edges and highland habitats. These pressures may be particularly important where populations are small or isolated.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect remaining mountain forest and maintain connected forest edges, flowering shrubs, native trees, and epiphytes. In Costa Rica, shade-grown farms and gardens can support the species when they retain native vegetation and avoid excessive pesticide use. Protecting flowering plants throughout the year helps provide both nectar and insect prey.

profile.overview: The Lesser Violetear (Colibri cyanotus) is a medium-sized hummingbird of humid mountain regions from Costa Rica and western Panama south through the Andes to Bolivia, with additional populations in northern Venezuela. It is named for the bright violet ear patches on the sides of its head. This active, metallic-green species visits flowering trees, shrubs, forest edges, gardens, and clearings, where it feeds on nectar and small insects and often defends productive feeding areas.
profile.classification: The Lesser Violetear belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the order Apodiformes. It is closely related to other violetears and was formerly included with the Mexican Violetear in a broader species concept.
profile.identification: Adults are mostly shining green, with conspicuous glittering violet patches behind the eyes and on the sides of the neck. The bill and legs are black. The throat and upper breast are bright green, while the tail is blue-green to bronzy with a distinct dark subterminal band. Females are generally duller below, and juveniles show buffy or rusty edging on the head and upperparts. Its repeated, dry-sounding calls and habit of perching high in exposed positions are useful field clues.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Lesser Violetear occurs in Costa Rica mainly in the country's highlands south of the Cordillera de Guanacaste, including the Cordillera de Tilarán, the Central Volcanic Cordillera, and the Talamanca range. It is associated with humid montane forest, cloud forest, woodland edges, secondary growth, scrub, pastures with scattered trees, clearings, and gardens. In Costa Rica it is most numerous at roughly 1,600–3,000 meters, though it may descend to about 1,000 meters outside the breeding season. It often uses flowering shade trees and open forest margins.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally resident in Costa Rica but undertakes local altitudinal movements. Birds may move downslope during the rainy season or when flowering conditions change, while some highland areas, including Cerro de la Muerte, show seasonal changes in abundance. It is not a long-distance migrant.
profile.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding is concentrated in the highlands and commonly occurs from about October through March, although timing can vary with elevation and local conditions. The female builds a small, sturdy cup nest from plant fibers, moss, fern scales, grass, and spider webbing. Nests are typically placed 1–3 meters above the ground on a drooping twig, bamboo stem, forest edge, roadside bank, or near a stream. The female alone incubates the eggs and cares for the young.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of nectar from trees, shrubs, and vines, supplemented by small insects and other arthropods that provide protein. In Costa Rica, the species may gather at flowering Inga trees and other nectar-rich plants in cloud forest edges, gardens, and shade-grown agricultural areas. It usually forages alone, often at middle and upper levels, and may defend a feeding territory when flowers are abundant.
profile.behavior: The Lesser Violetear is energetic, vocal, and territorial. Males commonly sing from high, exposed perches in the canopy or above open areas, sometimes repeating their dry call for long periods while displaying to females or challenging rivals. Several birds may use the same flowering area without forming a true lek. It can be aggressive around food but may be subordinate to larger or more dominant high-elevation hummingbirds in Costa Rica. The violet ear patches can be raised during aggressive interactions.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not considered to indicate a major species-level decline, although precise population estimates are unavailable.

profile.overview: The Purple-crowned Fairy (Heliothryx barroti) is a slender, long-tailed hummingbird of humid forests from southern Mexico through Central America to western Panama. It is named for the violet-purple crown of the adult, which contrasts with glossy green upperparts and mostly white underparts. This canopy-loving species often visits flowers high in trees but may also forage along forest edges, in gardens, and in shaded clearings. Costa Rica lies within its regular resident range.
profile.classification: The Purple-crowned Fairy belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the genus Heliothryx. It is closely related to the Green-breasted Mango and other large hummingbirds, but its long tail, white underparts, and purple crown help distinguish it.
profile.identification: Adults have glossy green upperparts, a dark mask through the eye, a violet or purple crown, and pale to white underparts. The long tail is deeply forked, with the central feathers usually darker than the outer feathers. The bill is long and slightly curved. Females and immature birds may show less vivid crown coloration and more grayish or buff tones below. Its strong, direct flight and habit of perching high in trees are also useful field marks.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southern Mexico through Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama. In Costa Rica it is found mainly in humid lowlands and foothill forests on both the Caribbean and Pacific sides, including forest edges, tall secondary growth, plantations, and shaded gardens. It generally uses evergreen or semi-evergreen habitats with abundant flowering plants and substantial tree cover, and may occur from the lowlands into lower mountain elevations.
profile.migrationStatus: The Purple-crowned Fairy is generally considered resident rather than a long-distance migrant in Costa Rica. Local movements may occur in response to flowering patterns, food availability, and seasonal changes in rainfall, and birds can shift between forest, edge, and nearby cultivated habitats.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited compared with that of some common hummingbirds. The female builds a small cup nest, typically using fine plant material and fibers, and incubates the eggs without help from the male. As in other hummingbirds, the female alone provides care for the young. Nest placement is usually associated with vegetation that offers shelter, often in forest or along a protected edge. Breeding activity may vary geographically with rainfall and flowering conditions.
profile.dietFeeding: The Purple-crowned Fairy feeds mainly on nectar from forest trees, vines, shrubs, and other flowering plants. Its long bill allows it to exploit tubular flowers, and it may defend productive flower patches from other hummingbirds. It also takes small insects and other arthropods, especially when feeding young. Foraging often occurs in the canopy or at mid-levels, although birds may visit flowers in gardens and plantations.
profile.behavior: This hummingbird is usually encountered singly or in pairs and often perches quietly in the upper or middle levels of vegetation between feeding flights. It makes rapid, direct movements between flowers and may aggressively exclude other hummingbirds from favored resources. Its long, forked tail and white underparts are conspicuous in flight. Individuals may use forest edges and clearings but generally remain associated with areas that retain mature vegetation and plentiful flowers.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not known with precision. The species remains fairly widespread, but abundance can vary locally with habitat quality and the availability of flowering plants.

profile.overview: The Green-breasted Mango is a large, powerful hummingbird of tropical lowlands and foothills. Males have glossy green plumage, a dark blue to violet throat and breast, and a long, slightly curved bill. Females are duller and usually show a pale or white central stripe below. It feeds mainly on nectar but also takes small insects. In Costa Rica, it is a regular hummingbird of suitable habitats, especially in warm lowland regions.
profile.classification: The Green-breasted Mango belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the genus Anthracothorax. It is one of several large mango hummingbirds found in the American tropics.
profile.identification: This is a relatively large hummingbird with a long, slightly decurved black bill and a moderately long tail. The adult male is mostly bright green, with a dark blue or violet throat and breast that may appear nearly black in poor light. Females are less strongly colored, with greener upperparts, paler underparts, and a conspicuous whitish central stripe. Juveniles resemble females and may have buff-edged feathers. Its strong, direct flight and large size help distinguish it from many smaller Costa Rican hummingbirds.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Green-breasted Mango ranges from Mexico through Central America to parts of northern South America and occurs on several Caribbean islands. In Costa Rica it is found mainly in warm lowlands and foothills, particularly in open woodland, forest edges, gardens, plantations, second-growth vegetation, and flowering shrubs near human settlement. It can occur on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes, although local abundance varies with elevation, habitat, and food availability. It generally favors disturbed or semi-open habitats rather than dense, mature forest interiors.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is generally resident in Costa Rica, but individuals may make local or seasonal movements in response to flowering and food availability. It is not considered a regular long-distance migrant there.
profile.breeding: Breeding can occur during periods when food is abundant, with timing varying across the species’ broad range. The female builds a small cup-shaped nest, usually from plant fibers, down, and other soft materials, secured with spider silk and often decorated externally with bits of lichen or bark. The nest is commonly placed on a slender branch. She incubates the eggs and raises the young alone, while the male may defend feeding territories rather than provide parental care.
profile.dietFeeding: The Green-breasted Mango feeds chiefly on nectar from tubular or otherwise nectar-rich flowers, including flowers of trees, shrubs, vines, and cultivated plants. It also captures small insects and other tiny arthropods, especially when feeding young. Its long bill and tongue allow it to reach deep flowers. It may defend productive flowering plants or feeding areas from other hummingbirds and often visits gardens, forest edges, and plantations where nectar sources are concentrated.
profile.behavior: This species is active, fast-flying, and often territorial around rich nectar sources. It may perch conspicuously on exposed twigs while watching for intruders, then make rapid chases or short display flights. Like other hummingbirds, it can hover while feeding and can maneuver quickly through vegetation. Males are usually more brightly colored and may appear dark when viewed against shade. Individuals commonly use semi-open habitats and may visit feeders where these are provided responsibly.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not considered to indicate a major decline, although local populations may be affected by habitat change and variation in food resources.
conservation.threats: Local threats may include loss of flowering habitat, removal of native vegetation, intensive agricultural practices, and inappropriate pesticide use. These pressures are not currently considered sufficient to place the species in a threatened global category.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect native flowering plants and retain connected vegetation in gardens, farms, and forest edges. Reduce pesticide use, provide clean feeders only when they can be maintained hygienically, and conserve lowland and foothill habitats used by hummingbirds in Costa Rica.

profile.overview: The Veraguan Mango (Anthracothorax veraguensis) is a large, long-tailed hummingbird of southern Central America. It is closely related to the Green-breasted Mango and was formerly treated as part of that species by some authorities. The bird is named for Veraguas in Panama, within much of its known range. It uses forest edges, clearings, gardens, and other habitats with abundant flowering plants, and is an important pollinator of tropical flowers.
profile.classification: The Veraguan Mango belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the genus Anthracothorax. It is a member of the mango group of large hummingbirds.
profile.identification: This is a large hummingbird with a long, slightly curved bill and a conspicuously long, forked tail. Adults are mainly green, with darker wings and tail feathers. The male has a dark central stripe on the underparts and contrasting blue to purplish coloration on the throat and breast, although appearance can vary with light and viewing angle. Females and immature birds are duller below and may show pale or grayish underparts. Care is needed to distinguish it from the similar Green-breasted Mango.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Veraguan Mango occurs in southern Central America, especially Costa Rica and western Panama, with its distribution centered on lowland and foothill areas. In Costa Rica, it is associated mainly with the Pacific side and adjoining southwestern regions, where it may occur in forest edges, secondary growth, plantations, gardens, mangroves, and other partly open habitats. It generally favors places with flowering trees, shrubs, and hummingbird-pollinated plants, and can use human-modified landscapes when suitable nectar sources remain available.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally considered resident or locally dispersive rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, individuals may move short distances in response to flowering conditions, but regular seasonal migration is not well established.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited compared with that of more widespread hummingbirds. Like other Anthracothorax species, the Veraguan Mango is expected to build a small cup-shaped nest, usually in vegetation above the ground, with the female handling incubation and most care of the young. Nest placement may be near forest margins or other open, flower-rich habitats. Timing can vary geographically and may be influenced by rainfall and local flowering cycles.
profile.dietFeeding: The Veraguan Mango feeds mainly on nectar from tubular or otherwise hummingbird-pollinated flowers. It also takes small insects and other arthropods, which provide protein, especially during breeding. Its large size and strong flight allow it to defend productive flowers from smaller hummingbirds and other nectar feeders. It may visit flowering trees, shrubs, vines, gardens, and cultivated plants, and can sometimes forage in disturbed habitats with reliable floral resources.
profile.behavior: This hummingbird is active and maneuverable, typically hovering while taking nectar and making rapid flights between flowering plants. It may perch conspicuously on exposed twigs while watching its feeding area. Individuals can be territorial around especially rich flowers and may chase other hummingbirds or nectar-feeding birds. Courtship and territorial displays are likely to include aerial pursuits and changes in body posture that emphasize the male’s colorful throat and breast.

conservation.populationTrend: The population trend is not well documented in detail. There is no reliable evidence presented here of a major global decline.

profile.overview: The Green Thorntail (Discosura conversii) is a very small hummingbird of humid forests and woodland edges in Central and northwestern South America. It is recognized by its compact body, glittering green plumage, narrow pointed bill, and, in adult males, elongated tail feathers. The species usually forages actively in the middle and upper levels of vegetation, visiting small flowers and defending feeding areas. Costa Rica forms part of its northern range.
profile.classification: The Green Thorntail belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae. It is placed in the genus Discosura, a group of small, long-tailed Neotropical hummingbirds.
profile.identification: This tiny hummingbird has mainly green upperparts, a short, slender bill, and a relatively long, narrow tail. Adult males are especially distinctive because the central tail feathers are extended and the throat and breast show bright green coloration. Females and immature birds are less ornate and may show paler underparts. Its quick flight, hovering at flowers, and small size help separate it from larger Costa Rican hummingbirds, although careful observation is often needed.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Green Thorntail occurs from Costa Rica and Panama south through western Colombia and northwestern Ecuador. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon to locally common resident of humid Caribbean-slope lowlands and foothills, with records extending into suitable forested areas at moderate elevations. It uses wet evergreen forest, forest edges, clearings, gardens, plantations, and second growth where flowering plants and cover remain available. It is generally associated with humid habitats rather than dry open country.
profile.migrationStatus: The Green Thorntail is generally considered resident in Costa Rica and across most of its range. It may make local or seasonal movements in response to flowering and food availability, but it is not known for long-distance migration.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited compared with that of many better-studied hummingbirds. Like other hummingbirds, the female is expected to build a small cup-shaped nest, usually with plant fibers, down, and spider silk, and to raise the young without male assistance. Nesting is associated with forested or edge habitats that provide flowers, concealment, and perches. Breeding timing can vary geographically and may be influenced by rainfall and local flowering patterns.
profile.dietFeeding: The Green Thorntail feeds mainly on nectar from small flowers, including flowers in forest trees, shrubs, vines, and cultivated plants. It also catches small insects and other tiny arthropods, which provide important protein, especially for females and growing young. It typically hovers while feeding and may defend productive flower patches from other hummingbirds. Its small body and rapid wingbeats allow it to exploit flowers in dense vegetation and forest edges.
profile.behavior: This species is active, agile, and often inconspicuous as it moves rapidly through foliage. It usually forages alone, although several individuals may gather where flowers are abundant. Males may display their elongated tail feathers and bright plumage during territorial or courtship interactions. The Green Thorntail frequently perches on exposed twigs between feeding visits and may use gardens, plantations, and other modified habitats when suitable flowering plants and nearby cover are present.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to face a severe overall conservation decline, although local populations may be affected by habitat loss and degradation.

profile.overview: The Rufous-crested Coquette is a tiny hummingbird of the family Trochilidae. It is named for the male’s striking rufous, spiky crest, which is especially noticeable during display. The species has a patchy distribution from eastern Central America through the Andes to Bolivia. It is generally uncommon and local, and its small size, quiet movements, and preference for forest edges can make it difficult to find. In Costa Rica, it is exceptionally rare and known from very few records.
profile.classification: The Rufous-crested Coquette belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the coquette genus Lophornis. Some taxonomic treatments have debated the status of related forms, but Lophornis delattrei is widely used for this species.
profile.identification: This is a very small hummingbird with a short, straight bill and a compact body. The adult male is distinguished by a prominent rufous-orange crest with elongated, pointed feathers, along with green upperparts and a mainly green-and-white underside marked by rufous tones. Females and immature birds lack the spectacular crest and appear plainer, with a rufous forehead and more subdued green, gray, and whitish plumage. Its rapid wingbeats and hovering flight are typical of hummingbirds.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species has a disjunct range extending from eastern Panama and northwestern Colombia through the Andes of Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia. It uses humid lowland and montane evergreen forest, forest edges, clearings, and sometimes secondary vegetation, generally from low elevations to about 2,000 meters. In Costa Rica it is not a regular, widespread hummingbird. Historical specimens came from the central part of the country, and later records, including a recent record from Cartago, indicate that it can occur there but remains exceptionally uncommon and localized.
profile.migrationStatus: No regular long-distance migration is known. The Rufous-crested Coquette is generally considered resident where established, although local or elevational movements may occur. In Costa Rica, its very small number of records makes its seasonal status uncertain; it should be treated as a rare, irregular occurrence rather than a predictable migrant.
profile.breeding: The species’ breeding biology is not well documented across its range. Like other coquettes, it is expected to be solitary and territorial, with the female responsible for nest construction, incubation, and care of the young. The nest is a small cup attached to vegetation, and breeding is probably associated with periods of suitable flowering and insect abundance. Reliable, detailed information on nesting dates and breeding sites in Costa Rica is especially limited.
profile.dietFeeding: The Rufous-crested Coquette feeds mainly on nectar from small flowers and supplements this diet with tiny insects and other arthropods. It usually forages alone, hovering at flowers and sometimes making short sallies to capture insects. Coquettes may defend productive flowers or feeding patches, particularly when nectar is concentrated. In Costa Rica, its specific food plants and feeding behavior have not been documented in detail because sightings are so scarce.
profile.behavior: This hummingbird is generally solitary and can be unobtrusive despite the male’s ornate crest. Males may perform brief display flights or expose the crest during interactions with other hummingbirds. It moves quickly between flowers and perches in vegetation between feeding bouts. The species is usually encountered in forest edges, clearings, and other semi-open habitats rather than in dense, dark forest interiors. Its rarity in Costa Rica may partly reflect genuine scarcity and partly the difficulty of detecting such a small bird.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well known.

profile.overview: The Black-crested Coquette (Lophornis helenae) is a very small hummingbird of humid tropical forests and adjoining gardens, clearings, and second-growth vegetation. The male is distinctive for its black crest, white collar, and ornamental facial feathers, while the female is less dramatically marked and has a spotted breast. It feeds mainly on small flowers and tiny arthropods. The species occurs from southern Mexico through Central America to western Panama, including localized areas of Costa Rica.
profile.classification: The Black-crested Coquette belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the genus Lophornis, the coquettes. It is one of several small, sexually dimorphic hummingbirds known for elaborate male head and neck plumage.
profile.identification: This is a tiny, short-tailed hummingbird with a slender bill. The adult male has mostly green upperparts, a prominent black crest, a white collar, and elongated, spotted facial feathers that can form a ruff around the head. The underparts are largely greenish or pale. The female lacks the male’s elaborate crest and facial ornamentation and is generally duller, with a pale, heavily spotted or scaled-looking throat and breast. Its small size and quick flight can make identification difficult.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Black-crested Coquette ranges from southern Mexico through Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and into western Panama. In Costa Rica it is associated mainly with the humid Caribbean lowlands and foothills, where it is local and generally uncommon rather than widespread. It uses mature evergreen forest edges, forest gaps, gardens, plantations, streamside vegetation, and second growth, especially where flowering shrubs, vines, and small trees provide nectar and cover. It is usually found from low elevations into the lower foothills.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is generally considered resident, but local movements may occur in response to flowering and food availability. In Costa Rica it is not normally treated as a regular long-distance migrant; records are localized, mainly on the Caribbean side and nearby foothills.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited compared with that of more familiar hummingbirds. Like other coquettes, the female is expected to build a tiny cup-shaped nest, usually from plant fibers, moss, and other soft materials secured with spider silk. She alone incubates the eggs and cares for the young. Nest placement is likely in a protected shrub, small tree, or similar vegetation, often near forest edge or other semi-open habitat. Timing may vary geographically and with local rainfall and flowering conditions.
profile.dietFeeding: The Black-crested Coquette feeds primarily on nectar from small flowers, including flowers of trees, shrubs, vines, and epiphytes. It also captures very small insects and other arthropods, which provide important protein, especially for females and growing young. It usually forages near forest edges, clearings, flowering vegetation, and gardens. Males may defend temporary feeding areas, although the species’ small size and localized occurrence can make its feeding behavior difficult to observe.
profile.behavior: This coquette is active and fast-moving, often hovering briefly at flowers before darting to another perch or feeding site. It may make short aerial sallies to capture insects and can perch quietly in foliage between feeding bouts. Males use their crest and elongated facial feathers during courtship displays, making them especially distinctive when viewed closely. The species is typically solitary or encountered singly, although several individuals may gather where flowering plants are concentrated.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population trend is not well documented and may be decreasing in some areas because of habitat loss and degradation.

profile.overview: The White-crested Coquette (Lophornis adorabilis) is a very small hummingbird restricted to the Pacific slope of Costa Rica and adjacent western Panama. It is especially notable for the adult male’s bright white crest, elongated cheek plumes, sparkling green throat, and warm rufous body markings. Females are less ornate and mainly green and buff. This regional endemic uses forest edges, clearings, secondary growth, gardens, and other places with abundant small flowers.
profile.classification: The White-crested Coquette belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the genus Lophornis, known as the coquettes. It is closely related to other small, ornamented hummingbirds of Central and South America.
profile.identification: The adult male is tiny, with a short, straight bill, a conspicuous white crest, dark facial markings, elongated pale cheek plumes, a glittering green gorget, and rufous-buff sides and underparts. The female lacks the elaborate crest and cheek plumes and is predominantly green above, with buffy or whitish underparts marked by green spotting. Both sexes have a compact shape and rapid wingbeats typical of hummingbirds. Immature males resemble females until adult ornamentation develops.
profile.rangeHabitat: The White-crested Coquette is a regional endemic of the Pacific slope of Costa Rica and the Pacific slope of far western Panama. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly from the Central Pacific region southward through the Osa Peninsula, Golfo Dulce, Térraba Valley, and nearby foothills, with records extending inland toward the Cordillera Central. It occupies humid lowland and foothill forest, forest edges, clearings, tall secondary growth, hedgerows, plantations, and flowering gardens, generally from sea level to about 1,200 meters.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered resident in Costa Rica rather than a long-distance migrant. Individuals may make local or irregular movements, sometimes described as nomadic, in response to flowering conditions and the availability of nectar-rich trees and shrubs.
profile.breeding: Breeding in Costa Rica has been recorded mainly during the early dry season, approximately December through February. The female builds a tiny cup nest from plant fibers and down, binds it with spider silk, and decorates the outside with lichens. Nests may be suspended from branches in clearings or at forest edges, sometimes several meters above the ground. The usual clutch is two eggs, and young leave the nest roughly three weeks after hatching.
profile.dietFeeding: The species feeds primarily on nectar from small flowers, often foraging in the canopy but also visiting flowers at forest edges, in secondary vegetation, and around gardens. It may follow regular routes between flowering plants. Small insects and other arthropods provide protein and are captured by hovering or gleaned from leaves and flowers. Its short bill and small body allow it to exploit flowers that are less accessible to larger hummingbirds.
profile.behavior: White-crested Coquettes are usually solitary while feeding and may be difficult to locate except where flowering plants concentrate them. Males defend feeding areas and perform elaborate courtship displays, including rapid side-to-side movements while facing a perched or hovering female. The species can be relatively tolerant of people and may visit flowering gardens. Numbers and local presence can change quickly as birds track changing supplies of nectar-producing plants.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains locally regular in suitable habitat and protected areas.

profile.overview: The Green-crowned Brilliant is a large, robust hummingbird of humid mountain forests from Costa Rica to western Ecuador. Males are especially striking, with glittering green plumage and a small blue throat patch, while females have white underparts heavily spotted with green. This species usually feeds in the middle and upper forest layers, visiting nectar-rich flowers and sometimes feeders. Its relatively straight bill and strong build distinguish it from many smaller hummingbirds sharing its range.
profile.classification: Scientific name: Heliodoxa jacula. It belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the order Apodiformes.
profile.identification: This hummingbird has a straight bill, sleek body, and fairly long tail. The adult male is largely shining emerald green, with a glittering crown and a small blue or violet-blue throat patch that may appear dark in poor light. The female has green upperparts and whitish underparts marked with prominent green spots. She also shows a white stripe beside the bill and a white spot behind the eye. Females have blackish tails with white tips on the outer feathers.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Green-crowned Brilliant occurs from the highlands of Costa Rica through Panama and western Colombia to western Ecuador. It inhabits humid subtropical and montane forest, including cloud forest, forest edges, clearings, secondary growth, and wooded stream corridors. It is generally associated with middle elevations, commonly occurring around 700 to 2,000 meters, although elevation varies across its range. The species tolerates some disturbed or fragmented forest and may visit gardens and feeding stations near suitable woodland.
profile.migrationStatus: Mostly resident. Local or seasonal elevational movements may occur, as suggested by occasional records from lower elevations.
profile.breeding: Breeding timing varies geographically, extending approximately from July or August to January in Costa Rica and from May to September in Colombia. The female builds a bulky cup nest saddled on a thin, often downward-sloping branch, sometimes near a stream. Plant fibers and tree-fern scales form the cup, while liverworts, mosses, lichens, and spiderweb provide camouflage. The usual clutch contains two whitish, elongated eggs. The female alone builds the nest and incubates the eggs.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of flower nectar, supplemented by small arthropods that provide protein. Marcgravia vines are an important nectar source, and females also visit smaller understory flowers. The bird usually forages in the middle and upper forest layers. It often clings to a flower while feeding rather than hovering continuously. Individuals may follow regular circuits between flowering plants, while males sometimes defend especially productive flower patches. The species also visits hummingbird feeders.
profile.behavior: Green-crowned Brilliants are active, powerful fliers that often feed alone. Males may defend concentrated nectar sources and chase other hummingbirds, but they also use trap-lining routes between scattered flowers. Their calls include loud, squeaky notes, with sputtering sounds during pursuits and repeated sharper notes in display. When perched, the bird may appear dark green until direct light reveals its brilliant iridescence. By carrying pollen among flowers, it serves as a pollinator within montane forest communities.

conservation.populationTrend: Decreasing; the global population size has not been quantified reliably.

profile.overview: The Talamanca Hummingbird (Eugenes spectabilis) is a large hummingbird of the high mountains of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is a striking member of the mountain-gem group and was formerly treated as the southern form of the Magnificent Hummingbird. Males show a dark head with iridescent purple and turquoise areas, while females are more subdued and mottled. The species is regularly seen in suitable cloud-forest habitats and often visits hummingbird feeders.
profile.classification: The Talamanca Hummingbird belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the mountain-gem tribe Lampornithini. It is one of two currently recognized species in the genus Eugenes.
profile.identification: This is a very large hummingbird, about 13 cm long. Adult males are mainly green, with a dark-looking head that can show a brilliant purple crown and turquoise throat in good light. Females are duller, with grayish, mottled underparts, green sides, and a conspicuous white spot behind the eye that extends into a pale eyeline. Females usually have a somewhat longer, slightly more downcurved bill. Immature birds resemble females but have buff-edged, scaly-looking plumage.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Talamanca Hummingbird is restricted to highland Central America, occurring in Costa Rica and extending into western Panama near Volcán Barú. In Costa Rica, it is found in the Cordillera Central and Cordillera de Talamanca, generally from about 2,000 m to treeline, with most records above 2,500 m and occasional birds as low as roughly 1,850 m. It favors montane oak forest, mossy cloud forest, forest edges, clearings, nearby secondary growth, and highland gardens.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally a resident, non-migratory species in Costa Rica. Some individuals may make local or seasonal movements to lower elevations or between flowering areas, but there is no known regular long-distance migration.
profile.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding activity is reported mainly from November through March. The nest is a small cup made from plant fibers and other fine materials, often decorated with moss and lichens. It is typically placed on a dangling stem, such as bamboo, above the ground. Detailed information on incubation and nesting success remains limited, but young remain in the nest for at least about 25 days after hatching.
profile.dietFeeding: The Talamanca Hummingbird feeds chiefly on nectar from a variety of flowering plants in montane forests and adjacent gardens. Males commonly defend productive flower patches, especially in the lower forest levels, while females often forage by trap-lining along repeated routes between flowering plants. It may also take small arthropods, although its insect-feeding behavior is less well documented than its nectar feeding.
profile.behavior: Males are territorial around favored flower patches and may chase other hummingbirds during disputes. The species forages in forest understory, edges, clearings, and sometimes the canopy. It is often attracted to hummingbird feeders in Costa Rican mountain lodges and gardens. Its flight is powerful and direct, and its large size makes it distinctive among the hummingbirds of the Talamancan highlands.

conservation.populationTrend: The population size is not well known, but the overall trend is considered stable and the species remains fairly common in suitable high-elevation habitat.

profile.overview: The Long-billed Starthroat (Heliomaster longirostris) is a medium-sized hummingbird of tropical forests, woodland edges, gardens, and other partly open habitats. It is named for its unusually long, straight bill and the male’s brilliant, star-like throat patch. The species ranges from Costa Rica and Panama through much of northern and central South America, with an additional population on Trinidad. It often perches conspicuously and makes rapid visits to flowers, especially in sunny clearings and forest margins.
profile.classification: The Long-billed Starthroat belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the genus Heliomaster. It is one of the starthroats, a group of relatively large hummingbirds associated with the mountain-gem lineage.
profile.identification: This hummingbird has a long, mostly straight black bill, green upperparts, and a noticeable white mark behind the eye. Adult males show a dark face and a brilliant iridescent throat patch that can appear reddish, purplish, or bluish depending on the light, often bordered by pale feathers. The underparts are generally pale gray or whitish. Females and immature birds are duller, with less vivid throat coloration. Its long bill and relatively sturdy body help separate it from many smaller Costa Rican hummingbirds.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Long-billed Starthroat occurs from Costa Rica and Panama south through Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, the Guianas, Brazil, and Trinidad. In Costa Rica it is a localized species rather than a uniformly common hummingbird, occurring mainly in the eastern and southwestern parts of the country, including lowland and foothill regions. It uses humid forest edges, clearings, second growth, plantations, gardens, river margins, and flowering trees or shrubs. It may also enter more open agricultural landscapes where suitable nectar plants and perches remain.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally considered resident or locally sedentary across its range. In Costa Rica, it is present year-round in suitable areas, although local movements and changes in detectability may occur as flowering conditions change. It is not regarded as a regular long-distance migrant in the country.
profile.breeding: The female builds a small cup-shaped nest, usually from plant fibers, spider silk, and other fine materials, placed on a slender branch or other sheltered support. She normally incubates the eggs and feeds the nestlings without assistance from the male. As in other hummingbirds, the young hatch helpless and remain in the nest until sufficiently developed for short flights. Detailed information on nesting dates and breeding density varies among regions, and Costa Rican breeding records are more localized than the species’ broad continental range.
profile.dietFeeding: The Long-billed Starthroat feeds mainly on nectar from flowering trees, shrubs, vines, and herbs. Its long bill allows it to exploit flowers with deep corollas, though it also visits a variety of accessible blossoms. It supplements nectar with small insects and other arthropods, which provide protein and other nutrients. Individuals may trap insects in flight, glean them from vegetation, or defend productive flowering patches and favored perches.
profile.behavior: This species often perches quietly in exposed positions while watching for feeding opportunities or intruders. It can be territorial around rich flower patches and may make rapid chases against other hummingbirds. Its flight is fast and highly maneuverable, with hovering at flowers followed by direct movements to nearby perches. The bright male throat patch is most striking when viewed at the correct angle to the light. Activity is usually greatest during daylight, especially when flowers are abundant.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly established. Available information does not currently indicate that the species meets the criteria for a threatened category.

profile.overview: The Plain-capped Starthroat is a large hummingbird of dry forests, woodland edges, thorn scrub, and other open habitats in Mexico and Central America. Its plumage is mostly green, gray, and brown, and the male has a small reddish or rose-colored throat patch that can be difficult to see. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon species associated mainly with the drier northwestern Pacific region, although records also occur elsewhere.
profile.classification: The Plain-capped Starthroat belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the genus Heliomaster. It is one of the mountain-gem hummingbirds and is sometimes placed with the starthroats as a distinct group.
profile.identification: This is a relatively large hummingbird, about 10–15 cm long, with a long, straight bill, a dull green back, and pale grayish or buff underparts. A broad white whisker stripe and a white patch near the rump or wing base are useful field marks. Adult males have a reddish throat center bordered by darker feathers, but the color may be inconspicuous in poor light. Females and immature birds are duller and lack a strongly visible gorget.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from western and southern Mexico through Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and into northwestern Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is most reliably associated with dry forest, scrub, woodland edges, open hillsides, gardens, and flowering trees, especially in Guanacaste and adjacent northwestern areas. It is generally found at low elevations, although occasional records have come from higher sites and from other provinces, indicating some dispersal beyond its usual Costa Rican range.
profile.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Plain-capped Starthroat is best treated as a resident or irregular seasonal species rather than a regular long-distance migrant. Local movements may follow flowering and rainfall, and the species appears to be more regularly encountered in the dry northwest. Records elsewhere in Costa Rica may represent dispersal, seasonal movements, or occasional wandering; the extent of migration remains poorly documented.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited. In Costa Rica, nesting has been reported or inferred mainly from October through January, during part of the seasonal transition into the dry season. The nest is a small, shallow cup made from plant fibers and soft down, often decorated with lichens and placed on a slender branch. As with other hummingbirds, the female is expected to handle incubation and chick rearing, while the male does not provide parental care.
profile.dietFeeding: The Plain-capped Starthroat feeds primarily on nectar from flowering trees, shrubs, vines, and other plants, especially in open or seasonally dry habitats. Its long bill allows it to use tubular flowers. It also captures small insects and other arthropods, either by short aerial sallies or while moving among vegetation. It may defend productive flowers or feeding areas from other hummingbirds and is often seen hovering briefly before perching.
profile.behavior: This hummingbird usually forages in open woodland, forest edges, scrub, and clearings rather than in dense forest interiors. It often perches conspicuously on exposed twigs and makes rapid, direct flights between feeding sites. Displays and chases can occur around flowers or territories. The species is generally quiet or gives sharp chips and high, thin calls, and its subdued plumage can make it easy to overlook despite its fairly large size.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is believed to be declining, but the decline is not currently considered severe enough to place the species in a threatened IUCN category.

profile.overview: The Fiery-throated Hummingbird is a medium-sized, brilliantly colored hummingbird of the high mountains of Costa Rica and western Panama. Its plumage can show glowing copper, orange, green, blue, and violet tones as the bird changes position in the light. It is especially associated with cool, humid cloud forests and other high-elevation habitats. The species is a characteristic hummingbird of Costa Rica’s Central and Talamanca cordilleras, where it may be seen at flowering plants, forest edges, clearings, and feeders.
profile.classification: The Fiery-throated Hummingbird belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the order Apodiformes. It is the only species in the genus Panterpe.
profile.identification: This hummingbird has a mostly green body, a dark bluish tail, and a highly iridescent head, throat, and upper breast. Depending on the angle of light, the throat may appear fiery orange, copper, gold, green, blue, or violet. The crown and face often show deep blue or purplish tones. Its bill is straight and of moderate length. Males and females are generally similar, although females may appear somewhat less intensely colored. The species is often conspicuous when perched on exposed branches between feeding flights.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Fiery-throated Hummingbird is found in Costa Rica and western Panama. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly along the Cordillera de Tilarán, the Central Volcanic Cordillera, and the Talamanca Mountains, including highland areas near volcanoes such as Poás and Irazú and forests around Cerro de la Muerte. It inhabits montane evergreen forest, cloud forest, elfin forest, forest edges, secondary growth, tree-rich pasture, and the lower edges of páramo. It is most often associated with elevations from roughly 1,500 meters to the high mountain zone, with local variation.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally resident in Costa Rica rather than a long-distance migrant. Individuals may make local or seasonal altitudinal movements, descending to somewhat lower elevations when flowering patterns, weather, or food availability change.
profile.breeding: Breeding occurs in the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama, with timing varying by locality and conditions. The female builds a small cup-shaped nest using plant fibers, moss, lichens, and spider silk, usually placing it in sheltered vegetation. She is responsible for incubation and care of the young. As in other hummingbirds, the nest is carefully camouflaged and the young are fed with regurgitated nectar and small animal prey. Detailed information on nesting sites and seasonal timing is incomplete across the species’ range.
profile.dietFeeding: The Fiery-throated Hummingbird feeds mainly on nectar from flowering plants in montane forests, forest margins, shrublands, and highland gardens. It visits a variety of tubular flowers and may defend productive feeding areas from other hummingbirds. It also captures small insects and spiders, particularly when feeding young or when additional protein is needed. In Costa Rica, it readily visits hummingbird feeders in suitable high-elevation habitats, although natural flowering plants remain important to its diet.
profile.behavior: This species is active and fast-flying, moving frequently between flowers and lookout perches. It commonly pauses on exposed twigs or branches, where its iridescent throat and crown flash brightly in the light. Individuals can be territorial around rich nectar sources and may chase other hummingbirds. Most activity occurs in the forest canopy, along edges, and in clearings, but birds may forage lower in shrubs. Local abundance can change noticeably with elevation and the seasonal availability of flowers.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not known to be declining at a rate that places the species in a threatened category; available assessments generally treat its population as stable or without a clearly established negative trend.

profile.overview: The White-bellied Mountain-gem is a medium-sized hummingbird of the humid mountain forests of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is named for the male’s mostly white underparts, which contrast with a dark green back and a violet-purple throat patch. This localized Central American species usually occupies cool, wet forest rather than open countryside. In Costa Rica, it is a resident bird of several major mountain ranges and is one of the characteristic hummingbirds of the Caribbean-facing highlands.
profile.classification: The White-bellied Mountain-gem belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae. It is traditionally placed in the genus Lampornis, although some taxonomic treatments have proposed the separate genus Prodosia because of its distinct evolutionary history.
profile.identification: Adults have dark green upperparts, a white postocular stripe, and predominantly white underparts with green spotting or shading along the flanks. The male has a purple to violet gorget that can appear dark or subdued depending on the light. Females lack the showy throat patch and are generally duller below. The tail is moderately forked, and the bill is straight and adapted for feeding at tubular flowers. Its relatively low-elevation range helps distinguish it from several other Costa Rican mountain-gems.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from north-central Costa Rica through the Caribbean slope into western Panama, reaching the Veraguas region. In Costa Rica it is recorded mainly in the Tilarán, Central, and Talamanca cordilleras, including humid foothill and montane forests on the Caribbean side. It inhabits cool, very wet subtropical evergreen forest, especially the canopy, edges, gaps, and flowering clearings. It generally avoids heavily altered open areas and is less associated with extensive secondary vegetation than some other hummingbirds.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered resident in Costa Rica, but it makes local elevational movements. Birds commonly breed at about 700–1,400 meters and may descend after breeding to roughly 400–1,000 meters, probably following food availability and flowering patterns. It does not undertake long-distance migration.
profile.breeding: Breeding has been documented in the Costa Rican mountains, particularly in humid forest between approximately 700 and 1,400 meters. As in related mountain-gems, the female is responsible for nest construction, incubation, and care of the young. The small cup nest is typically attached to vegetation and built from soft plant fibers, moss, and other materials, often with external camouflage. Detailed information on clutch size, incubation, and nestling periods is limited compared with that available for better-studied hummingbirds.
profile.dietFeeding: The White-bellied Mountain-gem feeds mainly on nectar from flowering trees, shrubs, vines, and epiphytes. It is especially associated with flowers of Ericaceae and Columnea, among other tubular-flowered plants. It supplements nectar with small insects and other arthropods, which provide protein. The bird forages at several levels of the forest, including the canopy and forest edges, and may defend productive flowers or feeding areas from other hummingbirds.
profile.behavior: This hummingbird is usually active and watchful, moving through forest in regular feeding circuits as flowers become available. Males may defend flowering territories and display the violet gorget during confrontations or courtship. It often perches quietly between feeding bouts, making detection easier by call than by sight in dense vegetation. Its movements between breeding elevations and lower post-breeding areas indicate a flexible response to seasonal changes in flowering and local conditions.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly quantified, but the species is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Purple-throated Mountain-gem is a medium-sized hummingbird of Central American highlands. Males have metallic green upperparts, a blue crown, bold white facial stripes, and a brilliant purple throat. Females are less colorful, with a pale or buffy throat and similar facial markings. This forest-associated species commonly visits flowering shrubs along cloud-forest edges, clearings, secondary growth, and highland gardens. It is distributed from southern Nicaragua through Costa Rica to western Panama.
profile.classification: The Purple-throated Mountain-gem belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the genus Lampornis, known as the mountain-gems. Three subspecies are generally recognized, including forms occurring in northern, central, and southern Costa Rica.
profile.identification: Adults are about 10–11.5 cm long. The male is recognized by his glittering purple gorget, blue crown, green back, and strong white stripe behind the eye, combined with a dark tail. The female lacks the vivid purple throat and usually shows a paler, buffy throat and less contrasting head pattern. In Costa Rica, careful comparison may be needed with other mountain-gems, especially females, which can have overlapping patterns and habitats.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Nicaragua through the mountains of Costa Rica to western Panama. In Costa Rica it occurs chiefly in the Cordillera de Guanacaste, Cordillera Central, and northern and central Cordillera de Talamanca, with additional southern populations associated with the form homogenes. It inhabits humid montane evergreen forest and cloud forest, especially steep or broken terrain, forest edges, clearings, secondary vegetation, and flowering gardens. It is usually found from about 800 to 2,500 m, locally lower in northern areas.
profile.migrationStatus: It is primarily resident in Costa Rica, but individuals may make local elevational movements. After breeding, some descend from higher forests to lower elevations, occasionally reaching about 300 m where suitable flowering habitat is available.
profile.breeding: Breeding is associated mainly with the rainy season and has been reported from approximately October through April. The female builds a small, deep cup nest from plant down and other fine materials, often with moss or external fibers that help camouflage it. She alone incubates the eggs and cares for the young. As in other hummingbirds, the male does not provide parental care and instead defends feeding territories or display areas.
profile.dietFeeding: Nectar forms most of the diet and is taken from a wide range of tubular flowers in forest understory, edges, clearings, and gardens. The species is an important pollinator of some flowering plants, including Psychotria elata and Palicourea lasiorrachis. It also captures small insects and other arthropods. Males often hawk insects from exposed perches, while females commonly glean prey from foliage during hovering flights.
profile.behavior: Males are strongly territorial around productive flower patches and may chase hummingbirds of either sex, including rivals of their own species. Females are generally less territorial and often follow trap-lines, visiting a sequence of flowering plants. The species is active and agile, typically feeding in shaded vegetation, forest gaps, and edges. Its movements are influenced by flowering conditions and elevation rather than by long-distance seasonal migration.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered decreasing, although it remains relatively widespread and is estimated at roughly 50,000–499,999 mature individuals.

profile.overview: The White-throated Mountain-gem is a small hummingbird of Central American highlands. It is associated mainly with humid montane forests, especially oak woodland, forest edges, and shrubby clearings. Males have a white throat and bright green upperparts, while females are more subdued and have rufous underparts. The species is resident rather than a long-distance migrant. Taxonomic treatments vary, and some populations in southern Costa Rica have been treated as the Gray-tailed Mountain-gem, Lampornis cinereicauda.
profile.classification: The White-throated Mountain-gem belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the genus Lampornis. It is sometimes included in a broader mountain-gem species complex because of close similarities with related forms.
profile.identification: This hummingbird is about 12 cm long and has a straight, medium-length black bill. Adult males show dark bronzy-green upperparts, an emerald-green crown, a white chin and throat, bright green sides of the neck and upper breast, and a dark gray lower breast and belly. Females have green upperparts, a darker rufous throat and belly, and paler outer tail feathers. The white throat and highland habitat help distinguish the male from other mountain-gems.
profile.rangeHabitat: The White-throated Mountain-gem occurs in the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama. In Costa Rica, it is reported as a resident of montane oak forests, especially in the Cordillera de Talamanca and adjacent south-central highlands, extending southward toward Panama. It uses forest interiors, edges, secondary growth, shrubby clearings, and sometimes gardens near woodland. Records and taxonomic treatments differ in southern Costa Rica, where some birds have been assigned to the Gray-tailed Mountain-gem. It generally occupies elevations from about 1,500 m to timberline.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally considered a year-round resident in Costa Rica and elsewhere in its range. Local movements may occur with flowering conditions or elevation, but regular long-distance migration is not known.
profile.breeding: Breeding has been reported mainly from October through April. The female builds a small cup-shaped nest from fine plant fibers, with moss and sometimes lichen attached to the outside. Nests are placed in vegetation in montane forest or nearby shrubby habitat. Available information on clutch details, incubation duration, and nestling development is limited, and the male is not known to provide parental care.
profile.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on nectar from a variety of flowering plants and is an important pollinator of highland vegetation. Males often defend flower patches in the forest interior, while females may forage more frequently in shrubby areas and along edges. It also captures or gleans small arthropods from foliage, which provide essential protein, especially during breeding and when feeding young.
profile.behavior: White-throated Mountain-gems are active during daylight and usually forage alone. Males are territorial and can dominate smaller hummingbirds at rich flower sources, although larger hummingbirds may displace them. The species commonly moves rapidly between flowers, perches in shaded vegetation, and gives sharp, high-pitched calls. Its preference for forest edges and clearings allows it to use both relatively undisturbed woodland and suitable human-modified highland habitats.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population size and population trend are not well quantified.

profile.overview: The Magenta-throated Woodstar (Philodice bryantae) is a very small hummingbird restricted mainly to the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is associated with humid montane landscapes but also uses forest edges, clearings, second growth, gardens, and other semi-open habitats with abundant flowers. The male is named for his brilliant magenta throat, while both sexes have a compact, bee-like appearance and distinctive tail posture. Costa Rica contains most of the species’ known range.
profile.classification: The Magenta-throated Woodstar belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the bee-hummingbird group, Mellisugini. It is currently placed in the genus Philodice and is considered a monotypic species.
profile.identification: This tiny hummingbird is about 7–8 cm long. The adult male has a striking iridescent magenta throat, green upperparts, pale underparts, and a relatively long, deeply forked tail that is often held cocked while feeding. The female lacks the bright throat and is mainly green above with pale underparts and subtle facial markings. Its rapid wingbeats, hovering flight, small size, and habit of perching in shrubs help distinguish it from larger Costa Rican hummingbirds.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species has a restricted range in the Talamancan highlands of Costa Rica and adjacent western Panama, especially Chiriquí. In Costa Rica it occurs in the Central and Talamanca mountain ranges, including well-known highland areas such as Monteverde and other elevated sites in the provinces of Puntarenas, San José, Cartago, Heredia, and Alajuela. It uses humid montane forest edges, clearings, shrubby pastures, gardens, shaded coffee landscapes, secondary growth, and flowering areas, generally from about 800 to 3,000 meters.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally regarded as resident rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, individuals may make seasonal altitudinal movements, occupying higher elevations during the breeding period and using somewhat lower mountain habitats at other times of year.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited. In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported mainly from November through March or April, although timing may vary with elevation, rainfall, and flowering conditions. Males perform diving display flights, sometimes alone or in loose groups. The nest, incubation period, and fledging period have not been reliably described in detail, and the female is believed to be responsible for most or all nesting duties, as in many hummingbirds.
profile.dietFeeding: The Magenta-throated Woodstar feeds primarily on nectar from flowering shrubs, herbs, and trees. It visits both native flowering plants and cultivated gardens, and may defend productive feeding areas. It also takes small arthropods, capturing them by short aerial sallies from exposed perches or by gleaning insects from foliage. Its small size and hovering ability allow it to exploit flowers that may be inaccessible to larger hummingbirds.
profile.behavior: This active hummingbird usually forages at forest edges, clearings, gardens, and flowering shrubs, moving rapidly between feeding sites. Males may display by diving and may open or spread the tail during aggressive encounters or courtship. Individuals can be territorial around rich flower patches and may chase other hummingbirds. The species often perches quietly between feeding bouts, making its distinctive magenta throat and tail posture useful field marks when viewed at close range.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered decreasing, although the decline is not currently judged severe enough to qualify the species as threatened under the global assessment.
conservation.threats: The principal concern is loss and fragmentation of high-elevation habitat through deforestation, agricultural expansion, intensive farming, and development. Degradation of flowering forest edges and other semi-open montane habitats may reduce feeding and breeding opportunities, particularly outside protected areas.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore montane forest, forest edges, and flowering corridors in Costa Rica and western Panama. Maintaining shade-grown farms, planting native nectar-producing vegetation, reducing pesticide use, and supporting protected mountain reserves can help preserve food resources and habitat. Birdwatchers should keep a respectful distance from displaying or nesting birds and report well-documented observations to national monitoring programs.

profile.overview: The Ruby-throated Hummingbird is a small, fast-flying hummingbird best known for the adult male’s brilliant ruby-red throat. It breeds across much of eastern North America and southern Canada, then migrates south for the nonbreeding season. The species is an important pollinator and feeds on flower nectar, small insects, and spiders. In Costa Rica, it is a seasonal visitor rather than a resident breeding hummingbird, and it shares the country with many native tropical hummingbird species.
profile.classification: The Ruby-throated Hummingbird belongs to the order Apodiformes and family Trochilidae. Its scientific name is Archilochus colubris.
profile.identification: This hummingbird is about 7.5–9 centimeters long, with a long, straight bill and rapidly beating wings. Adults have metallic green upperparts and pale gray-white underparts. The adult male has a vivid red, iridescent throat bordered by dark feathers, while the female lacks the red throat and usually shows a pale throat and outer tail feathers with white tips. Immature birds resemble females, although young males may develop scattered red throat feathers. Its hovering flight, sudden darts, and high-pitched calls are distinctive.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Ruby-throated Hummingbird breeds throughout much of the eastern United States and southern Canada. During the nonbreeding season it occurs from Mexico through Central America, including Costa Rica, where it is present mainly from about October through March. In Costa Rica it uses forest edges, clearings, gardens, plantations, second-growth vegetation, scrub, and other open habitats with flowering plants. It is not known as a regular breeding species in Costa Rica and is generally encountered as a migrant or wintering visitor.
profile.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Most individuals leave eastern North America in late summer and autumn and spend the nonbreeding season in Mexico and Central America. In Costa Rica, it is primarily a wintering migrant, with records concentrated roughly between October and March; some birds may also pass through during migration.
profile.breeding: Breeding takes place in eastern North America and southern Canada, not normally in Costa Rica. The female usually builds a tiny, flexible cup-shaped nest on a slender horizontal branch, often using plant fibers, down, spider silk, and lichens for camouflage. She commonly lays two small white eggs and raises the young alone. Nest sites occur in woodland edges, open forests, orchards, parks, gardens, and other habitats where shelter and flowering plants are available.
profile.dietFeeding: Ruby-throated Hummingbirds obtain energy mainly from nectar, especially from tubular or brightly colored flowers. They also capture small insects and spiders, which provide protein and other nutrients, particularly during the breeding season. They feed while hovering and may defend rich flower patches or feeders from other hummingbirds. In Costa Rica, they use both native flowering plants and cultivated or disturbed habitats that retain a dependable supply of nectar and small arthropods.
profile.behavior: This species is highly active and territorial, often making rapid chases, dives, and short flights between perches and feeding sites. It can hover precisely, fly backward, and briefly perch on exposed twigs while scanning its surroundings. Males generally defend feeding territories, whereas females spend more time searching for food and caring for young. During migration and winter in Costa Rica, individuals may occur singly or in low numbers among flowering vegetation and forest edges.

conservation.populationTrend: Generally stable to increasing or relatively stable in available long-term assessments, although trends can vary among regions and monitoring programs.

profile.overview: The Volcano Hummingbird (Selasphorus flammula) is a tiny hummingbird of the highest mountains of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is especially associated with páramo, stunted high-elevation woodland, shrublands, and open areas near the tree line. Males show striking regional variation in throat color, while females are mostly green above and pale below with a spotted or lightly marked throat. The species is well adapted to cool, windy mountain environments.
profile.classification: The Volcano Hummingbird belongs to the hummingbird family Trochilidae and the genus Selasphorus. Three geographically separated subspecies are commonly recognized: flammula, simoni, and torridus.
profile.identification: This is a very small, compact hummingbird with a short, straight bill, green upperparts, and a dark, somewhat forked tail. Adult males have a glittering gorget whose color varies among mountain ranges, including reddish, pinkish, purplish, or grayish tones. Females and immature birds lack the bold male throat and show pale underparts with dusky spotting. Its tiny size and high-elevation range help distinguish it from larger mountain hummingbirds, although it can resemble the related Scintillant Hummingbird.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Volcano Hummingbird occurs in Costa Rica and extends into extreme western Panama around Volcán Barú. In Costa Rica it is a characteristic resident of the Cordillera Volcánica Central, including the high mountains around Poás, Barva, Irazú, and Turrialba, and of the Cordillera de Talamanca, including high peaks such as Cerro de la Muerte and Chirripó. It uses páramo, subpáramo, elfin and dwarf woodland, shrubby clearings, forest edges, landslide openings, volcanic disturbance areas, and high-elevation gardens.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally resident in Costa Rica rather than a long-distance migrant. Individuals make local or seasonal altitudinal movements, sometimes descending from the highest páramo and exposed mountain slopes to lower montane edges during unfavorable weather or outside the breeding season.
profile.breeding: Breeding has been reported mainly during the wetter part of the year, with timing varying among mountain regions. The female builds a very small cup-shaped nest from plant fibers, down, moss, lichen, and spider web, usually placed on a shrub or small tree and often sheltered by overhanging vegetation. She incubates the eggs and raises the young alone. Nest placement may occur along forest edges, steep slopes, trails, or shrubby highland clearings.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of nectar from small high-elevation flowers, supplemented by tiny insects and other arthropods. It forages by hovering at flowers and may also take insects in short aerial sallies. In Costa Rica it visits flowering shrubs and plants in páramo, montane scrub, forest edges, disturbed clearings, and suitable gardens. Its ability to use scattered flowers is important in the open, windy habitats of the upper mountains.
profile.behavior: Volcano Hummingbirds are active and quick, often moving rapidly between flowers and perches. They are commonly seen alone and may defend productive flower patches from other hummingbirds. Males perform brief displays and aerial chases, especially around feeding areas or during courtship. Birds often perch on exposed twigs or low shrubs, where their small size and subdued female plumage can make them difficult to detect despite their bright, flashing gorgets.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered stable.

profile.overview: The Scintillant Hummingbird (Selasphorus scintilla) is a very small hummingbird of the mountain ranges of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is named for the male’s brilliant orange-red throat, which can flash brightly in sunlight. This active species commonly uses forest edges, shrubby clearings, coffee plantations, gardens, and other partly open habitats. It is especially characteristic of middle-elevation landscapes and is among the smallest hummingbirds regularly seen in Costa Rica.
profile.classification: The Scintillant Hummingbird belongs to the order Apodiformes and the hummingbird family Trochilidae. It is one of the small, strongly territorial hummingbirds in the genus Selasphorus.
profile.identification: This hummingbird is about 6.5 centimeters long, with a short, straight, black bill and a small, slightly cocked tail. Adult males have bronzy green upperparts, a rufous tail, and a vivid orange-red or coppery gorget bordered below by a pale band. Females lack the bright throat and show a pale, lightly spotted throat, greener upperparts, and rufous tones on the flanks and tail. Immature birds resemble females but may show rusty feather edges.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs in Costa Rica and western Panama, principally along the Cordillera de Tilarán, the Central Volcanic Cordillera, and the Talamanca range. In Costa Rica it is a resident, locally uncommon to common bird of the Pacific-facing highlands, with some records on the Caribbean side near Cartago and the upper Reventazón Valley. It usually occupies elevations from about 900 to 2,100 meters, using forest edges, second growth, brushy clearings, coffee farms, rural gardens, and open woodland. Occasional records occur lower, and nonbreeding birds may reach roughly 2,450 meters.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally resident in Costa Rica rather than a long-distance migrant, but it makes seasonal elevational movements. After breeding, some individuals move uphill, while others may descend to lower elevations; movements can vary with flowering and food availability.
profile.breeding: Breeding in Costa Rica is reported mainly from September through February, although timing may vary locally. The female builds the small cup nest, usually placing it low, often about one to four meters above the ground on an outer branch, grass clump, or shrub beside an open area.
