conservation.populationTrend: The overall short-term trend is uncertain to relatively stable, but the species has experienced substantial historical declines because introduced predators reduced or eliminated colonies on some breeding islands. Some populations have benefited from predator removal and habitat protection.
conservation.threats: Important threats include introduced rats, cats, and other predators at breeding colonies; disturbance or degradation of nesting islands; oil spills in marine areas; and possible effects from plastic pollution and changes in ocean conditions that reduce prey availability. Because breeding colonies are concentrated on islands, localized disasters can affect many birds.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect offshore breeding islands and remove or prevent invasive predators. Reduce the risk of oil pollution, keep plastics and fishing waste out of the ocean, and support responsible marine transportation and fisheries practices. Coastal observers and boat operators can contribute useful records by documenting offshore sightings with accurate locations and dates, especially in Costa Rican Pacific waters.

profile.overview: Markham’s Storm-Petrel (Hydrobates markhami) is a dark, ocean-going seabird of the eastern Pacific. It spends most of its life at sea and comes ashore mainly to breed in desert regions of coastal Peru and northern Chile. The species is poorly known because it is difficult to observe away from colonies and is usually active around breeding sites at night. In Costa Rica, it is a scarce pelagic migrant recorded over Pacific waters, including around Isla del Coco.
profile.classification: It belongs to the storm-petrel family Hydrobatidae and the order Procellariiformes. The accepted scientific name is Hydrobates markhami; older literature may use Oceanodroma markhami.
profile.identification: This is a medium-sized, slender storm-petrel with almost entirely dark brown to blackish plumage. A pale gray or whitish diagonal bar across the upper wing is often visible in good views. The rump may appear slightly paler, and the tail is slightly forked. It flies with rapid wingbeats interspersed with glides, often close to the sea surface. Identification at sea can be difficult, especially where it overlaps with Black and other dark storm-petrels.
profile.rangeHabitat: Markham’s Storm-Petrel breeds in arid coastal areas of Peru and northern Chile, where it nests in natural cavities, rock crevices, and sheltered spaces in desert terrain. Outside the breeding season it occupies open tropical and subtropical Pacific waters, often far from land. In Costa Rica it is not a resident coastal or terrestrial bird; it occurs as a marine migrant over the Pacific, with documented records from offshore waters and the Isla del Coco region. It is most likely to be encountered during pelagic surveys or boat trips.
profile.migrationStatus: Migratory. After breeding in the deserts of Peru and Chile, individuals disperse through the eastern Pacific. Costa Rica is a nonbreeding passage and marine-use area, with records from Pacific waters and around Isla del Coco rather than from the mainland interior.
profile.breeding: Breeding colonies are located in extremely dry coastal desert landscapes, especially in northern Chile and Peru. The species nests in cracks, crevices, and other protected cavities, generally returning to colonies at night. It lays a single egg, as is typical of many procellariiform seabirds, and both adults contribute to incubation and chick care. Breeding colonies can be difficult to detect because birds spend daylight hours at sea and visit nesting sites mainly after dark.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet is believed to consist mainly of small marine organisms, including planktonic crustaceans, small fish, and cephalopods, with other soft-bodied prey taken opportunistically. It forages from the sea surface and may pick prey from the water while fluttering or gliding. Like other storm-petrels, it can concentrate around productive ocean fronts, upwelling areas, floating organic matter, and feeding seabird groups.
profile.behavior: Markham’s Storm-Petrel is highly pelagic and normally avoids land outside the breeding season. Its flight is light and fluttering, with frequent glides and banking close to the water. It is generally solitary or occurs in small groups, although larger concentrations may form where food is abundant. Adults return to colonies after dark, which reduces exposure to many daytime predators. The species is often under-recorded because of its remote habitat and resemblance to other dark storm-petrels.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining. Available estimates and monitoring remain limited, so the exact rate and geographic pattern of decline are uncertain.
conservation.threats: Important threats include introduced predators and disturbance at breeding colonies, artificial lighting that can disorient fledglings, habitat degradation in coastal desert nesting areas, and mortality associated with fishing operations. Marine pollution, plastic ingestion, oil contamination, and changes in ocean productivity may add further pressure. Because Costa Rica supports migrants at sea, local risks may include accidental capture, pollution, and disturbance from intensive offshore activities.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and monitor breeding colonies in Peru and Chile, prevent the introduction of rats and other predators, and reduce artificial lighting near nesting areas. Improve monitoring of pelagic seabirds in Costa Rican Pacific waters, including around Isla del Coco, and promote fishing practices that reduce seabird bycatch. Reducing plastic and oil pollution, safeguarding marine protected areas, and reporting well-documented sightings can also support conservation and improve knowledge of this poorly studied species.

profile.overview: The Least Storm-Petrel is a tiny ocean-going seabird and one of the smallest members of the storm-petrel group. It breeds on rocky islands off western Mexico and spends most of its life far from land. With rapid wingbeats, dark plumage, and a low, fluttering flight over waves, it can be difficult to detect. Outside the breeding season, it moves through the tropical and subtropical eastern Pacific, including offshore waters near Central America and Costa Rica.
profile.classification: The Least Storm-Petrel belongs to the order Procellariiformes and family Hydrobatidae. Its accepted scientific name is Hydrobates microsoma; older literature may use Oceanodroma microsoma or Halocyptena microsoma.
profile.identification: This is a very small, mostly black or dark brown storm-petrel, about 13–15 cm long with a wingspan near 32 cm. It has relatively short, rounded or wedge-shaped wings and a short, wedge-shaped tail. The flight is fast, fluttering, and low over the sea, often giving the bird a bat-like appearance. Its small size helps distinguish it from larger dark storm-petrels, although identification at sea can be difficult in poor light or rough conditions.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Least Storm-Petrel breeds on rocky islands off the Baja California Peninsula and in the Gulf of California, Mexico. Away from colonies it is strictly marine, using warm offshore waters, especially the eastern tropical and subtropical Pacific. In Costa Rica it occurs as an uncommon migrant or non-breeding visitor, mainly offshore rather than over land. Records include Pacific waters associated with Costa Rica and surveys around Cocos Island, so it is most likely to be encountered during pelagic trips or offshore research.
profile.migrationStatus: Migratory. After breeding in western Mexico, it disperses south through the eastern Pacific; in Costa Rica it is an uncommon offshore migrant and non-breeding visitor, with sightings apparently concentrated in marine waters rather than along the mainland coast.
profile.breeding: Breeding colonies are located on remote rocky islands off western Mexico. Pairs nest in rock crevices, among boulder piles, or in other protected cavities, generally without constructing a substantial nest. The species lays one white egg, and both adults are believed to share incubation and chick-rearing. Adults visit colonies mainly at night, when they are less exposed to predators. Breeding information remains less detailed than for many other seabirds, partly because colonies are remote and activity is nocturnal.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet is not well documented but appears to consist mainly of zooplankton and other very small marine organisms, including tiny crustaceans. Larval spiny lobsters have also been reported as food. The Least Storm-Petrel usually feeds by fluttering low over the water and picking prey from the surface, rather than diving deeply. It may associate with other seabirds where plankton or other prey become concentrated.
profile.behavior: This storm-petrel spends most of its time at sea and is an agile, low-flying bird. Its rapid, deep wingbeats and erratic movements help it maneuver close to wave surfaces. It usually rests and feeds far offshore, making it difficult to observe from land. Like other storm-petrels, it is strongly tied to darkness at breeding colonies, where adults enter crevices and communicate with soft whirring, twittering, or squeaking calls.

conservation.populationTrend: Probably stable overall, although monitoring is limited and population estimates and long-term trend data are uncertain.

profile.overview: The Galápagos Petrel (Pterodroma phaeopygia), also called the Dark-rumped Petrel, is a large gadfly petrel endemic as a breeding bird to the Galápagos Archipelago of Ecuador. It spends most of its life over the eastern tropical Pacific, flying far offshore in search of prey. The species nests in burrows on forested and shrub-covered volcanic slopes and is notable for its swift, twisting flight and nocturnal visits to breeding colonies.
profile.classification: The Galápagos Petrel belongs to the order Procellariiformes and family Procellariidae, which include petrels, shearwaters, and fulmars. Its scientific name is Pterodroma phaeopygia.
profile.identification: This medium-large petrel has long, narrow wings, a strongly contrasting pattern, and a dark or gray-brown upper surface. The head is usually dark-capped, while the face and underparts are largely white. Dark markings form a broad border along the wings, and the rump and tail are dark, giving the species its alternative name, Dark-rumped Petrel. In flight it appears slim and agile, using rapid wingbeats followed by long glides and twisting turns close to the sea surface.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Galápagos Petrel breeds only in the Galápagos Islands, where colonies occur on humid, elevated volcanic slopes of islands including Santa Cruz, San Cristóbal, Santiago, Isabela, and Floreana. It nests in dense upland vegetation, volcanic soil, natural cavities, or burrows. At sea it forages mainly around the archipelago and may range widely through the eastern tropical Pacific. In Costa Rica it is not a regular coastal bird; it has been documented only rarely in offshore waters, including the pelagic zone around Cocos Island and other waters far from the mainland.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally considered a resident breeding species of the Galápagos rather than a long-distance migrant. Individuals make extensive feeding movements over the Pacific, and rare nonbreeding or wandering birds reach Central American waters. In Costa Rica, records are exceptional and are associated with offshore pelagic areas, especially around Cocos Island, rather than with the mainland coast.
profile.breeding: Breeding takes place in colonies on humid upper slopes, where pairs use deep burrows or natural cavities protected by dense vegetation. Adults are mainly active around the colony at night, which reduces exposure to predators. The species normally lays a single egg, and both parents share incubation and care of the chick. Young birds remain in the burrow until well developed and then leave for the sea. Breeding success is strongly affected by introduced predators and degradation of nesting habitat.
profile.dietFeeding: The Galápagos Petrel feeds chiefly on squid, small fish, and crustaceans, which it captures at or near the ocean surface. It is an oceanic forager that may travel considerable distances from breeding islands while searching for productive waters. Like other gadfly petrels, it can use dynamic soaring and fast, low flight to cover large areas efficiently. Feeding usually occurs far offshore, making direct observation difficult, including in Costa Rican waters.
profile.behavior: This species is highly pelagic and spends most of its time alone or in small groups over open ocean. Its flight is fast, buoyant, and erratic, with alternating wingbeats, glides, and sharp changes in direction. Adults return to colonies mainly after dark and use distinctive calls around nesting areas. Outside the breeding season, birds disperse widely across the eastern tropical Pacific, but their movements remain poorly documented because they spend little time near land.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is declining. Historical losses and continuing reproductive problems have caused major reductions at some breeding colonies, although conservation work has improved monitoring and habitat protection in parts of the archipelago.
conservation.threats: The main threats are introduced black rats, feral pigs, cats, dogs, and other mammals that prey on eggs, chicks, and adults. Invasive plants can obstruct burrow entrances and alter nesting habitat, while agriculture, livestock trampling, and habitat degradation reduce suitable breeding areas. Marine threats may also include changes in prey availability, bycatch, pollution, and climate-related changes in ocean conditions.
conservation.howToHelp: Support conservation programs that remove invasive predators and plants from Galápagos breeding colonies, restore native upland vegetation, and monitor nesting populations. Responsible visitors should follow Galápagos National Park rules, avoid disturbing nocturnal colonies, and prevent the transport of organisms between islands. In Costa Rica, observers can contribute useful information by documenting exceptionally rare offshore sightings carefully and submitting records to recognized bird-monitoring databases.

profile.overview: The Tahiti Petrel (Pseudobulweria rostrata) is a medium-sized tropical seabird of the family Procellariidae. It spends most of its life at sea and comes ashore mainly at night to breed on remote Pacific islands. Despite its name, it is not restricted to Tahiti. The species breeds across parts of French Polynesia, Melanesia, American Samoa, Fiji, and New Caledonia, and disperses widely across the tropical Pacific outside the breeding season.
profile.classification: The Tahiti Petrel belongs to the petrel and shearwater family Procellariidae in the order Procellariiformes. It is the only widely recognized species in the genus Pseudobulweria, although regional subspecies have been described.
profile.identification: This petrel has dark brown upperparts, a paler face and throat, and largely white underparts, with darker markings around the head and under the wings. Its bill is strong and hooked, and its long, broad wings give it a steady, languid flight. It is usually identified at sea by its relatively large size, dark-and-white plumage, straight-winged flight, and dark cap contrasting with the pale underside. It is rarely seen close enough for detailed field marks.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Tahiti Petrel breeds on mountainous and forested islands, using soil burrows, rock crevices, and cavities beneath vegetation. Breeding sites may range from low rocky islets to high mountain slopes. At sea it occupies warm tropical and subtropical waters of the Pacific. In the Costa Rica region, it is an uncommon offshore visitor rather than a breeding or land-based species. Reliable records occur in the Pacific Ocean west and southwest of Costa Rica, including waters associated with Isla del Coco, and birds may also be encountered during pelagic surveys farther offshore.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is a wide-ranging disperser rather than a strongly seasonal migrant. After breeding, individuals spread across the tropical Pacific and reach the eastern tropical Pacific, including offshore waters of Costa Rica. It is rarely observed from the mainland coast and has no known breeding population in Costa Rica.
profile.breeding: Tahiti Petrels usually breed in isolated colonies on tropical Pacific islands. Pairs nest in burrows or rock cavities, often in forest, dense vegetation, mountain ridges, or steep rocky terrain. One white egg is laid, and both adults share incubation and chick-rearing duties. Incubation is about 54–56 days in studied colonies, while chicks may remain in the nest for roughly 110–120 days. Adults generally visit colonies at night, which makes the species difficult to survey.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of squid and fish, with other marine prey such as crustaceans also taken. Studies indicate that the species often feeds on deep-water organisms and may seize dead or weakened prey floating at the surface. It forages over open tropical ocean, sometimes working around productive areas where prey is concentrated. Like other procellariiform seabirds, it can travel long distances from breeding islands while searching for food.
profile.behavior: Tahiti Petrels are powerful ocean fliers that often travel with slow, gliding wingbeats and shallow banking movements. They are mainly pelagic and spend extended periods away from land. Breeding adults are strongly nocturnal at colonies, reducing exposure to predators, and may call near nest sites after dark. At sea they are usually solitary or seen in small numbers, although they can join mixed-species seabird groups where food is available.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining, although trends are poorly known in several breeding regions. Surveys in the eastern tropical Pacific indicated a substantial reduction between the late 1980s and late 1990s, and declines have been reported at some island colonies.
conservation.threats: Introduced predators, especially feral cats and rats, can kill adults, chicks, and eggs at breeding colonies. Dogs and pigs may also disturb or dig into nests. Artificial lights can disorient fledglings and adults near settlements, causing collisions and grounding. Habitat disturbance and mining affect some colonies in New Caledonia, while localized harvesting has been reported in parts of French Polynesia. Offshore threats may include incidental capture in fisheries, although the scale for this species is not well established.
conservation.howToHelp: Protecting breeding islands through removal or control of introduced cats, rats, dogs, and pigs is a major conservation priority. Safeguarding native forest and nesting habitat, reducing artificial lighting near colonies, and monitoring remote breeding sites can improve survival. In Costa Rica, observers can contribute by submitting well-documented pelagic records from the Pacific, especially around Isla del Coco, while avoiding disturbance to any storm-driven or grounded birds and supporting marine wildlife monitoring.

profile.overview: The Spectacled Petrel (Procellaria conspicillata) is a large, dark seabird of the South Atlantic. Its name comes from the bold white markings surrounding the eyes, which contrast with its blackish head and body. It breeds only on Inaccessible Island in the Tristan da Cunha group. Although its population has recovered from historical lows, the species remains vulnerable because its entire breeding population is concentrated at one small island and it faces risks at sea.
profile.classification: The Spectacled Petrel belongs to the petrel family Procellariidae in the order Procellariiformes. It was once treated as a subspecies of the White-chinned Petrel but is now recognized as a separate species.
profile.identification: This is a large petrel, about 55 centimetres long, with an overall dark brown to black plumage. Its most distinctive feature is the conspicuous pale or white pattern around the eyes, giving the impression of spectacles. The bill is yellowish with a darker tip. It can resemble a White-chinned Petrel, but the latter lacks the sharply contrasting eye markings. In flight, it shows long, broad wings and a powerful, gliding style typical of large Procellaria petrels.
profile.rangeHabitat: Spectacled Petrels breed only on the high western plateau of Inaccessible Island in the Tristan da Cunha group, in the South Atlantic. Away from the colony, they forage over oceanic waters, mainly between South America and southern Africa, with many birds occurring off southern Brazil. They usually use open sea rather than coastal habitats. In Costa Rica, the species is an accidental visitor: the first national record was a fatigued individual found at Laguna Penitencia, Tortuguero, on February 24, 2022.
profile.migrationStatus: It is a dispersive, non-breeding seabird rather than a conventional land migrant. After breeding, birds range widely across the South Atlantic. Costa Rica lies far north of the species’ usual range, and its presence there is exceptional; the Tortuguero bird in February 2022 was reportedly the first record for Costa Rica and the Northern Hemisphere.
profile.breeding: Breeding is restricted to Inaccessible Island, where colonies occur in wet heath, bog fern heath, and areas of Phylica woodland at roughly 250–500 metres elevation. Spectacled Petrels nest in burrows and usually lay a single white egg. Both adults contribute to incubation and chick care. Breeding takes place during the austral spring and summer, with activity generally extending from about September through March. The species has high dependence on the security of its single breeding island.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of squid and other cephalopods, along with fish and crustaceans. Spectacled Petrels take prey from the ocean surface and by shallow dives. They may also follow fishing vessels to consume discarded fish or offal, behavior that can increase exposure to fishing gear. Feeding occurs over productive oceanic waters, including areas near continental shelf edges and waters used by commercial fisheries.
profile.behavior: Spectacled Petrels are strongly marine and spend most of their lives at sea. They are powerful fliers that use dynamic soaring and can travel long distances over open water. Birds may gather around fishing vessels or food concentrations. At the breeding colony they are active in and around burrows, especially at night. Like other burrowing petrels, they have a single-chick breeding strategy and generally show strong attachment to their nesting site.

conservation.populationTrend: The breeding population has increased substantially since historical lows, following the disappearance of introduced pigs from Inaccessible Island. Recent estimates indicate tens of thousands of breeding pairs, but the population remains vulnerable because all birds depend on one small island.
conservation.threats: Incidental capture in longline fisheries, particularly in the South Atlantic, is a major at-sea threat. The species is also highly exposed to accidental events because it breeds at only one locality. The introduction of rats or mice to Inaccessible Island could seriously harm eggs, chicks, and adults. Marine pollution, changes in prey availability, and poorly managed fishing activity may add further pressure.
conservation.howToHelp: Support seabird-safe fisheries that use bird-scaring lines, weighted lines, and night setting to reduce longline bycatch. Protect Inaccessible Island through strict biosecurity, careful control of landings, and prevention of invasive rodents. In Costa Rica, report unusual sightings through established bird-recording programs and avoid disturbing exhausted seabirds; records can improve understanding of this rare accidental visitor.

profile.overview: Parkinson's Petrel, also called Black Petrel or tākoketai, is a medium-sized seabird endemic as a breeding species to New Zealand. It is the smallest member of the Procellaria petrel group and spends most of its life at sea. The species nests in burrows on a small number of islands in the Hauraki Gulf, then travels across the Pacific Ocean after breeding. Costa Rica forms part of its non-breeding range, where it is an uncommon offshore visitor.
profile.classification: Parkinson's Petrel belongs to the petrel family Procellariidae within the order Procellariiformes. Its scientific name is Procellaria parkinsoni.
profile.identification: This is a stocky, uniformly very dark brown to black petrel with dark wings, black legs, and black feet. Its bill is pale yellowish or horn-colored, with a conspicuous dark tip and dark markings between the bill plates. It is smaller and less bulky than Westland Petrel and White-chinned Petrel, which can look similar at sea. Parkinson's Petrel usually flies low over the water, with strong wingbeats and occasional gliding.
profile.rangeHabitat: Parkinson's Petrel breeds only on Aotea or Great Barrier Island and Hauturu or Little Barrier Island in New Zealand's Hauraki Gulf. During the breeding season it forages mainly in subtropical and temperate waters around northern New Zealand, particularly near shelf edges and productive ocean areas. After breeding, it moves into the eastern tropical Pacific. It has been reported in offshore waters of Costa Rica, generally as a rare or uncommon pelagic species rather than a coastal or land-based bird.
profile.migrationStatus: Migratory. After breeding, most birds move east and north into the eastern tropical Pacific, where they occur off Costa Rica, Panama, Ecuador, and other Pacific coasts. They return to New Zealand waters and colonies for the breeding season.
profile.breeding: Parkinson's Petrels are colonial, monogamous burrow nesters. Their breeding colonies are restricted to two predator-managed islands in the Hauraki Gulf. Adults attend colonies mainly from October through July, and each pair normally lays one egg between mid-November and late January. Both parents share incubation, which lasts about 57 days, and feed the chick by regurgitation. Chicks remain in the burrow for roughly three to four months before fledging, and young birds usually return to colonies after several years.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet includes squid, small fish, crustaceans, and other marine prey, with scavenged material sometimes taken near fishing vessels. Birds feed at the surface and by diving, including shallow nighttime dives; recorded dives can reach several tens of metres. They may gather in small feeding groups around dolphins, whales, or boats where prey or discarded fishing material is concentrated.
profile.behavior: Parkinson's Petrels are generally solitary at sea but may associate with cetaceans and fishing vessels. They are powerful fliers that often travel close to the sea surface and can soar when conditions allow. Adults visit breeding colonies after dark and usually leave before dawn. The species is relatively quiet at sea, but birds become vocal around nesting burrows, where harsh calls help maintain pair and colony contact.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is declining overall, particularly at the main colony on Great Barrier Island. Long-term monitoring has documented an ongoing decrease, although the Little Barrier Island colony has benefited from introduced-predator removal and protection.
conservation.threats: Major threats include predation by introduced rats, cats, pigs, and other mammals at breeding colonies, along with habitat loss and disturbance. At sea, accidental capture on longlines and in trawl fisheries is a serious concern, especially because the birds are attracted to bait and fishing vessels. Marine pollution, changing food availability, and other ocean changes may add further pressure.
conservation.howToHelp: Support protection and predator control at the two New Zealand breeding colonies. Fisheries can reduce risk by using effective seabird bycatch measures, sinking baited hooks rapidly, managing offal and discards, and avoiding practices that attract petrels to fishing gear. In Costa Rica, pelagic observers and birders can document offshore sightings and report unusual concentrations or stranded birds to appropriate wildlife authorities, helping improve knowledge of the species' non-breeding distribution.

profile.overview: Cory’s Shearwater (Calonectris borealis) is a large Atlantic seabird in the petrel family. It spends most of its life at sea and comes ashore mainly to breed. The species has long, narrow wings, a brownish-gray back, pale underparts, and a large pale bill with a dark tip. Cory’s Shearwaters breed on islands in the eastern North Atlantic and undertake long-distance movements across the Atlantic outside the breeding season.
profile.classification: Cory’s Shearwater belongs to the order Procellariiformes and family Procellariidae. It was formerly treated as part of a broader Cory’s Shearwater complex that included Scopoli’s Shearwater, but Calonectris borealis is now generally recognized as a separate species.
profile.identification: This is a large shearwater with a wingspan of roughly 118–126 cm. Its upperparts are brownish gray, while the face and underparts are mostly white. The broad head and heavy, pale pinkish-yellow bill with a dark tip are distinctive. In flight, it shows long, stiff wings and an effortless, gliding style, often alternating several shallow wingbeats with long arcs close to the sea. It is larger and browner overall than many smaller shearwaters.
profile.rangeHabitat: Cory’s Shearwater breeds on the Azores, Madeira and nearby island groups, the Canary Islands, and the Berlengas off Portugal. Outside the breeding season it ranges widely across the Atlantic, including waters off North and South America and southern Africa. In Costa Rica it is a very uncommon offshore visitor, recorded mainly during pelagic trips in the Caribbean Sea, including off Limón. It is not a regular coastal or land-based bird of Costa Rica.
profile.migrationStatus: A long-distance trans-equatorial migrant. Birds leave Atlantic breeding colonies mainly after the breeding season, spend the nonbreeding period over tropical and southern Atlantic waters, and return to breeding islands in spring. In Costa Rica, records are scarce and involve birds at sea rather than a predictable passage or wintering population.
profile.breeding: Cory’s Shearwaters breed colonially on oceanic islands, using rocky crevices, caves, and cavities for nesting. They usually return to colonies in spring and lay a single egg. Both parents share incubation and chick care, making repeated feeding trips over the sea. Adults commonly visit colonies at night, when their calls can be prominent. Chicks remain in the nest until fully developed and then leave independently for the open ocean.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small pelagic fish and squid, with other marine prey taken opportunistically. Cory’s Shearwaters generally forage in open ocean waters, taking prey from near the surface and sometimes making shallow dives. They may follow productive fronts, schools of fish, marine predators, or fishing vessels. Feeding patterns can vary among individuals and between seasons as prey availability changes.
profile.behavior: Cory’s Shearwaters are highly pelagic and spend most of their time flying, resting on the water, or foraging far from land. Their flight is characterized by powerful wingbeats followed by long, graceful glides. They are social at sea and may gather in groups where food is concentrated. At breeding colonies they are largely nocturnal, arriving after dark and using loud calls to communicate with mates and neighbors.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not reliably known. The species has a large range and a substantial breeding population, so it does not currently meet the criteria for a threatened category.

profile.overview: The Pink-footed Shearwater is a large Pacific seabird that breeds only on a few Chilean islands and spends most of the year at sea. It is named for its pinkish bill base and feet, although these features can be difficult to see at a distance. The species is strongly associated with productive upwelling waters and moves across much of the eastern Pacific during the non-breeding season, including offshore waters near Costa Rica.
profile.classification: The Pink-footed Shearwater belongs to the petrel and shearwater family Procellariidae and the genus Ardenna. Its scientific name is Ardenna creatopus.
profile.identification: This shearwater is about 45–51 cm long, with a wingspan of roughly 109 cm. It has dark brown to gray-brown upperparts, pale underparts, and contrasting pale wing linings bordered by darker feathering. The bill is heavy, with a pinkish base and dark tip, while the legs and feet are pink. In flight, it shows broad, pointed wings and slow, powerful wingbeats followed by long glides. It is larger and paler below than many similar shearwaters.
profile.rangeHabitat: Pink-footed Shearwaters breed on Isla Mocha and the Juan Fernández Islands off central Chile, nesting in burrows on steep slopes in forested or open habitats. At sea they use coastal waters, continental-shelf edges, slopes, and offshore areas influenced by productive upwelling. In Costa Rica, the species occurs offshore in the Pacific Ocean rather than as a land bird. Reliable records indicate regular passage or seasonal presence, especially from May to June and again from September into the later autumn migration period.
profile.migrationStatus: A trans-equatorial migrant. After breeding, many birds move north through Peruvian waters and onward across the eastern Pacific, while others remain off Peru. In Costa Rican waters, it is a regular but oceanic migrant, most likely encountered during northbound and southbound passage, particularly in May–June and September–November.
profile.breeding: Breeding is restricted to three Chilean island areas: Isla Mocha and the Juan Fernández Islands, including Robinson Crusoe and Alejandro Selkirk islands. Pairs nest in underground burrows, often on steep slopes in forest or open vegetation. The female lays one egg, and both adults participate in incubation and chick care. Breeding takes place during the austral spring and summer, after which adults and fledged young leave the colonies for extended movements across the eastern Pacific.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small fish and squid, along with other marine prey taken near the surface or during shallow dives. Pink-footed Shearwaters often forage where prey is concentrated by oceanic upwelling, currents, fronts, dolphins, tuna, other seabirds, or fishing activity. They commonly feed from the water surface and can plunge or dive briefly, but they are not deep-diving seabirds.
profile.behavior: At sea, Pink-footed Shearwaters may travel alone or gather in loose groups with other shearwaters. Their flight combines several strong wingbeats with long glides close to the water, and they can cover very large distances during migration. They spend nearly their entire lives over the ocean and are usually silent away from breeding colonies. Individuals may rest on the water between feeding bouts and can associate with marine mammals or fishing vessels where prey is available.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining.
conservation.threats: Important threats include accidental capture in fishing gear, especially longline and other South American fisheries, as well as predation on eggs and chicks by introduced mammals. Habitat degradation, disturbance, and changes in marine food supplies may also affect the restricted breeding colonies. Because the species passes through several countries and ocean regions, threats during migration and at sea require international cooperation.
conservation.howToHelp: Support seabird-safe fishing practices, including methods that reduce longline and other fishing bycatch. Protect and restore breeding-island habitat, control introduced predators, and limit disturbance near colonies. In Costa Rica, responsible pelagic birding, accurate reporting of offshore records, and participation in marine monitoring can improve knowledge of the species’ seasonal movements and help guide conservation measures.

profile.overview: The Flesh-footed Shearwater is a medium to large oceanic seabird of the Indo-Pacific. It spends most of its life at sea and comes ashore mainly to breed on islands in Australia, New Zealand, and nearby regions. Its dark plumage, pale bill with a dark tip, and pinkish or flesh-colored feet distinguish it from many other shearwaters. The species is an uncommon visitor far from its usual range, including a documented record in Costa Rican Pacific waters.
profile.classification: The Flesh-footed Shearwater belongs to the order Procellariiformes and the family Procellariidae, which includes shearwaters, petrels, and fulmars. Its scientific name is Ardenna carneipes.
profile.identification: This shearwater has dark brown to blackish upperparts and generally dark underparts, with some paler areas on the face, throat, and underwing. The bill is pale horn-colored with a contrasting dark tip, while the legs and feet are distinctly pinkish or flesh-colored. It has long, narrow wings and a relatively heavy body. In flight, it alternates strong wingbeats with long glides close to the sea surface. Care is needed to separate it from similarly dark shearwaters.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Flesh-footed Shearwater breeds on offshore islands in southern Australia, New Zealand, and other parts of the southwestern Pacific, nesting in soil burrows or natural cavities. Outside the breeding season it ranges widely across the Indo-Pacific, using open ocean waters and areas where prey concentrates. In Costa Rica it is exceptionally rare: the first documented record was an individual observed on January 10, 2025, over the Middle America Trench in the Pacific, feeding offshore. It should be regarded as a rare oceanic visitor rather than a regular coastal species.
profile.migrationStatus: It is a long-distance migrant. Birds breeding in the South Pacific move northward and widely across the Pacific after breeding. Occurrence in Costa Rica is exceptional and currently documented by a first photographic record from January 10, 2025, in offshore Pacific waters; regular seasonal presence has not been established.
profile.breeding: Breeding is colonial and takes place on islands, usually in burrows or other sheltered cavities. Adults generally return to the same breeding areas, and pairs show strong site fidelity. A single egg is laid, and both parents share incubation and chick-rearing. Chicks remain in the burrow until they are fully developed and then depart for the sea. Breeding colonies can be vulnerable because introduced rats, cats, and other predators reach nesting islands and because adults are concentrated in predictable places.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet includes fish, squid, and other marine animals, especially prey associated with productive ocean fronts, schools of fish, and other feeding aggregations. The species forages by seizing prey at or below the surface and can make shallow dives. It may also scavenge discarded fish or offal around fishing vessels. The Costa Rican individual was observed feeding in a mixed seabird flock associated with spotted dolphins, suggesting localized prey concentration.
profile.behavior: Flesh-footed Shearwaters are highly adapted to life at sea, using long glides and strong, efficient flight over open water. They are often gregarious when feeding and may gather with other seabirds and marine mammals. Adults usually approach breeding colonies at night, which reduces exposure to predators. At sea they can travel great distances between feeding areas and nesting islands. Their burrowing lifestyle and strong attachment to breeding colonies make them especially sensitive to disturbance and introduced predators.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining. Available assessments estimate roughly 148,000 mature individuals, although population estimates remain uncertain for some breeding groups.
conservation.threats: Important threats include accidental capture in commercial longline and other fisheries, introduced predators at breeding colonies, disturbance and habitat degradation on nesting islands, and ingestion of or entanglement in marine plastic. Changes in marine food supplies and climate conditions may also affect breeding success and survival. Because the species concentrates at colonies and overlaps with fisheries, local impacts can have wide population consequences.
conservation.howToHelp: Support fisheries that use effective seabird-bycatch measures, such as night setting, bird-scaring lines, and properly weighted lines. Protect and restore breeding islands by controlling introduced rats, cats, and other predators, and by limiting disturbance during the nesting season. Reduce plastic use and never discard fishing line or other waste at sea. In Costa Rica, reporting and documenting offshore sightings can improve knowledge of this exceptionally rare visitor and its use of Pacific waters.

profile.overview: The Great Shearwater is a large oceanic seabird of the petrel family. It breeds on a few remote islands in the South Atlantic and spends much of the nonbreeding season over the North Atlantic, traveling thousands of kilometers between hemispheres. It is powerful in flight, using long glides and wind-assisted arcs above waves. Although it is included on Costa Rica’s bird list, it is an accidental and exceptionally rare visitor rather than a regular coastal species.
profile.classification: The Great Shearwater belongs to the order Procellariiformes and family Procellariidae. Its scientific name is Ardenna gravis; older literature often used Puffinus gravis or the common name Greater Shearwater.
profile.identification: This is a large shearwater with long, narrow wings, a heavy dark bill, and a broad, blunt-looking tail. Adults have a dark gray-brown cap and upperparts, a contrasting white collar and face, and white underparts marked by brownish smudging on the belly and underwings. The flight is strong and purposeful, with long glides on stiff wings close to the sea. Its size, dark cap, white collar, and belly smudges help separate it from similar shearwaters.
profile.rangeHabitat: Great Shearwaters breed on Gough Island, islands in the Tristan da Cunha group, and Kidney Island in the Falkland Islands. Outside the breeding season they range widely across the Atlantic, from southern waters north toward the Arctic. They use open ocean, continental-shelf waters, fronts, and areas where prey concentrates. In Costa Rica, the species is recorded only as an accidental or extremely rare visitor, most plausibly in offshore Caribbean waters; it is not a regular bird of either Costa Rican coast.
profile.migrationStatus: A long-distance trans-equatorial migrant. It breeds in the South Atlantic, then moves north into the North Atlantic during the boreal summer before returning south. Costa Rica lies outside its normal migration corridor, so occurrences there are accidental and very uncommon, with no established seasonal passage pattern.
profile.breeding: Great Shearwaters breed colonially on remote, predator-free or predator-limited South Atlantic islands. They nest in burrows or sheltered cavities among grass and other island vegetation. Adults return to colonies, court, and mate before females lay a single egg. Both parents share incubation and chick-rearing duties. The chick remains at the nest while the adults forage at sea, and breeding colonies are visited only during the species’ South Atlantic breeding season.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small fish and squid, along with crustaceans and other marine prey. Great Shearwaters often forage where prey is concentrated near the surface, including productive ocean fronts and shelf waters. They may feed in groups, follow marine predators, seize prey while sitting on the water, and take discarded fish or offal around fishing vessels. Their hooked bill and strong swimming ability help them handle slippery prey.
profile.behavior: Great Shearwaters are highly pelagic and spend most of their lives at sea. They are usually seen singly or in loose flocks, sometimes gathering around feeding activity created by fish schools, cetaceans, or fishing boats. In flight they alternate strong wingbeats with long glides and can soar and wheel in strong winds. They rest on the water between feeding bouts and come ashore mainly to breed.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable, although monitoring is limited and population estimates are not equally strong across all breeding colonies.

profile.overview: The Wedge-tailed Shearwater is a medium-large tropical seabird of the family Procellariidae. It spends most of its life over warm ocean waters and comes ashore mainly to breed on islands. Its long, pointed, wedge-shaped tail and buoyant flight distinguish it from many other shearwaters. The species has both pale and dark plumage forms. It is widespread across tropical and subtropical parts of the Indian and Pacific Oceans, including waters of the eastern tropical Pacific.
profile.classification: The Wedge-tailed Shearwater belongs to the order Procellariiformes and family Procellariidae. Its scientific name is Ardenna pacifica; older sources may use Puffinus pacificus.
profile.identification: This shearwater is about 38–45 cm long, with a wingspan of roughly 1–1.1 m. It has a slender body, long narrow wings, a slim grayish bill, and a conspicuously long wedge-shaped tail. The common pale form is gray-brown above and whitish below, often with subtle pale feather edges on the back. The dark form is dark brown overall. In flight it combines shallow wingbeats with smooth, low glides over the sea.
profile.rangeHabitat: Wedge-tailed Shearwaters breed on tropical and subtropical islands across the Indian and Pacific Oceans, usually in low coastal colonies. Outside the breeding season they occupy open ocean, often over warm waters and near productive areas where predatory fish, dolphins, or other seabirds concentrate prey. In Costa Rica, the species is a rare and irregular visitor to Pacific waters rather than a commonly encountered coastal bird. Documented records include offshore sightings and observations associated with marine-bird feeding activity, including the southern Pacific region near Golfo Dulce.
profile.migrationStatus: The species disperses widely across tropical oceans after breeding, but its movements are better described as seasonal oceanic dispersal than as a single, well-defined migration route. In Costa Rica it occurs only sporadically in Pacific offshore waters, and it is not considered a regular land-based migrant or common coastal species.
profile.breeding: Wedge-tailed Shearwaters breed colonially on islands, usually nesting in underground burrows, rocky cavities, or sheltered sites beneath vegetation. Pairs are generally monogamous and both adults help excavate the nest, incubate the egg, and feed the chick. One white egg is laid per breeding season. Incubation lasts about seven to nine weeks, and the chick remains in the burrow for approximately 15 weeks before fledging. Adults commonly visit colonies at night, when the birds are highly vocal.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small fish and squid, with crustaceans and other small marine animals also taken. Birds often forage where predatory fish drive prey toward the surface, and they may gather with terns, boobies, jaegers, dolphins, and other seabirds. They catch prey by flying low and dipping the head or bill into the water, but they also rest and feed while sitting on the ocean surface.
profile.behavior: At sea, Wedge-tailed Shearwaters are usually seen singly or in feeding groups that can contain hundreds or more birds. Their flight is relaxed and buoyant, with stiff wingbeats followed by glides on slightly bowed wings. They are strong swimmers and spend little time on land except during breeding. Colonies are mainly nocturnal, and adults communicate with loud, drawn-out calls. The species is long-lived and typically begins breeding only after several years.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall global trend is not precisely quantified, although the species remains widespread and locally abundant. Trends can differ among breeding colonies.

profile.overview: The Sooty Shearwater is a medium-large oceanic seabird of the southern Pacific and southern Atlantic regions. It spends most of its life at sea and comes ashore mainly to breed in large colonies on islands and coastal headlands. Famous for long-distance migrations, individuals may travel between subantarctic breeding grounds and productive waters of the North Pacific. In Costa Rica, it is a pelagic visitor, seen over Pacific waters rather than inland or along most sheltered beaches.
profile.classification: The Sooty Shearwater belongs to the shearwater family Procellariidae, within the order Procellariiformes. Its scientific name is Ardenna grisea; it was formerly often placed in the genus Puffinus.
profile.identification: This shearwater is about 40–45 cm long, with a long, narrow-winged shape and a dark brown to sooty overall appearance. The underparts are somewhat paler than the upperparts, and silvery or pale flashes may show across the underwings in good light. It has a relatively long, slender, all-dark bill. In flight, it uses rapid wingbeats followed by long glides close to the sea surface. It can resemble other dark shearwaters, especially Short-tailed Shearwater.
profile.rangeHabitat: Sooty Shearwaters breed mainly on islands and coastal areas around New Zealand, southern Australia, and southern South America, nesting in burrows or beneath dense vegetation. Outside the breeding season they disperse widely across the Pacific, Atlantic, and sometimes Indian Ocean. They are strongly pelagic, favoring offshore waters, continental-shelf edges, fronts, and other areas rich in prey. In Costa Rica, the species occurs as an irregular to locally common or abundant non-breeding visitor in Pacific waters, especially offshore, with records concentrated from roughly May through October.
profile.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Birds leave southern-hemisphere breeding colonies after breeding and move northward through major oceanic routes. In Costa Rica, it is a non-breeding Pacific visitor, generally recorded offshore from May to October; it does not breed there.
profile.breeding: Breeding takes place in the southern hemisphere, generally during the austral spring and summer. Pairs nest colonially in burrows, crevices, or sheltered ground among vegetation, returning to colonies year after year. The female lays a single egg, and both adults share incubation and chick care. Chicks remain in the nest until well developed and are fed regurgitated food. Adults usually forage at sea, sometimes traveling considerable distances from colonies before returning to feed their young.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet includes small fish, squid, crustaceans, and other marine animals. Sooty Shearwaters locate prey from the air and surface, then seize it while swimming or diving. They can make substantial underwater dives and may forage cooperatively in large flocks where prey is concentrated. Feeding areas often form around ocean fronts, upwellings, schools of fish, and other productive waters. They may also follow fishing vessels to take discarded fish or offal.
profile.behavior: Sooty Shearwaters are highly social at sea and may gather in flocks numbering from dozens to many thousands. Their flight is typically a series of quick, deep wingbeats followed by stiff-winged glides close to the waves. They are powerful fliers capable of crossing entire ocean basins. At breeding colonies they are mainly nocturnal, which reduces exposure to some predators. On land they are much less agile than in flight and on water.

conservation.populationTrend: Suspected declining globally, although estimates and trend data vary among breeding colonies and regions. Some colonies have decreased while others have remained stable or increased, so the overall rate of decline is uncertain.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include accidental capture in fishing gear, reduced prey availability, changing marine conditions associated with climate change, disturbance or predation at breeding colonies, introduced predators on islands, and local harvesting of chicks. Offshore pollution and ingestion of marine debris may add further risks. In Costa Rica, the main relevant concerns are threats affecting pelagic waters, including fisheries bycatch, prey depletion, and marine pollution.
conservation.howToHelp: Support sustainable fisheries and efforts to reduce seabird bycatch, especially through safer fishing practices and effective monitoring. Protect breeding islands from introduced predators and disturbance, and support marine protected areas that safeguard important feeding zones. In Costa Rica, responsible boating, reduced plastic pollution, and reporting well-documented sightings through established bird-monitoring programs can improve knowledge of this uncommon offshore visitor.

profile.overview: The Christmas Shearwater is a tropical Pacific seabird that spends most of its life over open ocean and comes ashore mainly to breed. It is a dark, compact shearwater with long wings, a short rounded tail, and a black bill. The species nests on remote islands scattered across the tropical Pacific. Although seldom recorded along the American coast, it has been documented offshore from Costa Rica, where it is considered an accidental or very uncommon visitor.
profile.classification: The Christmas Shearwater belongs to the order Procellariiformes and family Procellariidae. Its scientific name is Puffinus nativitatis.
profile.identification: This medium-sized shearwater is mostly dark brown to blackish, with slightly paler brown areas on the face, throat, and underparts. It has long, narrow wings, a relatively short rounded tail, dark legs, and a slender black bill with a hooked tip. In flight it shows a dark overall appearance without strong white markings. At sea, its identification can be difficult because it resembles other uniformly dark tropical shearwaters, especially under poor light or at a distance.
profile.rangeHabitat: Christmas Shearwaters breed on small, remote tropical and subtropical islands across the central and eastern Pacific, including parts of Hawaii, Micronesia, Polynesia, the Phoenix and Marquesas island groups, the Pitcairn and Tuamotu islands, and islands near Easter Island. At sea they use open tropical waters, often around oceanic islands and productive offshore areas. In Costa Rica, the species is not a regular coastal bird, but accepted records and observations place it offshore in the Pacific, including deep water west of the Nicoya Peninsula.
profile.migrationStatus: It is a dispersive seabird rather than a strictly seasonal migrant. After breeding, many birds range widely across the tropical Pacific. In Costa Rica it occurs as a very uncommon, non-breeding visitor or wanderer over deep Pacific waters; records include April observations roughly 35 to 50 km west of the Nicoya Peninsula.
profile.breeding: Christmas Shearwaters breed colonially on predator-free or relatively undisturbed islands, often nesting beneath vegetation, among rocks, or in shallow crevices rather than in deep burrows. The female lays one egg, and both adults share incubation and chick-rearing duties. Breeding seasons vary among island groups but commonly extend through much of the warmer part of the year. Nesting colonies are generally remote, and the species returns to land mainly after dark or during periods of reduced activity.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet includes small fish, squid, and crustaceans taken at sea. Christmas Shearwaters forage over open water and may feed alone or in association with other seabirds where prey is concentrated. They capture food by seizing items at or near the surface and by making shallow dives or plunge-dives. Their narrow wings and streamlined bodies support efficient flight over long distances while searching for patchy marine prey.
profile.behavior: This species is highly pelagic and usually rests on the sea or flies low over the water with measured wingbeats and gliding phases. It is generally encountered singly or in small groups, although several birds may gather where food is abundant. Like many shearwaters, it is most closely associated with land during breeding. Its remote nesting sites and oceanic lifestyle make its population difficult to monitor, and many aspects of its behavior remain poorly documented.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population trend is not well quantified, but the species remains widely distributed and is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Galapagos Shearwater (Puffinus subalaris) is a small seabird endemic to the Galapagos Islands. It belongs to the petrel and shearwater family, Procellariidae, and spends most of its life at sea. The species breeds on rocky islands and coastal cliffs, then forages over warm tropical waters. Although its breeding range is restricted to the Galapagos, individuals may travel beyond the archipelago, including offshore waters of Central America.
profile.classification: The Galapagos Shearwater is in the order Procellariiformes and family Procellariidae. Its scientific name is Puffinus subalaris; it was formerly treated as a subspecies of Audubon's Shearwater.
profile.identification: This is a slender, small shearwater measuring about 29–31 centimeters in length, with a wingspan of roughly 63–70 centimeters. It has dark brown upperparts and dark flight feathers beneath the wings, contrasting with white underparts. Some birds show a darker collar across the upper breast. The bill is narrow and the wings are long and pointed. In flight, it typically alternates several rapid wingbeats with short, low glides over the sea.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species is an endemic breeder of the Galapagos Islands, where it nests on small islets and on cliffs or rocky slopes of larger islands. At sea it uses warm tropical waters around the archipelago and may range farther west and north. In Costa Rica, it is not a resident land bird or breeding species; reliable records concern birds seen offshore in Pacific waters, where it occurs irregularly or as a passage visitor during pelagic seabird observations.
profile.migrationStatus: Largely sedentary around the Galapagos, but capable of wider movements at sea. In Costa Rica it is recorded offshore along the Pacific coast, apparently as an uncommon passage or wandering seabird rather than a regular coastal or terrestrial migrant.
profile.breeding: Galapagos Shearwaters breed colonially on rocky islands, cliffs, and other protected sites in the Galapagos. They nest in crevices, cavities, or burrows where available, sheltering the single egg and chick from exposure and predators. Adults commute between nesting areas and nearby feeding grounds at sea. Breeding is tied to local oceanographic conditions and food availability, and detailed information on the timing and productivity of colonies remains more limited than for many widely studied shearwaters.
profile.dietFeeding: The species feeds at sea on small fish, squid, and other marine prey, and may also take floating food or offal. It often forages socially with other shearwaters, boobies, and seabirds where prey is concentrated. Its flight is typically low over the water, with rapid wingbeats followed by shallow glides. Feeding areas are likely influenced by currents, fronts, and locally productive waters around the Galapagos and adjacent tropical Pacific.
profile.behavior: Galapagos Shearwaters are gregarious seabirds and are commonly seen in groups while traveling or feeding. They fly close to the sea surface and can move efficiently across open water using alternating flapping and gliding. Like other shearwaters, they return to land mainly for breeding and are otherwise strongly marine. Their dark-and-white plumage and low, fast flight help distinguish them from larger shearwaters and from more uniformly dark tropical seabirds.

conservation.populationTrend: Stable according to the current global assessment.

profile.overview: The Manx Shearwater is a medium-sized seabird of the family Procellariidae. It is dark brown or black above and white below, with long, narrow wings and a streamlined body adapted for efficient flight over the ocean. Most of its life is spent at sea, while breeding adults come ashore only at night. The species is famous for long-distance movements between North Atlantic breeding colonies and South Atlantic wintering waters.
profile.classification: The Manx Shearwater is Puffinus puffinus in the family Procellariidae, the tubenose seabirds that also includes petrels and fulmars. It belongs to the order Procellariiformes.
profile.identification: This shearwater measures about 30–38 centimeters long and has a wingspan of roughly 76–82 centimeters. Its upperparts are sooty black or dark brown, contrasting with white underparts. The face is usually dark and smudged, with white extending behind the cheek. It has a slender black bill, narrow stiff wings, and a characteristic low flight that alternates rapid wingbeats with gliding. It is usually identified at sea rather than from land.
profile.rangeHabitat: Manx Shearwaters breed mainly on rocky islands and coastal cliffs around the United Kingdom, Ireland, and nearby North Atlantic islands, with smaller colonies in northeastern North America. Outside the breeding season, they range widely across the Atlantic and winter chiefly in the South Atlantic off Brazil and Argentina. In Costa Rica, the species is an extreme rarity or accidental visitor. A documented sighting from the Caribbean coast near Tortuguero in November 1997 is regarded as an early or possibly first national record; it is not a regular coastal species there.
profile.migrationStatus: Highly migratory. After breeding in the North Atlantic, most birds move south through the Atlantic to wintering waters off South America. In Costa Rica, it is not a regular migrant; records are exceptional and may involve storm-driven or otherwise unusual vagrants in offshore or Caribbean coastal waters.
profile.breeding: Manx Shearwaters breed colonially, usually on predator-free or relatively protected islands. Adults return to the same nesting areas and use burrows, natural cavities, or spaces beneath dense vegetation. They are largely nocturnal at colonies, arriving after dark to reduce the risk from gulls and other predators. The female lays one egg, and both parents incubate it and feed the chick. Young birds leave the burrow and fly to sea after several months of development.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small schooling fish, including herring-like fishes, as well as squid and other marine invertebrates. Birds search over productive ocean waters and capture prey from the surface or by shallow to moderate dives. They may follow fronts, currents, or concentrations of baitfish, and adults can travel considerable distances from colonies while feeding for themselves and their chicks.
profile.behavior: Manx Shearwaters are highly pelagic and spend most of their lives far from land. Their flight is fast and low, with stiff-winged glides close to the water followed by quick, shallow wingbeats. They are strongly social around breeding colonies but may be encountered alone or in small groups at sea. Their calls are loud and eerie at night, especially when adults gather near burrow colonies. They are rarely seen on land during daylight.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered large, but precise worldwide trend estimates are limited because burrow-nesting colonies are difficult to survey. Some breeding colonies are stable or increasing, while others have experienced local declines.

profile.overview: The Black-vented Shearwater is a small Pacific seabird that breeds mainly on islands off the western coast of Baja California and in the Gulf of California, Mexico. It spends most of its life at sea, usually over relatively shallow coastal waters, and returns to land primarily to nest. The species is notable for its dark undertail coverts, a feature that helps distinguish it from several other small shearwaters. Costa Rica lies well south of its main range.
profile.classification: The Black-vented Shearwater belongs to the family Procellariidae, which includes shearwaters, petrels, and fulmars. It is placed in the genus Puffinus and is recognized as the species Puffinus opisthomelas.
profile.identification: This small shearwater measures about 30–38 centimeters long and has a wingspan of roughly 76–89 centimeters. Its upperparts are brownish to dark gray, while the underparts are mostly white. The head may appear dusky or dirty white, and the dark undertail coverts contrast strongly with the pale belly and flanks. It has a long, slender bill and narrow wings. In flight it alternates rapid wingbeats with gliding close to the sea surface.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Black-vented Shearwater breeds on islands off Baja California and in the Gulf of California, with important colonies on Isla Guadalupe, Isla Natividad, the San Benito Islands, and other Mexican islands. It nests in burrows and crevices on relatively dry, rocky or sandy islands. At sea it commonly uses coastal waters over the continental shelf. In Costa Rica it is a very rare visitor to Pacific waters, known from only a small number of records and apparently occurring mainly as an accidental or exceptional disperser rather than a regular species.
profile.migrationStatus: After breeding, some birds disperse northward and southward along the Pacific coast, with movements reaching California and occasionally farther south. In Costa Rica, records are exceptionally scarce and indicate irregular post-breeding dispersal or vagrancy, rather than a predictable seasonal migration. It is not a regular coastal or offshore migrant in the country.
profile.breeding: Breeding occurs colonially on Mexican islands, where pairs nest in underground burrows, rock crevices, or cavities beneath vegetation and surface debris. The species is generally active at colonies at night, which reduces exposure to predatory birds. A single egg is laid, and both adults share incubation and chick-rearing. Young birds remain in the burrow until they are developed enough to leave for the sea. Exact timing varies among colonies but breeding is concentrated in the warmer months.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small fish, squid, and other marine organisms, with crustaceans and fish offal possibly taken when available. Black-vented Shearwaters forage at or near the surface, often in productive coastal waters and around schools of prey. They may feed alone or in groups and can associate with other seabirds, dolphins, or predatory fish that drive prey toward the surface.
profile.behavior: This species is highly pelagic and spends most of its time at sea. It is an efficient flier, using alternating strong wingbeats and glides, often traveling low over the waves. Birds are generally quiet away from colonies but become vocal at nesting sites, especially at night. Like many burrow-nesting seabirds, adults usually approach and leave colonies after dark. Outside the breeding season they may form loose feeding flocks where prey is concentrated.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered declining or potentially declining, although abundance estimates and trends remain uncertain for some colonies.
conservation.threats: Important threats include introduced rats, cats, and other predators at breeding colonies; disturbance and habitat degradation on nesting islands; accidental capture in fishing gear; pollution; and changes in marine food availability. Because the species nests on a small number of islands, local threats can affect a substantial portion of the population. Climate-driven changes in ocean conditions may also alter prey distribution and breeding success.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore breeding islands by controlling introduced predators and preventing new introductions. Reduce seabird bycatch through effective fishing regulations and gear modifications, and protect productive marine feeding areas. Monitoring colonies, documenting records in Costa Rican Pacific waters, limiting disturbance near nesting sites, and supporting marine conservation and responsible fisheries can also benefit the species.

profile.overview: The Sargasso Shearwater (Puffinus lherminieri) is a small tropical seabird of the petrel family. It is associated mainly with the Caribbean Sea and western Atlantic Ocean, where it breeds on small islands and rocky islets. Formerly grouped with several similar shearwaters under the name Audubon's Shearwater, it is now generally treated as a separate species. It spends most of its life at sea and usually approaches land only for breeding or during unusual movements.
profile.classification: Kingdom Animalia; class Aves; order Procellariiformes; family Procellariidae; genus Puffinus; species Puffinus lherminieri. The species belongs to a complex of closely related small shearwaters that has been divided differently by various taxonomic authorities.
profile.identification: This is a compact shearwater with long, narrow wings, a dark gray-brown back and upperwings, and mainly white underparts. The head is dark, with a dusky cap and face contrasting with the white throat and lower cheeks. The underwing is generally pale with darker margins and axillaries. In flight it uses rapid wingbeats followed by low glides close to the sea. Identification at sea can be difficult because it resembles other small Puffinus shearwaters.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Sargasso Shearwater breeds on islands and rocky coastal sites in the Caribbean, the Bahamas, and nearby western Atlantic areas. It nests in crevices, burrows, or sheltered ground sites and forages over warm ocean waters, especially around productive coastal and offshore zones. In Costa Rica it is a very rare or accidental species, recorded mainly as an offshore visitor or vagrant on the Caribbean side rather than as a regular coastal bird. There is no reliable evidence that it breeds in Costa Rica.
profile.migrationStatus: It is not a long-distance seasonal migrant in the usual sense, but adults disperse widely through the western Atlantic outside the breeding period. In Costa Rica it is an irregular, rare visitor, with records most likely from Caribbean coastal or offshore waters; it is not a regular inland or Pacific-coast species.
profile.breeding: Breeding takes place in colonies on small islands, rocky islets, and other predator-free sites. The species is largely nocturnal at breeding colonies, where adults may call, court, and visit nest sites in darkness. A single egg is laid in a natural crevice, burrow, or sheltered depression. Both parents participate in incubation and chick care. Chicks are fed at night, and fledglings generally leave the colony after several weeks of development, departing directly toward the sea.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of small fish and squid, with other small marine organisms probably taken opportunistically. It feeds by seizing prey at the surface and by diving beneath the water. Underwater, it can propel itself with its wings and maneuver effectively. Feeding may occur during both daylight and darkness. Unlike some larger shearwaters, it does not usually follow ships or gather consistently around fishing vessels.
profile.behavior: The Sargasso Shearwater is highly marine and spends most of its time flying low over the ocean or resting on the water. It is agile in flight and often alternates quick wingbeats with gliding. At colonies it is active mainly at night, which reduces exposure to some predators. Birds may travel singly or in small groups, and they generally avoid approaching boats closely. Its dark upperparts and white underside provide useful camouflage in changing sea conditions.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population trend is uncertain, but declines have been reported or suspected at some breeding colonies, particularly where islands have experienced human disturbance, introduced predators, or habitat changes.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include disturbance and habitat degradation at breeding colonies, predation by introduced rats, cats, and other mammals, harvesting or persecution in some areas, and accidental capture in fishing gear. Marine pollution, artificial light near colonies, and changes in prey availability may add further pressure. Because the species is colonial and concentrated on relatively few islands, local losses can have disproportionate effects.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and monitor breeding islands, remove introduced predators where feasible, and limit human access during the nesting season. Reduce seabird bycatch through effective fishing practices and support monitoring of offshore populations. On Caribbean and Costa Rican coasts, avoid disturbing grounded or storm-driven birds, report unusual sightings to local bird-monitoring groups, and reduce artificial lighting near coastal nesting areas.

profile.overview: The Maguari Stork (Ciconia maguari) is a large South American stork associated mainly with open wetlands and seasonally flooded grasslands. It is the only New World member of the genus Ciconia and one of three native storks found in the Americas. Its broad white wings and body contrast with black flight feathers, while its long legs and bill are adapted for wading and capturing prey in shallow water.
profile.classification: The Maguari Stork belongs to the stork family Ciconiidae and the order Ciconiiformes. Its scientific name is Ciconia maguari.
profile.identification: A large, long-legged stork with mostly white plumage, black flight feathers, a black bill, and reddish or pinkish legs. Adults have a dark facial area around the eye and a distinctive black tail and wing pattern visible in flight. The species is similar to the Wood Stork and Jabiru, but the Maguari Stork has a straighter, more pointed bill, a slimmer appearance, and less extensive black on the head and neck. Juveniles are duller and often show darker legs and bill.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Maguari Stork occurs mainly east of the Andes, from Venezuela and eastern Colombia through the Guianas, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil, Uruguay, and Argentina. It uses open lowland habitats such as freshwater marshes, flooded savannas, shallow lagoons, mudflats, wet grasslands, rice fields, and seasonally flooded agricultural areas, generally avoiding dense forest. In Costa Rica it is an accidental or extremely rare vagrant, with documented occurrence near the Gulf of Nicoya, including the Chomes area; it is not a regular resident.
profile.migrationStatus: Movement patterns are not fully understood, but the species makes seasonal movements linked to rainfall, flooding, and food availability. Some populations form large dry-season or nonbreeding aggregations. In Costa Rica, it is not a regular migrant or breeding species; records represent rare wandering individuals, including a documented occurrence near Chomes on the Gulf of Nicoya.
profile.breeding: Breeding is associated with seasonal rains and shallow freshwater wetlands. Pairs may form or reunite in gatherings before nesting, and the species can breed colonially. In much of Brazil and Argentina, nests are large platforms of reeds and other wetland vegetation built on the ground or above shallow water, although shrubs may be used in parts of the northern range. Clutches commonly contain about three or four eggs. There is no reliable evidence of breeding in Costa Rica.
profile.dietFeeding: The Maguari Stork is an opportunistic carnivore that feeds in shallow water and wet grassland. Its prey includes fish, eels, frogs, tadpoles, aquatic invertebrates, crustaceans, snakes, small reptiles, earthworms, insects, and small mammals such as rodents. It usually hunts visually, walking slowly with its bill near the water surface, but may also probe muddy bottoms. Outside the breeding season, it can forage in dry fields where prey has been concentrated or disturbed.
profile.behavior: It is usually solitary or found in pairs during breeding, but may gather in flocks outside the breeding season and sometimes joins other wading birds. Individuals walk slowly through shallow water and may compete for concentrated prey, including occasional food stealing among storks. The species is primarily diurnal and adapted to open landscapes. Its ground-level nesting and defensive behavior by chicks are unusual among storks and reflect the risks of nesting in exposed wetlands.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable, although precise population estimates and movement patterns remain limited.

profile.overview: The Jabiru (Jabiru mycteria), also called the Jabiru Stork, is one of the largest flying birds in the Americas and the tallest stork in the New World. It lives mainly in lowland wetlands, where its long legs and massive bill help it forage in shallow water. Adults are mostly white with a black head and neck marked by a red throat pouch. In Costa Rica, it is a scarce and locally important wetland bird.
profile.classification: The Jabiru belongs to the stork family Ciconiidae and is the only species in the genus Jabiru. It is not closely related to the smaller Wood Stork, despite sharing wetland habitats.
profile.identification: This very large stork stands about 1.2–1.4 meters tall and has a broad wingspan. Adults have white plumage, black bare skin on the head and upper neck, and a conspicuous red pouch at the base of the neck. The heavy, slightly upturned bill is black. In flight, the bird shows broad wings, a long neck, and long legs extending beyond the tail. Young birds are duller and lack the strongly developed red throat pouch.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Jabiru ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and much of tropical South America, mainly east of the Andes. In Costa Rica it is highly localized, occurring chiefly in the lower Tempisque basin and northern lowlands around Caño Negro, Medio Queso, Upala, and nearby wetlands. It uses freshwater marshes, seasonal lagoons, flooded savannas, shallow ponds, drainage channels, rice fields, and other open wetlands. Nesting commonly occurs in tall trees standing in or near seasonally flooded woodland.
profile.migrationStatus: The Jabiru is generally resident or locally dispersive rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica it occurs year-round in suitable wetland regions, but numbers and records may increase seasonally, especially from roughly November to March, when water conditions and food availability change. Individuals can move between the Tempisque wetlands and northern Caribbean-slope lowlands.
