profile.breeding: Jabirus form large stick nests high in mature trees, often in floodplain or wetland woodland. Nest trees reported in Costa Rica include white guanacaste, kapok, rosewood-related species, and other large native trees. The nest may be very broad and is usually placed well above the ground on strong branches. Both adults participate in nest construction and care for the young. Breeding success depends on retaining suitable nesting trees, nearby shallow feeding areas, and quiet conditions around active nests.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of fish, including swamp eels and other small wetland fish, but also includes frogs, small reptiles, aquatic invertebrates, crustaceans, and occasionally other small animals. Jabirus usually walk slowly through shallow water or soft mud, probing and snapping with the bill. In Costa Rica they forage in marshes, lagoons, canals, and flooded agricultural fields, sometimes alone and sometimes among other waterbirds.
profile.behavior: Jabirus are usually quiet, deliberate birds that spend much of the day walking through wetlands or resting in tall trees. They may soar on broad wings during local movements and often gather where prey is concentrated. Courtship and social displays can include raised wings, bill movements, and postural displays. Despite their size, they are capable fliers. They are sensitive to disturbance near nests and may leave protected wetlands temporarily to feed in nearby farmland or artificial water bodies.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not considered strongly stable across the entire range, and declines or continuing range reductions have been reported in some areas. In Costa Rica, the population is small and has declined markedly from historical levels; published national estimates have generally placed the remaining population at fewer than 100 individuals, although the exact current number is uncertain.
conservation.threats: Important threats in Costa Rica include the loss and alteration of freshwater wetlands, drainage and conversion of marshes, contamination by pesticides and other pollutants, disturbance at nesting sites, and the removal of large mature trees used for nesting. Dependence on shallow wetlands and specific nesting trees makes the national population especially vulnerable. Feeding in agricultural landscapes can also expose birds to contaminated water and human disturbance.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore the lower Tempisque, Caño Negro, Medio Queso, and other northern lowland wetlands. Retain large native trees near marshes and safeguard active nests with an adequate disturbance buffer. Reduce pesticide and fertilizer runoff, maintain shallow-water feeding areas, and support wetland monitoring and local conservation programs. Visitors should observe Jabirus from a distance, avoid approaching nests, and report sightings through reputable bird-monitoring projects.

profile.overview: The Wood Stork (Mycteria americana) is a large New World stork and one of the most distinctive wading birds in the Americas. It has a white body, black flight feathers, a long thick bill, and a bare, dark head and neck. Wood Storks live in freshwater and brackish wetlands, where they feed in shallow water. In Costa Rica, they are associated mainly with lowland wetlands, river basins, marshes, lagoons, and coastal habitats.
profile.classification: The Wood Stork belongs to the stork family Ciconiidae and the genus Mycteria. It is the only Mycteria species found in North and Central America.
profile.identification: Adults are large, long-legged birds measuring roughly 90–115 cm in length, with a wingspan of about 150–165 cm. The body is mainly white, while the flight feathers and tail are black. The featherless head and upper neck are gray to black, and the heavy bill is dark and slightly downcurved. Juveniles have a less strongly patterned head and a paler bill. In flight, the Wood Stork holds its neck and legs extended and often soars in groups.
profile.rangeHabitat: Wood Storks range from the southeastern United States through Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and much of South America. In Costa Rica, they occur in lowlands on both slopes, especially around the Tempisque River basin and other wetlands of Guanacaste, as well as Caño Negro and the Río Frío region in the north. They use marshes, shallow lagoons, flooded savannas, mangroves, estuaries, ponds, rice fields, and forested wetlands for feeding, roosting, and nesting. Important Costa Rican sites include Palo Verde and nearby wetlands.
profile.migrationStatus: Wood Storks are generally nonmigratory, but they make local and regional movements in response to water levels and prey availability. Costa Rican birds may range between wetland complexes and coastal lowlands rather than following a fixed long-distance migration route.
profile.breeding: Wood Storks breed colonially, usually nesting in trees standing in or beside shallow water. Both adults help build a platform nest from sticks, and the female generally lays several eggs. The parents share incubation and feeding duties, bringing regurgitated food to the chicks. Colonies may include many nests and can be vulnerable to disturbance, falling water levels, and changes in wetland conditions. In Costa Rica, documented breeding has included colonies in the Tempisque drainage, including Isla Pájaros and other sites in Guanacaste, as well as the Río Frío area.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small fish, but also includes amphibians, aquatic invertebrates, reptiles, and occasionally small mammals. Wood Storks feed by wading through shallow water with the bill partly open and using sensitive touch to detect prey. When contact is made, the bill snaps shut rapidly. They feed most effectively where falling or fluctuating water levels concentrate fish and other aquatic animals in shallow pools.
profile.behavior: Wood Storks are social birds that roost, forage, soar, and nest in groups. They often spend long periods standing quietly in shallow water, then move slowly while probing with the bill. Adults and juveniles frequently soar on rising air currents, sometimes forming large, loose flocks. They are usually quiet away from colonies, where nestlings and adults may produce low calls, bill-clattering, or other sounds during interactions.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered generally stable to increasing, although trends differ among regions and local colonies.

profile.overview: The Magnificent Frigatebird is a large tropical seabird famous for its long, narrow wings, deeply forked tail, and effortless soaring. It spends much of its life in the air over coastal and offshore waters. Males are mostly black with a bright red throat pouch that they inflate during courtship, while females have a dark head and a contrasting white breast. The species is commonly seen gliding above beaches, bays, islands, and fishing areas in Costa Rica.
profile.classification: The Magnificent Frigatebird belongs to the order Suliformes and the family Fregatidae, the frigatebirds. Its scientific name is Fregata magnificens.
profile.identification: This is a very large, slender seabird with exceptionally long, angular wings and a long, forked tail. Adults are mainly black, although females have a white breast and juveniles have a white head and breast. Adult males are distinguished by their inflatable red throat pouch. The wings are often held in a shallow V while soaring, and the bird rarely flaps. Its size, narrow wings, forked tail, and buoyant flight make it distinctive along the Costa Rican coast.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs in tropical and subtropical coastal waters of the Americas, including the Pacific and Caribbean coasts of Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is regularly observed over beaches, estuaries, bays, mangroves, coastal lowlands, and offshore islands, including waters around Isla del Coco. It usually remains near the sea but may travel inland over coastal areas. Breeding colonies are generally located on low, predator-free islands or other undisturbed coastal sites with shrubs or trees for nesting.
profile.migrationStatus: Magnificent Frigatebirds are generally resident or dispersive rather than long-distance migrants. In Costa Rica they occur along both coasts throughout the year, with local and seasonal movements between coastal waters, feeding areas, and nesting colonies. Individuals may wander widely offshore, and numbers at particular sites can vary with weather, food availability, and breeding activity.
profile.breeding: Breeding takes place in colonies, usually on islands or secluded coastal sites. The male displays by inflating his red throat pouch, spreading his wings, and calling from a perch. The nest is a loose platform of sticks placed in shrubs or low trees. The female usually lays one egg, and both parents share incubation and care of the chick. Frigatebirds have a long breeding cycle, and young birds depend on adults for an extended period after hatching.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small fish, flying fish, squid, jellyfish, and other marine animals. Magnificent Frigatebirds often capture prey while gliding low over the water, taking items from the surface without landing. They also harass gulls, terns, boobies, and other seabirds until those birds drop or regurgitate food, a behavior called kleptoparasitism. Along Costa Rica’s coasts they may also feed around fishing activity and productive estuaries.
profile.behavior: This species is highly aerial and can soar for long periods on rising warm air and coastal winds. Its wings are adapted for gliding, while the forked tail provides precise control. Magnificent Frigatebirds often gather in groups above beaches, ports, fishing boats, and roosting islands. They usually avoid landing on the water because their plumage is not highly waterproof. Courtship displays are most conspicuous at colonies, where males compete for attention from passing females.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not monitored consistently enough for a precise trend, but the species remains widespread. Some breeding colonies have experienced local declines.

profile.overview: The Great Frigatebird (Fregata minor) is a large, highly aerial seabird of tropical oceans. It has extremely long, narrow wings, a deeply forked tail, and a long hooked bill. Males are mostly black with a bright red throat pouch, while females usually have dark upperparts and a white breast and belly. It spends much of its life over the open sea and returns to remote tropical islands to breed. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon offshore visitor and is easily confused with the more widespread Magnificent Frigatebird.
profile.classification: The Great Frigatebird belongs to the frigatebird family Fregatidae and the order Suliformes. Its scientific name is Fregata minor.
profile.identification: This species is recognized by its very large size, long angular wings, deeply forked tail, and effortless soaring flight. Adult males are largely black, often showing a greenish or purplish sheen, with a conspicuous red inflatable throat pouch during courtship. Females have a dark head and back with a contrasting white breast and belly. Juveniles have a pale head and breast. In Costa Rica, careful identification is important because Magnificent Frigatebirds are much more commonly encountered and can look similar at a distance.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Great Frigatebird has a broad pantropical distribution, breeding on remote islands in the Indian and Pacific oceans and in the eastern Pacific, including the Galápagos. It uses open tropical seas, coastal waters, oceanic upwellings, and offshore islands, usually roosting or nesting in trees and shrubs on predator-free islands. In Costa Rica it is not a regular breeding species; it occurs mainly as an uncommon or rare visitor over Pacific waters and near offshore areas, with occasional records along the Pacific coast. It is much scarcer than the Magnificent Frigatebird.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is not a conventional long-distance migrant. It disperses widely from breeding colonies and makes seasonal or weather-related movements over tropical oceans. In Costa Rica, individuals are best treated as irregular, nonbreeding Pacific visitors rather than a predictable migrant or resident population.
profile.breeding: Great Frigatebirds breed colonially on remote tropical islands, often in trees, shrubs, mangroves, or low vegetation. The nest is a platform of sticks, and both adults participate in incubation and care of the single chick. Breeding colonies may be used repeatedly, but reproduction is slow and young birds remain dependent for a long period. Courtship includes males inflating their red throat pouches and displaying their wings and bills. Costa Rica has no known major breeding colony of this species.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of flying fish, squid, and other marine animals taken near the sea surface. Great Frigatebirds often feed around tuna, dolphins, and other predators that drive fish upward. They also seize prey from the water or capture food near fishing activity. A notable behavior is kleptoparasitism: the frigatebird chases gulls, terns, boobies, and other seabirds until they drop or regurgitate their food, which it catches in flight.
profile.behavior: Great Frigatebirds are superb fliers and can soar for hours on thermals and wind currents with little wing flapping. They may travel far from land while foraging and can remain airborne for extended periods. They usually avoid landing on the water because their plumage is not well suited to swimming. Birds gather at roosts and breeding colonies, while males defend small display areas during courtship. Offshore sightings in Costa Rica may involve solitary birds or small groups moving along productive coastal waters.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining, but the magnitude and causes of the overall trend are not well quantified. Regional colonies may show different patterns.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include disturbance at breeding colonies, loss or degradation of nesting habitat, introduced predators on islands, human harvest in some regions, marine pollution, entanglement or interactions with fishing activities, and changes in food availability. Because Great Frigatebirds depend on remote islands and productive ocean areas, pressures affecting both nesting sites and marine ecosystems can reduce breeding success and survival.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect remote island nesting colonies and prevent introduced rats, cats, pigs, and other predators from reaching breeding sites. Reduce disturbance around colonies, support sustainable fisheries and efforts to limit seabird bycatch, and reduce marine plastic and other pollution. In Costa Rica, report unusual sightings with photographs and precise locations, especially from offshore waters, while avoiding disturbance to resting or nesting seabirds.

profile.overview: The Red-footed Booby is a tropical oceanic seabird recognized by its bright red feet, long pointed wings, and variable plumage. It is the smallest of the boobies and is unusual among its relatives because it usually nests in trees or shrubs rather than on bare ground. Red-footed Boobies spend much of their lives at sea, where they capture flying fish and other prey through agile aerial pursuit and plunge-diving. They gather in colonies on remote tropical islands.
profile.classification: The Red-footed Booby belongs to the booby and gannet family Sulidae and the order Suliformes. Its scientific name is Sula sula.
profile.identification: Adults have vivid red feet, a long bluish or pinkish bill, and a relatively slender body with long, narrow wings. Several color forms occur. The common light morph has a white head and underparts with dark wings and back, while dark morphs are mainly brown or gray-brown. Juveniles are generally darker above and paler below, with less brightly colored feet. In flight, the species appears long-winged and graceful, often gliding low over the sea.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Red-footed Booby has a pantropical distribution, breeding mainly on remote oceanic islands and coral atolls. In Costa Rica it occurs primarily in Pacific waters and around Isla del Coco, where it is associated with offshore island habitat and may breed or roost in island vegetation. It can also be encountered at sea away from land. Typical breeding habitat includes coastal woodland, shrubs, and other vegetation on predator-free or lightly disturbed islands; adults forage over pelagic and nearshore waters.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally non-migratory, but makes extensive local and post-breeding movements over the ocean. In Costa Rica, birds are associated mainly with the Pacific and Isla del Coco rather than seasonal passage along the mainland coast. Immature birds may disperse more widely than adults, and individuals can travel far from colonies while foraging.
profile.breeding: Red-footed Boobies breed colonially, usually in trees or shrubs and sometimes on grass, cliffs, or artificial structures. Courtship includes bill-raising, wing displays, calling, and showing the red feet. The pair normally lays a single egg, which both adults incubate with their feet for roughly six weeks. Both parents feed the chick, which remains dependent for several months. In Costa Rica, breeding activity on Pacific islands is generally associated with the local tropical breeding season, but timing can vary.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of flying fish, small fish, squid, and other marine animals. Red-footed Boobies often catch flying fish in the air or at the water’s surface and also dive from flight to seize prey below the surface. They may forage alone or in small groups, sometimes gathering where predatory fish drive prey toward the surface. Adults can travel considerable distances from nesting islands to find food.
profile.behavior: This is a highly aerial and social seabird. It commonly glides and circles over open water, sometimes following boats or resting on vessels far from land. At colonies, birds roost in vegetation and maintain pair bonds through repeated displays and mutual preening. Red-footed Boobies show strong attachment to breeding colonies, while young and nonbreeding birds are generally more mobile. Their relatively light build and long wings suit sustained flight over tropical seas.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not precisely known because many colonies are remote and monitoring is incomplete; available assessments generally indicate a suspected decline.
conservation.threats: Important local threats include disturbance at breeding colonies, loss or degradation of nesting vegetation, introduced predators on islands, collection of eggs or birds, and reduced food availability. Fishing activity may also cause competition for prey or accidental bycatch. Climate-related changes, including stronger storms and changing marine food conditions, may affect nesting success and foraging.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect remote island breeding colonies and their surrounding waters, prevent the introduction of rats, cats, and other predators, and keep visitors and boats away from active nesting areas. Support sustainable fisheries that reduce seabird bycatch and protect forage fish. Monitoring colonies in Costa Rica, especially around Isla del Coco, can improve knowledge of population size, breeding success, and local threats.

profile.overview: The Brown Booby (Sula leucogaster) is a large tropical seabird of warm ocean waters, rocky islands, and coastal areas. It is named for the dark brown plumage covering the head, neck, back, and wings, which contrasts with its white belly. The species is a powerful plunge-diver that captures fish and squid below the surface. Brown Boobies often rest on rocks, buoys, boats, and low offshore vegetation, and usually nest in loose colonies rather than dense aggregations.
profile.classification: The Brown Booby belongs to the booby and gannet family Sulidae and the genus Sula. Several geographic forms have been recognized, and taxonomic treatment of some eastern Pacific populations has changed in recent years.
profile.identification: Adults have dark brown upperparts and head, a sharply contrasting white belly, a long pointed bill, and relatively short legs with grayish or yellowish feet. Females are generally larger than males, while males often have a bluish facial skin area around the bill. Juveniles are browner overall, with less distinct belly contrast and pale edging on the feathers. In flight, the species shows broad wings, a relatively long tail, and strong, direct wingbeats alternating with gliding.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Brown Booby occurs widely in tropical and subtropical oceans, especially around small islands, rocky stacks, coastal cliffs, and sheltered marine waters. In Costa Rica it is a resident breeding seabird found locally along both the Pacific and Caribbean coasts, with birds using offshore islands and coastal islets for nesting and nearby waters for feeding. Pacific records include birds around Cabo Blanco and other rocky islands. It is generally associated with warm coastal seas rather than inland habitats.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is mainly resident near breeding islands and is not a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, Brown Boobies occur throughout the year, although local movements and dispersal may follow changes in food availability. Adults commonly forage offshore and may travel between neighboring islands and coastal waters.
profile.breeding: Brown Boobies usually nest on the ground on flat rock, soil, or sparsely vegetated parts of islands and islets. In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported from suitable Pacific coastal islands, including Cabo Blanco, and nesting activity may occur over an extended season, with a likely peak from about September through April. The usual clutch contains two eggs, but normally only one chick survives. Both parents incubate the eggs for roughly 40 to 44 days and continue feeding the chick after hatching.
profile.dietFeeding: Brown Boobies feed mainly on small to medium-sized fish and squid. They locate prey from the air and plunge into the sea, sometimes diving from considerable height. Birds may forage alone, in pairs, or in groups, especially where schools of fish are concentrated. They can also gather around predatory fish, fishing activity, or mixed seabird feeding groups. Compared with some other boobies, they often forage relatively close to shore.
profile.behavior: This species spends much of its time at sea but regularly returns to islands, rocks, boats, pilings, and other elevated resting sites. It is often social around roosts and nesting areas, although pairs generally defend small territories around their nests. Brown Boobies are strong fliers and capable divers. Young birds may remain near the colony after fledging and continue receiving food from their parents while learning to forage independently.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable, although precise population size and long-term trends are not well known in all regions.

profile.overview: The Cocos Booby (Sula brewsteri) is a large tropical seabird of the eastern Pacific Ocean. It was formerly treated as a geographic form of the Brown Booby but is now recognized as a separate species by several taxonomic authorities. It breeds colonially on oceanic and coastal islands, including islands associated with Costa Rica, and spends much of its time over offshore waters. Its name refers to the important population on Cocos Island, Costa Rica.
profile.classification: The Cocos Booby belongs to the booby and gannet family Sulidae and the genus Sula. It includes geographically distinct populations in the eastern Pacific, including the nominate form in the Gulf of California and western Mexico and the Central and South American form Sula brewsteri etesiaca.
profile.identification: This is a large, long-winged seabird with dark brown upperparts, white underparts, a dark head and neck, and a relatively slender, pointed bill. Adult males often show frosty white on the forehead, crown, or neck, while females and immature birds may have darker heads. The bill is typically yellow-based with pinkish tones toward the tip. Compared with Brown Boobies of other regions, Cocos Boobies often show more dark markings across the underwing coverts and a slimmer bill. Identification can be difficult, especially for females and young birds.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Cocos Booby occurs across the tropical and subtropical eastern Pacific, from the Gulf of California and islands off western Mexico south through Central America to Colombia. In Costa Rica it is a breeding and marine species associated especially with Cocos Island and other Pacific offshore islands or waters. Birds may also be seen along the Pacific coast and over the Gulf of Nicoya, although many individuals remain offshore. It nests on rocky or vegetated islands and forages over pelagic and nearshore ocean waters.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally resident near breeding colonies but disperses widely over the eastern Pacific. In Costa Rica, birds occur year-round around breeding islands such as Cocos Island and in surrounding offshore waters; additional individuals may range along the Pacific coast and Gulf of Nicoya. It is not considered a regular long-distance migrant, although nonbreeding and immature birds can travel far from colonies.
profile.breeding: Cocos Boobies breed colonially on predator-free islands, rocky islets, and coastal islands. The nest is a simple platform made from sticks, vegetation, and other available material, usually placed on the ground or in low vegetation. Both parents share incubation and chick care. Breeding timing varies among colonies, and published information for Costa Rican colonies is limited. Cocos Island and other Costa Rican Pacific islands provide important nesting habitat, while nearby ocean waters supply food for adults and young.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small to medium marine fish, including flying fish and other schooling species, with squid and other marine prey also taken. Cocos Boobies usually hunt by plunge-diving from flight, entering the water at speed and pursuing prey near the surface or at moderate depth. They may forage singly or in loose groups and can associate with other seabirds where fish are concentrated.
profile.behavior: Cocos Boobies are powerful fliers that spend much of the day traveling between colonies, roosts, and feeding areas. They rest on rocks, cliffs, or vegetation and show strong attachment to established breeding colonies. During the breeding season, adults defend small areas around nests and use displays, calls, and bill movements in courtship and territorial interactions. Young birds and nonbreeding individuals may wander widely across the Pacific before returning to breeding areas.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered relatively large and not currently believed to be declining at a rate that would qualify the species for a threatened category. Local colonies may nevertheless fluctuate with food availability, weather, disturbance, and breeding success.
conservation.threats: Potential concerns include disturbance at breeding colonies, introduced predators on islands, entanglement or accidental capture in fishing gear, plastic pollution, and reductions in marine prey caused by overfishing or changing ocean conditions. These pressures may be particularly important for small or isolated colonies in Costa Rica.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect Costa Rica’s Pacific islands and surrounding marine feeding areas, prevent the introduction of rats and other predators to nesting islands, and keep people and boats away from active colonies. Responsible fishing practices, reduction of plastic waste, and long-term monitoring of Cocos Booby colonies and offshore abundance can help identify and reduce emerging threats.

profile.overview: The Masked Booby is a large tropical seabird found over warm oceans worldwide. It is named for the dark skin around the eyes and bill. Adults are powerful fliers and spectacular plunge-divers that capture fish and squid from the sea. They spend most of their lives offshore and return to small tropical islands to breed in colonies. In Costa Rica, the species is associated mainly with the Pacific Ocean and offshore islands, especially Isla del Coco.
profile.classification: The Masked Booby belongs to the booby and gannet family Sulidae and the order Suliformes. Its scientific name is Sula dactylatra.
profile.identification: Adults are large, long-winged seabirds with mostly white plumage, black flight feathers, a black tail, and a conspicuous dark mask at the base of the stout yellow bill. The head and body are cleaner white than those of Brown Boobies. Juveniles and immatures are browner overall, with pale or mottled underparts that gradually become whiter. In flight, the broad black trailing edge of the wings and black tail are useful identification marks. It is generally silent at sea.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs across tropical and subtropical oceans, breeding on remote, low islands, coral atolls, and rocky volcanic islands. It forages over pelagic and coastal waters, often far from land. In Costa Rica, Masked Boobies occur in Pacific waters and are associated with Isla del Coco, where small numbers have been reported breeding or attempting to breed. They may also be encountered offshore around other Pacific islands and during boat-based seabird surveys, but they are not a typical mainland coastal bird.
profile.migrationStatus: Masked Boobies are mainly resident near breeding islands rather than long-distance migrants. After breeding, adults and young may disperse widely across nearby tropical waters. In Costa Rica, individuals associated with Isla del Coco can occur year-round, while birds seen farther offshore may reflect local or post-breeding dispersal rather than regular seasonal migration.
profile.breeding: Masked Boobies breed colonially on open ground, usually on flat or gently sloping island surfaces with little vegetation. The nest is a shallow scrape that may be surrounded by stones, shells, or other objects. The female usually lays one or two eggs, but normally only one chick is raised because the older chick commonly outcompetes or ejects the younger one. Both parents incubate with their feet and feed the chick. Breeding seasons vary among colonies; Costa Rican breeding activity is associated with Isla del Coco.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small to medium-sized marine fish and squid, with occasional other marine prey. Masked Boobies locate prey while flying over the ocean and capture it by plunging from the air, sometimes entering the water at high speed. They may forage singly or in small groups, and feeding activity can occur near schools of fish, tuna, or other predators that drive prey toward the surface.
profile.behavior: Masked Boobies are highly aerial and spend much of their time flying over open water. They use strong, direct wingbeats mixed with gliding and can travel substantial distances from breeding colonies. Courtship includes wing displays, head movements, calling, and presenting nesting material. On land they walk with a deliberate, somewhat awkward gait, but they are agile in the air and water. Birds commonly rest on rocky shores, low islands, boats, or other exposed structures.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not reliably quantified, but no major range-wide decline is established for the species.

profile.overview: The Nazca Booby (Sula granti) is a large tropical seabird of the eastern Pacific Ocean. It is closely related to the Masked Booby but is recognized as a separate species. Nazca Boobies spend most of their lives at sea, returning to isolated oceanic islands to breed in dense colonies. They are powerful fliers and plunge-divers that feed mainly on fish and squid captured in offshore waters.
profile.classification: The Nazca Booby belongs to the booby and gannet family Sulidae, within the order Suliformes. It was formerly treated as a subspecies of the Masked Booby but is now recognized as a distinct species.
profile.identification: Adults are large seabirds with a mostly white body, dark brown to black wings and tail, and a conspicuous black facial mask around the eyes and bill. The long, pointed bill is usually orange, pinkish, or yellowish, while the feet are gray. Immature birds are browner overall and develop adult plumage gradually. In Costa Rica, careful identification is important because Nazca Boobies can resemble Masked, Cocos, and Blue-footed Boobies.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species is distributed across the tropical eastern Pacific, breeding on isolated islands including the Galápagos, Malpelo, Clipperton, and Cocos Island. In Costa Rica, it is a breeding seabird of Isla del Coco and nearby rocky islets, where it uses open ground and cliff-top or coastal nesting sites. It also forages widely in offshore Pacific waters. Individuals have occasionally been recorded in waters off the mainland and, rarely, in the Caribbean side of Costa Rica.
profile.migrationStatus: The Nazca Booby is not a regular long-distance migrant. Adults generally remain associated with breeding islands and nearby oceanic waters, while juveniles and nonbreeding birds disperse more widely. In Costa Rica, it is resident at Isla del Coco but can occur irregularly offshore, with occasional vagrant records beyond the Pacific, including Caribbean waters.
profile.breeding: Nazca Boobies breed colonially on remote tropical islands, usually in open, sparsely vegetated terrain. They defend small territories around a nest made from loose vegetation, soil, and other available material. The female normally lays one egg, and both parents share incubation and care of the chick. Breeding timing varies among colonies and may be influenced by food availability. Colonies on Cocos Island form part of the species' small Central American breeding range.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small to medium-sized marine fish, along with squid and other available oceanic prey. Nazca Boobies usually forage offshore, often several kilometers from breeding colonies. They locate prey from the air and dive steeply into the water, sometimes entering at high speed from considerable height. Adults may also take advantage of tuna and other predatory fish that drive schooling prey toward the surface.
profile.behavior: Nazca Boobies are highly aerial seabirds that spend much of the day soaring, traveling, and searching for prey over open ocean. They are strongly colonial during breeding but defend space around their nests with displays, calls, bill movements, and aggressive postures. At sea they may forage alone or in loose groups, particularly where large predatory fish concentrate prey. Young birds disperse widely after fledging before returning to breeding areas.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains widely distributed and locally abundant at several major colonies.

profile.overview: The Blue-footed Booby is a medium-sized Pacific seabird famous for its bright blue feet and dramatic plunge-diving. It feeds mainly on small fish captured after dropping from the air into the sea. The species nests on open ground, often on islands and coastal sites, and is especially associated with the eastern Pacific. Its breeding colonies are vulnerable to changes in marine food supplies, although the species remains widespread and globally assessed as Least Concern.
profile.classification: The Blue-footed Booby belongs to the family Sulidae, which includes boobies and gannets. Its scientific name is Sula nebouxii, and two commonly recognized subspecies occur in the eastern Pacific.
profile.identification: Adults have a long, pointed bill, a streamlined body, long narrow wings, and contrasting dark brown wings with a white head, neck, breast, and underside. The large feet are vivid blue, with the color usually stronger in adults and males. Juveniles are browner and more muted, with pale or grayish feet. In flight, the species shows broad dark wings and a white body. Its direct plunge-diving behavior is also a useful field clue.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Blue-footed Booby occurs along the Pacific coast and offshore islands from the Gulf of California and western Mexico southward to Peru, including the Galápagos region. In Costa Rica, it is found mainly along the Pacific coast, around offshore islands, and in surrounding marine waters; it is also associated with Isla del Coco, where breeding has been reported. It uses open ocean for feeding and rocky, sandy, or sparsely vegetated coastal ground for resting and nesting.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is not a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica it is generally present year-round in Pacific marine waters and around suitable coastal islands, although individuals may move locally or disperse according to breeding activity and the availability of schooling fish.
profile.breeding: Blue-footed Boobies usually nest colonially or in loose groups on open ground, where their droppings may leave conspicuous white-stained areas. Both parents share incubation and chick care. The species commonly lays two or three eggs, but sibling competition can result in only one chick surviving. Courtship includes raised-foot displays, wing movements, head and bill gestures, and calling. In Costa Rica, breeding is associated with suitable Pacific islands and undisturbed coastal sites, including Isla del Coco.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of small schooling fish, including anchovies, sardines, and other nearshore or pelagic species. It locates prey from the air and dives steeply, sometimes singly and sometimes in coordinated groups. The bird can also seize fish near the surface. Feeding success depends strongly on the abundance and accessibility of small fish in surrounding marine waters.
profile.behavior: Blue-footed Boobies are highly aerial and marine, spending much of their time flying, fishing, or resting on exposed rocks and shorelines. They often travel in groups and may perform spectacular synchronized plunge dives when fish are concentrated. On land they walk with a distinctive, somewhat awkward posture. Adults use foot displays and vocalizations during courtship and territorial interactions, while nesting birds defend the immediate area around their nest.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered large, but available evidence indicates that it may be declining in parts of its range. The scale and causes of the overall trend remain uncertain.
conservation.threats: Important potential threats include reductions in small schooling fish caused by changing ocean conditions, climate variability, and overfishing. Disturbance at breeding colonies, accidental capture in fishing gear, introduced predators on islands, pollution, and extreme weather can also affect local populations.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect Pacific coastal waters and offshore islands, maintain sustainable fisheries, and reduce disturbance around nesting colonies. Visitors should keep well away from nesting birds, avoid landing on restricted breeding sites, prevent litter and plastic from entering the sea, and support marine protected areas and responsible wildlife monitoring.

profile.overview: The Peruvian Booby (Sula variegata) is a highly social seabird of the cool, nutrient-rich Humboldt Current along the Pacific coast of South America. It is strongly associated with anchovy-rich marine waters and breeds in large colonies on coastal islands and cliffs. Most of its population occurs from northern Peru to central Chile, with occasional northward movements or vagrancy reaching farther along the Pacific coast, including rare records in Costa Rica.
profile.classification: The Peruvian Booby belongs to the family Sulidae, which includes boobies and gannets, and the genus Sula. It is a monotypic species without currently recognized subspecies.
profile.identification: This is a large, long-winged booby with a white head, neck, breast, and belly, contrasting with dark brown to black upperparts and wing margins. Adults have a grayish bill, dark facial skin, and gray feet. The plumage often shows white spotting or scaling on the dark wing coverts. In flight, it appears sleek and strongly contrasting black and white. It can resemble Blue-footed or other dark-backed boobies, but its gray feet and mostly coastal South American distribution are useful clues.
profile.rangeHabitat: The main range follows the Pacific coast from southwestern Ecuador and northern Peru southward through Chile to the Chiloé region. It uses cold, productive coastal waters, usually close to shore, where it plunge-dives for schooling fish. Breeding colonies are located on offshore islands, rocky shores, cliffs, and sloping guano-covered terrain. In Costa Rica it is not a regular resident or breeder; it is a very rare visitor or vagrant, chiefly associated with the Pacific coast and offshore waters. Records should be carefully documented because the species is uncommon there.
profile.migrationStatus: Generally sedentary or dispersive rather than a long-distance migrant. Individuals may move widely in response to changes in prey availability, especially during El Niño conditions. In Costa Rica it occurs only exceptionally as a rare Pacific-coast or offshore vagrant, with no established seasonal population known.
profile.breeding: Peruvian Boobies breed colonially, often in dense aggregations on bare islands, rocky slopes, and cliff ledges. Nesting material commonly includes guano, small stones, vegetation, and other debris. Both adults share incubation and chick-rearing duties. Usually several eggs may be laid, although clutch size and breeding success vary with food availability. Incubation lasts about six weeks, and young remain dependent in the nest for several months before fledging. Breeding is concentrated in Peru and Chile, not Costa Rica.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small schooling marine fish, especially Peruvian anchoveta, with sardines and other pelagic fish also taken. The species forages by flying over the sea and diving steeply into the water, often entering at high speed. It commonly feeds in groups where prey schools are concentrated and may forage within a few kilometers of breeding colonies, although birds can travel farther when food is scarce.
profile.behavior: This is a strongly gregarious seabird that rests, travels, and feeds in groups. Birds often fly low over the sea in lines or loose formations and gather in large colonies during breeding. Territorial displays at nest sites include head movements, pointing postures, threats, and bill jabbing. Peruvian Boobies are powerful fliers and capable divers. Their movements and breeding success are closely linked to ocean conditions and the availability of anchovy and other schooling fish.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly established. Numbers may vary markedly between years because food supply, ocean temperature, and breeding conditions affect colony attendance and reproductive success.

profile.overview: The Anhinga is a long-necked waterbird of the warmer parts of the Americas. It is often called a snakebird because it swims with only its slender neck and head above the surface. Unlike many waterbirds, its feathers are not highly waterproof, allowing it to dive efficiently but requiring frequent wing-spreading to dry. Anhingas hunt mainly by swimming underwater and stabbing fish with their sharp, pointed bills.
profile.classification: The Anhinga belongs to the order Suliformes and family Anhingidae. Its scientific name is Anhinga anhinga.
profile.identification: Anhingas are large, slim waterbirds with very long necks, pointed bills, broad wings, and long tails. Adult males are mostly glossy black, with striking silvery-white markings on the wings and back. Females and immature birds have brown bodies and paler brown heads and necks. The species can be distinguished from cormorants by its sharply pointed bill, longer neck and tail, and habit of swimming low in the water. It often perches with its wings spread to dry.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Anhinga occurs from the southern United States through Mexico and Central America to much of South America and the Caribbean. In Costa Rica it is a widespread but generally uncommon resident of the lowlands on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes. It uses freshwater lakes, slow rivers, marshes, lagoons, ponds, reservoirs, mangroves, and quiet coastal wetlands. Important Costa Rican areas include the Tempisque and Bebedero lowlands, Río Frío, and Caño Negro, where suitable nesting and feeding wetlands support higher numbers.
profile.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Anhinga is considered primarily resident and can occur throughout the year. Northern populations are partly migratory, but individuals in Costa Rica generally do not undertake regular long-distance seasonal movements. Local movements may occur when water levels, prey availability, or wetland conditions change.
profile.breeding: Anhingas usually nest in trees or shrubs standing near or over water, sometimes alone and sometimes in small mixed colonies with other waterbirds. The nest is a shallow platform made from sticks and leafy material. A typical clutch contains about three to five pale bluish or greenish eggs. In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported mainly in lowland wetlands, with nesting activity extending through much of the year and often increasing during the wetter months.
profile.dietFeeding: The Anhinga feeds chiefly on fish, but it also takes aquatic insects, crustaceans, amphibians, and occasionally other small aquatic animals. It hunts by diving and swimming underwater, using its powerful feet for propulsion and its pointed bill to spear or seize prey. After feeding, it commonly rests on exposed branches, snags, or mangrove limbs, where it spreads its wings to dry.
profile.behavior: Anhingas are strong swimmers and divers but are less buoyant than ducks because their feathers become waterlogged. They may swim with only the head and neck visible, then dive suddenly when approaching prey. They are often seen singly or in small groups, although larger gatherings may form near productive wetlands or nesting sites. Their long necks may be held in an S-shape, and they sometimes soar on rising air currents.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable to increasing, although local numbers may vary with wetland conditions and habitat quality.

profile.overview: The Neotropic Cormorant is a medium-sized, dark waterbird found from the southern United States through Central and South America. It is strongly associated with freshwater and coastal wetlands, where it swims, dives, and rests on exposed branches, rocks, or shores. Although its plumage is mostly black, adults often show a narrow white border around the facial skin and a small white throat patch. The species is adaptable and commonly occurs near human-modified wetlands.
profile.classification: The Neotropic Cormorant belongs to the cormorant family Phalacrocoracidae. It was formerly often placed in the genus Phalacrocorax but is now generally treated as Nannopterum brasilianum.
profile.identification: Adults are medium-sized, slender cormorants with glossy black plumage, a long neck, a fairly small head, and a long, hooked bill. The facial skin is yellowish, with a narrow white outline that is especially noticeable at close range. In flight, the species shows broad wings and a long tail. Juveniles are browner and paler below. It can be distinguished from larger cormorants by its smaller size and relatively compact build.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Neotropic Cormorant ranges from the southern United States and Mexico through Central America and much of South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs in both coastal and inland lowlands, using estuaries, mangroves, lagoons, reservoirs, rivers, fishponds, and other calm or slow-moving waters. It may be seen on both the Pacific and Caribbean sides, although local abundance varies with wetland conditions and food availability. It often roosts on trees, snags, pilings, rocks, and mudbanks.
profile.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Neotropic Cormorant is generally considered a resident or regular year-round species rather than a long-distance migrant. Individuals may make local or seasonal movements among wetlands, rivers, reservoirs, estuaries, and coastal areas in response to water levels, breeding conditions, and prey availability. Birds from more northern populations can be more mobile.
profile.breeding: Breeding usually takes place in colonies, often with other waterbirds. The species builds a platform nest from sticks in trees, shrubs, mangroves, or other vegetation near water, and may also nest on islands or protected shoreline sites. Both adults share incubation and care for the young. Nesting timing varies across its broad range and is influenced by rainfall, water conditions, and food supply. In Costa Rica, breeding may occur when suitable wetland and colony conditions are available.
profile.dietFeeding: The Neotropic Cormorant feeds mainly on fish, but also takes crustaceans, amphibians, aquatic insects, and other small aquatic animals. It usually captures prey by diving and pursuing it underwater, using its feet for propulsion. Birds may forage alone or in groups, sometimes cooperating to concentrate fish. After feeding, they commonly perch with wings spread to dry their plumage.
profile.behavior: This cormorant is an active swimmer and diver that spends much of the day feeding or resting near water. It frequently perches with its wings extended, a behavior that helps dry the plumage. Neotropic Cormorants are social at roosts and breeding colonies and may travel in lines or loose groups between feeding and resting areas. They are capable fliers and often commute between wetlands, rivers, reservoirs, and coastal habitats.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly established; regional populations may increase or decrease depending on wetland condition, persecution, disturbance, and food availability.

profile.overview: The White Ibis (Eudocimus albus) is a sociable wading bird of wetlands, river margins, mangroves, estuaries, and shallow coastal waters. It probes soft mud and shallow water with its long, down-curved bill to find aquatic prey. Adults are mostly white with black wing tips, while young birds are brown and white. In Costa Rica, it is a resident species most strongly associated with the Gulf of Nicoya and the Tempisque River basin.
profile.classification: The White Ibis belongs to the ibis and spoonbill family, Threskiornithidae, in the order Pelecaniformes. Its scientific name is Eudocimus albus.
profile.identification: Adults are medium to large white wading birds with black tips on the flight feathers, a long red bill that curves downward, red facial skin, and pinkish-red legs. The eyes are pale blue to gray-blue. Juveniles are noticeably brown on the head, neck, back, and upper wings, with increasing white plumage as they mature. In flight, the black wing tips contrast clearly with the white wings and body.
profile.rangeHabitat: The White Ibis occurs from the southeastern United States and Mexico through Central America and parts of northern South America and the Caribbean. In Costa Rica it is a resident, concentrated especially around the Gulf of Nicoya and the Tempisque River basin, including mangroves, estuaries, lagoons, shallow lakes, river edges, and seasonally flooded wetlands. It is also found locally along the Pacific coast and seasonally in some lowland wetlands, but is uncommon or sporadic in many other areas.
profile.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the White Ibis is generally considered resident rather than a regular long-distance migrant. It may make local or seasonal movements in response to rainfall, flooding, water depth, and food availability. Northern populations are more migratory, but Costa Rican birds are primarily associated with permanent or seasonally suitable lowland wetlands.
profile.breeding: White Ibises breed colonially, often nesting with other wading birds in trees or mangrove vegetation near wetlands. In Costa Rica, breeding is documented at Isla Pájaros in the Tempisque River. The nesting season begins near the start of the rainy season, with activity commonly peaking around June. The nest is a bulky platform of sticks and plant material, and the usual clutch contains about two pale eggs marked with brownish or greenish spotting.
profile.dietFeeding: The White Ibis eats aquatic and wetland animals, including crayfish, crabs, small fish, frogs, insects, worms, snails, and other invertebrates. It usually feeds by walking slowly through shallow water or wet mud and probing with its sensitive bill. Groups may forage together in marshes, mangrove margins, flooded fields, and riverbanks, where changing water levels expose prey.
profile.behavior: This is a highly social species that commonly feeds, roosts, and flies in flocks. White Ibises use tactile feeding, sweeping or thrusting the bill through mud and shallow water rather than relying mainly on sight. They often gather at communal roosts and nesting colonies. Their flight consists of rapid wingbeats mixed with short glides, and they may travel considerable distances between feeding and roosting sites.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable to increasing overall, although local populations may vary with wetland conditions and habitat changes.

profile.overview: The Glossy Ibis (Plegadis falcinellus) is a medium-sized wading bird recognized by its long, down-curved bill and dark plumage that shines green, purple, and bronze in good light. It is widespread across parts of Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia, and the Americas. The species uses shallow wetlands and often feeds in small groups, probing soft mud for aquatic invertebrates and other prey. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon to rare visitor rather than a regular resident.
profile.classification: The Glossy Ibis belongs to the ibis and spoonbill family, Threskiornithidae, within the order Pelecaniformes. Its scientific name is Plegadis falcinellus.
profile.identification: Adults are about 48–66 cm long, with a long, slender, decurved bill, long legs, and a relatively short tail. The body appears nearly black at a distance but shows rich chestnut, bronze, green, and purple iridescence at close range. Breeding adults develop brighter facial colors and a narrow pale border around the facial skin. Juveniles and nonbreeding birds are duller brown. In Costa Rica, careful identification is important because the species may be confused with other dark ibises, although White-faced Ibis is not a regularly established Costa Rican species.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Glossy Ibis has a very broad, discontinuous distribution across the Old World and parts of the Americas. It occupies freshwater marshes, seasonal ponds, flooded grassland, rice fields, mangroves, estuaries, mudflats, and other shallow wetlands. In Costa Rica it is recorded as an uncommon or rare visitor, with occurrences reported particularly from wetland areas in the northwestern Pacific lowlands. It is not known as a widespread breeding species in the country, and sightings are generally localized and opportunistic.
profile.migrationStatus: Globally, many populations are migratory or partly migratory, while others are resident or nomadic. In Costa Rica, the Glossy Ibis is best treated as an uncommon to rare migrant or vagrant, with no evidence that it forms a regular resident population.
profile.breeding: Glossy Ibises usually breed colonially, often alongside herons, egrets, and other waterbirds. The nest is a bulky platform made from sticks and wetland vegetation, placed in low shrubs, trees, reeds, mangroves, or sometimes on the ground on an island. Both adults help build the nest and care for the young. Clutch size is commonly three or four eggs, and nesting is closely associated with wetlands that provide shallow feeding areas and safe nesting cover. Regular breeding in Costa Rica has not been established.
profile.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly in shallow water and soft mud, using its long curved bill to probe and sweep through the substrate. Food includes aquatic insects, insect larvae, crustaceans, mollusks, worms, small fish, frogs, tadpoles, and occasionally small reptiles or other animals. It may also forage in flooded fields and wet grassland. Glossy Ibises often feed methodically while walking, sometimes in flocks, and may take advantage of temporarily flooded habitats.
profile.behavior: Glossy Ibises are usually social outside the breeding season and may gather in small or large flocks. They walk through shallow water or wet vegetation while probing for prey, and they commonly roost communally in trees, reeds, or mangroves. In flight they extend the neck and show broad, rounded wings, alternating rapid wingbeats with gliding. Their calls are generally low, guttural grunts or croaks, especially when birds are gathered at nesting or roosting sites.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered large, and available assessments do not indicate a globally threatened status. Some regional populations are increasing or expanding, although local trends may differ.

profile.overview: The White-faced Ibis is a medium-sized wading bird with a long, downcurved bill and dark, glossy plumage that can show green, bronze, and purple tones. Adults usually have a pale feathered border around the face and reddish eyes, while immature birds are duller and lack the strongly contrasting facial pattern. It feeds in shallow wetlands, wet grasslands, rice fields, and other open habitats where it probes soft mud for aquatic and terrestrial prey.
profile.classification: The White-faced Ibis is a member of the ibis and spoonbill family, Threskiornithidae, and the genus Plegadis. It is closely related to the Glossy Ibis and Puna Ibis.
profile.identification: This ibis is about 46–56 cm long, with a wingspan of roughly 80–95 cm. Its body is slender, with long legs and a long, decurved bill. In good light, adults appear dark chestnut or purplish-brown with a greenish sheen, and the pale facial border is especially noticeable around the lores and cheeks. The legs are usually reddish or pinkish. Immatures are browner, less glossy, and have a less distinct pale face.
profile.rangeHabitat: The White-faced Ibis breeds mainly in western and central North America and in parts of southern South America. It uses freshwater marshes, shallow lakes, wet meadows, flooded fields, rice fields, and seasonally wet grasslands. In Costa Rica it is a scarce or uncommon visitor, generally recorded during the nonbreeding season rather than as a resident or breeding species. Sightings are most likely in suitable lowland wetlands and open flooded areas, especially on the Pacific slope, although records may be localized and irregular.
profile.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the White-faced Ibis is primarily a nonbreeding migrant and occasional winter visitor. It is not known as a regular breeding species there. Some records may involve dispersing or wandering birds, so its occurrence is generally considered uncommon and local rather than widespread.
profile.breeding: White-faced Ibises usually breed colonially in freshwater marshes, shallow lakes, wet meadows, and sometimes irrigated agricultural landscapes. Nests are commonly built above water in emergent vegetation such as bulrushes, cattails, or reeds. The female typically lays several eggs, and both adults help incubate them and feed the young. Breeding timing varies across the broad range, but colonies generally form during the local spring and summer wetland season.
profile.dietFeeding: The species feeds by walking through shallow water, mud, and wet vegetation while probing with its bill. Its diet includes insects, aquatic invertebrates, crayfish, small fish, frogs, and other small vertebrates. It also takes earthworms and other soil animals in wet grasslands and agricultural fields. White-faced Ibises often forage in groups, especially where shallow water or recently flooded ground provides concentrated food.
profile.behavior: White-faced Ibises are social and are often seen in flocks while feeding, roosting, or migrating. They fly with steady wingbeats in lines or loose formations and commonly roost communally in marsh vegetation or trees. Foraging birds walk actively through shallow water and mud, repeatedly inserting the bill to locate prey. They may associate with other ibis species, herons, egrets, and shorebirds in productive wetlands.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered stable to increasing, but some local populations may be affected by wetland loss, drought, changing water management, and degradation of breeding or stopover sites.

profile.overview: The Green Ibis (Mesembrinibis cayennensis), also called the Cayenne Ibis, is a dark, forest-associated wading bird of the ibis family. Its plumage can show green, bronze, and blue iridescence in good light, although birds in shaded habitats often appear nearly black. Unlike many ibises, it is usually secretive and is most often encountered alone or in pairs along quiet streams, forest swamps, muddy paths, and wet lowland woodland.
profile.classification: The Green Ibis belongs to the ibis and spoonbill family Threskiornithidae and is the only living species in the genus Mesembrinibis. It is classified in the order Pelecaniformes.
profile.identification: This medium-sized ibis has an overall dark greenish-black appearance with subtle metallic green or bronze reflections, especially on the neck, breast, and upperparts. It has a long, slender, downcurved bill that is greenish with a paler or yellowish tip, and relatively short, dull green legs. The body looks compact and heavy compared with the more slender Glossy Ibis. In Costa Rica, its quiet, forested wetland habitat and dark plumage help distinguish it from more open-country ibises.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Green Ibis ranges from eastern Honduras and Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama, then across much of tropical South America to northern Argentina and Paraguay. It uses swampy forest, wooded marshes, flooded woodland, forested river margins, gallery forest, muddy pools, and occasionally mangrove-edge wetlands, mainly in the lowlands. In Costa Rica it is a resident but localized species, occurring chiefly in Caribbean-slope lowlands, including the Río Frío area and coastal wetlands north and south of Limón. It may also occur locally in suitable forested wetlands around Sarapiquí.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally resident in Costa Rica and across most of its range. Regular long-distance migration is not known, although birds may make short local or seasonal movements, particularly as water levels and feeding conditions change.
profile.breeding: The Green Ibis breeds in wooded wetlands and along forested waterways, where it places its nest in vegetation, usually above or near water. Available observations indicate that nesting activity can occur in Costa Rica, including the Sarapiquí region. The nest is a platform made from sticks and other plant material. Detailed information on clutch size, incubation, and parental care is limited for this secretive species, and breeding timing may vary with local rainfall and flooding patterns.
profile.dietFeeding: It feeds mainly in shallow water, wet mud, leaf litter, and saturated ground. The curved bill is used to probe and sweep through soft substrate for invertebrates such as insects, worms, and snails. It may also take small aquatic animals, including amphibians or fish, as well as some plant material. Feeding usually takes place along quiet forest streams, marsh edges, muddy trails, and openings beside wooded wetlands.
profile.behavior: Green Ibises are generally shy and less social than many other ibises. They are most often seen singly or in pairs, though small groups may gather where food is concentrated. They frequently remain under forest cover and can be difficult to detect until they move into a muddy opening or wetland margin. Activity is often greatest around dawn and dusk, when their rolling calls may reveal their presence. Their flight is strong but somewhat heavy, with the neck extended.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to be undergoing a sufficiently rapid decline to qualify for a threatened category. Precise population estimates and detailed national trend information are limited, especially for localized populations in Central America.

profile.overview: The Bare-faced Ibis (Phimosus infuscatus) is a medium-sized South American ibis recognized by its dark plumage, long reddish bill, and bare red skin around the face and throat. It usually lives in open wetlands, flooded grasslands, rice fields, marshes, wet pastures, and the edges of shallow water. The species often feeds in small groups by probing soft mud and wet ground. In Costa Rica, it is considered a rare or accidental visitor rather than a regularly occurring resident.
profile.classification: The Bare-faced Ibis belongs to the ibis and spoonbill family Threskiornithidae and the order Pelecaniformes. It is the only species in the genus Phimosus.
profile.identification: This ibis is about 46–56 centimeters long. Adults are largely dark brown to blackish, often showing a subtle greenish or purplish sheen in good light. The long bill is strongly downcurved, reddish near the base and darker toward the tip. The face and throat are mostly bare and deep red, creating the species’ distinctive name. The legs are generally reddish. Juveniles are duller and may have less brightly colored bare facial skin.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Bare-faced Ibis is native mainly to northern, central, and eastern South America, where it occupies wet grasslands, marshes, rice fields, flooded pastures, shallow ponds, muddy stream margins, ditches, and the edges of rivers and lagoons. It is most closely associated with open, low-lying habitats rather than dense forest. In Costa Rica, it is listed as rare or accidental, so records are unusual and do not indicate an established national population. Any occurrence is best treated as a vagrant or exceptional visitor.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is generally regarded as resident or locally mobile across much of its South American range. Long-distance migration is not well documented, but movements related to rainfall and changing water conditions occur. In Costa Rica, it is a rare or accidental visitor, with no reliable evidence of regular seasonal migration or a resident breeding population.
profile.breeding: Bare-faced Ibises usually breed in colonies or loose groups, often near wetlands. They build platform-like nests from sticks and plant material in trees, shrubs, reedbeds, or other vegetation near water. The female commonly lays several eggs, and both adults participate in incubation and care of the young. Breeding timing varies across the range and is often associated with local rainfall and water conditions. No regular breeding population is reliably documented in Costa Rica.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet includes insects, insect larvae, earthworms, other invertebrates, small aquatic animals, and occasionally small vertebrates or carrion. The ibis usually walks through shallow water, mud, flooded grassland, or wet pasture while probing with its downcurved bill. It may feed singly or in groups and can forage in human-modified wetlands such as rice fields, drainage areas, and seasonally flooded farmland.
profile.behavior: Bare-faced Ibises are active, social foragers that often gather in small flocks, especially where food is concentrated. They walk steadily while searching the ground and shallow water, using touch as well as sight to locate prey. They roost in trees or dense vegetation and may travel between feeding and roosting sites as water levels change. Their flight is strong and direct, with the neck extended and broad wings beating steadily.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable, although precise population estimates are limited.

profile.overview: The Roseate Spoonbill (Platalea ajaja) is a large, social wading bird recognized by its pink plumage and broad, spoon-shaped bill. It belongs to the ibis and spoonbill family and lives in shallow wetlands across the Americas. The species sweeps its partly open bill from side to side through water and soft mud to locate prey. Its pink coloration develops with age and is influenced by pigments in its diet.
profile.classification: The Roseate Spoonbill belongs to the family Threskiornithidae, which includes ibises and spoonbills. It is the only spoonbill species native to the Americas.
profile.identification: Adults have a mostly pink body, white neck and upper back, bright red shoulder and wing areas, and a long, flattened bill with a rounded spoon-shaped tip. The bare head is pale greenish to yellowish, becoming brighter during the breeding season. Juveniles are duller and less intensely colored. The species is distinguished from flamingos by its much broader bill, shorter neck, and more compact wading-bird shape.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Roseate Spoonbill occurs from the southern United States through Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and much of South America. In Costa Rica it is locally common but unevenly distributed, especially around the Tempisque River basin, the Gulf of Nicoya, and Río Frío. It also occurs in smaller numbers along other Pacific coastal wetlands and is rare or sporadic on the Caribbean slope and in the Central Valley. Typical habitats include mangroves, estuaries, tidal flats, marshes, lagoons, and shallow freshwater wetlands.
profile.migrationStatus: Generally resident or locally mobile, rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, seasonal movements are linked mainly to changing water levels and wetland conditions; numbers may vary between sites during the wet and dry seasons.
profile.breeding: Roseate Spoonbills nest colonially, often with herons, egrets, ibises, or other wading birds. The nest is a sturdy platform or cup of sticks placed in mangroves or other trees above water. Both adults incubate the eggs and care for the young. In Costa Rica, breeding is especially associated with wetlands of the Tempisque basin, including Isla Pájaros, and nesting commonly takes place near the beginning of the dry season. Clutches usually contain two to four eggs.
profile.dietFeeding: The species feeds in shallow fresh, brackish, and salt water. Its diet includes small fish, crustaceans, aquatic insects, mollusks, and other small aquatic animals. While wading, it moves its bill from side to side through submerged mud or water, detecting prey by touch. It often forages in groups and may feed alongside storks, herons, egrets, and ibises.
profile.behavior: Roseate Spoonbills are highly social and commonly feed, roost, and nest in groups. They spend much of the day wading slowly through shallow water or resting in trees and mangroves. Adults communicate with soft calls and body movements, especially around nesting colonies. Their broad bills are usually held partly open while feeding, allowing them to sweep through the water efficiently as they search for prey.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered generally stable, with increases documented in some parts of the species’ range.

profile.overview: The Rufescent Tiger-Heron is a secretive, medium-sized wading bird of tropical wetlands. It has rich rufous-brown plumage, dark barring, and a long, pointed bill suited to catching fish and other small aquatic animals. Adults are often difficult to see because they stand motionless among dense vegetation or along shaded waterways. Costa Rica lies within the species’ range, where it occurs mainly in suitable lowland wetlands, river edges, mangroves, and forested waterways.
profile.classification: The Rufescent Tiger-Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and the genus Tigrisoma. It is one of three tiger-heron species.
profile.identification: Adults have a long neck, sturdy pointed bill, relatively short legs, and predominantly rufous-brown plumage marked with darker streaks and bars. The head and neck are strongly patterned, while the body is usually warmer brown or chestnut than that of many other herons. Juveniles are more heavily streaked and mottled, with less distinct coloration. In flight, the broad rounded wings and long neck help distinguish it from smaller herons. Its quiet, patient posture is characteristic.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Mexico through Central America and across much of tropical South America. In Costa Rica, it is a locally distributed bird of lowland wetlands and waterways rather than a widespread species of upland habitats. It may be found beside slow rivers, ponds, marshes, oxbow lakes, mangroves, flooded forest, and forested streams, especially where dense bankside vegetation provides cover. It generally avoids open, heavily disturbed areas unless suitable wetland vegetation remains.
profile.migrationStatus: Generally resident, including in Costa Rica, but it may make local movements in response to water levels, food availability, and seasonal flooding. It is not considered a regular long-distance migrant in Costa Rica.
profile.breeding: Rufescent Tiger-Herons usually breed solitarily or in loose, low-density groupings near wetlands. They build a platform-like nest of sticks in a tree, shrub, or dense vegetation, often above or close to water. The female commonly lays a small clutch, and both adults take part in incubation and care of the young. Nesting timing varies across its broad range and is influenced by local rainfall and wetland conditions. The young remain dependent while developing their flight and hunting skills.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of fish, frogs, tadpoles, aquatic insects, crustaceans, and other small animals found in or beside water. It usually hunts from the edge of a stream, pond, marsh, or flooded forest, standing still before delivering a quick bill thrust. Its cryptic plumage and slow movements help it approach prey without being noticed. Individuals may also search among wet vegetation and shallow mud for suitable food.
profile.behavior: This tiger-heron is usually solitary, quiet, and cautious. It spends long periods motionless in dense vegetation, relying on camouflage rather than conspicuous activity. When disturbed, it may freeze, move slowly into cover, or fly a short distance along the waterway. It is mainly active during daylight but can also feed at dawn and dusk. Its deep, resonant calls are more often heard during the breeding season than outside it.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is thought to be broadly stable, although local numbers may decline where wetlands, riverside vegetation, and mangroves are lost or degraded.
conservation.threats: Local threats include drainage and conversion of wetlands, clearing of riverbank vegetation, destruction of mangroves, water pollution, disturbance at nesting sites, and alteration of natural flooding patterns. In Costa Rica, protection and restoration of lowland wetlands and riparian habitats are important for maintaining suitable habitat.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect wetlands, mangroves, rivers, and forested stream margins; maintain native vegetation along waterways; reduce pesticide and other pollutant runoff; and avoid disturbing birds near suspected nests. Supporting protected areas and responsible wetland monitoring in Costa Rica can also help conserve the species and its habitat.

profile.overview: The Bare-throated Tiger-Heron is a large, secretive heron of tropical wetlands, mangroves, rivers, lagoons, and marshes. It is named for the exposed yellow or greenish-yellow skin on its throat. Usually found standing motionless near water, it waits for prey before striking with its long bill. The species ranges from Mexico through Central America to northwestern Colombia and is a regular resident of suitable lowland wetlands in Costa Rica.
profile.classification: The Bare-throated Tiger-Heron belongs to the heron family, Ardeidae, and the genus Tigrisoma. It is a member of the order Pelecaniformes.
profile.identification: This stocky heron is about 76–80 centimeters long, with a relatively short-legged appearance and a heavy bill. Adults have a black crown, gray cheeks, finely barred gray-brown upperparts, a rusty-brown neck pattern, and dull cinnamon-brown underparts. The bare throat is yellow, greenish-yellow, or orange, and the legs are greenish. Juveniles are more strongly marked, with warm buff-brown plumage and bold black barring. The black crown and yellow throat help distinguish it from similar tiger-herons.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from coastal and lowland Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama to northwestern Colombia, with a separate population in northwestern Peru. In Costa Rica it is a widespread resident on both Caribbean and Pacific lowlands, including mangroves, slow-flowing rivers, freshwater marshes, lagoons, ponds, wet meadows, swamps, and vegetated stream edges. Most Costa Rican records are at low elevations, generally below about 500 meters, although it may occur higher where suitable habitat remains.
profile.migrationStatus: Generally resident and nonmigratory throughout its range. In Costa Rica, it is present year-round in suitable wetlands; local movements may occur as water levels and prey availability change.
profile.breeding: The Bare-throated Tiger-Heron usually breeds singly rather than in large heron colonies. It builds a small, loose platform of sticks in a tree, often near water or wetland vegetation. Costa Rican observations include nests placed in tree forks, with young recorded in the nest. Available accounts indicate a small clutch, commonly around two or three pale greenish-white eggs. Details of breeding timing and nesting success in Costa Rica remain incompletely documented.
profile.dietFeeding: It is an opportunistic ambush predator that feeds mainly in shallow water or along wet margins. Its documented and likely prey include fish, frogs, crabs, and other aquatic animals. It may also take snakes and other small vertebrates when available; observations in Costa Rica include predation on an arboreal frog. The heron often remains completely still before making a sudden thrust with its bill. It feeds mostly during daylight but may also move around dawn or dusk.
profile.behavior: This species is usually solitary, quiet, and difficult to notice because its barred plumage blends with vegetation and shaded wetland edges. It stands motionless for long periods while watching for prey, then moves slowly or strikes suddenly.
