Bare-throated Tiger-Herons may perch or nest in trees near water and can fly with heavy wingbeats when disturbed. Their broad habitat use includes both wooded wetlands and some more open marshes, but they generally remain close to water.

conservation.populationTrend: The species is widespread, but its total population and long-term global trend are not well quantified. It remains locally common in parts of its range, including suitable areas of Costa Rica.

profile.overview: The Fasciated Tiger-Heron is a secretive, medium-sized heron associated with clear, rocky streams in forested foothills and mountains. It usually hunts alone from the water’s edge or from rocks in fast-flowing channels. Adults have dark, finely pale-striped heads, necks, and upperparts, with a subdued reddish-brown belly and yellow eyes. Its compact shape and preference for rushing streams help distinguish it from other tiger-herons. The species is represented in Costa Rica by the salmoni form.
profile.classification: The Fasciated Tiger-Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and the genus Tigrisoma. It is closely related to the Rufescent and Bare-throated Tiger-Herons.
profile.identification: Adults are dark grayish to blackish overall, marked with narrow pale buff or whitish barring and streaking on the head, neck, back, and wings. The underparts are generally gray to dull cinnamon or reddish brown, while the flanks are gray. The iris is yellow, and the bill is short and stout, with a dark upper mandible and a yellowish-green lower base. Immatures are more heavily and evenly barred and can be difficult to separate from young tiger-herons without habitat clues.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Costa Rica south through Panama and the Andes to Bolivia and northern Argentina, with a separate population in southeastern Brazil and northeastern Argentina. In Costa Rica it is a localized resident, especially along the Caribbean-slope foothills from the Guanacaste Cordillera near Bijagua south toward Panama. It favors forested, hilly terrain with rocky, swift rivers and streams, commonly around 250–800 meters, although local records may reach about 2,400 meters. It may also use streams near artificial fishponds.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered resident in Costa Rica, with no well-established regular long-distance migration. Local movements may occur along streams or with changes in water conditions and food availability.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is poorly documented. The Fasciated Tiger-Heron builds a platform nest from sticks and woody vines, placed in vegetation near its forested river habitat. Reliable details about the Costa Rican breeding season, clutch size, incubation, and division of parental care remain limited. Because the species is local, secretive, and associated with difficult-to-access rushing streams, nesting behavior is observed much less often than its feeding behavior.
profile.dietFeeding: The Fasciated Tiger-Heron feeds mainly in and beside fast-flowing streams. It stands motionless on rocks or banks, often with the neck partly extended, and seizes aquatic prey with a quick thrust of the bill. Its diet is believed to include small fish, aquatic insects, crustaceans, and other stream-dwelling animals. Feeding is usually solitary, and birds may space themselves along productive stretches of river.
profile.behavior: This heron is generally solitary or occurs in pairs and is often difficult to detect because it remains still among rocks, shadow, and streamside vegetation. It favors secluded sections of clear, rushing water and may perch or stand close to the channel while hunting. Individuals can occupy separate fishing sites along the same stream. When disturbed, it may retreat into dense vegetation or fly a short distance along the watercourse.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified. Available assessments do not identify the species as globally threatened, but it is local and uncommon in parts of its range.

profile.overview: The Boat-billed Heron (Cochlearius cochlearius) is a distinctive tropical waterbird named for its unusually broad, flattened bill. Although it belongs to the heron family, it has a compact body, short legs, large eyes, and largely nocturnal habits that give it a different appearance from many typical herons. It usually lives near quiet freshwater, brackish wetlands, mangroves, and forest waterways in tropical parts of Central and South America.
profile.classification: The Boat-billed Heron is in the heron family, Ardeidae, and is the only living species in the genus Cochlearius. It is sometimes placed with night herons because of its nocturnal behavior and body form.
profile.identification: Adults have a large, dark, scoop-shaped bill that is broad enough to appear almost as wide as the head. The crown and upper back are dark, while the face, neck, and underparts are generally gray to pale gray. The body is stocky, the legs are relatively short, and the eyes are large and adapted to low light. Young birds are browner and less sharply patterned. Its slow wingbeats and unusual silhouette are distinctive.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Boat-billed Heron ranges from Mexico through Central America and much of tropical South America. In Costa Rica it occurs in suitable lowland wetlands on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes, including mangrove forests, river edges, marshes, lagoons, swamps, and densely vegetated waterways. It is associated mainly with coastal and near-coastal lowlands, although it may also use inland wetland habitats. Important Costa Rican areas for the species include Tortuguero, Corcovado, Palo Verde, and other protected wetland landscapes.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally resident and rather sedentary. In Costa Rica, Boat-billed Herons are considered year-round birds rather than regular long-distance migrants, although local movements between roosting, nesting, freshwater, and tidal feeding sites may occur.
profile.breeding: Boat-billed Herons nest singly or in small colonies, usually in trees, shrubs, reed beds, or other vegetation above or close to water. Both adults help build the nest, incubate the eggs, and feed the young. Clutches commonly contain two or three pale bluish eggs. The chicks hatch dependent on their parents and remain in or near the nest for several weeks. Breeding may be colonial where suitable wetland nesting habitat is concentrated.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet includes small fish, crustaceans, aquatic insects, worms, frogs, and other small wetland animals. Feeding is mainly nocturnal, when the heron moves quietly along shallow water, muddy edges, or branches overhanging channels. Its broad bill can be used to seize prey from the water or vegetation, and tactile feeding may help it detect prey in dark or turbid conditions.
profile.behavior: During the day, Boat-billed Herons usually roost quietly in dense vegetation, often alone or in groups. They become more active after dusk and may produce harsh, croaking or squawking calls. Birds may gather communally at roosts, while feeding is often more dispersed. Courtship includes crest raising, bill movements, and vocal or chattering displays. Their secretive habits and nocturnal activity can make them easy to overlook even where they are established.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable.

profile.overview: The Agami Heron (Agamia agami) is a striking, secretive heron of tropical Central and South America. It has a dark blue-green back, chestnut underparts, a long narrow bill, and pale blue facial markings. Unlike many conspicuous herons, it usually stays in dense vegetation along forest streams, swamps, lagoons, and mangroves. The species often nests in small colonies and is difficult to observe because it tends to forage quietly in shaded wetlands.
profile.classification: The Agami Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and is the only living species in the genus Agamia. It is sometimes called the Chestnut-bellied Heron.
profile.identification: Adults are medium-sized herons with a long, pointed bill, elongated neck, and relatively short legs. The crown and upperparts are dark greenish blue, while the neck and body are rich chestnut, with pale blue skin around the eye and throat. Breeding birds may show elongated plumes on the head and neck. Juveniles are duller and browner. Its combination of deep chestnut underparts, dark upperparts, and secretive forest-wetland habits helps distinguish it from other Central American herons.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Agami Heron ranges from eastern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and central South America to the Amazon Basin. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon resident of lowland wet forests and wetlands, especially on the Caribbean slope and around the Golfo Dulce and Osa Peninsula, generally near rivers, lagoons, flooded forest, and mangroves. It favors quiet, densely vegetated freshwater or brackish habitats, usually from near sea level into the low foothills.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is generally considered resident, including in Costa Rica. Clear long-distance migration is not established, but local or regional movements may occur, particularly after breeding or during seasonal changes in water conditions.
profile.breeding: Agami Herons breed colonially, often in small, secluded rookeries in flooded forest, mangroves, or vegetation beside wetlands. They may nest near other waterbirds, including other herons and ibises. In Costa Rica, breeding has been documented, including colonies in the Caribbean lowlands, and more recent observations indicate that additional nesting sites may occur in suitable wetlands. Both adults contribute to nest building, incubation, and care of the young. Colonies are vulnerable to disturbance because suitable nesting habitat is limited.
profile.dietFeeding: The Agami Heron mainly eats small fish, but also takes crustaceans, frogs, aquatic insects, and other small wetland animals. It usually forages alone in shallow water or along muddy banks, often beneath dense vegetation. The bird may stand motionless before making a quick thrust with its long bill. Its narrow body and long neck allow it to move through tangled vegetation and hunt along shaded forest streams.
profile.behavior: This heron is notably secretive and is more often heard or glimpsed than seen clearly. It commonly moves slowly and deliberately through shadowed vegetation, keeping its body low while foraging. Individuals may perch quietly in trees or dense shrubs near water. Agami Herons are usually solitary outside the breeding season, but can gather at nesting colonies. Their quiet habits and preference for remote wetlands make population monitoring difficult.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although its total population size and detailed regional trends are not well known because the species is difficult to survey.
conservation.threats: Major concerns include the loss, degradation, and fragmentation of lowland wet forests, flooded forests, mangroves, and other wetlands. Drainage, agricultural conversion, logging, development, pollution, and disturbance at breeding colonies can reduce feeding and nesting habitat. Because Agami Herons often nest in small colonies, damage or repeated disturbance at a single rookery may affect many birds.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore lowland rivers, wetlands, mangroves, and forested waterways in Costa Rica and throughout the species’ range. Keep known nesting colonies undisturbed, especially during the breeding season, and support protected areas that include both feeding and roosting sites. Avoid clearing streamside vegetation, reduce pollution and pesticide runoff, and report sightings of colonies to local conservation authorities or bird-monitoring programs.

profile.overview: The American Bittern (Botaurus lentiginosus) is a secretive, medium-sized heron of freshwater marshes. Its streaked brown, buff, and white plumage provides excellent camouflage among cattails, reeds, sedges, and other tall vegetation. It is usually seen alone, standing motionless or walking slowly at the edge of shallow water while hunting. During the breeding season, males are famous for their deep, resonant booming calls, which carry across wetlands and are often heard before the bird is seen.
profile.classification: The American Bittern belongs to the heron family, Ardeidae, and the order Pelecaniformes. It is one of the large bitterns in the genus Botaurus.
profile.identification: This stocky heron measures about 60–85 cm in length. Adults have warm brown upperparts, heavily streaked brown-and-white underparts, a broad buffy neck, a long pointed bill, and yellowish legs. A dark stripe extends from the eye down the side of the neck. In flight, the wings show pale coverts contrasting with darker flight feathers. Juveniles are generally browner and lack the strongly defined dark neck stripe. Its slow movements and bill-up concealment posture help distinguish it from other marsh birds.
profile.rangeHabitat: The American Bittern breeds across much of Canada and the northern and central United States, then winters mainly in the southern United States, Mexico, and Central America. In Costa Rica it is a rare winter visitor rather than a breeding species, with records from several provinces, including Cartago, Puntarenas, Alajuela, and Limón. It uses freshwater marshes, lake margins, wet grasslands, and other wetlands with tall emergent or floating vegetation and nearby shallow water.
profile.migrationStatus: It is a long-distance migrant. Birds reaching Costa Rica generally arrive during the Northern Hemisphere winter, most often from about September through March, and depart northward for the breeding season. In Costa Rica it is uncommon to rare and irregular, so it is not expected at every suitable wetland.
profile.breeding: Breeding takes place in northern North America, usually in freshwater marshes with dense stands of cattails, bulrushes, reeds, or sedges. The female normally builds a platform or mound just above shallow water, using dry wetland vegetation. She incubates the eggs and raises the young with little or no assistance from the male. A clutch typically contains two to seven eggs, and incubation lasts roughly 24–28 days. American Bitterns usually nest singly rather than in dense colonies.
profile.dietFeeding: The American Bittern eats a varied diet of fish, frogs, tadpoles, salamanders, crayfish, aquatic insects, grasshoppers, dragonflies, reptiles, and occasionally small mammals. It commonly hunts at dawn, dusk, or in dim conditions along the edges of shallow water and dense vegetation. The bird may stand completely still, slowly lower its bill, and then strike rapidly to seize prey, usually swallowing aquatic animals head first.
profile.behavior: American Bitterns are solitary, wary, and difficult to detect. When threatened, one may stretch its neck vertically and point its bill upward, swaying slightly with surrounding reeds to imitate vegetation. It usually walks slowly through marsh plants or remains motionless for long periods. Males produce a distinctive low booming call during the breeding season. The species generally makes short, low flights over wetlands and is often heard more frequently than seen.

conservation.populationTrend: Population trends vary geographically. Broad monitoring indicates declines in some regions of the United States and Canada, while the overall continental population remains relatively large.
conservation.threats: Loss, drainage, alteration, and degradation of freshwater marshes are the main concerns. Pollution, nutrient enrichment, siltation, invasive plants, pesticide exposure, and disturbance near breeding wetlands can reduce habitat quality or the availability of prey.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore marshes, wet grasslands, lake margins, and other shallow wetlands used by migratory birds. Maintain natural water levels and tall emergent vegetation, limit pollution and pesticide runoff, control invasive plants where appropriate, and avoid disturbing secluded marsh areas, especially during the breeding season. Reporting well-documented sightings in Costa Rica can also improve knowledge of this rare winter visitor.

profile.overview: The Pinnated Bittern (Botaurus pinnatus) is a large, secretive heron of freshwater marshes and seasonally flooded grasslands in the Neotropics. It is often difficult to see because it remains motionless among reeds, sedges, cattails, and tall grasses, where its streaked brown plumage provides excellent camouflage. Although widespread from Central America through much of South America, its distribution, abundance, and movements remain incompletely documented because of its elusive behavior.
profile.classification: The Pinnated Bittern belongs to the heron family, Ardeidae, and the bittern genus Botaurus. It is also called the South American Bittern.
profile.identification: This large bittern has a long, heavy bill, a thick body, long legs, and strongly patterned buff, brown, and black plumage. The upperparts are streaked and barred, while the neck and underparts show dark vertical markings. In flight, the broad wings and contrasting darker flight feathers are noticeable. It is usually identified by its size, cryptic plumage, and habit of standing upright and still in dense marsh vegetation. Sexes are similar, although males are generally larger.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Pinnated Bittern occurs from southeastern Nicaragua and Costa Rica south through much of Central and South America, including the Guianas, Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, and northern Argentina. In Costa Rica it is a local resident of both Caribbean and Pacific lowlands, with records especially associated with the Tempisque lowlands, the Río Frío region, Medio Queso Wetlands, Palo Verde, and other marshes. It uses freshwater marshes, cattail and reed beds, wet savannas, flooded pastures, drainage ditches, and sometimes rice fields, generally at low elevations.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is generally considered resident or locally dispersive in Costa Rica. Seasonal changes in wetland conditions may cause short-distance movements, but recent evidence does not support a consistent, regular long-distance migration pattern across the range.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited because the species is difficult to observe. It builds a nest above or close to shallow water in dense marsh vegetation, using reeds, grasses, or other emergent plants. The nest may be a platform or a shallow structure concealed among stems. Clutches of about two to three eggs have been reported. In Costa Rica, nesting has been documented in cattail marshes, including a record of a nest containing three eggs at Taboga during the rainy season.
profile.dietFeeding: The Pinnated Bittern is an ambush hunter that often stands motionless before striking quickly. Its diet includes fish, eels, frogs, other amphibians, reptiles, insects and other arthropods, mollusks, worms, and small mammals or birds when available. It usually forages alone in shallow water or along marsh edges, using its long bill to seize prey from close range.
profile.behavior: This bittern is solitary, cautious, and largely crepuscular or otherwise most active during quiet periods of the day. When threatened, it may freeze with its body lowered and neck held vertically, relying on camouflage rather than immediately flying away. It usually flushes only when approached closely. Its secretive habits and preference for dense vegetation make vocalizations, patient scanning, and slow movement important for detection.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population trend is not precisely known because the species is difficult to survey, but available broad assessments describe it as stable. Recent research also indicates that its actual distribution may be broader than older range maps suggest.

profile.overview: The Least Bittern is the smallest heron in the Americas, a secretive marsh bird that often remains hidden among reeds and cattails. It has a compact body, a short neck, and long toes suited to walking across floating vegetation. Despite its small size, it is an effective hunter of fish and other wetland animals. The species occupies freshwater and brackish marshes from North America through Central America and parts of the Caribbean and South America.
profile.classification: The Least Bittern belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and the order Pelecaniformes. Its current scientific name is Botaurus exilis; some older references use Ixobrychus exilis.
profile.identification: Adults are about 28–36 cm long, with a short, thick body and long legs and toes. Males are strikingly patterned, with a black crown and back, buffy yellow wings, and pale underparts marked with brown. Females are duller and more uniformly brown. Juveniles resemble females but are heavily streaked. The bird’s small size, broad buff wing patches, and habit of clinging to reeds help distinguish it from larger bitterns and herons.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Least Bittern occurs from southeastern Canada and the United States through Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and parts of northern South America. Costa Rica lies near the southern edge of its Central American range; the species is recorded locally on both Caribbean and Pacific sides, especially in lowland wetlands. It uses freshwater and brackish marshes with tall cattails, sedges, reeds, bulrushes, and other dense vegetation mixed with open water. It may also use mangroves, ponds, and managed wetlands.
profile.migrationStatus: Northern populations are migratory and move south in autumn to Mexico, the Caribbean, Central America, and northern South America. In Costa Rica, the species occurs locally as a breeding-range bird and may also be encountered during seasonal movements or in the nonbreeding period. Birds in tropical parts of the range may remain year-round where suitable wetlands persist.
profile.breeding: Least Bitterns usually nest in dense emergent vegetation over shallow water, often in cattails, reeds, sedges, or bulrushes. The nest is a small platform made from wetland plants and may be attached to standing stems. Several eggs are laid, and both adults participate in caring for the young. Pairs may produce more than one brood in favorable conditions. Breeding in Costa Rica is associated with suitable lowland marsh habitat, but the species is generally local and difficult to detect.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small fish, frogs, tadpoles, aquatic insects, crayfish, other crustaceans, and occasionally small snakes, mammals, and amphibians. The Least Bittern hunts quietly from cover, often standing motionless before making a rapid thrust with its bill. Its long toes allow it to grasp reeds and walk across floating plants, giving it access to shallow water and dense marsh vegetation that larger herons cannot easily use.
profile.behavior: This species is highly secretive and is more often heard or briefly glimpsed than seen clearly. It moves through reeds by grasping stems with its long toes and may freeze with its bill pointed upward when threatened, using its streaked plumage as camouflage. It is most active during daylight but may also forage at dawn and dusk. Short, rapid flights usually remain low over the marsh, and the bird often drops quickly back into cover.

conservation.populationTrend: The global trend is not precisely known. Regional evidence indicates long-term declines in parts of North America, while some monitored areas show stable or uncertain recent trends. Costa Rican population trends are not well documented.
conservation.threats: The principal concern is loss and degradation of freshwater and brackish marshes through drainage, conversion, development, pollution, altered water levels, and invasive vegetation. Disturbance during breeding and the loss of connected wetland habitat may also reduce local occupancy.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore marshes, reedbeds, mangroves, and other shallow wetlands in Costa Rica and across the species’ range. Maintain natural water levels and native emergent vegetation, limit pollution and unnecessary disturbance, and support wetland monitoring. Reporting well-documented sightings to recognized bird-monitoring programs can improve knowledge of this elusive species.

profile.overview: The Yellow-crowned Night Heron is a medium-sized wading bird of the Americas, named for the yellow crown and long yellow plumes of the adult. It is strongly associated with coastal wetlands but also uses freshwater habitats inland. Unlike many herons, it specializes in crabs, crayfish, and other aquatic invertebrates. It is most active at dusk and during the night, although individuals may forage in daylight when tides or food availability make this advantageous.
profile.classification: The Yellow-crowned Night Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and the order Pelecaniformes. Its scientific name is Nyctanassa violacea.
profile.identification: Adults have a slate-gray to purplish body, a bold black-and-white head pattern, a thick dark bill, and a yellow crown with long pale plumes. The legs are yellowish. Juveniles are brown, heavily streaked and spotted, and can resemble juvenile Black-crowned Night Herons. Yellow-crowned juveniles usually have a heavier bill, longer-looking legs and neck, and fewer, smaller pale spots on the wings. In flight, the legs extend beyond the tail.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from the southeastern United States through Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America. In Costa Rica it is recorded on both the Caribbean and Pacific lowlands, mainly below about 500 meters, although occasional individuals have been found at higher elevations. It uses mangroves, tidal creeks, mudflats, lagoons, marshes, river margins, ponds, and wet forest edges. Mangroves and gallery forests are especially important for roosting.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident and migratory populations both occur in Costa Rica. The species is present year-round in suitable lowland wetlands, while some individuals—especially from northern populations—move south during the nonbreeding season. Costa Rican records are generally more frequent along the coasts and in lowland wetland habitats.
profile.breeding: Yellow-crowned Night Herons usually nest in trees or shrubs near water, including mangrove stands, wooded swamps, and other wetland forests. They may nest in colonies with other herons or as isolated pairs. The nest is a platform of sticks, and both adults help incubate the eggs and feed the young. Nesting activity and local breeding status in Costa Rica are less thoroughly documented than in the northern part of the species’ range, so regional timing can vary with rainfall and habitat conditions.
profile.dietFeeding: Crabs and crayfish are the principal foods in many parts of its range. The species also takes other crustaceans, aquatic insects, fish, frogs, small reptiles, and other small aquatic animals. It usually forages by standing still or walking slowly through shallow water, mudflats, marsh vegetation, or along mangrove edges. Prey is seized with a quick lunge and may be shaken, dismembered, or swallowed whole.
profile.behavior: This heron often rests quietly in trees or dense vegetation during the day and becomes more conspicuous at dusk or after dark. It is mainly crepuscular and nocturnal but may feed by day, especially around changing tides. Individuals commonly forage alone and maintain a deliberate, hunched posture while stalking prey. Its flight is steady, with the neck retracted and the long legs projecting beyond the tail.

conservation.populationTrend: The species is widespread and globally secure, although available assessments indicate a slight overall decline, probably linked to habitat loss and degradation.
conservation.threats: Loss, degradation, and disturbance of coastal wetlands, mangroves, marshes, and nesting habitat can reduce feeding and breeding opportunities. Human disturbance near roosts and colonies may also affect nesting success.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore mangroves, marshes, lagoons, and other shallow wetlands. Keep a respectful distance from roosting and nesting birds, avoid disturbing colonies, support wetland conservation, and report sightings through reputable bird-monitoring programs.

profile.overview: The Black-crowned Night Heron is a stocky, medium-sized heron found across much of the world. It is named for its mainly nocturnal feeding habits and distinctive black crown and back in adults. This adaptable species uses freshwater and coastal wetlands, often roosting quietly in trees during the day. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon but regular wetland bird, occurring in suitable habitats rather than being one of the country’s most frequently seen herons.
profile.classification: The Black-crowned Night Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and the genus Nycticorax. Its scientific name is Nycticorax nycticorax.
profile.identification: Adults have a black crown and back, pale gray wings, a whitish face and underparts, red eyes, a thick dark bill, and yellowish legs. Two or three long white plumes extend from the back of the head during the breeding season. Juveniles are brown overall with prominent pale streaks and spots, making them look unlike adults. The species has a compact body, broad rounded wings, and a short tail. Its harsh, barking call is often heard at dusk or night.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Black-crowned Night Heron has a broad distribution in North and South America, Europe, Africa, and Asia. It occupies marshes, swamps, ponds, lakes, rivers, lagoons, mangroves, tidal flats, canals, rice fields, and other shallow-water habitats, with trees or dense vegetation nearby for roosting and nesting. In Costa Rica, it is recorded in lowland wetlands and along rivers, lakes, lagoons, mangroves, and other suitable aquatic areas. It is considered uncommon but regular there, including sites such as Caño Negro.
profile.migrationStatus: Costa Rica supports both resident or locally occurring birds and migrants from farther north. Northern populations commonly move south after breeding, and some reach Central America during the nonbreeding season. The species is therefore present in Costa Rica year-round in suitable areas, but numbers and visibility may increase during migration and winter.
profile.breeding: Black-crowned Night Herons usually breed in colonies, sometimes alongside other herons, egrets, ibises, or gulls. Nests are loose platforms of sticks, reeds, and twigs placed in trees, shrubs, marsh vegetation, or occasionally on the ground. A clutch commonly contains three to five pale bluish or greenish eggs, which hatch asynchronously after about three to four weeks. Both adults care for the young. In Costa Rica, breeding activity has been reported mainly during the rainy-season period, including July and August.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet is varied but often includes fish, frogs, aquatic insects, crustaceans, mollusks, small mammals, snakes, and other small aquatic or wetland animals. The heron usually hunts by standing still or walking slowly at the edge of shallow water, then thrusting its bill at prey. It feeds most actively from dusk through the night, although breeding birds may also forage during daylight.
profile.behavior: During the day, Black-crowned Night Herons commonly remain motionless in trees, shrubs, reeds, or other sheltered vegetation, often in groups. They become more active at dusk, flying to nearby feeding sites with steady wingbeats and giving loud, harsh calls. They are generally patient ambush hunters and may defend a small feeding area. The species commonly nests and roosts communally, while pairs defend the immediate area around their nest.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered broadly stable, although trends vary among regions. Some local populations have declined, while others have stabilized or increased after earlier pesticide-related losses.

profile.overview: The Whistling Heron is a medium-sized heron of tropical and subtropical South America. Unlike many herons, it often feeds on land rather than in deep water, walking through grasslands, wet fields, savannas, and lightly wooded areas. Its contrasting gray, buff, yellow, black, and pink coloration makes it distinctive. The species is the only member of the genus Syrigma and is known for clear whistling calls and a generally deliberate, terrestrial feeding style.
profile.classification: The Whistling Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae. Two subspecies are generally recognized: Syrigma sibilatrix fostersmithi in northern South America and the nominate S. s. sibilatrix farther south and east.
profile.identification: This heron is about 50–58 centimeters long and has a gray body and wings, a yellowish-gold neck and upper breast, and dark crest feathers. The face shows blue skin around the lores, while the large bill is pinkish with a black tip. The legs are dark. In flight, buff or pale wing edges can be noticeable. Its upright posture, long legs, terrestrial habits, and distinctive whistled calls help separate it from other herons.
profile.rangeHabitat: The main range extends from Colombia and Venezuela south and east through Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil, Uruguay, and northern Argentina. It uses wet savannas, marshy grasslands, rice fields, muddy margins, shallow wetlands, drainage ditches, rural areas, and open landscapes with scattered trees or woodland remnants. In Costa Rica it is an exceptionally rare accidental visitor rather than an established species. The first documented national record was an individual observed foraging at Manzanillo, Limón Province, on February 16, 2016, representing the northernmost documented record at that time.
profile.migrationStatus: Generally resident within its South American range, with local movements and dispersal rather than a well-defined long-distance migration. In Costa Rica it is known from rare accidental occurrence, and there is no reliable evidence that it has established a resident or regular migratory population.
profile.breeding: Whistling Herons usually nest in mature trees, including trees in small woodlots, forest remnants, and open rural landscapes. The nest is a loose platform of sticks, commonly placed on a substantial horizontal branch several meters above the ground. They generally breed alone or in small, scattered groups. Clutches usually contain three or four pale blue, speckled eggs. Incubation lasts about 28 days, and young remain associated with adults after leaving the nest.
profile.dietFeeding: The species takes a broad variety of small animals, especially insects such as grasshoppers, dragonflies, beetles, and mantises. It also eats earthworms, spiders, crustaceans, frogs, small reptiles, and other small vertebrates when available. It commonly forages in grasslands and shallow wet places, walking slowly and pausing upright before making a quick stab or lunge. Individuals may feed alone or in pairs.
profile.behavior: Whistling Herons are often active during daylight and spend considerable time on the ground. They walk slowly through open habitat, sometimes making short runs or catching flying insects. Birds may perch or roost in trees and can tolerate relatively open, human-modified landscapes. They are usually solitary or found in pairs, though larger gatherings may occur at roosts. Communication includes clear whistles and hissing sounds, particularly in family groups.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable overall, and the species is locally common to abundant in parts of its South American range. Its occurrence in Costa Rica is too rare and recent to support a separate national population assessment.

profile.overview: The Little Blue Heron (Egretta caerulea) is a medium-sized wading bird found from the southern United States through Central America and the Caribbean to much of South America. Adults have slate-blue bodies, violet-maroon heads and necks, and dark-tipped, pale gray bills. Young birds are mostly white and can resemble Snowy Egrets. The species usually hunts alone in shallow wetlands and often nests in mixed colonies with other herons and egrets.
profile.classification: The Little Blue Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and the order Pelecaniformes. Its scientific name is Egretta caerulea.
profile.identification: Adults are about 60 centimeters long, with long legs, a long pointed bill, and dark blue-gray plumage. The head and neck may appear purplish, especially in good light. The bill is pale gray or bluish with a darker tip, and the legs are dark. Immatures are largely white during their first year, often showing pale greenish legs and a gray-and-black bill. Their slow wingbeats and slim shape help distinguish them from larger herons.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Little Blue Heron ranges from the southeastern United States and Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean to northern and central South America. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly in the lowlands of both the Pacific and Caribbean slopes, where it uses freshwater marshes, ponds, lakes, slow rivers, rice fields, mudflats, estuaries, mangroves, salt ponds, and other shallow wetlands. It is commonly associated with open wetland edges and sheltered roosting or nesting vegetation.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is resident in much of the tropics, while northern populations migrate southward after breeding. In Costa Rica it is primarily a passage migrant and winter visitor, with some individuals remaining during the breeding season; it is generally not considered a regular breeding resident there.
profile.breeding: Little Blue Herons usually breed colonially, often alongside Great Egrets, Snowy Egrets, Tricolored Herons, and other waterbirds. They build a platform of sticks in trees, shrubs, mangroves, or dense wetland vegetation near feeding areas. Both adults incubate the eggs and care for the young. Northern populations commonly lay about three to six eggs, while clutches in Central America are often smaller. Reliable sources do not indicate that Costa Rica supports a major regular breeding population.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small fish, frogs, tadpoles, aquatic insects, crustaceans, and other small aquatic animals. The heron usually walks slowly through shallow water or stands motionless before making a quick strike with its bill. It may forage along muddy margins, flooded fields, streams, ponds, estuaries, and mangrove channels. Individuals commonly feed alone, although several may gather where prey become concentrated.
profile.behavior: Little Blue Herons are generally quiet and solitary while feeding, and they often occur singly or in pairs rather than in large feeding flocks. They may congregate with other waders at roosts, nesting colonies, and rich feeding sites. Adults fly with slow, deliberate wingbeats and the neck folded back. Young birds remain white for much of their first year, a coloration that may reduce aggression from adult herons in mixed colonies.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining, although the species remains widespread and numerous enough to be classified as Least Concern.
conservation.threats: Important threats include loss, drainage, pollution, and degradation of wetlands; disturbance of nesting colonies and communal roosts; removal of wetland vegetation; and reduced availability of shallow feeding habitat. Declines have been reported in parts of North America, so continued protection of wetlands and breeding colonies is important even though the global assessment is Least Concern.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore marshes, ponds, mangroves, estuaries, and other shallow wetlands. Avoid disturbing nesting colonies and roosts, especially during the breeding season, and support conservation of Costa Rica’s wetland reserves and coastal habitats. Reducing pesticide and chemical runoff, keeping dogs and people away from sensitive colonies, and reporting sightings through established bird-monitoring programs can also help improve knowledge and conservation planning.

profile.overview: The Tricolored Heron (Egretta tricolor) is a slender, medium-sized heron of the Americas. Its blue-gray body, white belly, and narrow white stripe down the front of the neck create a distinctive pattern. It usually hunts alone in shallow coastal and inland wetlands, often moving quickly through the water while chasing small fish. The species is also known as the Louisiana Heron and commonly nests in mixed colonies with other wading birds.
profile.classification: The Tricolored Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and the order Pelecaniformes. It is placed in the genus Egretta, which includes several slender herons and egrets.
profile.identification: Adults are mostly slate blue or blue-gray above, with a white belly, white rump, and a long, narrow bill. A white line runs down the front of the dark neck. During breeding, adults may show buffy plumes on the back and warmer blue, purple, or orange tones on the neck and face. Immature birds are browner, especially on the neck and upperparts, and can resemble young Little Blue Herons but retain a contrasting pale belly.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from the southern United States through Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America. In Costa Rica it is primarily found in the lowlands of both the Pacific and Caribbean slopes, especially around mangroves, estuaries, mudflats, coastal lagoons, marshes, river mouths, and other shallow wetlands. It is generally uncommon but widespread in suitable lowland habitat, and may occasionally occur at higher elevations, including parts of the Central Valley.
profile.migrationStatus: Tricolored Herons from northern breeding populations migrate south in the nonbreeding season, while populations in Central and South America may be resident or locally mobile. In Costa Rica, it is mainly a winter resident and passage visitor, although some individuals may remain year-round and local breeding has been recorded, including on the Pacific side.
profile.breeding: The Tricolored Heron usually nests colonially with other herons and egrets. It builds a platform of sticks in mangroves, shrubs, low trees, or dense wetland vegetation, often on islands or near coastal waters. Both adults help incubate the eggs and feed the young. Clutches commonly contain three or four eggs. In Costa Rica, breeding has been documented locally, including in coastal wetland areas, but the species is more often encountered there outside the main breeding season.
profile.dietFeeding: Small fish make up most of the diet. The heron also takes shrimp, crabs, aquatic insects, frogs, lizards, and other small aquatic animals when available. It usually feeds in shallow water along marsh edges, mudflats, lagoons, mangroves, and estuaries. Its hunting style is active: it may walk, run, pause abruptly, spread its wings, or dart after prey before striking with its long bill.
profile.behavior: This species is generally solitary while feeding, although it gathers with other wading birds at roosts and breeding colonies. It is mainly active during daylight and often returns to trees or mangroves to rest. Tricolored Herons are strong fliers, traveling with the neck folded back and the legs extended. Their quick, changeable movements while hunting are a useful field mark and distinguish them from slower, more deliberate herons.

conservation.populationTrend: The species remains widespread and globally secure, although available large-scale monitoring indicates an overall decline in recent decades and regional trends vary.

profile.overview: The Reddish Egret (Egretta rufescens) is a medium-sized coastal heron known for its energetic, unusual hunting style. It often runs, leaps, spins, and spreads its wings while pursuing small fish in shallow water. The species occurs mainly around warm coastal regions of the Americas, including the Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, Central America, and parts of northern South America. It uses open tidal habitats more than freshwater wetlands and is uncommon across much of its range.
profile.classification: The Reddish Egret belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and the genus Egretta. It is closely related to other egrets and small herons, but its distinctive plumage and active feeding behavior make it readily recognizable.
profile.identification: This long-legged egret has a fairly heavy, straight bill with a pinkish or flesh-colored base and a dark tip. Adults occur in dark and white color morphs. The dark morph, most often seen in Costa Rica, has a slate-gray body, reddish-brown head and neck, dark legs, and shaggy neck feathers. The white morph is entirely white but retains the characteristic bill shape and active feeding behavior. Immature birds are generally duller and have darker bills.
profile.rangeHabitat: Reddish Egrets are distributed along tropical and subtropical coasts from the southern United States and Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean. In Costa Rica, they are uncommon coastal birds, with records concentrated along the Pacific coast, especially around the Gulf of Nicoya and Golfo Dulce. They use tidal mudflats, shallow lagoons, salt pans, estuaries, mangrove edges, and other sheltered coastal waters. They are rarely found far inland and are not normally associated with forest or upland habitats.
profile.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Reddish Egret is best described as an uncommon winter visitor or seasonal resident. It is reported mainly on the Pacific coast from approximately November through March, while records on the Caribbean coast are much scarcer and are associated chiefly with autumn migration, especially around September. It does not appear to be a regular breeding species in Costa Rica.
profile.breeding: Breeding usually occurs in coastal colonies, often on low islands, mangrove-covered sites, or thorny coastal vegetation. The species commonly nests near other herons and places its stick nest above ground or over shallow water. Both parents incubate the eggs and feed the young. Reliable evidence of regular breeding in Costa Rica is lacking, so the country is more important as a nonbreeding and seasonal-use area than as a documented breeding region.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small fish, with crustaceans, frogs, insects, and other aquatic animals taken occasionally. Reddish Egrets usually feed in shallow water during daylight. Their characteristic technique involves running rapidly, changing direction, spinning, jumping, and holding the wings partly open to reduce glare or shade the water. They may also stand quietly before making a sudden strike with the bill.
profile.behavior: Reddish Egrets are active and conspicuous foragers compared with many other herons. Individuals often defend feeding areas from other egrets and may show displays involving raised feathers, bill movements, or posturing. They usually roost in mangroves, shrubs, or other coastal vegetation. Outside the breeding season they are often seen alone or in loose associations with other wading birds, especially around productive tidal flats and lagoons.

conservation.populationTrend: The population appears broadly stable or slightly declining in the short term, but it remains well below historical levels after severe declines in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
conservation.threats: Major concerns include loss and degradation of mangroves, tidal flats, estuaries, and shallow coastal wetlands; coastal development; dredging and shoreline alteration; disturbance at nesting and feeding sites; and the effects of sea-level rise. Human activity can reduce feeding opportunities or cause birds to abandon otherwise suitable habitat. The small, geographically concentrated population also increases vulnerability to local habitat changes.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect mangroves, estuaries, tidal mudflats, salt pans, and coastal lagoons, including important sites in Costa Rica such as the Gulf of Nicoya and Golfo Dulce. Keep boats, vehicles, dogs, and pedestrians away from roosting, feeding, and nesting birds. Support wetland restoration, responsible coastal development, long-term monitoring, and citizen-science reporting of sightings. Avoid disturbing birds for photographs and help maintain clean, undisturbed shoreline habitat.

profile.overview: The Snowy Egret is a slender, elegant heron of wetlands throughout the Americas. Its bright white plumage contrasts with a black bill and legs and vivid yellow feet. It often feeds in shallow water, using quick movements and foot-stirring behavior to disturb small aquatic prey. Once heavily hunted for its ornate breeding plumes, the species recovered after protective laws were introduced and is now widespread and locally common.
profile.classification: The Snowy Egret belongs to the heron family, Ardeidae, and the genus Egretta. Its scientific name is Egretta thula.
profile.identification: Adults are medium-sized, entirely white egrets with a slim black bill, black legs, and bright yellow feet. During the breeding season, long delicate plumes extend from the head, neck, and back. The yellow facial skin may become more vivid. Juveniles resemble adults but generally have duller facial colors and less-developed plumes. The black bill and legs with contrasting yellow feet help distinguish it from the larger Great Egret, which has a yellow bill and black feet.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Snowy Egret ranges from the United States and southern Canada through Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and much of South America. In Costa Rica it is a native wetland bird recorded on both Pacific and Caribbean lowlands, especially around coastal lagoons, estuaries, mangroves, river mouths, marshes, ponds, lakes, and other shallow-water sites. It may also forage in flooded fields and open agricultural areas, generally favoring lowlands rather than high elevations.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is resident in much of tropical America, including Costa Rica, where it occurs year-round in suitable wetlands. Northern populations are partly or strongly migratory, and birds from the United States and Canada may pass through or winter in Costa Rica. Local movements follow water conditions and food availability.
profile.breeding: Snowy Egrets usually breed colonially with other herons, egrets, ibises, or cormorants. They build a platform nest of sticks in a tree, shrub, mangrove, or marsh vegetation, often over or near water. Both adults help with nest construction, incubation, and feeding the young. Breeding colonies require relatively undisturbed nesting vegetation and nearby shallow wetlands that provide abundant fish and other aquatic prey. Breeding in Costa Rica is less extensively documented than passage and winter occurrence.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet includes small fish, frogs, tadpoles, crustaceans, aquatic insects, worms, snails, and occasionally small reptiles. The Snowy Egret usually feeds in shallow water, walking actively while stabbing prey with its bill. It may run, shuffle its feet, or spread its wings to startle hidden animals. Individuals sometimes forage together, particularly in productive coastal wetlands, and may also feed in flooded fields and along quiet river margins.
profile.behavior: This species is active mainly during the day and often roosts communally in trees, mangroves, or dense wetland vegetation. It is an agile, energetic forager that may chase prey through shallow water rather than standing motionless. Snowy Egrets commonly associate with other wading birds and can be wary when approached. Outside the breeding season they may gather in loose groups, moving among wetlands as water levels and prey availability change.

conservation.populationTrend: The species remains widespread, but regional populations may vary with wetland conditions, disturbance, and habitat quality. A precise current global trend is not consistently established.

profile.overview: The Striated Heron (Butorides striata) is a small, compact waterbird of the heron family. It is usually found alone along quiet freshwater and coastal margins, where it waits motionless before striking at prey. The species has a broad distribution across tropical regions of the Americas, Africa, and Asia. In Costa Rica, it is recognized as part of the national heron fauna and occurs mainly around suitable wetlands, rivers, streams, ponds, mangroves, and sheltered coastal waters.
profile.classification: The Striated Heron belongs to the order Pelecaniformes and the family Ardeidae. Its scientific name is Butorides striata.
profile.identification: This small heron has a short neck, rounded wings, a relatively short tail, and a long, pointed bill. Adults are generally dark gray or slate-colored above, with a darker crown, streaked neck and breast, and greenish or yellowish legs. Plumage varies geographically, and some individuals may appear browner or more richly colored. Juveniles are browner and more heavily streaked or spotted. It can resemble the closely related Green Heron, but range and plumage details help separate them.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Striated Heron has a wide tropical and subtropical range extending through much of South America, Central America, parts of the Caribbean, Africa, and southern and eastern Asia. In Costa Rica, it is recorded as a resident heron rather than a regular long-distance migrant. It uses lowland and foothill wetlands, slow-moving rivers, forest streams, ponds, canals, mangroves, estuaries, and quiet coastal edges. Dense vegetation, overhanging branches, muddy margins, and shallow water provide important feeding and resting habitat.
profile.migrationStatus: Generally resident in Costa Rica, with no regular seasonal migration pattern documented for the national population. Local movements may occur as water levels and food availability change.
profile.breeding: The species usually breeds near water, often in trees, shrubs, mangroves, or other dense vegetation. It builds a loose platform nest from sticks, commonly positioned above or close to the water. The female typically lays a small clutch of pale bluish or greenish eggs, and both adults participate in incubation and care of the young. Breeding timing varies across its broad range and is often linked to local rainfall and wet-season conditions. Costa Rica supports resident populations and likely local breeding where suitable habitat is available.
profile.dietFeeding: Striated Herons feed mainly on small fish, crustaceans, aquatic insects, frogs, tadpoles, and other small aquatic animals. They usually hunt from a low perch, exposed root, rock, or water-edge branch, remaining still before making a quick downward thrust with the bill. They may also walk slowly along muddy margins or shallow water. Like some related herons, individuals can occasionally use floating objects or other material to attract prey within striking range.
profile.behavior: This is usually a solitary and secretive heron. It spends long periods standing quietly or crouched on a perch, then moves with sudden, deliberate actions when hunting. It is active during the day but may also feed at dawn, dusk, or under shaded conditions. When disturbed, it may fly low over the water and give a sharp call. Dense waterside vegetation is important for concealment, roosting, and escape from predators.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified, although the species remains widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Green Heron (Butorides virescens) is a small, compact heron found around freshwater and coastal wetlands in the Americas. It often hunts alone from a low perch beside quiet water, waiting motionless before striking fish or other prey. Its dark greenish back, chestnut neck, short legs, and strong pointed bill give it a distinctive appearance. The species is also notable for sometimes using small objects as bait to attract fish.
profile.classification: The Green Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and the genus Butorides. It is a separate species from the closely related Striated Heron, Butorides striata.
profile.identification: Adults are small herons with a dark greenish-black back and crown, rich chestnut neck and breast, grayish underparts, and yellowish legs. The bill is dark and sharply pointed, while the face usually shows yellow skin around the eye and lores. In flight, the bird appears compact with broad, rounded wings. Juveniles are browner and more heavily streaked, with less distinct chestnut and green coloration. It often crouches low and extends its neck while hunting.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Green Heron ranges from the eastern and western parts of North America through Mexico, Central America, and parts of northern South America. In Costa Rica it occurs widely, especially around the Caribbean slope, central elevations, and suitable lowland wetlands; it has also been recorded on the Pacific side and Isla del Coco. It uses mangroves, estuaries, marshes, ponds, lagoons, rivers, streams, and other shallow waters bordered by dense shrubs or trees, generally from sea level to about 1,850 meters.
profile.migrationStatus: Costa Rica supports both resident Green Herons and North American migrants. Resident and wintering birds occur mainly on the Caribbean slope and in the central highlands, while migrants move chiefly along the Caribbean coast during September–October and April–May.
profile.breeding: Green Herons usually nest in trees, shrubs, or dense thickets near water, sometimes in vegetation overhanging a wetland. The nest is a small platform of sticks, and both parents generally participate in incubation and care of the young. Clutches commonly contain several pale bluish or greenish eggs. In Costa Rica, resident birds may breed where suitable wetland habitat is available, but detailed information on local breeding distribution and timing is limited.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet includes small fish, frogs, tadpoles, crustaceans, aquatic and terrestrial insects, spiders, and other small animals. The bird usually hunts from a low branch, stump, or concealed bank beside shallow water. It may stand motionless for long periods before making a rapid stab with its bill. Green Herons are among the birds known to use bait, such as feathers, insects, or small floating objects, to draw fish within reach.
profile.behavior: Green Herons are commonly solitary and secretive, especially when feeding. They move carefully through dense vegetation and often crouch low while stalking prey. When disturbed, they may fly with quick wingbeats and a short, harsh call. Adults defend feeding or nesting areas and use postures such as stretching the neck, raising the crest, and pointing the bill during interactions. Their activity is mainly diurnal, although they can also forage during crepuscular periods.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered to be declining, with long-term reductions reported across much of its range, despite the species remaining common in many areas.
conservation.threats: The main concerns are destruction, drainage, and degradation of wetlands; loss of mangroves and vegetated stream margins; water pollution; and disturbance near nesting or feeding sites. Conversion of shallow-water habitat and removal of shoreline vegetation can reduce suitable cover and prey availability.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect wetlands, mangroves, ponds, rivers, and vegetated shorelines. Support conservation of natural watercourses and avoid clearing dense bank vegetation. Reduce pesticide and fertilizer runoff, keep domestic animals away from nesting areas, and observe herons from a respectful distance. Reporting sightings through reputable bird-monitoring programs can also help document resident and migratory populations in Costa Rica.

profile.overview: The Western Cattle-Egret is a small, adaptable heron that often feeds in open grassland, pasture, farmland, and seasonally flooded areas rather than standing in water. It commonly follows cattle, horses, and other large animals, catching insects and other prey disturbed by their movement. During the breeding season, adults develop orange-buff feathers on the head, chest, and back. The species has expanded widely from its original Old World range and is now established across much of the Americas, including Costa Rica.
profile.classification: The Western Cattle-Egret belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and is classified as Ardea ibis. It was formerly widely placed in the genus Bubulcus; some sources still use Bubulcus ibis.
profile.identification: This egret is a compact, short-necked white heron with a stout, yellowish bill, yellow to dark legs, and a relatively short, rounded wing profile. Adults in nonbreeding plumage are mostly white. In breeding plumage, orange-buff feathers appear on the crown, back, and breast, while the bill and legs may become more strongly colored. Juveniles are duller and lack the adult breeding colors. It is smaller and more stocky-looking than the Great Egret and often walks on land while feeding.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Western Cattle-Egret occurs across tropical and subtropical regions of Africa, southern Europe, western Asia, and the Americas. In Costa Rica it is a widespread and abundant resident, reported through much of the country, especially in lowlands and other open areas below about 2,000 meters, although it may occasionally occur higher. Typical habitats include cattle pasture, agricultural fields, savannas, roadsides, wet grassland, marsh margins, rice fields, and other landscapes where grazing animals or mowing disturb prey.
profile.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Western Cattle-Egret is primarily resident rather than a regular long-distance migrant. Local and seasonal movements may occur in response to rainfall, flooding, food availability, and changes in grazing conditions. Birds from northern populations can also move southward, but Costa Rican records generally represent an established breeding population present throughout the year.
profile.breeding: Western Cattle-Egrets usually breed colonially, often with other herons and egrets. They build a platform nest of sticks in trees, shrubs, reed beds, or vegetation near wetlands, lakes, rivers, and sometimes human settlements. Both adults participate in nest construction, incubation, and feeding the young. Clutch size is commonly several pale blue or greenish eggs, and the young are fed regurgitated food. Breeding timing varies geographically and is often linked to the rainy season and resulting increases in prey.
profile.dietFeeding: The main food consists of grasshoppers, crickets, beetles, caterpillars, flies, and other large insects. It also takes frogs, lizards, small snakes, fish, crustaceans, and occasionally small mammals or birds. Unlike many herons, it frequently feeds in dry or open habitats. Individuals often walk among cattle, horses, or other large mammals and seize prey flushed by their movements. They may also forage around agricultural machinery, recently mown fields, and shallow wetlands.
profile.behavior: Western Cattle-Egrets are social and commonly gather in flocks while feeding, roosting, and nesting. They are active walkers and may spend much of the day on land rather than standing in water. Birds often follow grazing animals closely, sometimes riding on them briefly or waiting for insects to be disturbed. At night they form communal roosts in trees or dense vegetation. Their flight is steady, with regular wingbeats and the neck held retracted, as in other herons.

profile.overview: The Great Egret (Ardea alba) is a large, elegant heron found on wetlands across much of the world. It is recognized by its entirely white plumage, long neck and legs, yellow bill, and slow, deliberate movements while hunting. The species uses both freshwater and coastal habitats and often shares nesting colonies with other herons and egrets. In Costa Rica, it is a familiar wetland bird and may be seen in both lowland and coastal areas.
profile.classification: The Great Egret belongs to the heron family, Ardeidae, in the order Pelecaniformes. It is also called the Great White Egret or Great White Heron in some regions.
profile.identification: A Great Egret is a tall, slender, completely white wading bird with a long, S-shaped neck, long black legs, and a long, pointed yellow bill. It is larger and more slender than a Snowy Egret, which has a black bill and yellow feet. During the breeding season, adults develop long ornamental plumes on the back, and the facial skin near the bill may become greenish. In flight, the neck is folded and the broad wings beat slowly.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species has a broad distribution in the Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australasia. It occupies marshes, swamps, ponds, lakeshores, flooded fields, rice fields, river edges, mangroves, estuaries, mudflats, and sheltered coastal waters. In Costa Rica, Great Egrets occur widely in suitable lowland wetlands, along rivers, around lakes and ponds, in mangroves, and on coastal mudflats. They are recorded on both the Pacific and Caribbean sides of the country, as well as inland.
profile.migrationStatus: Great Egrets in Costa Rica include resident birds and seasonal visitors. Some local populations remain year-round, while additional individuals migrate south from North America and occur mainly during the nonbreeding season or passage periods. Numbers can therefore increase seasonally, especially in wetlands and coastal areas.
profile.breeding: Great Egrets usually breed in colonies, often with other herons, egrets, and ibises. Nests are built on trees, shrubs, or vegetation near water and are made from sticks. Both adults help incubate the eggs and feed the young. Several young may hatch, but competition among nestlings can be intense when food is scarce. Great Egrets breed in parts of their tropical range, including suitable wetland areas of Costa Rica, although timing varies with local rainfall and water conditions.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of fish, frogs, aquatic insects, crustaceans, and other small aquatic animals. Great Egrets may also take snakes, lizards, small mammals, and occasionally young birds. They commonly hunt by standing motionless in shallow water or walking slowly while watching for prey. When an opportunity appears, the bird thrusts its bill forward with a rapid stabbing motion. It may also forage in flooded fields, grasslands, and along tidal edges.
profile.behavior: Great Egrets are usually solitary while feeding but gather at communal roosts and breeding colonies. They are patient hunters and may remain still for long periods before striking. Birds often fly with slow, powerful wingbeats and the neck folded back. They are active during daylight and may move between wetlands as water levels and prey availability change. Outside the breeding season, they can travel widely and may appear in habitats far from traditional nesting sites.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is uncertain. The species is widespread and remains common in many regions, although local populations may increase or decline depending on wetland condition and protection.

profile.overview: The Great Blue Heron (Ardea herodias) is a large, widespread wading bird found across much of North and Central America. It is commonly seen standing motionless in shallow water before striking fish and other prey with its long, spear-like bill. Its blue-gray body, long legs, broad wings, and folded S-shaped neck make it distinctive. The species uses freshwater and marine wetlands and often nests colonially in trees near productive feeding areas.
profile.classification: The Great Blue Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and the order Pelecaniformes. Its scientific name is Ardea herodias.
profile.identification: Adults are very large herons with blue-gray upperparts, a pale head and neck, a dark stripe above the eye, and long blackish plumes extending from the head during the breeding season. The bill is long and yellowish, while the legs are dull yellow to gray. Juveniles are browner, lack the prominent head plumes, and have less contrasting markings. In flight, the neck is folded into an S shape and the long legs trail well beyond the tail.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from Alaska and Canada through the United States, Mexico, Central America, and parts of the Caribbean. It occupies lakes, rivers, ponds, marshes, mangroves, estuaries, mudflats, reservoirs, fishponds, and coastal shallows, and may forage in wet meadows or agricultural areas. In Costa Rica, the Great Blue Heron is recorded as the Garzón azulado and occurs in suitable wetlands, river margins, estuaries, mangroves, and coastal habitats, generally as a nonbreeding visitor rather than a regular breeding species.
profile.migrationStatus: Great Blue Herons are partly migratory: northern populations move south after breeding, while many birds farther south remain year-round. In Costa Rica, the species is principally encountered as a migrant or nonbreeding visitor, although individual birds may remain in the country for extended periods when food and open water are available.
profile.breeding: Breeding usually occurs in colonies called heronries, often in tall trees or shrubs near wetlands, lakes, rivers, or coastlines. The male selects and defends a nest site, while both adults build or repair a bulky platform of sticks. A typical clutch contains several pale blue eggs, and both parents incubate them and feed the young. Reliable evidence for regular breeding by Great Blue Herons in Costa Rica is limited; the country is primarily important to the species outside its main breeding range.
profile.dietFeeding: Fish are the principal food, but the diet also includes frogs, aquatic insects, crayfish, crabs, snakes, small mammals, and occasionally young birds. The heron usually hunts alone by standing still or walking slowly through shallow water, then thrusting its bill rapidly at prey. It may also feed in tidal flats, flooded fields, ponds, drainage channels, and other shallow habitats where prey can be seen and reached.
profile.behavior: Great Blue Herons are often solitary while feeding and may defend productive foraging spots from other herons. They are patient hunters and can remain motionless for long periods before making a sudden strike. Birds fly with slow, deep wingbeats and the neck folded back. Outside the breeding season they commonly roost in trees or dense vegetation, while nesting colonies can become noisy and crowded during courtship and chick rearing.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable to increasing overall, although local populations may vary with wetland condition, disturbance, and food availability.

profile.overview: The American White Pelican is one of North America’s largest flying birds. It has brilliant white plumage, black wing tips, a long yellow-orange bill, and a large expandable throat pouch. Unlike the Brown Pelican, it usually catches fish while swimming rather than diving from the air. It breeds colonially on inland lakes and islands and spends the nonbreeding season around lakes, rivers, reservoirs, estuaries, and sheltered coastal waters.
profile.classification: The American White Pelican belongs to the pelican family, Pelecanidae, and the order Pelecaniformes. Its scientific name is Pelecanus erythrorhynchos.
profile.identification: This very large pelican measures about 1.3–1.8 meters in length, with a wingspan commonly exceeding 2.4 meters. Adults are mostly white, with contrasting black outer flight feathers visible especially in flight. The bill and throat pouch are yellowish to orange, and the legs are short and pale. Breeding adults may develop a temporary raised plate on the upper bill. Juveniles are duller, with gray-brown markings and a less brightly colored bill.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species breeds mainly across inland western and central North America, from parts of Canada through the western and central United States, with additional breeding populations in Mexico and Texas. It winters mostly in the southern United States, Mexico, and occasionally farther south. In Costa Rica it is a rare or accidental visitor rather than a regular wintering species. A few records, including observations near the Gulf of Nicoya and the Caribbean coast, have involved solitary birds using open freshwater, wetland, river, or sheltered coastal habitats.
profile.migrationStatus: Most populations are migratory, moving south after breeding and returning north in spring. In Costa Rica, the American White Pelican is an irregular accidental migrant or vagrant, recorded mainly during the northern winter or migration periods; it does not breed there and is not a dependable seasonal species.
profile.breeding: American White Pelicans breed in large colonies, usually on remote islands in freshwater lakes or on isolated marshy ground that offers protection from terrestrial predators. Both adults help build a simple nest of soil, vegetation, or debris. A typical clutch contains two eggs, although usually only one chick survives. Parents share incubation and feeding duties. Young gather in groups, or crèches, after leaving the nest and become independent several weeks later.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of fish, but also includes amphibians, crayfish, and other aquatic animals. Pelicans often forage cooperatively, swimming in lines or semicircles to concentrate prey before scooping it up with their pouches. They may also feed alone, especially where prey is scattered. The pouch temporarily holds water and prey; the bird drains the water before swallowing its food.
profile.behavior: American White Pelicans are highly social outside the breeding season and commonly roost or travel in groups. Their broad wings allow efficient soaring, and flocks may circle on rising air for long periods. They are generally quiet away from colonies. Birds rest on sandbars, islands, mudflats, and shorelines, and they may swim readily between feeding areas. At breeding colonies, adults can become aggressive toward intruders and neighboring birds.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered large and is not currently recognized as undergoing a meaningful overall decline, although local colonies may fluctuate with water conditions, food supply, disease, and disturbance.

profile.overview: The Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) is a large coastal waterbird recognized by its long bill, expandable throat pouch, dark body, and broad wings. Unlike most pelicans, it captures fish by plunge-diving from the air. It is strongly associated with warm marine waters, estuaries, bays, beaches, and offshore islands. In Costa Rica, it is a familiar coastal species, especially along the Pacific shore, where groups commonly rest, fly, and feed near beaches and fishing areas.
profile.classification: The Brown Pelican belongs to the pelican family, Pelecanidae, in the order Pelecaniformes. It is one of the pelican species native to the Americas.
profile.identification: Adults have a gray-brown body, dark flight feathers, a pale or yellowish head, and a very long bill with a large throat pouch. Breeding adults may show brighter yellow, orange, or reddish coloration on the face and bill. The species has a heavy body, broad wings, and a distinctive flight style that combines strong wingbeats with gliding. It is often identified by its spectacular plunge-dives, in which it drops headfirst into the water to catch fish.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Brown Pelican occurs along the Pacific and Atlantic coasts of the Americas, from western and southern North America through Central America and into northern South America and the Caribbean. In Costa Rica it is resident and widespread along the Pacific coast, where it is generally common to abundant around beaches, bays, estuaries, mangroves, coastal wetlands, and offshore islands. It also occurs along the Caribbean coast, but is less numerous there. Important coastal breeding habitat includes Pacific islands and other undisturbed sites near shore.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is mainly resident in Costa Rica. Birds make local and seasonal movements along the coast in response to food supplies, weather, and breeding activity, while some individuals elsewhere in the range undertake broader coastal migrations. Costa Rica is used both by resident birds and by pelicans moving through or along the Central American coastline.
profile.breeding: Brown Pelicans breed colonially, usually on offshore islands or other protected coastal sites. Nests may be placed on the ground, in shrubs, or in low trees, depending on the location. Both parents help build the nest, incubate the eggs, and feed the young. Colonies require secure sites with minimal disturbance and nearby productive fishing waters. In Costa Rica, breeding is documented mainly on Pacific islands, including protected coastal islands such as Isla Bolaños. Breeding timing can vary with region and local conditions.
profile.dietFeeding: Fish form the main food, supplemented by marine invertebrates such as shrimp and other crustaceans. The Brown Pelican usually hunts by flying above shallow coastal water, folding its wings, and plunging into the sea. Its throat pouch briefly holds the catch and excess water, which is drained before the fish is swallowed. It often feeds in groups and may gather around schools of fish, productive estuaries, or areas where fishing activity concentrates prey.
profile.behavior: Brown Pelicans are social birds that commonly roost, travel, and feed in groups. They rest on beaches, pilings, rocks, mangrove edges, and offshore islands, often holding their wings open to dry or regulate body temperature. Their flight consists of powerful wingbeats alternating with glides close to the water. Adults are generally calm around one another, although birds may compete for food or favored roosting and nesting places. They are powerful swimmers and can take off directly from the water.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered relatively secure, although trends vary among regional populations and some areas may be stable, increasing, or declining.

profile.overview: The King Vulture is a large, distinctive New World vulture of tropical Central and South America. It is named for its striking appearance and dominance at carcasses, where its powerful bill can open tough skin for smaller scavengers. The species usually searches for food by soaring above forest and open areas, then descends to carrion on the ground. It plays an important ecological role by rapidly removing dead animals from the environment.
profile.classification: The King Vulture belongs to the vulture family Cathartidae and is the only living species in the genus Sarcoramphus. Its scientific name is Sarcoramphus papa.
profile.identification: This is a very large vulture with broad wings, a short tail, and mostly white plumage contrasting with black flight feathers and a black tail.
