conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is declining, with long-term monitoring in North America indicating a gradual decrease. The decline is not currently considered severe enough to place the species in a globally threatened category.
conservation.threats: Important threats include loss and fragmentation of wetlands, grasslands, meadows, and old fields; agricultural intensification; development; and succession of open farmland into dense woodland. Reduced prey availability, pesticide exposure, poisoned rodents, disturbance or trampling of ground nests, and occasional shooting can also affect local populations.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore wetlands, native grasslands, pastures, and other open habitats, including wintering areas. Maintain dense ground vegetation around suitable nesting sites and avoid disturbing suspected nests during the breeding season. Reduce unnecessary rodenticide and pesticide use, preserve natural prey populations, and support habitat conservation programs and responsible monitoring of migrating and wintering raptors.

profile.overview: The Tiny Hawk (Microspizias superciliosus) is one of the smallest birds of prey in the Americas. It is a forest-dwelling accipitrid that hunts mainly small birds, often by making quick, surprise attacks through dense vegetation. The species is generally secretive and is more often heard or briefly glimpsed than watched in the open. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon resident of suitable humid forest, where it can occur on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes.
profile.classification: The Tiny Hawk belongs to the order Accipitriformes and family Accipitridae. It was formerly widely known as Accipiter superciliosus; current classifications place it in the genus Microspizias.
profile.identification: This is a very small, short-winged hawk, with males substantially smaller than females. Adults are mainly slate-gray above, with fine barring on the whitish to rufous underparts, a darker crown, a relatively short tail, and a noticeable pale eyebrow. Juveniles are browner or rufous and usually show stronger warm tones below. It can be confused with the Semicollared Hawk, but the Tiny Hawk lacks that species’ prominent contrasting collar. It usually perches quietly inside or along the edge of forest.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Tiny Hawk occupies humid tropical and subtropical forest from Central America through much of northern and eastern South America. It uses lowland rainforest, moist foothill forest, forest edges, clearings, and sometimes more open woodland near forest. In Costa Rica, the subspecies fontainieri occurs locally on the Caribbean slope in the north and on both slopes in the southwest, extending through lowlands and hills. It is most likely in remaining mature forest and well-wooded landscapes, generally from low elevations into the foothills.
profile.migrationStatus: Generally resident and non-migratory. In Costa Rica it is considered a year-round species rather than a regular seasonal migrant, although local movements and irregular records may occur.
profile.breeding: The Tiny Hawk is believed to breed in forest habitats within its range, including Costa Rica. Available life-history information indicates a small clutch, usually about one or two eggs. As with other small forest hawks, nesting behavior is difficult to observe because adults remain inconspicuous and nests are placed in trees. Pairs likely defend territories and may be especially difficult to detect during the breeding season because much of their activity occurs under the forest canopy.
profile.dietFeeding: It feeds primarily on small birds, which it captures with rapid attacks through vegetation or from concealed perches. Hummingbirds and other small, agile forest birds may be taken, along with insects and possibly small reptiles or mammals when available. Its short wings and longish tail suit maneuvering through dense forest. The hawk often hunts alone and may wait quietly before making a sudden burst of speed.
profile.behavior: The Tiny Hawk is diurnal, solitary, and secretive. It commonly remains within dense forest, where its small size and subdued plumage make it easy to overlook. Individuals may perch near forest edges or in clearings, but they generally avoid prolonged exposure in open areas. When detected, it may give sharp calls and move quickly between perches. Its flight is fast and agile, especially when pursuing small birds through tangled vegetation.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains widespread and is not currently assessed as threatened.

profile.overview: The Double-toothed Kite (Harpagus bidentatus) is a small forest raptor of the Neotropics. It is named for two tooth-like notches on the cutting edge of its upper bill, an adaptation shared with its close relative, the Rufous-thighed Kite. This agile kite often hunts from concealed perches beneath the forest canopy and may soar over forest openings. It is generally associated with humid, mature woodland but can also use older second-growth habitats and edges.
profile.classification: The Double-toothed Kite belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae. Two commonly recognized subspecies are distributed in Central and South America, with H. b. fasciatus occurring from Mexico through Central America and western South America.
profile.identification: Adults have slate-gray upperparts, a white throat marked by a narrow dark central stripe, rufous to chestnut breast and belly, barred lower underparts, yellow legs, and red eyes. The fluffy white undertail coverts are especially noticeable in flight. The short, strongly hooked bill has two tooth-like projections. Immature birds are browner above and paler below, with prominent dark streaking. Its thin, high-pitched whistles may also help identify it.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and into northern and eastern South America. In Costa Rica it is a permanent resident found on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes, including lowland and middle-elevation forests, generally from sea level to about 1,200 meters. It favors mature moist and wet forest interiors, but also occurs along forest edges, openings, and older second growth. It is less characteristic of heavily cleared landscapes.
profile.migrationStatus: The Double-toothed Kite is considered largely resident rather than migratory. In Costa Rica it occurs throughout the year on both slopes, although local movements may follow food availability or changing conditions in forested areas.
profile.breeding: Breeding timing varies by region and is often associated with the local rainy season. The female builds, or helps build, a shallow saucer-shaped nest of small sticks in a tree fork, commonly near a forest edge and sometimes high above the ground. Clutches usually contain one or two eggs. The female performs most incubation, lasting about 42 to 45 days, while the male commonly supplies prey. Young usually leave the nest roughly a month after hatching.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of insects and small vertebrates. Documented prey includes cicadas and other large insects, lizards, frogs, bats, and occasionally other small animals. The kite usually hunts from a perch within or below the forest canopy, making quick sallies to snatch prey from vegetation or the air. In Costa Rica it may follow troops of White-faced or Squirrel Monkeys, capturing insects and other creatures flushed by the monkeys’ movements.
profile.behavior: This is an alert, agile, and mostly solitary or pair-living raptor. It spends considerable time perched quietly inside the canopy but may soar above the treetops, especially over gaps and clearings. Courtship includes display flights above the canopy, and males may bring food to females during courtship and incubation. Pairs communicate with thin whistles, while sharper calls may be given during territorial encounters or nest defense.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is reported as decreasing, although the species is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Mississippi Kite (Ictinia mississippiensis) is a slender, long-winged raptor that breeds mainly in the southern and central United States and migrates to South America. It is an agile aerial hunter, often catching insects while gliding or swooping. Adults are mostly gray with a pale head, dark wingtips, and a black tail. The species is sociable outside the breeding season and may gather in large groups during migration and winter.
profile.classification: The Mississippi Kite belongs to the order Accipitriformes and family Accipitridae. It is one of two species in the genus Ictinia, the other being the Plumbeous Kite.
profile.identification: Adults have a slim body, long pointed wings, and a fairly long dark tail. The head and underparts are pale gray to whitish, while the back is darker gray; a broad pale area on the upper wings is visible in flight. The eyes are reddish in adults. Juveniles are brown and heavily streaked, with pale-edged feathers. Its buoyant, falcon-like flight and frequent aerial insect hunting are useful identification clues.
profile.rangeHabitat: Mississippi Kites breed across parts of the southern Great Plains, lower Mississippi Valley, southeastern United States, and adjacent regions. They use mature bottomland forest, riparian woodland, savanna, shelterbelts, isolated groves, pasture edges, and increasingly urban parks and golf courses. In Costa Rica, they are nonbreeding migrants rather than residents. Occurrence is generally irregular or sporadic, with flocks recorded during migration in lowlands on both slopes and in the Central Valley, especially in spring and autumn.
profile.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant, it leaves North American breeding areas for wintering grounds in South America. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon, passage migrant, reported mainly from late March to early May and from about mid-September to mid-October; it does not normally breed there or remain year-round.
profile.breeding: Breeding takes place in North America, not Costa Rica. Pairs build a shallow stick nest in a tree, sometimes reusing an old nest or a squirrel nest. Nest placement ranges from low trees to tall mature forest trees. The usual clutch contains one to three dull-white eggs, incubated by both parents for roughly one month. Young generally leave the nest after about four to five weeks, although they may remain dependent nearby afterward.
profile.dietFeeding: Flying insects, including beetles, grasshoppers, cicadas, and leafhoppers, form much of the diet. Mississippi Kites commonly seize prey in midair and may eat it while still flying. They also take frogs, lizards, snakes, turtles, small birds, bats, and small mammals. Birds may forage over woodland edges, pasture, wetlands, farmland, roads, and urban areas, and sometimes capture prey from vegetation, shallow water, or the ground.
profile.behavior: Mississippi Kites are graceful, highly maneuverable fliers that soar on thermals and glide with their long pointed wings. They often hunt and roost socially, sometimes in groups of dozens. During the breeding season, adults vigorously defend nest areas and may dive at people, pets, crows, owls, or other perceived threats. Pairs usually remain together through the nesting period, and some breeding groups may include a year-old helper.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered increasing or stable overall, and the species remains fairly common across much of its breeding range.

profile.overview: The Plumbeous Kite (Ictinia plumbea) is a slim, long-winged bird of prey found from Mexico through Central America and across much of tropical South America. It is named for its overall plumbeous, or lead-gray, plumage. This kite often hunts insects from exposed perches or catches them in flight. In Costa Rica, it is best known as a seasonal migrant and passage bird, particularly during raptor migration along the Caribbean slope and other lowland areas.
profile.classification: The Plumbeous Kite belongs to the family Accipitridae, which includes kites, hawks, eagles, and harriers. It is one of two closely related species in the genus Ictinia, the other being the Mississippi Kite.
profile.identification: Adults are slender kites with long, pointed wings, a long tail, and mostly dark gray plumage. The head and underparts are usually paler gray than the back, while the flight feathers are darker and the tail is black with narrow pale bands. The eyes are reddish, and the legs are orange-red. Juveniles are browner and more heavily streaked, with pale-edged feathers and a more prominently banded tail. Its buoyant flight and narrow, pointed wings are useful field marks.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from Mexico and Central America south through northern and central South America. It uses humid and seasonally dry forests, forest edges, woodland clearings, gallery forests, plantations, and savanna-like habitats, generally in lowlands and foothills. In Costa Rica, Plumbeous Kites occur mainly as migrants and passage birds, using forested lowlands, open areas, and migration corridors. They are regularly noted during raptor movements along the Caribbean coast and at sites such as the Talamanca and Kèköldi region.
profile.migrationStatus: Northern populations are migratory, while many South American populations are resident or move locally. In Costa Rica, the species is chiefly a seasonal migrant and passage visitor. Migration can be observed from about August through November, with additional northbound passage in spring; timing and numbers vary by location and weather.
profile.breeding: Plumbeous Kites usually nest in trees within or near forest, often placing a small stick nest high above the ground. The female generally lays one or two eggs, and both adults participate in rearing the young. The species may breed in parts of Mexico, Central America, and South America, but detailed breeding information is uneven across its range. Costa Rica is more consistently documented as a migration area than as a major breeding center for the species.
profile.dietFeeding: Flying insects form the main part of the diet, including dragonflies, grasshoppers, beetles, cicadas, and other large insects. The kite often watches from a prominent perch before making a short aerial sortie to capture prey. It may also take insects while gliding or hawking through the air. Small vertebrates and other prey are probably eaten occasionally, but insects are the characteristic food.
profile.behavior: This kite is often seen soaring or gliding with its long wings held slightly forward, sometimes joining other raptors during migration. It commonly perches quietly on exposed branches, poles, or dead snags while scanning for prey. Individuals may be solitary outside migration, although several can gather where food is abundant or along established migration routes. Its flight is generally light and buoyant rather than powerful or rapidly flapping.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is assessed as decreasing, but the species is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Crane Hawk (Geranospiza caerulescens) is a distinctive tropical raptor of the Americas. It has unusually long legs, a long tail, and flexible ankle joints that help it search for prey in tree cavities, bromeliad clusters, tangled vegetation, and other difficult places. The species is usually secretive and spends much of its time perched inside forest or woodland. In Costa Rica, it is a local and uncommon resident of the lowlands on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes.
profile.classification: The Crane Hawk belongs to the order Accipitriformes and the hawk-and-eagle family Accipitridae. Geranospiza is a small genus containing this single species.
profile.identification: Adults are slender, long-legged hawks with a small head, long tail, and broad wings. The plumage is generally slate-gray to dark gray, with reddish eyes, a gray facial area, and long red legs. The tail has two conspicuous broad white bands, especially visible in flight. Immature birds are browner and have paler facial markings and less vivid eyes. Its loose wingbeats, low flight, and habit of climbing through branches help distinguish it from many other tropical hawks.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Crane Hawk occurs from Mexico and Central America through much of northern, western, and central South America, including Trinidad in some treatments. It uses humid lowland forest, forest edges, gallery forest, swamps, mangroves, second growth, plantations, and wooded areas near wetlands. In Costa Rica it is a local, uncommon resident of the lowlands along both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes. It is most likely in well-wooded sites with dense vegetation, water, and mature trees, rather than in open highland areas.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is generally considered resident rather than a regular long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, it occurs year-round, although local movements may follow food availability, water conditions, or changes in habitat. Seasonal variation in sightings does not by itself indicate passage migration.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is less thoroughly documented than for many widespread raptors. The Crane Hawk builds a stick nest in a tree, typically within forest or dense woodland, and breeding pairs are thought to defend territories. Nest placement provides concealment and may be associated with mature trees near wetlands or other productive feeding areas. The female lays a small clutch, and both adults participate in caring for the young. Timing varies geographically across its broad tropical range.
profile.dietFeeding: The Crane Hawk feeds mainly on small vertebrates and large invertebrates, including frogs, lizards, snakes, small birds, rodents, bats, crabs, and insects. It often hunts from low perches and moves deliberately through dense vegetation. Its long legs and unusually flexible joints allow it to reach into tree holes, bromeliads, epiphyte masses, nests, and tangled foliage while searching for concealed prey.
profile.behavior: This is a secretive, mostly solitary or paired hawk that is more often heard or briefly seen than observed in open flight. It commonly perches quietly in the forest understory or along edges. When foraging, it may climb or hop through branches and vegetation in a manner unlike most hawks. Its flight is usually low and direct, with relaxed wingbeats; it rarely spends long periods soaring high above the landscape.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered decreasing, although the species remains widespread and is not currently evaluated as globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Black-collared Hawk (Busarellus nigricollis) is a broad-winged raptor strongly associated with wetlands and shallow water. It is named for the dark crescent across the upper breast, below a pale buff-white head. Most of its range lies from southern Mexico through Central America and across tropical South America east of the Andes. It usually hunts from perches near marshes, ponds, slow rivers, flooded fields, and forest edges.
profile.classification: The Black-collared Hawk belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae. It is the only species in the genus Busarellus.
profile.identification: Adults are medium-sized hawks with broad wings, a short tail, and mainly cinnamon-rufous underparts. The head is pale buff or whitish, often with fine dark streaking, and a conspicuous black crescent forms a collar across the upper breast. The flight feathers are mostly black, while the tail is brown with dark bands. Immatures are browner and more heavily streaked, with less sharply defined adult markings.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of tropical South America east of the Andes, reaching southern Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, and northern Argentina. In Costa Rica it is a scarce, local resident rather than a widespread common hawk. Reliable records are concentrated around wetlands and lowland waterways, including Río Frío and Caño Negro, with additional occurrences near Tortuguero, the lower Tempisque and Bebedero basins, and parts of the Osa Peninsula. It uses shallow marshes, lagoons, slow rivers, flooded fields, riparian woodland, and open lowland habitats with trees for perching.
profile.migrationStatus: Generally resident and not considered a regular long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, it is regarded as a local resident, although individuals may make short-distance movements in response to water levels and prey availability.
profile.breeding: Black-collared Hawks build a large stick nest, usually in a tall tree near water, sometimes in an isolated or emergent tree above wetland vegetation. The nest is lined with smaller twigs and fresh leaves. Clutch size is commonly one or two eggs, though details vary across the range. Both adults participate in territorial activity and care for the young. A nesting record from Costa Rica confirms that the species breeds there, although breeding information for the country remains limited.
profile.dietFeeding: Fish make up most of the diet. The hawk usually watches from a low or moderate perch and drops or plunges into shallow water to seize fish with its long, strongly curved talons. Specialized roughened surfaces on the feet may help it hold slippery prey. It also takes aquatic invertebrates, amphibians, crustaceans, and other small animals when available. Hunting is closely tied to calm, shallow water and exposed wetland margins.
profile.behavior: This hawk often sits quietly on branches overlooking water, marsh edges, or flooded vegetation. It may make short flights between perches while searching for prey and can hover or plunge briefly when attacking fish. Pairs may perform high aerial displays involving circling, calling, dipping, and diving. It is usually solitary or seen in pairs, and its distribution is strongly patchy because suitable wetlands are unevenly distributed across the landscape.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered decreasing, but the species remains widespread and is not currently close to the thresholds for a threatened category.

profile.overview: The Snail Kite is a specialized wetland raptor that feeds mainly on freshwater snails. Its strongly curved bill is adapted for extracting snails from their shells. Adult males are dark gray, while females and young birds are brown and streaked. The species is broadly distributed from Florida and the Caribbean through Central America and much of South America. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon, local bird associated with suitable marshes, lakes, rivers, and seasonally flooded wetlands.
profile.classification: The Snail Kite belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae and the order Accipitriformes. Its scientific name is Rostrhamus sociabilis.
profile.identification: This medium-sized kite has broad wings, a short tail, and a distinctive white patch at the base of the tail. Adult males are slate gray to nearly black, with red eyes, an orange to reddish cere and legs, and a strongly hooked bill. Females and immature birds are brown with paler streaking on the head, neck, and underparts. In flight, it often shows slow, deep wingbeats and may circle low over marshes. Its specialized bill helps distinguish it from other Costa Rican kites.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Snail Kite ranges from Florida, Cuba, and southern Mexico through parts of Central America and across much of tropical South America. In Costa Rica it occurs locally and is generally uncommon, with records from wetland regions including the Tempisque Basin and Guanacaste marshes, as well as other lowland sites. It uses freshwater marshes, shallow lakes, flooded savannas, slow rivers, oxbow wetlands, and areas with emergent vegetation, especially where apple snails and perching sites are abundant.
profile.migrationStatus: The Costa Rican population appears to include resident birds, while some individuals recorded on the Caribbean slope may be northern migrants. Occurrence is local and irregular outside the principal wetland areas.
profile.breeding: Snail Kites usually nest near wetlands, often in low trees, shrubs, or emergent vegetation over or beside shallow water. They may breed singly or in loose colonies, depending on food availability and nesting habitat. Both adults participate in incubating the eggs and feeding the young. The species breeds in Central and South America, but reliable information on the frequency and distribution of breeding within Costa Rica is limited; documented Costa Rican records should therefore be interpreted as local rather than representative of the entire country.
profile.dietFeeding: Freshwater snails, especially apple snails and related ampullariid mollusks, make up most of the diet. The kite typically searches from a perch or while flying slowly over shallow water, then captures a snail with its feet. It carries the prey to a favored perch, grips the shell with one foot, and uses its narrow, sharply curved bill to remove the edible animal. Small crabs, crayfish, frogs, and other aquatic prey may occasionally be taken.
profile.behavior: Snail Kites are often seen singly, in pairs, or in small groups around wetlands. They perch conspicuously on dead branches, shrubs, or other elevated structures near feeding areas. Their flight is usually slow and buoyant, with broad wings and relaxed wingbeats. Birds may patrol the edge of marsh vegetation before dropping toward the water. Because their movements are closely tied to water levels and snail abundance, local numbers can vary between seasons and years.

conservation.populationTrend: Globally stable overall, with some regional increases in the northern part of the range and localized declines where wetlands have been damaged. Population size across the full range is not well quantified.

profile.overview: The Barred Hawk (Morphnarchus princeps) is a forest-dwelling raptor of humid tropical regions from Costa Rica and Panama south through the Andes to Peru. It is a stocky, relatively short-winged hawk with dark upperparts, a black chest, pale underparts marked with dark barring, and a dark tail crossed by a narrow white band. It usually hunts from concealed perches within dense vegetation rather than soaring conspicuously over open country.
profile.classification: The Barred Hawk belongs to the order Accipitriformes and family Accipitridae, which includes hawks, eagles, kites, and Old World vultures. Morphnarchus is a monotypic genus containing only this species.
profile.identification: Adults are medium-sized, broad-bodied hawks with slate-gray to blackish upperparts, a dark head and chest, and white underparts heavily barred with black. The tail is mostly dark and has a conspicuous narrow white band and pale tip. The cere and legs are yellow to orange. In Costa Rica, it can be confused with other dark forest hawks, but its bold barred belly, black bib, and forest habitat are useful field marks.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Barred Hawk occurs from Costa Rica and Panama through Colombia and Ecuador to Peru, primarily along humid mountain slopes and foothills. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, recorded in suitable forested areas including Caribbean-slope lowlands, foothills, and montane regions; it is generally local and less frequently encountered than common open-country raptors. It uses humid tropical lowland and montane forest, especially areas with mature vegetation, dense canopy, and relatively undisturbed habitat.
profile.migrationStatus: The species is considered resident rather than migratory. Barred Hawks occur in Costa Rica throughout the year, although local movements may follow food availability or changing conditions in mountainous terrain.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited compared with that of better-studied raptors. The species is believed to form territorial pairs in forest, with nesting associated with mature trees and secluded areas. As with many tropical forest hawks, the female probably performs most incubation while the male supplies food, but detailed information on nest structure, clutch size, incubation, and fledging is scarce. Costa Rican records indicate that the species breeds within its resident range, although timing may vary by region.
profile.dietFeeding: The Barred Hawk takes a varied selection of forest prey, including snakes, lizards, frogs, large insects, small mammals, and birds. It generally hunts by waiting quietly on a concealed perch and making short, direct flights to capture prey on or near the ground or within dense vegetation. Its slow, deliberate hunting style is well suited to humid forest where visibility is limited.
profile.behavior: Usually solitary or found in pairs, the Barred Hawk spends much of its time perched quietly inside or at the edge of forest. It may call with a clear, penetrating whistle and can become vocal around a mate or territory. It is not primarily a soaring raptor, although it may fly above the canopy or across valleys. Dense forest, rather than open thermals, is central to its daily activities.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not precisely quantified, and detailed trend information is limited. The species remains broadly distributed, but local abundance depends on the persistence of humid forest.

profile.overview: The Common Black Hawk (Buteogallus anthracinus) is a broad-winged raptor associated with rivers, wetlands, mangroves, and other warm lowland habitats. Adults are mostly black or dark charcoal, with a broad white band and white tip on the short tail, yellow legs, and a yellow-based bill. Juveniles are brown and heavily streaked. Despite its name, it is not closely related to the Zone-tailed Hawk and is generally more strongly tied to aquatic habitats.
profile.classification: The Common Black Hawk belongs to the order Accipitriformes and the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae. Its genus, Buteogallus, includes several large tropical black hawks.
profile.identification: Adults are nearly uniform black or dark gray, with broad wings, a short tail, yellow legs, and yellow skin at the base of the bill. A single broad white tail band and a white tail tip are conspicuous in flight. The underwing may appear somewhat paler than the body. Juveniles are brown above and pale below, with dark streaking, a dark facial stripe, and a more barred tail. It can be confused with the larger Great Black Hawk, which usually has more extensive white in the tail and wings.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from the southwestern United States and Mexico through Central America to northern South America, with additional populations in the Caribbean. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, locally common along both the Pacific and Caribbean coasts but uncommon or scarce inland. It uses mangrove swamps, estuaries, coastal woodland, river margins, wet lowland forest, and dry woodland near water. Large rivers can allow it to occur farther inland where suitable prey and nesting trees remain available.
profile.migrationStatus: Costa Rican populations are generally resident and do not undertake regular long-distance migration. The migratory portion of the species occurs mainly in the northern range, especially the southwestern United States and parts of northwestern Mexico; those birds move south in the nonbreeding season and may pass through or winter farther south.
profile.breeding: Breeding occurs in suitable lowland habitats, especially near rivers, estuaries, mangroves, and other wetlands. The nest is a bulky platform of sticks placed in a tree, often near water, and may be reused or repaired in later years. The female usually lays a small clutch, commonly one or two eggs. Both adults defend the nesting area, and the young remain dependent on the parents for an extended period after leaving the nest.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet varies with location and season. Common prey includes crabs, crayfish, fish, frogs, snakes, lizards, small mammals, and large insects. In coastal Central America, land crabs and other aquatic or shoreline animals can be especially important. The hawk often hunts from a low or exposed perch beside water, dropping to the ground or water's edge to seize prey, and may also search slowly along mudflats and mangrove margins.
profile.behavior: Common Black Hawks are often seen perched quietly in trees beside water or soaring on broad wings over wetlands and forest edges. They are generally less constantly active than many smaller hawks, but may make short flights between perches while hunting. Adults are territorial during breeding. Their calls are high, clear, and repeated, especially around the nest. They may tolerate some human-modified landscapes when riverside trees, wetlands, and adequate prey are retained.

conservation.populationTrend: The recognized population trend is decreasing.

profile.overview: The Savanna Hawk is a large, long-legged raptor of open tropical and subtropical country. Its striking plumage is mainly cinnamon or rufous, with gray-brown upperparts, fine dark barring below, reddish wings, and a black tail marked with a pale band and tip. It often hunts from low perches or on foot, and may follow fires through grasslands to catch animals fleeing the flames. The species is also called the Savanna Hawk or Savanna Buteogallus.
profile.classification: The Savanna Hawk belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae and the genus Buteogallus. It was formerly placed in the genus Heterospizias.
profile.identification: Adults are about 46–64 cm long and have a distinctive warm cinnamon to rufous body. The back is grayish brown with pale-edged feathers, while the underparts show fine dark barring. The wings are strongly reddish, and the black tail usually has a broad pale central band and a whitish tip. Long yellow legs, a yellow cere, broad wings, and a relatively short tail help separate it from other open-country hawks. Immatures are duller and more heavily mottled.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Panama and Trinidad through much of northern, central, and eastern South America to Bolivia, Uruguay, and central Argentina. It favors lowland savannas, seasonally flooded grasslands, marsh edges, ranchland, agricultural clearings, and other open areas with scattered trees, shrubs, or gallery forest. In Costa Rica it is very rare and irregular, with records concentrated in the southwestern lowlands, including the Coto 47 region and possible observations near the Osa Peninsula. It is generally treated as a vagrant or occasional visitor there rather than a widespread resident.
profile.migrationStatus: Generally resident or locally nomadic within its range, following changes in rainfall, flooding, fire, and prey availability. In Costa Rica it is an irregular, very rare visitor, and there is no reliable evidence that it undertakes regular seasonal migration through the country.
profile.breeding: Savanna Hawks usually breed as pairs in open landscapes containing scattered trees or strips of riparian woodland. The nest is a platform of sticks placed in a tree, often fairly low or at moderate height, and is lined with vegetation. A typical clutch is small, usually one or two eggs. Both adults participate in nest defense and care for the young. Breeding is well documented across the species’ main range, but a regular breeding population has not been reliably established in Costa Rica.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet is broad and includes small mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, crabs, frogs, snakes, lizards, and large insects. The hawk commonly watches from a low perch before dropping to the ground, but it may also seize prey in flight or stalk through grass on its long legs. In burned or recently burned fields, it sometimes walks behind the fire front to capture animals exposed by the flames.
profile.behavior: This is a conspicuous, mostly solitary or pair-living hawk of open country. It spends considerable time perched on fence posts, dead trees, shrubs, or utility structures, and it may soar over its territory. It frequently hunts on the ground and is more comfortable walking than many other large hawks. Its movements are influenced by local conditions, especially fire, flooding, grass growth, and concentrations of prey.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to be undergoing a sufficiently rapid decline for a threatened category. Local populations may nevertheless be affected by loss or alteration of open grassland and wetland habitats. In Costa Rica, it remains extremely rare and irregular, so its local status is less secure than its global assessment suggests.
conservation.threats: Conversion of natural savannas, seasonally flooded grasslands, and wetlands can reduce feeding and nesting habitat. Intensive agriculture, indiscriminate pesticide use, persecution of raptors, uncontrolled burning, and collisions with vehicles or power infrastructure may also cause local losses. Because records in Costa Rica are scarce, changes in its local occurrence should be monitored rather than assumed to reflect a stable population.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect remaining lowland savannas, wetlands, riparian woodland, and mixed-use open habitats, particularly in southwestern Costa Rica. Use fire carefully and maintain scattered native trees and safe hunting perches. Reduce unnecessary pesticide use, prevent persecution of birds of prey, and report well-documented sightings with photographs or recordings to national bird-monitoring programs so the species’ expanding or irregular presence in Costa Rica can be tracked.

profile.overview: The Great Black Hawk (Buteogallus urubitinga) is a large tropical raptor of the Americas. It is mostly black as an adult, with a broad white band across the tail and conspicuous yellow legs and cere. This powerful hawk often hunts from low perches or walks on the ground rather than soaring continuously. It uses forests, woodland edges, wetlands, river corridors, and semiopen country, and is generally associated with warm lowland and foothill environments.
profile.classification: The Great Black Hawk belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae and the genus Buteogallus. It is separate from the similar Common Black Hawk, Buteogallus anthracinus.
profile.identification: Adults are large, heavy-bodied black hawks with broad wings, a relatively short tail, yellow legs, and yellow skin at the base of the bill. The tail shows a contrasting broad white band, especially visible in flight. Immatures are mainly brown and heavily streaked, with a pale eyebrow and fine barring on the tail; they can be difficult to separate from immature Common Black Hawks. Great Black Hawks are generally larger and have a more substantial bill and body.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and much of South America. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon but widely distributed resident of both the Pacific and Caribbean slopes, occurring mainly in lowlands and middle elevations and locally reaching about 1,200 meters. It uses forest, forest edges, river and stream margins, marshy areas, and semiopen landscapes. It is usually less common in exposed coastal areas than in inland lowlands and foothills.
profile.migrationStatus: Great Black Hawks in Costa Rica are regarded as resident rather than regular long-distance migrants. Individuals may make local movements in response to food, water, or habitat conditions, but the species is present during all seasons.
profile.breeding: The Great Black Hawk usually builds a stick platform high in a tree, often near forest, rivers, wetlands, or other productive feeding areas. The nest may be large and bulky. A clutch generally consists of one white egg marked with reddish-brown or violet blotches. In Costa Rica, nests with small or nearly fledged young have been reported during the dry and early wet seasons, although breeding timing can vary by locality and conditions.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet is varied and includes reptiles, amphibians, fish, crabs, birds, small mammals, large insects, eggs, carrion, and occasionally fruit. It often hunts from a low perch, drops onto prey, or searches on foot along stream banks, wet ground, forest edges, and open patches. Its strong legs and bill allow it to handle relatively large or armored prey.
profile.behavior: Great Black Hawks are often seen perched quietly, flying low between trees, or soaring over forest and open country. They may forage on the ground and sometimes occur in small groups, particularly where food is concentrated. Adults are conspicuous and confident, while immatures can appear more secretive. Their broad wings and contrasting tail markings are useful for identification during flight.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered decreasing, although the species remains widespread and is not currently assessed as globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Solitary Eagle is a large, powerful forest eagle of the tropical Americas. It is mostly dark gray to black, with a broad wingspan, a short tail, and conspicuous white markings in the tail and wing coverts. It usually occurs alone or in pairs and is associated with mountain forests and adjacent open country. Despite its wide geographic range, it is uncommon and rarely seen, partly because it occupies extensive, remote areas.
profile.classification: The Solitary Eagle belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae. It is the only species in the genus Buteogallus commonly known by this English name, although it was formerly placed in the genus Harpyhaliaetus.
profile.identification: Adults are large, dark slate-gray eagles with a relatively short, broad tail marked by a prominent white central band and a dark terminal band. White patches may show on the upperwing when the bird is flying. The bill is large and hooked, and the legs are yellow. Juveniles are browner and more heavily streaked or mottled, with less sharply defined tail markings. Its heavy build and slow, deep wingbeats help distinguish it from smaller forest raptors.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Solitary Eagle ranges from Mexico through Central America and much of northern and western South America. It inhabits humid and montane forests, forest edges, wooded valleys, and nearby open slopes, generally in hilly or mountainous terrain. In Costa Rica it is a rare and local species, reported mainly from suitable forested mountain and foothill regions rather than being widespread across the country. Records are scarce, and the species may be overlooked because of its solitary behavior, low density, and preference for remote habitats.
profile.migrationStatus: The Solitary Eagle is generally considered resident rather than migratory. In Costa Rica, it is expected to remain year-round where suitable mountain and foothill habitat persists; seasonal movements may occur locally, but regular long-distance migration is not established.
profile.breeding: The Solitary Eagle is believed to nest mainly in tall trees or on cliffs in rugged, forested landscapes. It generally lays a single egg, and the breeding cycle is prolonged, as in many large eagles. Pairs defend large territories and may use soaring displays and vocalizations during courtship. Detailed information on nesting sites, timing, and reproductive success is limited, especially in Central America and Costa Rica, where the species is uncommon and difficult to study.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet includes medium-sized mammals, birds, reptiles, and possibly other vertebrates available in forest and edge habitats. The eagle often hunts from a high perch or while soaring, watching for prey below before making a powerful descent. It may also take prey in open areas near forest. Because it occurs at low density and is seldom observed, the full range of its prey and hunting methods is not well documented.
profile.behavior: The Solitary Eagle is usually seen alone, although pairs may occupy and defend a territory. It spends substantial time perched quietly or soaring over forested mountains and valleys. Its flight is strong and deliberate, with broad wings suited to ridge-soaring. The species is generally secretive and difficult to detect, and it may vocalize during territorial interactions or breeding. Large home ranges and low population density contribute to its name and its rarity in field observations.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is thought to be decreasing, but the species is poorly known and population estimates are uncertain. In Costa Rica, it appears to be rare and local, with relatively few documented records.

profile.overview: The Roadside Hawk (Rupornis magnirostris) is a small, widespread bird of prey found from Mexico through Central America and across much of South America. It is named for its habit of perching beside roads and other clearings while hunting. Adaptable and vocal, it uses forest edges, farmland, river margins, open woodland, and some urban areas. In Costa Rica, it is a familiar resident hawk and is often easy to observe from roadsides and rural settlements.
profile.classification: The Roadside Hawk belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae and the order Accipitriformes. It is the only species currently placed in the genus Rupornis.
profile.identification: This relatively small hawk has a compact body, broad wings, and a long, banded tail. Adults commonly show a gray head and upperparts, finely barred underparts, and noticeable rufous coloring on the wings and belly, although plumage varies among subspecies. The strongly hooked bill and yellow cere, legs, and feet are typical. Its sharp, repeated calls are often heard before the bird is located. It frequently sits upright on exposed branches, poles, fences, or roadside wires.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from Mexico through Central America and across much of South America east of the Andes. In Costa Rica, the Roadside Hawk is a widespread and commonly observed resident, occurring in both the Caribbean and Pacific regions, including lowlands, foothills, valleys, and some settled areas. It favors forest edges, secondary woodland, riparian vegetation, plantations, pasture with trees, agricultural landscapes, and roadsides. It generally avoids extensive unbroken rainforest and very open habitats lacking perches.
profile.migrationStatus: The Roadside Hawk is generally nonmigratory in Costa Rica and is considered a year-round resident there. Some northern populations farther north in the range may move seasonally, but Costa Rican birds do not normally undertake long-distance migration.
profile.breeding: Roadside Hawks build large stick nests, usually high in a tree and sometimes concealed among vines. Nests may be placed in forest edges, riparian woodland, farmland, or other habitats with scattered mature trees. Both adults help construct the nest and may line it with fresh green leaves. The usual clutch contains one or two eggs. Incubation lasts about 33–37 days, and young typically remain in the nest for roughly 38 days after hatching.
profile.dietFeeding: This hawk is an opportunistic predator whose diet varies with location and season. It takes large insects, amphibians, lizards, snakes, small mammals, and small birds. It usually hunts from a conspicuous perch, dropping quickly to the ground or vegetation to capture prey. Roadside Hawks may also exploit army-ant swarms, grass fires, or other disturbances that flush insects and small animals into the open.
profile.behavior: Roadside Hawks are conspicuous, vocal birds that often perch beside roads, trails, fields, and clearings. Their flight commonly consists of several rapid wingbeats followed by short glides, and they may wag the tail after landing. Pairs become especially noisy and active around nest sites, where they may circle together and defend the surrounding area. Their tolerance of modified habitats helps explain why they are frequently encountered in Costa Rican agricultural and suburban landscapes.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered increasing.

profile.overview: Harris's Hawk is a medium-sized, social bird of prey found from the southwestern United States and Mexico south through much of Central and South America. It is unusual among raptors because it commonly hunts in family groups, sometimes cooperatively surrounding prey. The species favors open, warm landscapes with scattered trees, thorn scrub, grassland, desert edges, and agricultural areas. In Costa Rica, it is associated mainly with open and seasonally dry habitats rather than humid forest.
profile.classification: Harris's Hawk belongs to the family Accipitridae, which includes hawks, eagles, and kites. It is the only species in the genus Parabuteo.
profile.identification: Adults have dark brown to nearly black upperparts, a rich chestnut shoulder and wing patch, and a broad white band across the base of the tail with a white tail tip. The rump is also white. The legs are yellow, and the hooked bill is dark with a yellow cere. Juveniles are browner and more heavily streaked, with less sharply defined chestnut and white markings. The species has broad wings and a long, barred-looking tail.
profile.rangeHabitat: Harris's Hawk ranges from the southwestern United States and Mexico through Central America and much of South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs locally in open, lowland and seasonally dry regions, especially where grassland, scrub, pasture, woodland edges, or agricultural land provide hunting areas and scattered perches. It generally avoids continuous wet forest and is more likely to be found in Guanacaste and other open landscapes than in densely forested or mountainous areas.
profile.migrationStatus: Harris's Hawk is largely resident, with movements usually local or regional rather than long-distance migration. In Costa Rica it is treated as a local or uncommon resident, and its presence may vary with habitat and food availability.
profile.breeding: The species usually nests in trees, shrubs, or other elevated sites within open habitats. The nest is a bulky platform made of sticks and lined with softer vegetation, feathers, or other material. Both members of a pair may participate in nest building, and helpers from the social group can assist with territorial defense and care of young. Breeding timing varies across its broad range and is influenced by local rainfall and food conditions. Several eggs are laid, and the young remain dependent after fledging.
profile.dietFeeding: Harris's Hawks eat mainly small to medium-sized mammals, birds, and reptiles, along with large insects when available. Common prey can include rodents, rabbits, lizards, snakes, and ground-dwelling birds. They often hunt from prominent perches, search on foot, or pursue prey across open ground. Cooperative hunting is a notable behavior: two or more birds may flush, surround, or distract prey, increasing hunting success for the group.
profile.behavior: This hawk is highly social and commonly lives in family groups consisting of a breeding pair and helpers or older offspring. Members perch close together, call to one another, groom, and defend a shared territory. Groups may hunt cooperatively and may stack or cluster on prominent perches. Harris's Hawks are agile and adaptable, but they depend on open ground for hunting and on suitable trees, poles, fences, or other elevated structures for lookout and roosting.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered generally stable, but regional trends can differ, and reliable long-term information for Costa Rica is limited.

profile.overview: The White-tailed Hawk (Geranoaetus albicaudatus) is a large, broad-winged raptor of open country in the tropical and subtropical Americas. It often hunts while soaring or hovering over grasslands, savannas, dry scrub, and agricultural landscapes. Adults are mainly slate gray above and white below, with reddish shoulders and a conspicuous white tail crossed by a black band. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon resident, especially in the northwestern lowlands.
profile.classification: The White-tailed Hawk belongs to the order Accipitriformes and family Accipitridae. It is closely related to other large soaring hawks and was formerly often placed in the genus Buteo.
profile.identification: Adults have long, broad wings, a slate-gray back, reddish or chestnut shoulders, white underparts, and a white tail with a bold black subterminal band. The wings extend noticeably beyond the tail when the bird is perched. Immatures are browner and more heavily marked, with a less sharply defined tail pattern. In flight, the species may hold its wings slightly bent at the shoulders while soaring. The tail pattern helps separate it from Short-tailed Hawk and Harris’s Hawk.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southern Texas and Mexico through Central America and much of South America to central Argentina. It favors open habitats such as grasslands, savannas, dry forest edges, scrub, pastures, cultivated areas, and plains with scattered trees or shrubs. In Costa Rica it is a very uncommon resident, concentrated mainly in the lowlands and foothills of Guanacaste, particularly near the Cordillera de Guanacaste. Older records came from parts of the central highlands, and possible residence has also been suggested for the Térraba savannas.
profile.migrationStatus: Generally resident in Costa Rica and not considered a regular long-distance migrant there. The Costa Rican official bird list classifies it as a resident species, although movements may occur locally or seasonally in response to food and weather.
profile.breeding: White-tailed Hawks build a substantial platform nest from sticks, sometimes adding leaves and other plant material. The nest is usually placed high in a tree in open savanna or similar habitat. Two white or lightly brown-marked eggs are commonly reported. In Costa Rica, a nest near Taboga in Guanacaste was observed in February with two downy young, supporting local breeding. Nesting sites are typically surrounded by open ground that provides access to hunting areas.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet is varied and consists mainly of small to medium-sized mammals, including rodents, along with reptiles, birds, large insects, and other available prey. The hawk commonly searches from soaring flight, hovering or kiting over open ground, and perches on trees, shrubs, poles, or other elevated lookouts. It may also exploit prey fleeing grass or brush fires, a behavior recorded in grassland habitats.
profile.behavior: This hawk is usually seen alone or in pairs, soaring over open landscapes on rising air currents. It often remains nearly stationary while facing into the wind and scanning the ground below. When not hunting, it perches conspicuously on isolated trees, shrubs, fence posts, or utility poles. Adults may defend breeding territories, and other small birds sometimes nest near its nest, apparently gaining some protection from predators.

conservation.populationTrend: Stable or possibly increasing overall, although reliable long-term information is limited in parts of its range.

profile.overview: The White Hawk (Pseudastur albicollis) is a striking forest hawk of tropical Central and South America. Its mostly white plumage, broad dark wing tips, and dark facial markings make it distinctive in flight. It usually hunts from elevated perches, watching for prey below, and is often associated with humid forest and forest edges. In Costa Rica, it is a regularly encountered resident, especially in lowland and foothill regions with suitable forest habitat.
profile.classification: The White Hawk belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae. It is the only species in the genus Pseudastur.
profile.identification: Adults are largely white, with black or very dark markings on the outer wings and tail and a dark mask around the eyes. The wings are broad, and the bird often soars with slow, deliberate wingbeats. From below, the contrast between the white body and dark wing tips is especially noticeable. Juveniles are generally browner and less sharply patterned than adults. Its medium-large size and distinctive black-and-white appearance help separate it from other Costa Rican raptors.
profile.rangeHabitat: The White Hawk occurs from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and central South America. In Costa Rica, it is found mainly in humid Caribbean-slope forests, foothills, and adjacent forest edges, and it also occurs locally on the Pacific slope where suitable woodland remains. It generally uses lowland and lower montane evergreen forest, river corridors, plantations near forest, and clearings with tall perches. It can occur from sea level into the foothills, but is less typical in heavily cleared areas.
profile.migrationStatus: The White Hawk is generally resident in Costa Rica and is not considered a regular long-distance migrant. Individuals may move locally in response to food availability, breeding activity, or habitat conditions.
profile.breeding: White Hawks usually breed in mature forest, placing a large stick nest high in a tree, often near the canopy. The nest is built from branches and may be reused or repaired in successive years. The species generally lays a small clutch, commonly a single egg, and both adults participate in territorial defense and care of the young. Breeding timing varies across its broad range; in Costa Rica, nesting may occur during different parts of the year depending on region and local rainfall patterns.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet includes reptiles, amphibians, birds, insects, and other small animals. The White Hawk commonly hunts from a high, exposed perch, scanning the ground and vegetation before making a short flight to capture prey. It may also search along forest edges and clearings. In some areas, it follows groups of foraging monkeys or mixed-species bird flocks, taking advantage of animals disturbed by their movement.
profile.behavior: White Hawks are usually seen alone, in pairs, or occasionally in family groups. They spend long periods perched quietly before soaring above the forest or moving between elevated perches. Pairs defend territories and may circle together while calling. Their broad wings and contrasting plumage make them conspicuous when soaring over forest canopies. They are generally less tolerant of extensive open farmland than more adaptable roadside raptors.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to be facing an immediate extinction risk, although local populations may decline where mature forest is lost or fragmented.

profile.overview: The Semiplumbeous Hawk is a small, compact forest raptor of humid lowland regions in Central and northwestern South America. It is named for its partly lead-gray plumage and is recognizable by its white underparts, dark head, bright yellow eyes, and orange cere and legs. This secretive hawk usually hunts from concealed perches in the forest canopy or middle levels, where it makes rapid attacks on small vertebrate prey.
profile.classification: The Semiplumbeous Hawk belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae and the genus Leucopternis. It is generally treated as a monotypic species.
profile.identification: Adults have dark bluish-gray upperparts, head, and breast, contrasting with white lower underparts. The face is dark, the eyes are yellow, and the cere and legs are orange to reddish orange. The wings are relatively short and rounded, and the tail is dark with pale barring. It is a small, stocky hawk, about 31–36 cm long. Its combination of gray plumage, white belly, yellow eyes, and orange facial skin helps distinguish it from similar forest hawks.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from eastern Honduras through Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama to Colombia and northwestern Ecuador. In Costa Rica it is a resident, especially associated with humid Caribbean lowlands and foothills, where it is locally common; it is seldom recorded above about 500 m. It occupies mature tropical and subtropical moist forest, forest edges, riparian woodland, and some forest fragments, but generally avoids extensively open countryside. It often remains within dense vegetation and is more easily detected by calls than by sight.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident and largely non-migratory. In Costa Rica, the species is present year-round in suitable humid lowland and foothill forest, including the Caribbean region; there is no reliable evidence that Costa Rican birds undertake regular long-distance migration.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited. Birds are usually solitary or seen in pairs during the breeding period. In Costa Rica, a nest has been reported in the middle level of vegetation, approximately 25 m above the ground. The nest is probably a stick structure placed in a tree or large shrub, but details such as clutch size, incubation period, nestling period, and breeding-season timing remain poorly documented. Both adults are expected to participate in territorial and parental behavior.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet includes small birds, particularly antbirds and other species flushed by army-ant swarms, as well as lizards, snakes, frogs, bats, and other small vertebrates. It commonly perches quietly in the canopy or middle levels and makes sudden, fast attacks when prey becomes exposed. In Costa Rica, observations include predation on small forest birds and reptiles. Following army-ant columns may allow it to capture birds fleeing the moving ants.
profile.behavior: The Semiplumbeous Hawk is secretive and usually keeps to forest cover rather than soaring over open landscapes. It often sits motionless on a concealed perch, watching the surrounding vegetation, then darts quickly after prey. Individuals may follow army-ant swarms and exploit the disturbance they create among understory birds. It is generally encountered alone or in pairs, and its presence is often revealed by a distinctive call before the bird is seen.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered decreasing, but the species is not currently assessed as threatened at the global level.

profile.overview: The Gray Hawk (Buteo plagiatus) is a small, broad-winged raptor of the tropical Americas. It is named for its mostly gray adult plumage and distinctive black-and-white banded tail. The species often hunts from exposed perches, watching for lizards, snakes, frogs, insects, and small birds. Gray Hawks commonly inhabit open woodland, forest edges, savannas, plantations, and other partly cleared areas. In Costa Rica, it is a resident species found mainly in suitable lowland and foothill habitats.
profile.classification: The Gray Hawk belongs to the family Accipitridae, which includes hawks, eagles, and kites. Its scientific name is Buteo plagiatus.
profile.identification: Adults are mostly slate-gray above and pale gray below, with fine dark barring on the underparts. The tail is dark with several narrow white bands and a broader pale terminal band. The wings are broad and rounded, and the head may appear slightly crested when the bird is alert. Juveniles are brown above, whitish below, and heavily streaked, with a distinctly banded tail. In flight, adults show broad wings and relatively short tails.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Gray Hawk occurs from the southwestern United States and Mexico through Central America to northern South America. In Costa Rica, it is a resident rather than a seasonal migrant, occurring mainly in the lowlands and foothills, including the Pacific northwest, Caribbean lowlands, river valleys, and other warm regions where suitable habitat remains. It uses dry and moist forest edges, open woodland, savanna, scrub, agricultural landscapes with scattered trees, plantations, and clearings, usually avoiding dense, unbroken forest.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica, with no regular long-distance migration known for the country. Some local movements may occur in response to food availability, weather, or habitat conditions.
profile.breeding: Breeding generally takes place during the local dry or early wet season, although timing varies across the species' broad range. The nest is a stick platform placed in a tree, often near a forest edge or in open woodland. The female usually lays a small clutch, and both adults help defend the territory and care for the young. Nest sites may be reused or rebuilt in subsequent breeding seasons.
profile.dietFeeding: The Gray Hawk is an active predator that usually hunts from a conspicuous perch. It feeds heavily on lizards and other small reptiles, but also takes frogs, snakes, large insects, small mammals, and birds. It may drop suddenly onto prey on the ground or seize animals from vegetation. In open habitats, roadside trees, fence posts, and utility structures can provide useful hunting perches.
profile.behavior: Gray Hawks are generally solitary or found in pairs, especially during the breeding season. They spend long periods perched quietly while scanning below, then make short, direct flights to capture prey. Their calls are high-pitched and repeated, particularly around breeding territories. They may soar over forest edges and clearings, and adults often become conspicuous when defending a nest or territory.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered severely threatened, although detailed population information is limited and trends may vary regionally.

profile.overview: The Gray-lined Hawk is a small to medium-sized Neotropical bird of prey found from southern Central America through much of South America. It is a compact, active hawk associated with forest edges, woodland, river corridors, and other partly open habitats. Adults are mainly pale gray with fine barring and a strongly banded black-and-white tail. In Costa Rica, it is distinguished from the similar Gray Hawk by its more extensive barring and its occurrence mainly in the southern part of the country.
profile.classification: The Gray-lined Hawk belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae and the genus Buteo. It was formerly grouped with the Gray Hawk, but the southern and northern forms are now generally recognized as separate species.
profile.identification: Adults are pale gray overall, with fine dark barring on the head, upperparts, underparts, and wings. The tail is dark with several contrasting white bands, and the legs and cere are yellow. In flight, the wings show barred primary tips and lack the prominent dark trailing edge typical of the Gray Hawk. Juveniles are brown above and pale below, with heavy dark streaking. The species is often seen perched conspicuously or soaring over open woodland.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Gray-lined Hawk ranges from El Salvador and Honduras south through Panama and across much of tropical South America to Argentina, including Trinidad. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly in the southern and southwestern portions of the country, especially in lowland and foothill landscapes on the Pacific side; the northern part is primarily occupied by the closely related Gray Hawk. It uses forest edges, gallery forest, tropical woodland, clearings, savanna-like areas, plantations, and agricultural land with scattered trees.
profile.migrationStatus: Generally resident, with no regular long-distance migration known. In Costa Rica, Gray-lined Hawks are present year-round in their southern and southwestern range, although local movements may follow food availability and breeding conditions.
profile.breeding: Gray-lined Hawks usually breed in wooded landscapes where tall trees stand near open hunting areas. The nest is a stick platform placed high in a tree, and the female generally lays a small clutch, commonly one or two eggs. Both adults defend a territory, and courtship and territorial displays include aerial activity and repeated calls. Nest sites are often near forest edges, rivers, roads, or clearings, where the adults can hunt efficiently around the nest.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet includes lizards, snakes, frogs, small mammals, birds, and large insects. The hawk commonly hunts from an exposed perch, scanning the ground and vegetation before making a rapid drop or short flight to seize prey. It may also patrol edges and clearings, taking advantage of animals moving between forest and open areas. Its broad diet allows it to use both natural habitats and modified landscapes with suitable cover and perches.
profile.behavior: This is usually a solitary or pair-living hawk. It often sits quietly on a prominent branch, utility wire, or other exposed perch, then makes short, direct hunting flights. It may soar above woodland during warm parts of the day and becomes more vocal during the breeding season. Gray-lined Hawks defend territories with calls and aerial displays. Their preference for edges and open forest makes them more visible than many forest-dwelling raptors.

conservation.populationTrend: Generally considered stable at the global level.

profile.overview: The Broad-winged Hawk is a medium-sized forest hawk that breeds across much of eastern North America and migrates to Central and South America. It is famous for forming large, swirling flocks called kettles during migration. In Costa Rica, it is primarily a common migrant and winter visitor rather than a breeding species. It often uses forest edges, open countryside, hillsides, and other areas where trees provide hunting perches and nearby clearings provide access to prey.
profile.classification: The Broad-winged Hawk belongs to the order Accipitriformes and the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae. Its scientific name is Buteo platypterus.
profile.identification: This stocky hawk has broad, rounded wings, a relatively short tail, and a large head. Adults usually show dark upperparts, pale underparts with fine barring, and a boldly banded tail with black and white bands. The dark trailing edge of the wings is noticeable in flight. Juveniles are browner and more heavily streaked below, with a banded tail. Its call is a high, thin, two-part whistle. Migrating birds are often identified in large soaring groups.
profile.rangeHabitat: Broad-winged Hawks breed in deciduous and mixed forests of eastern and central North America, usually near forest openings, wetlands, or other clearings. They winter from southern Mexico through Central America into northern and central South America. In Costa Rica, the species is a common winter resident on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes, from lowlands to at least about 2,000 meters. It is especially associated with forest edges, broken forest, open areas, hillsides, savannas, and woodland clearings, and is less frequent in intact forest except in some parts of Guanacaste.
profile.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, Broad-winged Hawks pass through mainly during fall migration from late September through mid-November, with especially notable movements along the Caribbean slope and highland routes. Spring migration generally occurs from early March through late May on both slopes. Many birds remain through the northern winter, making this one of Costa Rica’s most frequently observed wintering migratory raptors. Large flights may be seen soaring over ridges, valleys, and forested landscapes.
profile.breeding: Breeding occurs mainly in large deciduous or mixed forests of Canada and the United States, not generally in Costa Rica. The nest is a loose platform of sticks, often placed in the lower or middle part of a large tree, commonly near a forest edge, road, water body, or opening. The clutch usually contains two or three eggs. Both adults participate in incubation and care of the young. Pairs are generally solitary and defend a nesting territory during the breeding season.
profile.dietFeeding: The Broad-winged Hawk eats a varied diet of small mammals, frogs, snakes, lizards, insects, and occasionally small birds. It commonly hunts from a low or shaded perch, watching forest floors, roadside verges, grassy openings, and wet areas before dropping onto prey. In Costa Rica, wintering birds may forage along forest edges, in open woodland, and around clearings. Migrants may also take advantage of temporarily abundant insects and other prey during stopovers.
profile.behavior: Broad-winged Hawks are often quiet and difficult to detect when perched inside forest, but they become conspicuous during migration. They use rising columns of warm air to travel efficiently and may gather in flocks numbering in the hundreds or thousands. In Costa Rica, individuals may be seen alone or in small groups during the winter, while major movements can produce broad streams of soaring birds. The species typically hunts from perches and roosts in trees or forest margins.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered stable to increasing, with increases documented in parts of the North American breeding range.

profile.overview: The Zone-tailed Hawk is a dark, medium-sized raptor of the Americas. Its bold white tail bands and pale bars across the flight feathers are most visible when it soars. The species often resembles a Turkey Vulture in shape, flight style, and behavior, a resemblance that may help it approach prey unnoticed. It occupies forested mountains, canyons, dry woodland, foothills, and other rugged landscapes from the southwestern United States through Central America and much of South America.
profile.classification: The Zone-tailed Hawk belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae and the genus Buteo. Its scientific name is Buteo albonotatus.
profile.identification: Adults are mostly black or very dark brown, with silvery-white barring on the flight feathers and several broad white bands across the tail. The wings are long and narrow, and the bird commonly soars with the wings held in a shallow dihedral, rocking from side to side. The cere and feet are yellow, and a small pale area may show in front of the eye. Juveniles have more finely barred tails and less distinct wing markings. It is easily confused with Turkey Vulture and Common Black Hawk.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from the southwestern United States and Mexico through Central America to South America. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon but regularly recorded native hawk, listed as both resident and migratory. It occurs in several regions, including the northwest, Caribbean lowlands, foothills, and mountain landscapes, and has been recorded on both slopes. Breeding has been reported in northwestern Costa Rica, although the species is generally local and much less numerous than many migrant raptors. It favors forest edges, wooded valleys, dry forest, canyons, and open areas near forest.
profile.migrationStatus: Zone-tailed Hawks are short-distance migrants in the northern part of their range and mostly resident farther south. In Costa Rica, the species is considered both resident and migratory: some birds remain year-round, while others pass through or move seasonally. Records may increase during raptor migration periods, but it is not one of Costa Rica’s most abundant migrant hawks.
profile.breeding: The Zone-tailed Hawk usually nests in trees or on cliff ledges in rugged, relatively undisturbed terrain. The nest is a large stick platform lined with softer material, and the same territory or nest area may be used repeatedly. The female generally lays one to three eggs, and both adults participate in rearing the young. In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported in the northwest, but detailed information on nesting dates, productivity, and the full breeding distribution remains limited.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of small and medium-sized birds, mammals, reptiles, and amphibians. Depending on location, prey may include passerines, woodpeckers, quail, lizards, snakes, frogs, and small mammals. It commonly hunts from soaring flight or a concealed perch, then drops or glides toward prey. The hawk may associate with Turkey Vultures while searching for food, using a similar flight silhouette to reduce detection by potential prey.
profile.behavior: This hawk is often seen soaring high above forested hills, canyons, and valleys, especially where rising air currents allow it to travel with little effort. Its flight is distinctive: the wings are held in a slight V and the bird frequently rocks from side to side. It is usually solitary or seen in pairs, though several may gather during migration or over favorable thermal currents. Vocalizations are generally less noticeable than its aerial behavior.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to be undergoing a sufficiently rapid decline to qualify for a threatened category. Trend information is limited in parts of Central and South America.

profile.overview: The Short-tailed Hawk is a small to medium-sized bird of prey found from the southern United States through Central America and much of South America. It is named for its relatively short tail, although its broad wings are often the most noticeable feature in flight. Two main color forms occur: a pale form with a mostly white underside and a dark form that appears nearly black below. It often hunts by soaring over forest edges and open areas.
profile.classification: The Short-tailed Hawk belongs to the hawk and eagle family Accipitridae and the genus Buteo. Its scientific name is Buteo brachyurus.
profile.identification: Adults have broad wings, a short tail, and yellow legs and cere. In the pale form, the upperparts are dark brown while the underparts are largely white, with dark flight feathers and a dark trailing edge to the wings. The dark form is deep brown to black below but usually shows pale areas at the bases of the flight feathers when viewed from beneath. Immatures are generally browner and more heavily streaked, especially on the breast. The species may soar with wings held slightly raised.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Short-tailed Hawk ranges from southern Florida and northern Mexico south through Central America to northern Argentina. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon, local resident, reported especially along lower mountain slopes and ridges on the Caribbean side of the Central and Tilarán ranges, around the Arenal lowlands, and on both slopes of the Guanacaste range. It also occurs in forest, scattered-tree landscapes, forest patches, savannas, and open country near woodland. Records are more frequent in the Caribbean lowlands than in many Pacific lowland areas.
profile.migrationStatus: Costa Rica supports resident birds as well as seasonal migrants. Migration is especially noticeable from August to October and from February to April, when individuals may appear in or near larger movements of other hawks. Birds from northern populations can move south into Costa Rica, while many birds farther south are resident.
profile.breeding: The species generally nests in tall trees within or beside mature, often wet forest, including forest near wetlands or water. It usually lays a small clutch, and both adults participate in territorial defense and care of the young. The nest is a stick platform placed high above the ground.
