Their low-level movements, dark plumage in males, and preference for tangled vegetation can make them difficult to observe even where they are locally regular.

conservation.populationTrend: Decreasing.

profile.overview: The Chestnut-backed Antbird is a small, ground-dwelling antbird of humid tropical forests in Central and northern South America. It is usually encountered alone or in pairs, moving through dense understory and following army-ant swarms to capture insects disturbed by the ants. The species was formerly placed in the genus Myrmeciza and is now generally classified as Poliocrania exsul. It is a resident species in Costa Rica, where it occurs mainly in suitable lowland and foothill forest.
profile.classification: The Chestnut-backed Antbird belongs to the antbird family Thamnophilidae and the order Passeriformes. Its scientific name is Poliocrania exsul; older sources may list it as Myrmeciza exsul.
profile.identification: This antbird is compact and short-tailed, with a dark head and underparts contrasting with a rich chestnut or rufous back. Males are generally darker, with blackish plumage on the face, throat, and breast, while females are browner or more extensively rufous below. The species often keeps low in dense vegetation and may be detected first by its sharp calls or by its active behavior near army-ant swarms. Its unobtrusive habits can make visual identification difficult.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Chestnut-backed Antbird ranges from eastern Honduras and Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama into parts of northwestern South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident of the Caribbean slope and adjacent humid foothills, with additional occurrences in suitable wet forest habitats elsewhere in the country. It favors mature lowland rainforest, forest edge, dense second growth, thickets, and areas with tangled understory, generally from sea level into the lower foothills. It is less typical of open agricultural land and heavily disturbed habitats.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and across its range; it does not undertake regular long-distance migration. Individuals may make local movements in response to food availability, habitat conditions, or army-ant activity.
profile.breeding: The Chestnut-backed Antbird usually nests low in dense vegetation, where its nest is concealed among leaves, stems, or tangled understory. As in many antbirds, both adults participate in territorial defense and care of the young. The species typically lays a small clutch, often of two eggs, but nesting details can vary geographically. Breeding activity in Costa Rica is associated mainly with the wet season and periods of increased food availability, although timing may differ among regions.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of insects and other small arthropods, including beetles, ants, grasshoppers, and spiders. It searches through leaf litter, low vegetation, fallen branches, and dense ground cover. The species is a regular army-ant follower: it takes prey attempting to escape advancing ants rather than feeding on the ants themselves. It may also forage independently, usually by making short sallies or picking prey from leaves and the forest floor.
profile.behavior: The Chestnut-backed Antbird is generally secretive, territorial, and most often seen singly or in pairs. It moves deliberately through dense understory, frequently flicking or raising its tail while investigating vegetation and leaf litter. Pairs maintain contact with soft calls and defend territories with vocal displays. When army ants are present, several antbird species may gather nearby, but the Chestnut-backed Antbird usually remains close to the ground and forest edge of the swarm.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains widespread and is not currently close to the thresholds for a threatened category.

profile.overview: The Dull-mantled Antbird (Sipia laemosticta) is a small, secretive antbird of humid foothill forests in southern Central America. It spends much of its time on or near the forest floor, moving through dense tangles, streamside vegetation, and fallen branches. The sexes differ in plumage, and the species is often detected by its soft song before it is seen. Costa Rica is an important part of its range, especially along the Caribbean slope.
profile.classification: The Dull-mantled Antbird belongs to the antbird family Thamnophilidae and the genus Sipia. It was formerly placed in the broader genus Myrmeciza.
profile.identification: This compact antbird is about 13–14 cm long and has a distinctive red iris. The male has an olive-brown back, somewhat rufous wings and tail, a gray head and underparts, and a dark throat with pale spots on the wing coverts. The female is browner overall, with a black-and-white scaled throat and buffy or brownish wing spots. It is usually recognized by its low, deliberate movements and frequent tail raising in dense understory.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Costa Rica through western and eastern Panama, with records extending toward extreme northwestern Colombia. In Costa Rica it is a resident of the Caribbean-slope lowlands and foothills, occurring from roughly 300 to 750 m and locally reaching about 1,000 m or slightly higher in the southeast. It favors humid evergreen forest, especially shaded ravines, stream margins, steep slopes, and dense vegetation near small waterways. It may also use regenerating growth around tree falls and landslides.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident and apparently nonmigratory. In Costa Rica, it remains year-round on the Caribbean slope rather than arriving as a seasonal migrant. Its limited dispersal ability may make it sensitive to breaks in suitable forest habitat.
profile.breeding: Detailed breeding information is limited. In Costa Rica, breeding activity has been reported during at least April and May, but the full breeding season is not well defined. The species is believed to nest low in dense vegetation, near the ground, as is typical of closely related forest antbirds. Pairs probably maintain small territories in thick understory, ravines, and streamside tangles, where the adults forage and remain difficult to observe.
profile.dietFeeding: The Dull-mantled Antbird feeds mainly on insects and other small arthropods, including beetles, cockroaches, grasshoppers, insect larvae, spiders, and possibly ants and woodlice. It forages mostly below about one metre, walking or hopping through leaf litter and dense ground cover and sometimes turning over leaves or searching around fallen trunks. It may attend army-ant swarms occasionally, but it is not considered a persistent army-ant follower.
profile.behavior: This is a quiet, secretive understory bird that usually occurs singly or in pairs. It moves deliberately through tangled vegetation, along stream banks, and around fallen branches, often pausing with the tail lowered and then raising it slowly. Its soft song consists of a short series of high, subdued notes, and paired birds may respond to one another. Although it can join mixed-species flocks, it is more often detected by careful listening than by open views.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population size has not been quantified and is believed to be decreasing, although the decline is not currently considered rapid enough for a threatened-category assessment.
conservation.threats: Loss and fragmentation of humid foothill forest are the main potential concerns. Because the species has narrow habitat and elevational preferences and apparently limited dispersal ability, it may be vulnerable to the gradual degradation or isolation of streamside and understory forest.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore humid Caribbean-slope foothill forest in Costa Rica, especially ravines, stream corridors, and connected understory habitat. Support well-managed protected areas, retain native vegetation during development, reduce clearing on steep slopes, and contribute well-documented sightings to monitoring programs.

profile.overview: Zeledon's Antbird (Hafferia zeledoni) is a secretive forest antbird of Central America and northwestern South America. It usually stays in dense, humid understory, where it searches leaf litter and low vegetation for arthropods and small vertebrates. The species is often detected by its ringing, rapidly delivered song rather than by sight. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon resident, occurring mainly on the Caribbean slope and locally in suitable foothill and montane forests on the Pacific slope.
profile.classification: Zeledon's Antbird belongs to the antbird family Thamnophilidae, within the passerine order Passeriformes. It was formerly placed in the genus Myrmeciza but is now classified in Hafferia. Two subspecies are generally recognized.
profile.identification: This medium-sized antbird has a relatively long tail and pale bluish skin around the eye. The male is mostly black, with small white marks on the shoulders that may be concealed. The female is mainly dark brown, with a darker tail. Immature males resemble females. It often moves through dense vegetation close to the ground, pumping or slowly raising its tail. Its loud song is a rapid, slightly descending series of clear, ringing whistles.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama, with a separate population extending from eastern Panama through western Colombia to western Ecuador. In Costa Rica it occurs chiefly along the Caribbean slope, where it is fairly uncommon, and is rarer on the Pacific slope, mainly at higher elevations. It inhabits humid evergreen foothill forest, mature secondary forest, understory edges, ravines, steep hillsides, landslides, and tree-fall openings, generally from about 250 to 1,700 meters, with local variation.
profile.migrationStatus: Zeledon's Antbird is considered a year-round resident, not a regular migrant. In Costa Rica, individuals are present throughout the year in suitable forest, although local movements may occur in response to food availability or habitat conditions.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited and the timing appears to vary geographically. The known nest was a dome-shaped structure made mainly from dry leaves, small sticks, and grasses, placed on a steep forest slope. A clutch of two white eggs with reddish blotches was recorded. Both parents incubated during the day, while the female incubated at night. Incubation lasted at least 17 days, and the nestling period lasted about 14 days.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of arthropods, including insects and other small invertebrates, with occasional small lizards and frogs. The bird forages mostly on or near the ground, usually alone, in pairs, or in family groups. It gleans prey from leaf litter and low vegetation, rummages among debris, and sometimes pounces from a low perch. It regularly follows army-ant swarms and captures prey fleeing from the ants.
profile.behavior: Zeledon's Antbird is generally unobtrusive and remains in dense understory, often moving by short hops between feeding spots. It may forage with its tail lowered and then raise it slowly. Both sexes give sharp calls, including an explosive note and a rapid scolding series. The species sometimes joins army-ant activity with other antbirds, but it only occasionally participates in mixed-species feeding flocks. Its ringing song is often the easiest way to locate it.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains widespread and the global population is still estimated to include at least tens of thousands of mature individuals.

profile.overview: The Bicolored Antbird is a medium-sized antbird of humid lowland forests in Central and northern South America. It is strongly associated with army-ant swarms, which flush insects and other small prey from the leaf litter. The species often forages in noisy groups and may join mixed-species flocks. In Costa Rica, it is a resident of suitable evergreen forest, especially on the Caribbean slope and in nearby lowland regions.
profile.classification: The Bicolored Antbird belongs to the antbird family Thamnophilidae and the genus Gymnopithys. It is sometimes treated within a broader species complex that has undergone taxonomic revision.
profile.identification: This antbird has contrasting black, gray, and white plumage. Adults generally show a dark head and upperparts, a paler throat and underparts, and conspicuous white markings on the wings or sides of the body. The bill is fairly stout, and the tail is dark. It is usually detected by its sharp calls, active movements, and association with army-ant swarms rather than by prolonged views in dense understory.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Bicolored Antbird ranges from southern Mexico through Central America into northern South America, including parts of Colombia and western Ecuador. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly in humid Caribbean lowlands and foothill forests, where it uses mature evergreen forest, rainforest edges, and other wooded habitats with deep leaf litter. It is most characteristic of low elevations but may reach lower foothill zones. Protection of extensive forest is important because the species depends on intact ground-foraging habitat and regular army-ant activity.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and across its range; it does not undertake regular long-distance migration. Local movements may follow army-ant colonies and changes in food availability.
profile.breeding: The Bicolored Antbird is thought to breed during the wet-season or early dry-season period in much of Central America, although timing varies geographically. The nest is a small cup or pouch placed low in vegetation, often near the ground. Both adults participate in territory defense and care of the young. Detailed breeding information is limited, and the species' nesting biology is less thoroughly documented than that of some more widespread antbirds.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of insects and other arthropods, including ants, beetles, grasshoppers, and spiders. It commonly follows swarms of army ants, capturing prey that flee from the advancing ants. Individuals forage on or close to the ground, hopping through leaf litter and low vegetation, and may feed in coordinated groups with other ant-following birds.
profile.behavior: The Bicolored Antbird is active, vocal, and social. It often travels in pairs or small groups and may join mixed-species flocks in forest understory. Army-ant swarms can attract several individuals, which defend feeding positions and make frequent short flights to seize fleeing prey. Outside swarm activity, it searches through leaves, fallen branches, and low plants. Its calls help maintain contact in dense forest.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not precisely known and may be declining in some areas because of forest loss and degradation.
conservation.threats: Habitat loss, fragmentation, and degradation of humid lowland forest are the principal concerns. In Costa Rica, continuing protection of Caribbean lowland forest and forest corridors is important, especially because the species depends on mature habitat, intact leaf litter, and army-ant swarms.
conservation.howToHelp: Support protection and restoration of Caribbean lowland and foothill forests in Costa Rica. Maintaining large connected forest blocks, limiting further clearing, and preserving natural understory and leaf-litter conditions can benefit this species and other ant-following birds. Reporting sightings through established bird-monitoring programs can also improve knowledge of its distribution and population status.

profile.overview: The Spotted Antbird (Hylophylax naevioides) is a small forest bird of the typical antbird family, Thamnophilidae. It lives mainly in humid tropical lowland forests from Central America to northwestern South America. The species is usually encountered in dense understory, where it searches for insects and other small invertebrates. It is a resident bird rather than a long-distance migrant and is often detected first by its distinctive, repeated whistled song.
profile.classification: The Spotted Antbird belongs to the antbird family Thamnophilidae and the genus Hylophylax. Two commonly recognized subspecies are Hylophylax naevioides capnitis in Central America and Hylophylax naevioides naevioides farther south.
profile.identification: This is a small, compact antbird with a short tail and a relatively broad bill. Males are generally dark gray to blackish above, with conspicuous white spotting on the wings and underparts, while females are warmer brown or rufous, also marked with pale spots. It usually remains low in thick vegetation and moves by short hops. Its song consists of repeated, clear whistled phrases followed by short notes; both sexes may vocalize.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Spotted Antbird occurs from eastern Honduras and Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama to Colombia and western Ecuador. In Costa Rica it is a resident species found mainly on the Caribbean slope, with a smaller occurrence on the northwestern Pacific slope. It occupies humid lowland and foothill evergreen forest, including mature secondary forest, especially where dense understory and leaf litter are present. It generally occurs from sea level to about 900–1,000 meters.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout most of its range; it does not undertake regular long-distance seasonal migration. Local movements may occur in response to food availability or changing conditions.
profile.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding is associated mainly with the early wet season, approximately April through July. The nest is a small open cup, often made partly from fungal rhizomorphs and disguised among debris. It is usually attached to a low branch within about two meters of the ground. Clutches generally contain two spotted or streaked eggs. Both adults participate in incubation, although the female commonly incubates at night, and young leave the nest roughly 11 days after hatching.
profile.dietFeeding: The Spotted Antbird feeds chiefly on insects and other small arthropods, including spiders. It forages in the shaded understory and on or near the forest floor, searching among leaves, twigs, vines, and low vegetation. Like several antbirds, it may take advantage of insects flushed by army-ant activity, but it is not considered wholly dependent on army-ant swarms. Pairs or small family groups may forage together.
profile.behavior: This antbird is generally secretive and spends much of its time in dense vegetation, often close to the ground. It may join mixed-species feeding groups and can become more visible when following active army ants or responding to playback and neighboring birds. Pairs defend territories with songs and aggressive calls. The species commonly gives sharp alarm notes, churring sounds, and harsher vocalizations when disturbed.

conservation.populationTrend: No reliable evidence of a rapid global population decline is established in the available assessment information.

profile.overview: The Ocellated Antbird is a striking forest antbird named for the eye-like spots formed by bold markings on its back and underparts. It is closely associated with army-ant swarms, especially Eciton burchellii, and captures insects and other small animals fleeing the ants. Usually found near the forest floor, it lives in humid lowland and foothill forests from Honduras through western South America. In Costa Rica, it is a resident of suitable wet forest, especially on the Caribbean slope.
profile.classification: The Ocellated Antbird belongs to the antbird family Thamnophilidae and the subfamily Thamnophilinae. Its scientific name is Phaenostictus mcleannani, and it is the only species in its genus.
profile.identification: This is a relatively large antbird, about 20 cm long, with a long bill and tail. Both sexes are broadly similar. The head and upperparts are dark brown to blackish with conspicuous pale, oval spots that create an ocellated or scaled appearance. The underparts are warm cinnamon to rufous and heavily marked, while a large area of bare bluish skin surrounds the eye. It is most often detected moving quietly through dense understory near army-ant swarms.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from northern Honduras through Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama to western Colombia and northwestern Ecuador. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly on the Caribbean slope, including humid lowlands and foothills, and locally reaches about 1,200 m elevation. It favors mature evergreen or rain forest with dense understory, but can also use advanced secondary forest. Records include La Selva, the Arenal region, and the Área de Conservación Guanacaste, where it has been observed in wet forest at several elevations.
profile.migrationStatus: The Ocellated Antbird is considered a year-round resident throughout its range, including Costa Rica. It does not undertake regular seasonal migration, although local movements may follow army-ant activity and changing food conditions.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited, but the species is known to nest in humid forest, including at La Selva Biological Station in Costa Rica. The nest may be an open cup placed on or very close to the ground, sometimes between buttresses or among low vegetation. Clutches generally contain about two eggs, and both parents participate in incubation and feeding nestlings. Pairs maintain feeding areas and may nest within a smaller, repeatedly used portion of that range.
profile.dietFeeding: The Ocellated Antbird is an obligate army-ant follower. It specializes in taking arthropods flushed by advancing swarms, including insects, spiders, and other small invertebrates. Birds usually perch within about a meter of the ground near the front or edges of a swarm, then make short sallies to seize fleeing prey. In Costa Rica it is especially associated with Eciton burchellii swarms and may forage with other ant-following birds.
profile.behavior: It is generally seen in pairs, family groups, or small associations gathered around army ants. Individuals remain in dense forest understory and seldom cross open ground unless following a swarm. They are active and attentive, often perching quietly before darting after prey. Ocellated Antbirds may dominate feeding gatherings at ant swarms and defend access to productive portions of the swarm, while maintaining long-term pair territories or feeding ranges.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population size and detailed trend are not well quantified. Available information does not establish a clear global rate of change.

profile.overview: The Black-crowned Antpitta (Pittasoma michleri) is a secretive, ground-dwelling forest bird of Central America and northwestern Colombia. It belongs to the gnateater family, Conopophagidae, rather than the true antpittas. Usually encountered alone or in pairs, it moves quietly through dense understory and leaf litter, where its rounded body, short tail, and richly patterned underparts help it blend into shadowy forest. Its distinctive calls are often easier to detect than the bird itself.
profile.classification: The Black-crowned Antpitta is a passerine in the family Conopophagidae and genus Pittasoma. It is one of two recognized species in this genus.
profile.identification: This medium-sized bird is about 18–19 cm long. Adults have a dark blackish crown, brown to chestnut sides of the head, olive-brown upperparts, and a chestnut-brown tail and wings. The throat is dark, while the whitish to buff underparts are strongly marked with black, giving the breast and belly a scaled or barred appearance. The bird has a stout bill, longish legs, and a compact, rounded profile. It is more often heard or glimpsed briefly than seen in the open.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from eastern Costa Rica through Panama to northwestern Colombia. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly on the Caribbean slope, especially in humid foothill forests, generally from roughly 300 to 1,000 meters elevation. It favors mature evergreen or wet foothill forest with dense understory, tangled vegetation, and deep leaf litter. It forages close to the ground and may use forest edges or lightly disturbed habitat where dense cover remains, but it is strongly associated with humid forest conditions.
profile.migrationStatus: The Black-crowned Antpitta is considered a resident species. In Costa Rica, individuals are present year-round on the Caribbean slope; no regular long-distance migration is recognized.
profile.breeding: Reliable, detailed information on the breeding biology of the Black-crowned Antpitta is limited. The species is believed to breed within humid forest across its range. Like other small forest birds that forage near the ground, it likely places its nest in dense vegetation close to the forest floor, but nest structure, clutch size, incubation, and parental care are not sufficiently documented here to describe confidently.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of forest-floor invertebrates, including insects, spiders, scorpions, and other arthropods. It may also take small vertebrates such as frogs and small lizards. The bird searches through leaf litter and low vegetation, using short hops and pauses to locate prey. Its heavy bill and terrestrial habits are well suited to probing, picking, and seizing prey in damp, shaded understory.
profile.behavior: The Black-crowned Antpitta is shy, quiet, and highly skulking. It usually stays on or near the ground, moving through dense cover rather than crossing open areas. It often forages alone or in pairs and may remain motionless when approached, making it difficult to observe. Vocalizations can provide the first indication of its presence. The species is most likely to be encountered in undisturbed or well-developed humid forest understory with abundant leaf litter.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well documented. The species is locally uncommon and depends on humid forest, but it is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Scaled Antpitta (Grallaria guatimalensis) is a secretive, ground-dwelling songbird of humid forests in Central and northern South America. It spends much of its time walking or hopping through dense understory and leaf litter, where its rich, ringing song is often easier to detect than the bird itself. In Costa Rica, it is a resident of montane forests on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes, occurring mainly in middle-elevation forested regions.
profile.classification: The Scaled Antpitta belongs to the family Grallariidae, a group of mainly terrestrial Neotropical forest birds. It is placed in the genus Grallaria, which includes several large antpittas with powerful legs, short tails, and concealed forest-floor habits.
profile.identification: A medium-sized, compact antpitta with a short tail, long legs, and a slightly rounded body. The upperparts are brown and prominently marked with darker, scale-like feather edges, while the underparts are generally warm rufous or reddish brown, with paler areas on the throat and belly. It is usually seen briefly as it crosses a trail or probes among leaves. Its loud, repeated song is an important clue to its presence.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from Mexico through Central America and southward in parts of the northern Andes and adjacent regions. In Costa Rica, it occurs in montane forests between about 800 and 1,600 meters, on both slopes of the Guanacaste, Tilarán, Central Volcanic, and Talamanca mountain ranges. It favors humid evergreen forest, cloud forest, dense forest edge, and other well-developed understory with abundant leaf litter. It may occasionally appear in shaded gardens or disturbed forest near suitable cover.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica. It is not regarded as a regular long-distance migrant, and individuals generally remain in suitable forest habitats throughout the year.
profile.breeding: The species is believed to breed within its resident forest range, including Costa Rica, but detailed information on nesting biology is limited. Antpittas typically place their nests low above the ground or close to the forest floor in dense vegetation, where they are difficult to find. Breeding activity is most likely detected through singing and territorial behavior rather than direct nest observations. Local timing may vary with rainfall and elevation.
profile.dietFeeding: The Scaled Antpitta feeds mainly on small invertebrates found on or beneath the forest floor. Its diet likely includes insects, spiders, larvae, and other arthropods, along with earthworms and similar soft-bodied prey. It forages by walking slowly through leaf litter, pausing to listen, and turning or probing leaves and loose soil with its bill. It normally feeds alone or in pairs rather than in large flocks.
profile.behavior: This antpitta is shy, solitary, and strongly associated with dense ground cover. It often remains motionless or moves quietly through shadowy understory, making it difficult to observe even where it is regularly heard. The song is a clear, powerful, repeated whistle or ringing phrase, frequently delivered from concealed vegetation. When flushed, it usually flies only a short distance before disappearing back into thick cover. It is most active during the morning and in humid conditions.

profile.overview: The Streak-chested Antpitta (Hylopezus perspicillatus) is a shy, ground-dwelling forest bird of the humid Neotropics. It spends much of its time walking or hopping through leaf litter beneath dense vegetation, where it searches for small invertebrates. Its rich brown plumage, pale facial markings, and strongly streaked chest provide useful identification features, but it is more often detected by its distinctive, repeated whistle than by sight.
profile.classification: The Streak-chested Antpitta belongs to the antpitta family Grallariidae and the order Passeriformes. It is one of the ground-foraging antpittas of tropical Central and northern South America.
profile.identification: This medium-sized antpitta has a compact, rounded body, short tail, and relatively long legs. The upperparts are mainly brown, while the underparts are pale to buff with conspicuous dark streaking across the breast and upper belly. It also shows contrasting pale markings around the face and throat. It usually keeps low in dense cover and may stand upright briefly before quickly disappearing into vegetation. Its loud, clear, repeated whistle is often the best way to locate it.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from parts of southern Central America through northern South America, generally in humid lowland and foothill forests. In Costa Rica, it is a resident of suitable wet forest, especially in the Caribbean lowlands and adjacent foothills, where it uses dense understory, shaded forest floor, and areas with abundant leaf litter. It may occur in mature forest and well-developed secondary growth, but is most reliably associated with moist habitats offering dense ground cover and relatively undisturbed foraging conditions.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally considered resident and non-migratory. In Costa Rica, individuals are present year-round in suitable humid forest; local movements may occur in response to food availability or habitat conditions.
profile.breeding: Information on its breeding biology is less complete than for many conspicuous bird species. Like other antpittas, it is believed to nest close to the ground or in low vegetation, using a bulky structure made from plant material. Breeding activity is associated with the rainy season in at least parts of its range, when food is abundant. The species is secretive around nesting areas, and detailed information on nest sites, clutch size, and parental care remains limited.
profile.dietFeeding: The Streak-chested Antpitta feeds mainly on small animals found in leaf litter and soil, including insects, spiders, and other arthropods. It forages by walking and making short hops beneath dense vegetation, often pausing to listen before probing or flicking aside leaves. It may also take other small invertebrates when available. Its feeding behavior is quiet and deliberate, which helps it remain difficult to observe.
profile.behavior: This is a strongly terrestrial and secretive bird that usually stays in shaded understory rather than moving through the canopy. It often forages alone or in pairs and responds to danger by freezing, crouching, or slipping silently into cover. Its loud, far-carrying whistle contrasts with its unobtrusive appearance. Because it is more frequently heard than seen, patient observation along quiet forest trails is often needed for a visual encounter.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly quantified, and some populations may be affected by continuing forest loss. The species remains locally common in suitable habitat in parts of its range, including protected humid forests in Costa Rica.

profile.overview: The Thicket Antpitta (Myrmothera dives) is a small, secretive forest bird that spends most of its time walking or hopping through dense vegetation on or near the ground. It is recognized more often by its distinctive vocalizations than by direct views. The species inhabits humid tropical forests from Central America into northern South America and is associated with shaded, tangled understory, leaf litter, and areas with dense ground cover.
profile.classification: The Thicket Antpitta belongs to the antpitta family Grallariidae and the order Passeriformes. It is classified in the genus Myrmothera.
profile.identification: This is a compact, short-tailed antpitta with a rounded body, long legs, and a mostly brown plumage adapted to forest-floor conditions. Its subdued coloration helps it remain concealed in shadowy thickets. It is difficult to observe because it usually stays in dense vegetation and may freeze or move quietly when approached. Its clear, repeated calls are often the best way to detect its presence.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Thicket Antpitta occurs in humid lowland and foothill forests of Central America and northern South America. In Costa Rica, it is a local resident of suitable humid forest, particularly on the Caribbean side and in other wet forest regions where dense understory remains intact. It uses shaded forest with thick ground vegetation, tangled plants, and leaf litter, and is generally associated with mature or well-developed forest rather than open habitats.
profile.migrationStatus: The Thicket Antpitta is considered non-migratory. In Costa Rica it occurs as a resident species in suitable humid forest, with local movements possible within its territory but no regular long-distance migration.
profile.breeding: The breeding biology of the Thicket Antpitta is not as well documented as that of many more conspicuous birds. Like other antpittas, it is believed to form a pair bond and defend a forest territory through vocal displays. Nesting takes place in dense vegetation close to the ground or slightly above it, where the nest and young are protected by heavy cover. Breeding timing can vary geographically and may be linked to local rainfall patterns.
profile.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on small invertebrates found in leaf litter and low vegetation, including insects, spiders, and other arthropods. It forages by walking, hopping, and making short movements through dense understory, sometimes pausing before picking prey from the ground or vegetation. Its feeding behavior is usually difficult to watch because the bird remains concealed while searching in shaded forest-floor habitat.
profile.behavior: The Thicket Antpitta is shy, terrestrial, and strongly associated with dense cover. It usually occurs alone or in pairs and spends much of the day near the forest floor. Individuals may remain motionless when disturbed and often respond more readily to recorded or imitated calls than to visual searching. Its repeated, loud song is especially useful for locating the species in thick forest, where direct sightings are uncommon.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is not considered globally threatened, but it may be declining locally where humid forest is cleared, fragmented, or degraded. Reliable fine-scale population estimates are limited.
conservation.threats: Habitat loss and fragmentation caused by agricultural expansion, road building, logging, and other development can reduce suitable forest habitat. Degradation of dense understory may also make occupied sites less suitable. In Costa Rica, protection and maintenance of humid forest on both public and private lands are important for retaining local populations.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore humid lowland and foothill forest, especially on the Caribbean slope of Costa Rica. Maintaining connected forest, dense native understory, and intact leaf-litter habitat benefits this and other forest-floor birds. Supporting protected areas, responsible land management, and monitoring of antpitta populations can help identify local declines.

profile.overview: The Ochre-breasted Antpitta (Grallaricula flavirostris) is a small, secretive forest bird of the antpitta family. It spends most of its time on or near the ground in dense, humid mountain forest, where it searches among leaf litter and low vegetation for small invertebrates. Its rounded body, short tail, yellowish bill, and warm ochre breast are distinctive, but its skulking habits make it easier to hear than see. It ranges from Costa Rica through Panama and the Andes to Bolivia.
profile.classification: The Ochre-breasted Antpitta belongs to the family Grallariidae in the order Passeriformes. Several geographic subspecies are recognized, including the Costa Rican form, Grallaricula flavirostris costaricensis.
profile.identification: This is a small, compact antpitta with olive-brown to brown upperparts, a short tail, rounded wings, and a relatively stout yellowish bill. The underparts are warm ochre or buff, with the breast typically richer and more orange than the belly. Fine markings can vary among subspecies. It usually keeps its body low, moves by short hops, and disappears quickly into thick vegetation. In Costa Rica, its clear, repeated whistle is often the best way to detect it.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Costa Rica and western Panama south through the Andes of Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, the resident subspecies costaricensis is found mainly in humid montane and cloud forests, especially on the Caribbean slope from central Alajuela southward, with additional local populations on the Pacific slope from central San José southward. It favors mature, shaded forest with dense understory, moss, leaf litter, and relatively undisturbed ground cover, generally at middle to upper elevations.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered a resident species rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, it is present year-round in suitable montane forest, although local movements may occur with changes in food availability or conditions.
profile.breeding: The breeding biology of the Ochre-breasted Antpitta is not fully documented. Nests have been described in Costa Rica and are placed low in dense vegetation, where they are concealed near the forest floor. The nest is a small cup made from plant material, and both adults are believed to participate in territorial defense and parental care. Breeding activity has been recorded during the wet season in parts of its range, but timing may vary geographically.
profile.dietFeeding: It feeds mainly on small invertebrates, including insects, spiders, and other arthropods. The bird forages alone or in pairs on the forest floor, pausing frequently before hopping forward and probing leaf litter, loose soil, moss, and low vegetation. It may make short pounces to capture prey and generally remains under dense cover rather than feeding in exposed places.
profile.behavior: The Ochre-breasted Antpitta is shy, quiet, and strongly terrestrial. It usually moves slowly through shadowy understory and leaf litter, often freezing when disturbed and then slipping away without flying far. Its short wings and reduced tail reflect its ground-oriented lifestyle. Individuals defend territories with clear, repeated whistles, and pairs may respond to one another from dense vegetation. Sightings are uncommon because the species is more often heard than observed.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend has not been quantified reliably.

profile.overview: The Silvery-fronted Tapaculo is a small, secretive songbird of the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama. It belongs to a distinctive family of ground-dwelling birds called tapaculos. Usually detected by its sharp, repeated song rather than by sight, it moves through dense vegetation close to the ground. Its dark plumage, pale silvery forehead, and preference for wet mountain undergrowth help distinguish it from other Costa Rican birds.
profile.classification: The Silvery-fronted Tapaculo is a passerine in the tapaculo family Rhinocryptidae and the genus Scytalopus. Two subspecies are commonly recognized, including the nominate form found in Costa Rica.
profile.identification: This tapaculo is about 11 centimeters long and has mostly sooty black or dark gray plumage. The forehead is silvery gray, often extending into a small pale supercilium. The lower breast and belly are somewhat paler, while the flanks and undertail region show dusky brown barring. Females may appear browner and generally have less obvious pale facial markings. It is most often heard rather than seen, and its furtive movements can make visual identification difficult.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs in Costa Rica and western Panama. In Costa Rica, it is a resident of the country's mountain ranges, from the Cordillera de Guanacaste south through the highlands, including suitable areas around the Talamanca region. It occupies humid montane and cloud forests, dense shady understory, bamboo thickets, stream edges, ravines, and adjacent second growth. It is generally found from about 1,000 to 3,100 meters, with local lower-elevation records where cool, wet forest persists.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident and probably largely sedentary. In Costa Rica it remains in suitable highland forest year-round, with no regular long-distance migration known.
profile.breeding: Reliable published information on the Silvery-fronted Tapaculo's breeding biology is limited. Like other Scytalopus tapaculos, it is believed to nest close to the ground or within dense understory cover, where the nest and young are protected from view. Birds defend territories mainly through vocalizations. In Costa Rica, breeding is expected to take place within permanent montane forest habitat, but detailed information on nesting dates, clutch size, incubation, and parental care is insufficient for a fuller account.
profile.dietFeeding: The Silvery-fronted Tapaculo feeds mainly on small invertebrates found in leaf litter and dense ground vegetation. Reported prey includes insect larvae, pupae, beetles, earwigs, crickets, spiders, and spider egg cases. It creeps, hops, and probes along the forest floor, searching among leaves, moss, roots, fallen branches, and crevices. Its dark, compact body and secretive feeding style suit the dim, tangled understory of humid mountain forests.
profile.behavior: This is a highly secretive, ground-oriented bird that usually stays within thick vegetation and is difficult to observe. It moves cautiously through brush, often near streams and ravines, and may freeze or slip away when approached. Its presence is commonly revealed by a distinctive repetitive song or calls from concealed cover. Individuals are generally encountered alone or in pairs, and their vocal activity is especially useful for locating them in Costa Rican cloud forests.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified, but the species is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Black-faced Antthrush (Formicarius analis) is a secretive forest bird of the antthrush family, Formicariidae. It spends most of its time walking quietly on the forest floor, where its dark face and throat contrast with olive-brown upperparts and grayish underparts. Its clear, far-carrying song is often easier to detect than the bird itself. The species has a broad distribution from Central America through much of tropical South America and is generally considered locally common in suitable habitat.
profile.classification: The Black-faced Antthrush is a passerine in the family Formicariidae. Its scientific name is Formicarius analis.
profile.identification: This medium-sized antthrush is about 18 cm long. It has mainly olive-brown or grayish-brown upperparts, a black face, throat, and sides of the neck, and subdued gray or brown underparts. The wings and tail are darker, while the lower belly and undertail may show warmer brown tones. It is usually seen walking rather than flying, with a deliberate posture and frequent pauses while it searches among leaves and small plants.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from eastern Honduras through Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama, and across much of tropical South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly in humid lowland and foothill forests, especially on the Caribbean slope, including evergreen forest, floodplain forest, forest edges, and mature second growth. It generally favors dense, shaded habitats with a well-developed leaf-litter layer and may occur from the lowlands into lower foothill elevations, although it is replaced at higher elevations by other Formicarius species.
profile.migrationStatus: The Black-faced Antthrush is generally resident and does not undertake regular seasonal migration. In Costa Rica it is present year-round in suitable humid forest and is not regarded as a migratory species.
profile.breeding: Black-faced Antthrushes are believed to breed in secluded forest sites, with nesting activity associated with the wet or early part of the breeding season in different parts of the range. The nest is placed in a protected cavity or other concealed structure close to the ground, where the adults care for a small brood. Both parents participate in territorial defense and parental care. Detailed information on nesting sites and reproductive timing is limited for some populations, including those in Costa Rica.
profile.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on insects and other small invertebrates found in leaf litter and on the ground. It walks slowly through shaded forest, turning leaves or probing among debris with its bill. Antthrushes may take advantage of army-ant swarms and the disturbed prey they flush, although the Black-faced Antthrush also forages independently. Small seeds or other occasional plant material may be taken, but animal prey forms the main part of its diet.
profile.behavior: This is a quiet, terrestrial bird that is more often heard than seen. It normally travels alone or in pairs and maintains a territory in dense forest. Its rounded wings and short flights reflect its ground-dwelling habits. The song is a distinctive series of clear, ringing notes that may carry through thick vegetation. When alarmed, it may freeze, slip into cover, or move away on foot rather than making a conspicuous flight.

conservation.populationTrend: The species has a large range and is not currently considered globally threatened. Its overall population is generally regarded as stable, although local declines may occur where humid forest is extensively cleared or degraded.

profile.overview: The Black-capped Antthrush (Formicarius nigricapillus) is a secretive, ground-dwelling antthrush of humid mountain forests in southern Central America. It spends most of its time walking quietly through leaf litter, where it searches for small invertebrates. The species was formerly treated as part of the broader Black-headed Antthrush complex, but the Costa Rican and Panamanian form is now recognized as a separate species. Costa Rica is an important part of its limited range.
profile.classification: The Black-capped Antthrush belongs to the order Passeriformes and family Formicariidae. Its scientific name is Formicarius nigricapillus, and it is currently treated as a monotypic species following the separation of the former Chocó population as the Black-hooded Antthrush, Formicarius destructus.
profile.identification: This medium-sized antthrush is approximately 18 cm long. Adults have a dark brown body, a blackish cap, and black facial and throat areas, with a conspicuous bluish-white area of bare skin around the eye. The underparts are generally dark and subdued, while the back and wings are brown. It is usually detected by its deliberate walk, upright posture, and distinctive ringing or trilling song rather than by prolonged views.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Black-capped Antthrush occurs in Costa Rica and Panama, mainly in humid forests on the Caribbean slope and in suitable forest on both slopes of Panama. In Costa Rica, it is locally common but occupies a narrow elevational belt: roughly 400–800 m in the north and central regions, and about 600–1,200 m in the southeast. It favors primary wet forest and may occasionally enter adjacent mature secondary growth. It is replaced by related antthrushes at lower or higher elevations.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident, including in Costa Rica. No regular seasonal migration is known; individuals generally remain in suitable forest habitat throughout the year.
profile.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported mainly in April and May. A documented nest was a shallow cup made from leaf petioles and dry leaves, placed inside a hollow palm stump. The clutch consists of two eggs, which are described as dull white and soon becoming marked with brown. Information on incubation, nestling development, and parental care remains limited.
profile.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on arthropods, especially insects and spiders, and may also take very small reptiles and amphibians. It forages almost entirely on or close to the ground, walking slowly through leaf litter and probing crevices, tangles, and fallen vegetation. It may flick aside leaves to expose prey and can sometimes follow army-ant swarms to capture animals fleeing the advancing ants.
profile.behavior: Black-capped Antthrushes are shy, difficult-to-see forest birds that usually occur alone or in pairs. They move deliberately along the forest floor, often holding the tail cocked and pausing frequently while searching for prey. Both sexes may sing, commonly from low perches or near the ground. Their songs and calls are more often heard than the birds are seen, especially in dense, wet understory.

conservation.populationTrend: The population trend of the separately recognized Black-capped Antthrush is not well established. The species is locally common in parts of its range and occurs in protected forests, but it is uncommon in Costa Rica and has a geographically limited distribution.

profile.overview: The Rufous-breasted Antthrush is a secretive, ground-dwelling forest bird of the Neotropics. It belongs to a group known for slow, deliberate walking and loud, simple whistles. The species is usually detected by voice rather than seen, because it stays in dense vegetation on the forest floor. Its range is divided among Central America, the Andes, and adjacent foothill regions of Venezuela and Peru.
profile.classification: The Rufous-breasted Antthrush is a passerine in the antthrush family Formicariidae and the genus Formicarius. Several geographically separated subspecies are recognized, including the nominate form found in Costa Rica and Panama.
profile.identification: This is a chunky, short-tailed antthrush with a strongly contrasting rufous or chestnut breast, darker upperparts, and a relatively plain head and belly. It often holds its tail cocked while walking. The species is difficult to observe in thick understory, but its song is distinctive: typically two clear, whistled notes, sometimes with the second note slightly higher. Its deliberate, rail-like movements can help distinguish it from other forest-floor birds.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species has a disjunct range extending from Costa Rica and Panama through Colombia and Ecuador to Peru, with separate populations in Venezuela. In Costa Rica, it occurs locally in humid highland forests, especially along the Caribbean slope of the Cordillera de Tilarán southward through the country's mountain ranges. It generally occupies montane evergreen or very wet forest, mature second growth, ravines, steep slopes, landslide regrowth, and dense Heliconia or other understory thickets, usually from about 750 or 800 to 1,500 meters.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident and essentially non-migratory. In Costa Rica, it is present year-round in suitable highland forest rather than being a seasonal migrant, although local movements may occur with changes in conditions or food availability.
profile.breeding: The breeding biology of the Rufous-breasted Antthrush is poorly documented. Confirmed or reported breeding activity elsewhere in its range includes June in Colombia and October in Ecuador, but the timing in Costa Rica is not well established. Like related Formicarius antthrushes, it is expected to nest in a concealed cavity, hollow stump, or similar protected site, with both adults likely involved in incubation and care of the young; these details should be treated as general information for the genus rather than fully confirmed for this species.
profile.dietFeeding: Detailed dietary studies are lacking, but the species is believed to feed mainly on insects and other small invertebrates found in leaf litter and soil. It forages almost entirely on the ground, walking slowly through dense cover and probing or picking prey from the forest floor. It has occasionally been recorded near army-ant swarms, but a regular dependence on them has not been demonstrated.
profile.behavior: The Rufous-breasted Antthrush is secretive, terrestrial, and usually solitary or found in pairs. It moves quietly and deliberately through tangled understory with its tail raised, and it may remain hidden even when singing nearby. Its vocalizations are often the best way to locate it. The species is active by day and appears strongly associated with shaded, structurally complex forest-floor habitat.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is believed to be decreasing, although the decline is not currently considered severe enough to qualify the species for a threatened category.
conservation.threats: Loss and fragmentation of humid montane forest can reduce suitable dense understory habitat, particularly in areas affected by agricultural expansion, roads, and other land-use changes. Because the species is local and dependent on forest-floor cover, continued habitat degradation may affect some populations even where it remains globally secure.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore humid montane forest, maintain connected habitat along mountain slopes and ravines, and retain dense native understory during forest management. In Costa Rica, supporting protected areas and careful monitoring of local populations can help detect changes in distribution and abundance.

profile.overview: The Middle American Leaftosser, also called the Tawny-throated Leaftosser, is a secretive forest bird of the ovenbird family. It spends much of its time on the ground, using its bill to toss aside dead leaves while searching for small invertebrates. Its mostly brown plumage provides excellent camouflage, while the warm tawny throat and chest are useful identification features. The species is usually encountered alone or in pairs in humid tropical forest.
profile.classification: The Middle American Leaftosser belongs to the family Furnariidae, the ovenbirds and woodcreepers, and the subfamily Sclerurinae. Its scientific name is Sclerurus mexicanus.
profile.identification: This small, compact leaftosser is about 15–17 cm long. Adults are mainly dark brown above and below, with a distinctive tawny to rufous throat and upper breast. The back and wings are plain, the rump may appear somewhat warmer chestnut, and the tail is short and dark. It has a fairly long, pointed bill and strong legs suited to ground foraging. Its low posture, secretive behavior, and habit of flipping leaves help separate it from similar forest understory birds.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southern Mexico through much of Central America to western Panama. In Costa Rica it is a resident of humid forested areas, especially foothills, montane and premontane forest, and forested highlands; the Costa Rican population is associated with the form Sclerurus mexicanus pullus. It generally favors shaded, leaf-littered forest floors and can occur from lowlands into the highlands, commonly at roughly 700–2,200 meters, depending on locality. It is most likely in mature, continuous forest.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and across its range; it does not undertake regular long-distance migration. Local movements may occur in response to food, weather, or habitat conditions.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is best documented in Costa Rica, where nesting occurs mainly from December through April. Pairs are territorial and apparently monogamous. The nest is placed in a short burrow excavated in an earth bank or similar protected site, sometimes using a natural cavity or abandoned opening. It is lined with small sticks and leaves. The clutch typically contains two unmarked white eggs. Adults share territorial defense and care for the young, although many details of parental behavior remain poorly known.
profile.dietFeeding: The Middle American Leaftosser feeds mainly on small invertebrates, including insects, spiders, beetles, ants, roaches, larvae, and other arthropods. It forages primarily on the forest floor, hopping through damp leaf litter and turning leaves with its bill. It also probes rotting wood, loose soil, and decomposing vegetation. Individuals usually forage alone or in pairs, relying on stealth rather than conspicuous movement.
profile.behavior: This is a quiet, elusive bird that spends much of its time in dense understory or on the ground. It commonly moves by short hops while tossing leaves aside, and it may freeze or slip into cover when approached. Pairs defend territories and may remain in the same forest area throughout the year. Its song consists of a descending series of plaintive, drawn-out notes, while alarm calls are sharper and more abrupt. It is more often heard than seen.

conservation.populationTrend: A precise global population estimate and reliably quantified trend are not available.

profile.overview: The Scaly-throated Leaftosser is a secretive forest bird of the ovenbird family. It spends much of its time on the ground, where it tosses aside leaves while searching for small invertebrates. Its dark brown plumage, reddish-brown rump, and finely scaled throat provide useful identification clues. The species is associated mainly with humid evergreen forests and is usually encountered alone or in pairs rather than in conspicuous flocks.
profile.classification: The Scaly-throated Leaftosser belongs to the ovenbird family Furnariidae and the leaftosser genus Sclerurus. Three subspecies are generally recognized, with the nominate subspecies, Sclerurus guatemalensis guatemalensis, occurring in Costa Rica.
profile.identification: This medium-sized leaftosser is about 16.5 cm long. Adults have dark brown upperparts, a dark crown and nape with a scalloped or scaled appearance, a darker tail, and a reddish-brown rump and upper tail coverts. The throat is pale or buffy with distinct dark scaling, while the underparts are generally dark brown. It is often detected by movement in leaf litter or by its clear trill and sharp, piercing calls.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through much of Central America to western Panama, with additional populations in northern South America and western Ecuador. In Costa Rica, it occurs on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes and is a resident of suitable forest rather than a localized migrant. It favors humid lowland evergreen forest, especially mature primary forest with a closed canopy and sparse ground cover, but may also use mature secondary and montane evergreen forest. It is generally found from low elevations to roughly 1,200 meters in Central America.
profile.migrationStatus: The Scaly-throated Leaftosser is a year-round resident, including in Costa Rica. There is no reliable evidence of regular long-distance migration, although local movements may occur in response to habitat or food conditions.
profile.breeding: In Central America, breeding is generally reported from February through May, although nesting records from Costa Rica also include other months. The pair excavates a tunnel in a stream bank, soil bank, or the exposed root mass of a fallen tree. A shallow cup of leaf fibers is placed in the terminal chamber. The usual clutch is two eggs. Both adults help excavate the nest, incubate the eggs, and feed the nestlings.
profile.dietFeeding: The Scaly-throated Leaftosser feeds mainly on insects and other small invertebrates. It forages primarily on the forest floor, hopping rather than walking and using its bill to flip aside leaves, probe the litter, and inspect rotting logs. It usually feeds alone or in pairs and occasionally joins mixed-species foraging groups. Dense leaf litter and undisturbed soil are important for its ground-feeding behavior.
profile.behavior: This species is quiet, inconspicuous, and strongly associated with the shaded forest floor. It commonly moves beneath closed canopy and may remain difficult to see even when nearby. Pairs or solitary birds search methodically through leaf litter, often pausing before tossing leaves aside. Its song is a clear trill or a descending series of accented notes, while its calls include sharp, piercing squeaks or metallic-sounding notes. It is generally sedentary throughout its range.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, but the decline is not currently assessed as severe enough to place the species in a threatened category.

profile.overview: The Gray-throated Leaftosser (Sclerurus albigularis) is a secretive, ground-dwelling songbird of the ovenbird family. It is named for its habit of tossing aside dead leaves while searching for small prey. The species has a mainly brown and rufous plumage, a contrasting pale grayish throat, and a broad dark tail. It is usually detected by movement in leaf litter or by its sharp, distinctive calls rather than by prolonged views.
profile.classification: The Gray-throated Leaftosser belongs to the order Passeriformes and the ovenbird family Furnariidae. It is one of the leaftossers, a small group of forest birds specialized for feeding in leaf litter.
profile.identification: This medium-sized leaftosser is about 18 cm long. Its upperparts are generally warm rufous-brown, while the breast is darker and more reddish, creating a strong contrast with the whitish to grayish throat. The tail is broad, rounded, and dark. It has a sturdy, slightly curved bill and subdued earth-toned plumage suited to the forest floor. In Costa Rica, careful attention is needed to separate it from other brown forest-floor birds and leaftossers.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species has a disjunct range from Costa Rica and western Panama through northern and western South America, including parts of Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Brazil, and Trinidad and Tobago. In Costa Rica, the resident subspecies Sclerurus albigularis canigularis occurs locally in humid evergreen forest on both slopes, especially in foothill and lower montane areas, generally from about 600 m upward. It is absent or scarce in the dry northwest and favors mature forest with deep leaf litter.
profile.migrationStatus: Gray-throated Leaftossers are year-round residents. In Costa Rica, the species is not considered a regular migrant; individuals remain in suitable forest habitat throughout the year, although local movements may occur when conditions change.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited, particularly for Costa Rica. Elsewhere, nesting has been reported in natural cavities, banks, or similar sheltered sites near the ground, where the bird lays eggs and raises its young away from the open forest floor. The species' breeding season is documented from October to May in Trinidad, while records from Colombia include at least May and June. The exact nesting period and nest details in Costa Rica remain poorly documented.
profile.dietFeeding: The Gray-throated Leaftosser feeds mainly on small invertebrates and other prey found in leaf litter and surface soil. Recorded food includes beetles, spiders, cockroaches, and tiny frogs. It usually forages alone or in pairs, hopping across the ground while flipping leaves aside with its bill, probing beneath them, and gleaning exposed prey. It generally does not participate in mixed-species foraging flocks.
profile.behavior: This is a shy and inconspicuous forest-floor bird that usually stays under dense vegetation and is easy to overlook. It moves by hopping rather than walking and often pauses while searching beneath leaves. It is normally solitary or found in pairs. Its repeated leaf-tossing movements are characteristic, but the bird may freeze or retreat quickly when disturbed. Vocal activity can help reveal its presence in thick forest.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not reliably quantified, but the species is considered widespread and not currently facing a level of decline that meets a threatened-category threshold.

profile.overview: The Olivaceous Woodcreeper is a small to medium-sized tree-climbing songbird of the ovenbird family. It moves upward along trunks and larger branches while searching for insects, often in pairs or alone. Its subdued olive-brown plumage, grayish head, and lightly streaked throat help it blend into forest vegetation. The species ranges from Mexico through Central America and across much of South America. In Costa Rica, it is a resident species found in suitable forest habitats across much of the country.
profile.classification: The Olivaceous Woodcreeper belongs to the ovenbird family Furnariidae and the woodcreeper subfamily Dendrocolaptinae. Its scientific name is Sittasomus griseicapillus.
profile.identification: This woodcreeper has mostly olive-brown upperparts, a grayish head, and a relatively plain face. The throat and upper breast are usually pale with fine streaking, while the wings and tail may show warmer rufous tones. It has a long, narrow, slightly decurved bill and a stiff, pointed tail used for support while climbing. It is best identified by its fairly uniform coloration, slender shape, and habit of spiraling up trunks rather than flying rapidly between branches.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Olivaceous Woodcreeper occurs from central Mexico through Central America and across much of mainland South America. In Costa Rica, it is found in both lowlands and foothills, including parts of the Pacific and Caribbean slopes, and has been recorded in dry forest, moist forest, mature secondary woodland, forest edges, riverine vegetation, and wooded gardens. It generally uses trees and larger branches for foraging and can occur in moderately disturbed landscapes when sufficient tree cover remains.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered a resident species in Costa Rica, with no regular long-distance migration documented. Individuals may make local movements in response to food availability, weather, or changes in habitat conditions.
profile.breeding: The species nests in cavities, including natural hollows and abandoned woodpecker holes. The nest is built inside the cavity from plant material such as leaves, fibers, and other soft debris. Both members of a pair may participate in territorial defense and care of the young. Breeding timing varies across its broad range. In Costa Rica, nesting can occur during the local breeding period, but detailed information on its breeding biology in the country is limited.
profile.dietFeeding: The Olivaceous Woodcreeper feeds mainly on arthropods, including beetles, ants, termites, spiders, and other insects. It searches methodically on trunks, branches, bark crevices, and epiphytes, using its bill to probe or pick prey from surfaces. It may also take prey from foliage and occasionally consume small fruits. The species often follows mixed-species feeding flocks, where its climbing behavior complements birds that forage in other parts of the vegetation.
profile.behavior: It usually climbs tree trunks and large limbs in short hops, using its stiff tail as a brace. Individuals may forage alone, in pairs, or with mixed-species flocks. The species is generally unobtrusive, but its sharp calls and repeated notes can reveal its presence. It tends to remain within wooded habitat and may use forest edges, shaded plantations, and other areas with mature trees. Flight is typically direct and short between nearby trees or feeding sites.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not precisely known and is considered to be decreasing, but the species remains widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Piping Long-tailed Woodcreeper is a small, slender woodcreeper of humid forests in Central America and northern South America. It climbs trunks and large vines while searching for arthropods, often in shaded forest understory and middle levels. The species was formerly treated as part of a broader Long-tailed Woodcreeper complex but is now recognized separately. It is generally inconspicuous, and its piping song is often easier to detect than the bird itself.
profile.classification: The Piping Long-tailed Woodcreeper belongs to the ovenbird family Furnariidae and the woodcreeper subfamily Dendrocolaptinae. Its scientific name is Deconychura typica.
profile.identification: This is a small to medium-sized, brown woodcreeper with a noticeably long, graduated tail, a slender, slightly decurved bill, and cryptic plumage suited to shaded forest. The upperparts are generally warm brown, while the head and underparts show fine streaking or subtle scaling. It is usually seen clinging to or hitching up trunks and vines rather than perching openly. Its rapid series of piping notes is distinctive and may reveal its presence before the bird is located.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Piping Long-tailed Woodcreeper occurs from Honduras through Nicaragua and Costa Rica to Panama, with additional populations in northern Colombia. In Costa Rica it is found mainly on the Caribbean slope and in suitable humid forest areas, extending locally onto the Pacific side; it can occur from lowlands into foothills and has been recorded to roughly 1,200 meters. It favors the interior of mature, humid primary forest, but may use mature secondary woodland and forest edges where substantial tree cover remains.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered mainly resident. In Costa Rica, some local or elevational movements are suspected, but it is not regarded as a regular long-distance migrant.
profile.breeding: The breeding biology of the Piping Long-tailed Woodcreeper is poorly known. Available information suggests that breeding timing varies across its range, and at least one recorded clutch contained two eggs. Like other woodcreepers, it may nest in a cavity, hollow trunk, or similar protected site, but details of nest construction, incubation, parental care, and fledging are insufficiently documented. In Costa Rica, breeding records and seasonal patterns remain limited, so conclusions about its local nesting period should be treated cautiously.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet consists primarily of arthropods, although the exact composition is not well documented. It usually forages alone, in pairs, or with mixed-species feeding flocks from the lower understory to the canopy. The bird moves up trunks and vines, picking or gleaning prey from bark, crevices, foliage, and epiphytes. It sometimes makes short aerial sallies to capture insects. Adults may form an important part of its prey, rather than larvae alone.
profile.behavior: The Piping Long-tailed Woodcreeper is an active trunk-climber that typically moves upward in short hops, using its stiff tail for support. It is often quiet and difficult to see in dense forest, but it can respond strongly to the playback of its song. The song is a long, rapidly delivered series of piping notes that accelerates and rises before slowing and fading. It may sing at several times of day, especially during the morning and late afternoon.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered decreasing, although the rate and extent of decline are uncertain.
conservation.threats: The species appears sensitive to forest modification and may require nearly continuous mature forest. Clearing, fragmentation, degradation of humid forest, and the loss of large trees could reduce suitable habitat, including in Costa Rica. It is locally uncommon in parts of Central America, so isolated populations may be especially vulnerable to further habitat loss.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore large blocks of mature humid forest in Costa Rica, especially along the Caribbean slope and foothill regions. Maintain forest connectivity, retain large trees and natural cavities, and limit clearing or severe thinning of mature forest. Support protected areas, private forest reserves, and responsible ecotourism that contributes to habitat conservation. Documenting sightings and breeding evidence through well-verified bird records can also improve knowledge of the species in Costa Rica.

profile.overview: The Ruddy Woodcreeper (Dendrocincla homochroa) is a medium-sized tropical woodcreeper in the ovenbird family, Furnariidae. Its rich rufous-brown plumage, long slightly curved bill, and habit of climbing along trunks distinguish it from many related species. It is mainly a bird of humid forest, where it searches bark and branches for insects. Individuals are often solitary, but they may join mixed bird groups or gather at army-ant swarms to catch fleeing prey.
profile.classification: The Ruddy Woodcreeper belongs to the family Furnariidae and subfamily Dendrocolaptinae, the woodcreepers. Its scientific name is Dendrocincla homochroa.
profile.identification: This woodcreeper is predominantly warm reddish or rufous brown, with relatively plain plumage and subtle variation between geographic forms. It has a long, narrow, slightly decurved bill, a stiff tail used for support, and the upright posture typical of trunk-climbing woodcreepers. It moves by hitching upward along trunks and large branches, often pausing to probe bark crevices. Its call is a useful identification clue because the bird can be difficult to detect inside dense forest.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Ruddy Woodcreeper ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and into northern South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident, occurring on both Pacific and Caribbean slopes, although it is generally uncommon and less frequent in the lowest lowlands. It is found in humid evergreen forest, foothill forest, forest edges, mature secondary woodland, gallery forest, and partly open areas with trees. Costa Rican records extend from low elevations to roughly 1,350–1,500 meters, with especially suitable habitat in northern foothills and protected forest areas.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica; it is not considered a regular long-distance migrant. Its local movements may follow food availability, especially army-ant activity.
profile.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding has been documented mainly during May and June, although timing may vary by locality. The species nests in natural cavities, often in hollow trunks or bases of medium-sized trees, commonly a few meters above the ground. A Costa Rican observation reported two white eggs placed deep inside a vertical cavity. Little nest material may be used, though leaves, moss, wood chips, or other debris can occur. At least some nests may receive care predominantly from the female.
profile.dietFeeding: The Ruddy Woodcreeper feeds mainly on insects and other arthropods found on or beneath tree bark. It climbs trunks, branches, and stems below the canopy, using its bill to investigate crevices and loose bark. Recorded prey includes insects and spiders. It is particularly associated with army-ant swarms, following moving ants and capturing insects that flee from the advancing swarm. Most feeding is solitary, but two or more birds may forage together at these temporary food concentrations.
profile.behavior: This species is usually quiet and solitary while foraging, moving in short flights and upward climbs along trunks and branches. It may join mixed-species flocks, especially in forest understory and lower-canopy habitats. Army-ant swarms can attract several individuals and other insect-eating birds. The Ruddy Woodcreeper generally remains below the canopy and can be overlooked because its subdued plumage blends with tree bark. It may reuse a successful nest cavity in a later breeding season.

conservation.populationTrend: A precise global population trend is not well quantified, but the species is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Tawny-winged Woodcreeper (Dendrocincla anabatina) is a small forest woodcreeper of Central America. It climbs trunks and large branches while searching bark, crevices, foliage, and leaf litter for invertebrates. Its plumage is mostly warm brown, with noticeably tawny wings and a relatively plain appearance compared with many streaked woodcreepers. In Costa Rica it is a resident species of humid lowland and foothill forests, where it is usually found singly or in pairs and can be unobtrusive.
profile.classification: The species belongs to the woodcreeper subfamily Dendrocolaptinae within the ovenbird family Furnariidae. It is placed in the genus Dendrocincla, a group of mostly forest-dwelling woodcreepers.
profile.identification: This is a small to medium-sized woodcreeper with a slim, slightly decurved bill, stiff tail, and upright trunk-climbing posture. The upperparts are warm brown, while the wings and wing coverts have a distinct tawny or rufous tone that gives the species its common name. The underparts are generally buffy to brownish, with limited fine streaking compared with several similar woodcreepers. Identification is aided by its compact shape, plain facial pattern, and habit of moving methodically along trunks and larger limbs.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Tawny-winged Woodcreeper ranges from southern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and western Panama. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly in humid Caribbean-slope and southern Pacific forests, including lowlands and foothills, and has also been recorded at sites such as Los Cusingos.
