profile.overview: The Ochre-bellied Flycatcher (Mionectes oleagineus) is a small, mostly olive-green tyrant flycatcher of humid tropical forests. It is named for its warm ochre or tawny belly and is often detected by its quiet movements in shaded vegetation rather than by conspicuous behavior. Unlike many temperate flycatchers, it eats substantial amounts of fruit as well as insects. In Costa Rica it is a resident of lowland and foothill forest, especially in humid areas with dense understory.
profile.classification: The species belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Mionectes. It is one of the small Neotropical flycatchers sometimes called fruit-tyrants because fruit forms an important part of its diet.
profile.identification: This small flycatcher is about 13 cm long. Adults have olive-green upperparts, a grayish-olive head and throat, and a distinctly ochre, yellowish-tawny to orange-buff belly. The wings and tail are brownish with narrow buff or rufous edges. The bill is short and broad, often with a pale pinkish or orange base to the lower mandible. It is generally identified by its compact shape, plain olive coloration, ochre underparts, and preference for shaded forest vegetation.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Ochre-bellied Flycatcher ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern South America east of the Andes, including Trinidad and Tobago. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly in humid lowland and foothill forests on both slopes, locally extending to roughly 1,200 m and occasionally higher. It uses mature evergreen forest, forest edges, streamside vegetation, second growth, and shaded gardens or plantations with dense cover. It is especially associated with forest understory and middle levels rather than exposed, open ground.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally a year-round resident in Costa Rica, not a regular long-distance migrant. Individuals may make local movements in response to fruit availability, rainfall, breeding activity, or changes in elevation, but Costa Rican populations are not normally replaced seasonally by migrants.
profile.breeding: In northeastern Costa Rica, breeding activity has been recorded mainly from March through July. The species may use solitary courtship or small display areas known as leks. Its nest is a pear-shaped structure with a side entrance, made from plant fibers and other soft materials and often covered with moss. It is suspended from a vine, aerial root, or similar support, usually in shaded forest vegetation. Clutches commonly contain about three eggs, although detailed nesting information varies across the range.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet includes small fruits, especially berries and fruit with fleshy or aril-like parts, together with insects and other small arthropods. In Costa Rica it gleans small insects and spiders from leaves and also makes short flycatching sallies from a perch. It may hover briefly while taking food from foliage or fruit. Feeding commonly occurs in shaded understory and middle-level vegetation, and the species can join mixed-species flocks or concentrate at fruiting trees.
profile.behavior: The Ochre-bellied Flycatcher is usually quiet, unobtrusive, and solitary, although it sometimes joins mixed-species feeding groups. It moves through dense foliage with short flights between perches and often pauses before making a quick sally to seize an insect or fruit. During courtship, males may sing, flash their wings, raise the crown feathers, and display either singly or at leks. Its vocal activity is generally greater during the breeding season.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the rate and geographic pattern of change are not well quantified.

profile.overview: The Sepia-capped Flycatcher (Leptopogon amaurocephalus) is a small, quietly active tyrant flycatcher of tropical forests. It is usually found in shaded vegetation from the understory to the lower middle levels of the forest, where it makes short flights to capture insects and sometimes takes small fruits. Its broad distribution extends from Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and eastern South America. In Costa Rica, it is a resident species associated mainly with forested lowlands and foothills.
profile.classification: The species belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Leptopogon. Several geographic subspecies are recognized across its extensive range.
profile.identification: This small flycatcher has olive-green upperparts, a distinctly sepia-brown crown, and a grayish face with a pale throat. The underparts are generally pale gray to yellowish, becoming more yellow toward the belly, and the wings show contrasting pale edging or wingbars. It has a short, fairly broad bill and a compact shape. In Costa Rica, careful attention to the brown crown, subdued coloration, and forest-understory habits helps separate it from other small Leptopogon flycatchers.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Sepia-capped Flycatcher occurs from southern Mexico through much of Central America and across large parts of northern, western, and eastern South America. In Costa Rica, the northern Central American subspecies range reaches the central part of the country, with the species also occurring along the Pacific slope from central Costa Rica southward toward Panama. It uses lowland evergreen forest, mature secondary forest, forest edges, gallery woodland, and some plantations, generally from sea level into the foothills and lower subtropical elevations.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally considered a year-round resident rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, it is present as a resident in suitable forest habitat; major seasonal movements have not been reliably documented, although local or elevational movements may occur.
profile.breeding: Detailed information on breeding is limited across much of the species' range. The breeding season is geographically variable and is not well defined for Costa Rica. Records from Mexico indicate breeding activity at least during April and May, but this should not be assumed to represent the full Costa Rican season. The species is believed to breed within its Costa Rican range, but reliable published details on nest placement, clutch size, incubation, and parental care remain sparse.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects and other small arthropods, with fruits also taken. It usually forages alone or in pairs in shaded vegetation from the understory to the lower middle levels of the forest. Typical feeding involves short sallies from a perch to hover-glean prey from leaves or snatch insects and fruit. It may occasionally capture flying insects and can participate in mixed-species feeding flocks.
profile.behavior: This is a relatively unobtrusive forest flycatcher that often remains inside dense foliage rather than using exposed perches. Its movements are usually brief and deliberate, making it easier to detect by its calls than by prolonged views. Individuals commonly forage singly or in pairs, but they may join mixed-species flocks while feeding. As with many small tropical flycatchers, activity is concentrated in shaded woodland with a layered understory and abundant foliage.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend has not been quantified in detail, but the species is widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Slaty-capped Flycatcher (Leptopogon superciliaris) is a small, active tyrant flycatcher of humid forests in the American tropics. It usually stays within leafy vegetation, where it searches for insects and occasionally small fruits. The species has a broad distribution from Costa Rica through parts of Panama, northern South America, and the Andes. It is generally encountered singly or in pairs and often joins mixed-species foraging flocks.
profile.classification: The Slaty-capped Flycatcher belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Leptopogon. Some taxonomic treatments have separated certain southern populations, so range details can vary among references.
profile.identification: This is a small flycatcher with a distinctive slate-gray crown and a contrasting pale eyebrow. The face is finely patterned, the back is olive-green, and the wings are dark with pale edging and wing bars. The underparts are generally pale yellowish or whitish, often with subtle dusky streaking on the breast. Its compact shape, relatively short bill, active movements, and habit of flicking through foliage help distinguish it from similar forest flycatchers.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Costa Rica and western Panama south through parts of Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia, with additional populations in Trinidad under some taxonomic treatments. In Costa Rica it is a resident of humid foothill and montane forest on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes, most often at middle elevations, commonly from about 500 to 1,500 meters. It also uses mature secondary woodland, forest edges, and shaded coffee plantations, especially where vegetation remains dense and structurally diverse.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally considered a resident species in Costa Rica and across most of its range. Seasonal movements may occur locally in response to food availability or elevation, but it is not known as a regular long-distance migrant in Costa Rica.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is less thoroughly documented than for many widespread forest birds. The species is believed to nest during the local rainy-season breeding period, when insect food is abundant. As with related small forest flycatchers, it likely places a compact nest in sheltered vegetation, cavities, or other protected sites, but nest placement and parental behavior can vary among populations. In Costa Rica, breeding may occur wherever suitable humid woodland persists at foothill and montane elevations.
profile.dietFeeding: The Slaty-capped Flycatcher feeds mainly on insects and other small arthropods, including flying insects and prey gathered from leaves and twigs. It usually forages from low or middle levels of the forest, making short sallies to pick prey from vegetation or to intercept insects in the air. Small berries or other fruits may supplement the diet, particularly when insect availability is reduced.
profile.behavior: This flycatcher is alert and energetic, moving quickly through dense foliage while frequently turning its head and flicking its wings or tail. It often forages quietly but may give sharp calls that reveal its presence. Individuals are commonly seen alone, in pairs, or in mixed-species flocks with other insect-eating birds. It generally prefers cover rather than exposed perches and may remain difficult to observe despite its repeated movements.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not precisely quantified, but it is generally considered stable.

profile.overview: The Rufous-browed Tyrannulet is a small, active tyrant flycatcher of humid mountain forests in Central and northern South America. It is recognized by its olive-green upperparts, pale underparts, and distinctive rufous or rusty eyebrow. The species often remains high in the forest canopy, where it makes short flights to capture insects from leaves and twigs. Its distribution is patchy, and it can be difficult to detect despite its lively calls and restless behavior.
profile.classification: The Rufous-browed Tyrannulet belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Phylloscartes. It is divided into several geographically separated populations or subspecies across Central and South America.
profile.identification: This small tyrannulet has olive-green upperparts, a yellowish to pale underside, and a strongly contrasting rusty-rufous eyebrow extending behind the eye. The wings show contrasting darker flight feathers and pale edging, while the bill is short and slender. It is usually seen moving quickly through foliage, often perched horizontally with the tail slightly raised. Its high, lively song and sharp calls can be more useful for detection than its unobtrusive appearance.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species has a disjunct range from Costa Rica and western Panama south through parts of Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, and northern Peru. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly on the Caribbean slope, from the Cordillera de Guanacaste eastward through the Cordillera Central, generally in humid montane evergreen forest at roughly 600–1,200 meters, with some populations or records reaching higher elevations. It uses mature forest, forest edges, and sometimes adjacent wooded habitats with dense foliage.
profile.migrationStatus: The Rufous-browed Tyrannulet is considered a year-round resident rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, it remains in suitable humid mountain forests throughout the year, although local movements may occur in response to food availability or weather.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited. In Costa Rica, breeding is thought to occur mainly from March through May or June. The species is believed to nest in forest vegetation, but details about nest construction, clutch size, incubation, and care of young remain poorly documented. Its breeding season coincides with the beginning and middle of Costa Rica’s wetter period, when insect food is generally abundant in montane forests.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet is thought to consist mainly of insects and other small arthropods, with small fruits possibly taken occasionally. It forages actively in the canopy and sometimes at lower levels, making short sallies to hover-glean prey from leaves and twigs. Individuals may forage alone, in pairs, or in small family groups, and they often join mixed-species feeding flocks.
profile.behavior: The Rufous-browed Tyrannulet is energetic and quick-moving. It frequently shifts between exposed perches and leafy branches, raising or cocking its tail and making brief flights to inspect nearby foliage. It regularly participates in mixed-species flocks, which may help it locate food or detect predators. The species is more often heard than seen in dense forest, giving high, sharp, lively calls and a rapidly delivered song.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is believed to be decreasing, although the rate of decline is not well quantified.
conservation.threats: The principal potential threat is loss and fragmentation of humid montane forest, especially through agricultural expansion, logging, and other changes to forest structure. Its patchy distribution and dependence on mature, humid woodland may make local populations vulnerable when suitable habitat is isolated.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore humid montane forest, maintain connected forest corridors, and reduce clearing and degradation along mountain slopes. In Costa Rica, supporting protected areas and responsible management of forested watersheds can help preserve the species’ habitat. Careful bird monitoring is also valuable because the species is local and inconspicuous, and its population status is not well known.

profile.overview: The Black-capped Pygmy-Tyrant (Myiornis atricapillus) is a very small tyrant flycatcher of humid tropical forests from Costa Rica south through Panama and western Colombia to northwestern Ecuador. It is among the smallest passerines in the region. Despite its tiny size, it is an active insect hunter that often moves through shaded vegetation and forest edges. Its short tail, dark cap, compact shape, and quick movements are useful clues for identification.
profile.classification: The species belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Myiornis. It is sometimes discussed with the closely related Short-tailed Pygmy-Tyrant in a superspecies group.
profile.identification: This tiny, compact flycatcher has a very short tail, a relatively large head, and a short, broad bill. The upperparts are generally olive-green, while the crown is blackish, forming the prominent black cap that gives the species its name. The underparts are pale, often with a whitish throat and breast and yellowish tones toward the belly. It is easily overlooked because of its small size, rapid movements, and preference for dense vegetation.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Black-capped Pygmy-Tyrant ranges from the Caribbean slope of Costa Rica through Panama, western Colombia, and northwestern Ecuador. In Costa Rica it is a resident of humid lowland and foothill forest, especially on the Caribbean slope, and it may occur in mature forest, second growth, forest edges, gaps, and dense understory. It is generally associated with warm tropical habitats at low elevations, although local records may extend into foothill zones.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered resident rather than migratory. In Costa Rica, individuals are present year-round, particularly in humid Caribbean lowland and foothill forests; seasonal movements are not known to be a regular feature of the species.
profile.breeding: Reliable public information on the species' breeding biology is limited. Like other small tyrant flycatchers, it is expected to defend a breeding territory and feed nestlings largely on arthropods. Breeding activity has been reported within its tropical range, including Costa Rica, but detailed information on nest structure, clutch size, incubation, and parental care is not sufficiently consistent in accessible sources to summarize confidently.
profile.dietFeeding: The Black-capped Pygmy-Tyrant feeds mainly on small insects and other arthropods. It forages actively in shaded forest vegetation, often making short sallies from low perches to pick prey from leaves or capture it in the air. Its tiny size and quick, deliberate movements allow it to search dense foliage that is difficult for larger flycatchers to exploit.
profile.behavior: This species is usually encountered singly or in pairs and can be difficult to locate in thick vegetation. It often makes short, rapid movements between perches and may respond to nearby calls or the activity of mixed-species feeding groups. Its very short tail, compact posture, and habit of remaining within shaded understory vegetation distinguish it from many larger tyrant flycatchers.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not reliably quantified in the accessible assessment information, but the species is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Scale-crested Pygmy-Tyrant (Lophotriccus pileatus) is a tiny, active tyrant flycatcher of humid forests in Central and northern South America. It is named for the short, scale-like crown feathers that can form a small crest when the bird is alert. Despite its size, it often draws attention with sharp calls and energetic movements. In Costa Rica, it is a resident of forested foothills and lower mountain regions, where it may be easier to hear than see.
profile.classification: The species belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the small group of pygmy-tyrants in the genus Lophotriccus. Several geographic forms are recognized across its broad, discontinuous range.
profile.identification: This very small flycatcher has olive-green upperparts, a short tail, and pale underparts marked with fine dusky streaking on the throat and breast. Its most distinctive feature is the crown, where elongated dark feathers have pale or rufous edges and create a scaled appearance. The bill is short and broad, and the bird often flicks through dense vegetation. In Costa Rica, it can be confused with other tiny forest flycatchers, so its crown pattern, streaked underparts, calls, and habitat are useful clues.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Scale-crested Pygmy-Tyrant occurs from southeastern Honduras and Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama, with additional populations in Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it is found on both slopes, especially in humid foothills and lower montane zones; it occurs along much of the Caribbean slope and on the Pacific slope from the central region southward. It uses humid to wet evergreen forest, cloud forest, mature secondary growth, forest edges, and natural gaps, generally from low elevations into the foothills.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and across most or all of its range. It is not regarded as a regular long-distance migrant, although local movements may occur in response to conditions or elevation.
profile.breeding: The breeding season is not fully defined, and specific timing for Costa Rica remains poorly documented; nesting activity elsewhere in the range includes March through June. The nest is a domed, hanging bag with a side entrance protected by a small awning. It is woven from plant fibers, often with loose material dangling below, and suspended from a twig several meters above the ground. The clutch is two eggs, and the female is thought to perform the incubation; incubation and fledging periods are not well known.
profile.dietFeeding: It feeds mainly on small insects and other arthropods captured from foliage. The bird usually forages in dense understory and lower to middle vegetation, moving actively among leaves and twigs and making short flights to seize prey. It may search forest edges, vine tangles, gaps, and secondary growth as well as mature forest. Its small size and unobtrusive feeding style can make it difficult to locate even when it is calling nearby.
profile.behavior: Scale-crested Pygmy-Tyrants are active, alert birds that often remain within dense vegetation. They commonly forage singly or in pairs and may join mixed-species feeding flocks with other small insect-eating birds. The crown feathers can be raised during excitement, territorial interactions, or alarm. Their sharp, repeated calls are often the best way to detect them. In Costa Rica, observers frequently hear the species before obtaining a clear view in shaded foothill forest.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not well quantified, but the species remains widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Northern Bentbill (Oncostoma cinereigulare) is a small, compact tyrant flycatcher of humid tropical forests and dense second growth. It is named for its distinctive short bill, which curves slightly downward. The species occurs from southern Mexico through Central America to western Panama, including Costa Rica. It usually stays within thick vegetation, where its subdued gray-green plumage and quiet movements can make it difficult to detect except when it gives its rapid, trilling calls.
profile.classification: The Northern Bentbill belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Oncostoma. It is closely related to the Southern Bentbill (Oncostoma olivaceum).
profile.identification: This is a small, short-tailed flycatcher with a compact body and a noticeably broad, slightly hooked bill. The upperparts are generally olive-green to grayish olive, while the head and throat appear dull gray. The underparts are paler, often with a yellowish or olive wash, and the wings and tail are darker. Its short upward sallies from low perches, dense-vegetation habitat, and distinctive bent bill help separate it from other small Costa Rican flycatchers.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Northern Bentbill ranges from southern Veracruz and Oaxaca in Mexico through Belize and Central America to western Panama. In Costa Rica it is a resident on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes, occurring commonly in much of the country but less commonly on the Pacific side of northern Costa Rica. It inhabits humid lowland evergreen forest, semi-deciduous and deciduous forest, forest edges, secondary woodland, scrub, and other dense thickets, generally from sea level to about 1,100 meters in Costa Rica.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident and nonmigratory in Costa Rica; it is present throughout the year rather than occurring there only as a seasonal migrant.
profile.breeding: The breeding season is not fully defined, but breeding activity appears to include April in Costa Rica. The female builds an elongated, domed nest of plant fibers with a side entrance, sometimes with loose fibers hanging below it. The nest is suspended from a twig or leaf, usually from near ground level to about four meters high. Clutches contain two eggs. The female apparently incubates the eggs and provides most or all food for the nestlings.
profile.dietFeeding: The Northern Bentbill feeds mainly on arthropods, including insects and other small invertebrates, and sometimes takes small berries. It usually forages alone or in pairs in dense vegetation, especially in the understory and lower forest levels, although it may search as high as about six meters. From a concealed perch, it makes short upward flights to seize prey from leaves before moving to another perch.
profile.behavior: This species is generally unobtrusive and spends much of its time moving through tangled vegetation. It commonly forages alone or in pairs and is not known to regularly join mixed-species feeding flocks. Its typical feeding maneuver is a brief upward sally from a perch, followed by a return or movement to a new perch. Calls include rapid, harsh or toad-like trills and shorter sharp notes, which may reveal birds that are otherwise difficult to see.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although it remains relatively large and the species is common in much of its range, including much of Costa Rica.

profile.overview: The Slate-headed Tody-Flycatcher is a tiny, compact tyrant flycatcher of tropical lowlands and foothills. It is usually found in dense vegetation along forest edges, secondary growth, scrub, clearings, and gallery forest. The species often remains inconspicuous among leaves, where it makes short flights to capture small arthropods. Its broad distribution is divided between Middle America and northern South America, with Costa Rica forming part of its resident Central American range.
profile.classification: The Slate-headed Tody-Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Poecilotriccus. Its scientific name is Poecilotriccus sylvia.
profile.identification: This is a very small, short-tailed flycatcher with a relatively large head and a broad, flattened bill. The head and upperparts are mainly slate-gray to olive-gray, while the underparts are generally pale yellowish or buff, with a lighter throat. It can be difficult to see because it moves through dense foliage near the ground. In Costa Rica, its subdued colors and compact shape help separate it from brighter or more boldly marked tody-flycatchers.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species has a disjunct range. In Middle America it occurs from southern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama; separate populations occur in northern South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident, occurring on both slopes but reported especially from the Pacific slope from the Gulf of Nicoya southward, with additional records in Caribbean lowlands and foothills. It uses tropical evergreen and deciduous forest edges, gallery forest, secondary forest, scrub, overgrown clearings, and open woodland, generally from sea level to about 1,000 meters.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, individuals are expected to remain within the country throughout the year, although local movements may follow food availability or breeding conditions.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is incomplete and varies geographically. The breeding season overall appears to extend mainly from January through August, but the timing in Costa Rica is not precisely defined. The nest is a pear-shaped structure with a side entrance, made from moss, grasses, and other plant fibers. It is usually suspended from the tip of a branch, often with some overhead cover, and generally placed within about three meters of the ground. A typical clutch contains two creamy white eggs marked with brown spots.
profile.dietFeeding: The Slate-headed Tody-Flycatcher feeds mainly on small arthropods, including insects and other invertebrates, and may also take some fruit. It usually searches dense vegetation near the ground, picking prey from leaves and twigs or making short sallies from a perch. It sometimes forages higher in the vegetation, including the forest canopy, but most feeding activity occurs in shaded, leafy cover.
profile.behavior: This species is generally quiet and inconspicuous, although its short calls can help reveal its presence. It commonly forages in pairs and only rarely joins mixed-species feeding flocks. The bird makes short, deliberate movements through dense foliage and may show brief tail movements while feeding. Because it often stays inside vegetation rather than perching in the open, careful observation and attention to calls are useful for detecting it in Costa Rica.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly quantified, but the species is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Common Tody-Flycatcher (Todirostrum cinereum) is a small, active tyrant flycatcher of tropical America. It is usually found in open woodland, forest edges, second-growth vegetation, gardens, plantations, and other lightly wooded habitats rather than deep forest. The species often moves rapidly through low vegetation while searching for insects and is recognized by its broad bill, bold head pattern, olive upperparts, yellow underparts, and lively behavior. In Costa Rica, it is a widespread resident and a familiar bird in suitable lowland habitats.
profile.classification: The Common Tody-Flycatcher belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family Tyrannidae and the genus Todirostrum. Several geographic subspecies are recognized across its large range from southern Mexico through Central and South America.
profile.identification: This is a tiny flycatcher with a relatively broad, flattened bill, a dark crown, pale or whitish lores, and a noticeable pale eye-ring or facial markings. The back is olive-green, while the throat and breast are pale to yellowish and the belly is usually brighter yellow. The wings show pale bars or edging, and the tail is dark. It frequently flicks its wings and tail while moving through shrubs. Its small size, bold face, and broad bill help separate it from many other Costa Rican flycatchers.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southern Mexico through Central America and widely across northern and central South America. In Costa Rica it is a widespread resident, occurring on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes and in much of the central and eastern lowlands; it is generally common, although it is less frequent in the far northwest. It favors forest edges, secondary growth, scrub, mangroves, river margins, plantations, orchards, pastures with scattered trees, and gardens. It usually avoids extensive, closed-canopy forest and occurs mainly from sea level into the lower elevations.
profile.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Common Tody-Flycatcher is considered a permanent resident rather than a regular long-distance migrant. Local movements may occur in response to breeding, food availability, or habitat conditions, but seasonal migration is not a prominent feature of its ecology.
profile.breeding: Breeding information from Costa Rica indicates that nesting activity can begin around July and August, although timing may vary by region and rainfall. The hanging nest is a small, cone-shaped or basket-like structure made from plant fibers, fine roots, dried leaves, and spiderwebs. It is commonly attached to a slender branch a few meters above the ground, with a side entrance. The female generally lays two eggs, and both adults incubate and feed the young. Nestlings receive small arthropods, including caterpillars, flies, butterflies, and crickets.
profile.dietFeeding: The Common Tody-Flycatcher feeds mainly on small arthropods, especially insects such as flies, caterpillars, small moths, butterflies, and crickets. It searches actively through shrubs, vines, and low tree foliage, often making short flights to seize prey from leaves or twigs. It may hover briefly while gleaning and commonly returns to nearby perches. Adults carry similar prey to nestlings during the breeding season.
profile.behavior: This species is energetic, conspicuous, and often easier to detect by its repeated calls and constant movement than by a prolonged view. It usually forages alone, in pairs, or in family groups in the lower and middle levels of vegetation. Wing-flicking and tail movements are frequent. It may join mixed-species foraging groups but also defends a small territory during breeding. Its hanging nest and preference for edge habitats make it well adapted to human-modified landscapes.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable, although local numbers may vary with land-use change and habitat quality.

profile.overview: The Black-headed Tody-Flycatcher (Todirostrum nigriceps) is a small Neotropical tyrant flycatcher associated mainly with humid lowland forest. It has a striking dark head, pale throat, yellowish underparts, and contrasting wing markings. The species searches actively for small arthropods in leafy vegetation, often in the canopy or along forest edges. Its range extends from Costa Rica and Panama south through parts of Colombia, Venezuela, and western Ecuador.
profile.classification: The Black-headed Tody-Flycatcher belongs to the order Passeriformes and family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers. Its scientific name is Todirostrum nigriceps.
profile.identification: This small, active flycatcher has a glossy black or very dark head, a white throat, olive-gray upperparts, and pale yellow to yellowish underparts. The wings show yellowish or olive-edged markings, while the bill is short and relatively broad. It often flicks through foliage with quick movements and may be detected first by its high, thin single-note calls. Care is needed to separate it from other small Todirostrum flycatchers.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Costa Rica and Panama through northern and eastern Colombia, northwestern Venezuela, and western Ecuador. In Costa Rica it is primarily a resident of the Caribbean lowlands, locally reaching about 700 meters and occasionally occurring higher, to roughly 1,500 meters. It is uncommon or local on the Pacific side, where it mainly reaches the drainage through low passes in the Cordillera de Guanacaste. It uses very humid lowland forest, forest edges, tall second growth, shaded cacao, and partly open areas with mature trees.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout its range; it is not considered a regular long-distance migrant. Its local movements may reflect food availability or elevation.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited, but in Costa Rica nesting has been reported mainly from March to May. The nest is a short, pear-shaped, pendulous pouch made from pale plant fibers and plant down, with a side entrance protected by a small overhanging visor. It is usually attached 6–15 meters above the ground on a tree at a forest edge or in a partly open site. Nests may be placed near wasp nests, and both adults are believed to participate in construction and parental care.
profile.dietFeeding: The Black-headed Tody-Flycatcher feeds mainly on small insects and other arthropods. It forages actively among leaves and fine branches, especially in the upper and middle levels of humid forest and at edges. Rather than making long aerial sallies, it typically gleans or makes short advances within vegetation, pausing frequently as it searches. Its small size and quick movements allow it to exploit insects in narrow foliage and shaded forest structure.
profile.behavior: It is usually seen alone or in pairs and is an alert, fast-moving bird. Individuals frequently hop or flit through dense foliage, using short calls to maintain contact or advertise. The species can be difficult to observe because it remains among leaves and often moves suddenly from branch to branch. In Costa Rica it may be encountered in forest edges, gardens adjoining mature woodland, shaded farms, and other habitats retaining tall trees.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend has not been quantified reliably.

profile.overview: The Eye-ringed Flatbill is a stocky, broad-billed tyrant flycatcher of humid forests in Mexico, Central America, and northwestern South America. It is named for its conspicuous pale eye-ring, which contrasts with its olive-green plumage and subdued facial pattern. The species is usually quiet and unobtrusive, spending much of its time in shaded understory and lower-canopy vegetation. In Costa Rica, it is a resident forest bird found in suitable habitats across several regions, although it is not generally common.
profile.classification: The Eye-ringed Flatbill belongs to the order Passeriformes and the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae. Its scientific name is Rhynchocyclus brevirostris. Three subspecies are generally recognized.
profile.identification: This flycatcher has a broad, flattened bill, olive-green upperparts, and somewhat paler yellowish or olive underparts. The bold whitish eye-ring is its most useful field mark. The head and cheeks are grayish or dusky, and the wings may show inconspicuous pale edging or bars. It often sits upright and quietly on a shaded perch. Its appearance can be difficult to assess in dim forest light, but the combination of a wide bill, strong eye-ring, and sluggish behavior is distinctive.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Central America to Panama and extreme northwestern Colombia. In Costa Rica, it occurs on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes, including humid lowland forest, foothill forest, cloud forest, forest edges, ravines, and nearby secondary growth. It is usually associated with shady, structurally complex vegetation from the understory to the middle levels of the forest, and may occur from near sea level to roughly 2,100 meters, depending on region.
profile.migrationStatus: Mostly resident. In Costa Rica, the Eye-ringed Flatbill is considered a year-round resident rather than a regular long-distance migrant, although local or elevational movements may occur.
profile.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported mainly from March through June. The nest is a bulky, pear-shaped structure made from rootlets, plant fibers, and dead leaves, with a tubular entrance that slopes downward from the attachment point. It is usually suspended from a twig or vine, often above an open space or small stream. Clutches generally contain two eggs. Adults may also use the nest as a roost outside the breeding period.
profile.dietFeeding: The Eye-ringed Flatbill feeds mainly on insects and other arthropods, including beetles, caterpillars, and similar forest invertebrates. It also takes some berries and seeds. It commonly watches from a shaded perch and makes short upward or outward sallies to snatch prey from leaves and twigs, sometimes hovering briefly while gleaning. In Costa Rica, it has been observed attending army-ant swarms, where it captures arthropods disturbed by the ants.
profile.behavior: This species is generally secretive, slow-moving, and difficult to locate except by its thin, buzzy calls. It often forages alone, in pairs, or with mixed-species feeding flocks in the shaded understory and lower canopy. After making a short feeding flight, it usually returns to another perch rather than remaining in the air. Its unobtrusive behavior and preference for dense vegetation mean that it is often detected by sound before it is seen.

conservation.populationTrend: Probably decreasing overall, although the species remains widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Yellow-olive Flatbill is a small, rather inconspicuous tyrant flycatcher of the American tropics. It has olive-green upperparts, a grayish head, pale yellow underparts, a broad two-toned bill, and a narrow whitish eye-ring. Usually found singly or in pairs, it searches foliage from low and middle-level perches and gives thin, insect-like calls. In Costa Rica it is a common resident of suitable lowland and foothill woodland, including both humid and seasonally dry areas.
profile.classification: The Yellow-olive Flatbill belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, in the order Passeriformes. Its scientific name is Tolmomyias sulphurescens, and several geographic subspecies are recognized across its extensive Neotropical range.
profile.identification: This flatbill is predominantly olive above with a gray or olive-gray crown and face, a pale whitish eye-ring and supraloral line, and pale yellow underparts. Its broad bill is dark on the upper mandible and paler below. Yellowish edges on the wing feathers may be visible but do not form strong wingbars. In Costa Rica, the pale eye and spectacles, broad bill, and soft yellow belly help separate it from similar flatbills and other small flycatchers.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern, western, and eastern South America. In Costa Rica it is a widespread resident and is described as common in appropriate habitats, occurring on both slopes and in many regions, including the Pacific lowlands, Caribbean lowlands, foothills, and some interior valleys. It uses tropical evergreen and deciduous forest, woodland, gallery forest, forest edges, second growth, plantations, and other semi-open wooded habitats, generally from lowlands to roughly 1,000 to 1,650 meters.
profile.migrationStatus: The Yellow-olive Flatbill is regarded as a year-round resident rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica it occurs throughout the year; local movements may follow food availability or seasonal conditions, but regular passage or winter migration is not expected.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is incomplete, but Costa Rican records indicate nesting mainly from April through June, during the early rainy season. The nest is a hanging, pear-shaped or retort-like structure with a tubular entrance, built from plant fibers, grasses, rootlets, bark, fungal rhizomorphs, and spider web. It may be suspended from a branch or vine near a forest edge, roadside, or stream, sometimes close to a wasp nest. Clutches generally contain two or three eggs.
profile.dietFeeding: The Yellow-olive Flatbill feeds mainly on insects and other small arthropods, with some small berries or fruits also taken. It usually forages from the understory to middle levels and occasionally higher in the canopy. From a deliberate perch, it gleans prey from leaves and twigs, makes short outward or upward sallies, and may hover briefly while picking prey from vegetation. Individuals commonly forage alone or in pairs.
profile.behavior: This species is generally quiet and unobtrusive, spending much of its time inside foliage and often being detected by its thin, high-pitched, insect-like call. It tends to perch calmly while inspecting nearby leaves and branches, then moves to another perch after a short feeding sally. It may join mixed-species feeding flocks, especially in wooded habitats, but is also frequently encountered alone or in pairs. Adults may use the breeding nest as a roost outside the nesting period.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered large, with at least several million mature individuals, but is believed to be decreasing.

profile.overview: The Yellow-winged Flatbill (Tolmomyias flavotectus) is a small tyrant flycatcher of humid forests in southern Central America and northwestern South America. It was formerly treated as part of the Yellow-margined Flatbill complex, but is now recognized as a separate species. Its broad, flattened bill, olive upperparts, grayish head, pale eye-ring, and conspicuous yellow edging on the wings are useful identification features. It usually stays within forest vegetation and is more often detected by its sharp, emphatic vocalizations than by prolonged views.
profile.classification: The Yellow-winged Flatbill belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Tolmomyias. Its scientific name is Tolmomyias flavotectus; it was formerly treated as a subspecies of Tolmomyias assimilis.
profile.identification: This flatbill is about 13 cm long and has a large, broad bill typical of the genus. Adults have a dark grayish head, a distinct pale eye-ring, olive-green back and tail, and dusky wings with broad yellow margins that create the characteristic yellow-winged appearance. The throat and breast are pale gray with a yellowish wash, while the belly and undertail coverts are more clearly yellow. The bill is dark above and paler below, and the legs are gray.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama to western Colombia and northwestern Ecuador, west of the Andes. In Costa Rica it is a resident species occurring on both slopes, especially in humid lowland and foothill forest; it reaches roughly 600 m in northern Costa Rica and about 1,000 m farther south. It uses the interior and edges of wet forest, taller second growth, mature secondary vegetation, swamp forest in parts of its range, and some plantations.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout its range; it is not considered a long-distance migrant. Local movements may occur, but reliable evidence for regular seasonal migration is lacking.
profile.breeding: The breeding season is incompletely known but appears to include at least April through June. The nest is a pear-shaped hanging bag made from fine plant fibers and fungal rhizomorphs, with a tunnel-like entrance that slopes upward toward the lower part of the structure. Nests are suspended from the tip of a branch or vine, commonly several meters above the ground, and may be placed near a wasp nest. Clutch size, incubation, and fledging periods are poorly documented.
profile.dietFeeding: The Yellow-winged Flatbill feeds mainly on insects and other small invertebrates, with little fruit thought to be taken. It generally forages alone or in pairs and often joins mixed-species feeding flocks. Most feeding occurs in the middle levels of the forest and toward the canopy, although birds may work lower vegetation along forest edges. Its broad bill is suited to short sallies and gleaning prey from leaves and small branches.
profile.behavior: This species is generally unobtrusive and spends much of its time among dense foliage in the forest mid-story and canopy. It frequently participates in mixed-species flocks and may be easier to locate by voice than by sight. The song is a forceful series of short, harsh notes, often delivered from a concealed perch. Singing is reported mainly during the morning and late afternoon. Birds usually occur singly or in pairs outside flocking activity.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population size has not been quantified. It is believed to be decreasing, but the species remains fairly common in parts of its range, including Costa Rica, and occurs in protected areas.

profile.overview: The Yellow-bellied Tyrannulet (Ornithion semiflavum) is a very small forest flycatcher of the American tropics. It is named for its yellow underparts and belongs to a group of active insect-eating tyrant flycatchers. The species usually forages high in vegetation, where its small size, subdued upperparts, and quick movements can make it difficult to detect. In Costa Rica, it is a local bird of humid forest, especially in the Caribbean lowlands and adjacent foothills.
profile.classification: The Yellow-bellied Tyrannulet is a member of the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Ornithion. It is closely associated with other small Neotropical tyrannulets.
profile.identification: This is a tiny, short-tailed flycatcher with olive-green to grayish upperparts, a yellow throat and underparts, and a small, slender bill. The yellow is generally strongest below the throat and on the belly, while the head may appear relatively plain. It often keeps to the upper and middle levels of trees, moving rapidly between perches. Identification is helped by its small size, yellow underside, forest habitat, and high, thin calls.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Yellow-bellied Tyrannulet occurs from southern Mexico through Central America and into northern South America. In Costa Rica, it is a resident rather than a regular long-distance migrant, and records are associated mainly with the humid Caribbean slope, lowland evergreen forest, and foothill forests. It uses mature wet forest, forest edges, clearings with scattered trees, and sometimes shaded second growth. The species generally forages in the canopy or subcanopy, where dense foliage provides both food and cover.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered generally resident in Costa Rica. Local movements may occur with weather, food availability, or seasonal conditions, but there is no well-established regular migration pattern for the Costa Rican population.
profile.breeding: The breeding biology of the Yellow-bellied Tyrannulet is not as well documented as that of many larger tyrant flycatchers. Like related tyrannulets, it is thought to form a pair during breeding and to place its nest in a concealed position in vegetation, often in the forest canopy or subcanopy. Breeding activity in Central America is associated with the local wet-season cycle, but detailed information on nest structure, clutch size, incubation, and parental care remains limited.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of small arthropods, especially insects gathered from leaves, twigs, and other surfaces in the canopy and subcanopy. It usually hunts from short perches, making quick flights to pick prey from foliage before returning to a nearby perch. The species may join mixed-species foraging flocks, which can help it locate prey and may make this otherwise inconspicuous bird easier to find.
profile.behavior: The Yellow-bellied Tyrannulet is active, alert, and usually encountered singly, in pairs, or in small mixed-species flocks. It moves quickly through leafy branches and often remains high above the ground. Its small size and unobtrusive plumage make visual detection challenging, while its sharp, high-pitched calls can be more useful for locating it. It is primarily an arboreal species and rarely spends time on the forest floor.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is not considered to face a level of decline that currently qualifies the species for a threatened category. Local populations may be affected by habitat loss, but the global trend is not sufficiently severe for a higher-risk assessment.

profile.overview: The Brown-capped Tyrannulet (Ornithion brunneicapillus) is a very small insect-eating flycatcher of humid forests in Middle America. It is usually encountered high in the canopy, where its olive-green body, brown crown, pale throat, and yellowish underparts can be difficult to see among foliage. Like other tyrannulets, it makes short sallies to capture insects and often moves quietly through forest vegetation, sometimes joining mixed-species feeding flocks.
profile.classification: The Brown-capped Tyrannulet belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the subfamily Elaeniinae. It is the only widely recognized species in the genus Ornithion.
profile.identification: This tiny tyrannulet has olive-green upperparts and a distinctive brown or brownish-gray crown. The throat and upper breast are pale, while the lower underparts are generally yellowish, with some regional variation. It has a small, fairly pointed bill, a short tail, and often shows pale wingbars or edging on the wing coverts. Its quiet movements in dense foliage and preference for high forest levels can make it easy to overlook. Vocalizations are useful for detection.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Brown-capped Tyrannulet occurs from southern Mexico through Central America to Panama. In Costa Rica it is a resident of humid, mainly montane and premontane forest, including forest edges, woodland clearings, and mature second growth where suitable canopy remains. It is most often associated with moist evergreen forest and may occur on both Caribbean- and Pacific-slope mountains. It typically forages in the middle and upper canopy, rather than on the ground or in open agricultural habitats.
profile.migrationStatus: Generally resident in Costa Rica and across its range. It is not known for regular long-distance migration, although local movements may occur with changes in food availability, weather, or elevation.
profile.breeding: Reliable, widely applicable details about the Brown-capped Tyrannulet's nesting biology are limited. As a forest-dwelling tyrant flycatcher, it is believed to breed within its resident range, including Costa Rica, during the local rainy-season period when insects are abundant. The species likely places a small nest in vegetation, but nest placement, clutch size, incubation, and parental roles are not sufficiently documented here to describe confidently.
profile.dietFeeding: The Brown-capped Tyrannulet feeds mainly on small arthropods, especially insects collected from leaves, twigs, and other surfaces in the canopy. It commonly forages by making short flights from a perch to snatch prey from foliage or the air, then returning to a nearby branch. It may also take small fruits occasionally, as do several related tyrannulets, but insects are considered its principal food.
profile.behavior: This species is usually active but inconspicuous, moving through leafy branches with quick hops and short flights. It often remains high in the forest and may associate with mixed-species flocks, which can improve its chances of finding prey and detecting predators. The Brown-capped Tyrannulet is generally encountered singly or in pairs. Its small size, subdued plumage, and canopy habits mean that observers often hear it before seeing it.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population trend is not well documented, but the species is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Northern Beardless-Tyrannulet is a small, active flycatcher of the tyrant flycatcher family. It has a subtle gray-green appearance, a small crest, and very short or nearly absent rictal bristles around the bill. The species ranges from the southwestern United States through Mexico and Central America to northwestern Costa Rica. It often lives in open woodland, scrub, forest edges, and gardens, where it searches among foliage for insects and occasionally takes fruit.
profile.classification: The Northern Beardless-Tyrannulet belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the largest family of flycatchers, and the genus Camptostoma. It is closely related to the Southern Beardless-Tyrannulet, Camptostoma obsoletum, which occurs south of the Northern Beardless-Tyrannulet’s range.
profile.identification: This small tyrannulet has a grayish-green back, dusky wings with two pale wing-bars, a brownish head, a faint pale eyebrow, and a slightly raised crest. The underparts are pale gray on the throat and breast, becoming yellowish on the belly. Its bill is short and dark, and the tail is frequently flicked. It is generally duller and less strongly marked than the similar Southern Beardless-Tyrannulet. A distinctive loud, plaintive whistle can help locate it.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southeastern Arizona, southern New Mexico, and southern Texas south through Mexico and Central America to northwestern Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is associated mainly with the dry northwestern Pacific lowlands and nearby foothills, where it reaches the southern edge of its range and may overlap with the Southern Beardless-Tyrannulet. It uses open riparian woodland, dry forest, thorn scrub, brushy thickets, forest edges, semiopen countryside, and gardens with mature trees, generally at low to moderate elevations.
profile.migrationStatus: It is largely resident in Costa Rica, where it occurs within the species’ southern breeding range, although some northern populations are partial migrants and may move southward in winter. Seasonal movements within Central America are poorly documented.
profile.breeding: Breeding extends southward through Central America and includes northern and northwestern Costa Rica. The nest is a compact, rounded or domed structure with a side entrance, usually placed in an outer tree branch or large shrub and sometimes concealed among vegetation such as mistletoe or an old caterpillar web. It is built from grasses, plant fibers, leaves, seed pods, and soft lining materials. Clutches commonly contain two pale eggs marked with reddish or lilac blotches.
profile.dietFeeding: The Northern Beardless-Tyrannulet feeds mainly on small insects and other arthropods, including beetles, flies, caterpillars, and spiders. It forages actively through the outer foliage of trees and shrubs, often moving in a warbler- or vireo-like manner while making short sallies to capture prey. It also eats some berries, seeds, and other small fruits, especially when insect prey is less available.
profile.behavior: This is an energetic, alert bird that usually forages alone or in pairs in low trees and shrubs. It frequently flicks its tail and raises its small crest when excited, alarmed, or defending a territory. Males give a clear, whistled song during the breeding season. Both parents defend the nest and young, sometimes approaching or scolding potential predators closely. The species can be inconspicuous despite its sharp voice and constant movement.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not known to have a quantified decline. It remains fairly common across much of its range, although local abundance varies and monitoring is limited, particularly in Central America and Costa Rica.

profile.overview: The Southern Beardless-Tyrannulet is a small, active tyrant flycatcher of the American tropics. It occupies a broad range from Costa Rica and Panama south through much of South America, including Trinidad. Unlike many forest-dependent flycatchers, it often uses scrub, woodland edges, second growth, gallery forest, plantations, parks, and gardens. Its restless movements, raised crest, distinctive calls, and habit of searching foliage for insects make it easier to detect than its subdued plumage might suggest.
profile.classification: The Southern Beardless-Tyrannulet belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the subfamily Elaeniinae. It is one of two closely related species in the genus Camptostoma; the other is the Northern Beardless-Tyrannulet, Camptostoma imberbe.
profile.identification: This small tyrannulet is about 10–11 cm long, with olive-gray to gray-brown upperparts and paler underparts. The throat and breast are whitish or pale gray, while the belly is often washed yellow, especially in some populations. Two pale wing-bars, pale feather edging, a dark eye line, and a short, broad bill are useful field marks. The crown can look slightly peaked, particularly when the bird is excited or calling. Sexes are generally alike.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from Costa Rica and Panama across most of northern, western, central, and eastern South America, reaching Argentina, Uruguay, and southern Brazil. In Costa Rica it is a resident of the Pacific slope, especially southwestern areas, extending north toward the Tempisque Valley; it is not normally a widespread Caribbean-slope bird. It uses secondary forest, gallery forest, riparian thickets, dry woodland, scrub, forest edges, open country with scattered trees, plantations, parks, and gardens, generally from lowlands to about 1,200 m.
profile.migrationStatus: Southern Beardless-Tyrannulets in Costa Rica are resident rather than regular long-distance migrants. Individuals may make local movements in response to food, rainfall, or habitat conditions, but the Costa Rican population remains in the country year-round. The species is also resident across most of its South American range, although some regional or elevational movements occur.
profile.breeding: In Central America, breeding is generally reported during the dry-to-early-rainy-season period, with records in Costa Rica concentrated approximately from December through March, though timing can vary locally. The female builds a bulky, enclosed or globular nest with a side entrance, using plant fibers, grasses, bark, spider web, and other soft materials. Nests may be well concealed in shrubs or trees at variable heights. The usual clutch is two eggs, and both parents feed the nestlings.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects and other small arthropods, including beetles, flies, caterpillars, spiders, and similar prey. It usually forages actively through foliage in the lower and middle levels of trees and shrubs, picking prey from leaves and twigs. It also makes short sallies to capture flying insects and may take small fruits or berries, particularly when arthropod food is less available.
profile.behavior: This is a restless, conspicuous little flycatcher that often moves in pairs or small groups, sometimes joining mixed-species feeding flocks. It frequently flicks through foliage, pauses briefly on exposed twigs, and raises its crest while calling or investigating disturbances. Its calls are high, clear whistles and descending notes, and birds may respond strongly to imitations or recordings. It commonly occupies open, lightly wooded habitats and tolerates moderate human disturbance.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable.

profile.overview: The Cocos Tyrannulet (Nesotriccus ridgwayi) is a small insect-eating songbird endemic to Cocos Island, an isolated Pacific island administered by Costa Rica. It is one of the island’s distinctive endemic land birds and is found nowhere else in the world. Formerly often called the Cocos Flycatcher, it belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family and is closely associated with the humid forest and edge habitats of Cocos Island.
profile.classification: The Cocos Tyrannulet is a passerine in the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the subfamily Elaeniinae. It is generally treated as a distinct, monotypic species in the genus Nesotriccus.
profile.identification: This is a small, rather plain tyrant flycatcher with subdued grayish, brownish, and olive tones. It has a compact body, a short tail, and a slender bill suited to catching small insects. Its appearance can be difficult to separate from other small tyrannulets without attention to its isolated island range, behavior, and voice. The species is often active in forest edges and vegetation near clearings.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Cocos Tyrannulet is endemic to Cocos Island, located in the eastern Pacific about 550 kilometers southwest of Costa Rica’s mainland. Thus, in the Costa Rican regional context, it occurs only on Costa Rica’s Cocos Island and not on the mainland or other nearby islands. It uses humid tropical forest, woodland edges, clearings, and secondary vegetation, including areas near streams and human access routes. Cocos Island remains largely forested and protected as a national park.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident and breeding endemic of Cocos Island, Costa Rica. It is not known to undertake regular seasonal migration to the Costa Rican mainland.
profile.breeding: The species breeds on Cocos Island, but its nesting biology is not well documented compared with that of many mainland tyrant flycatchers. Pairs or territorial birds may remain in suitable forest throughout the year, and vocal activity is especially noticeable in forest-edge habitats. Detailed information on nest placement, clutch size, incubation, and parental care remains limited, so these aspects should be treated as poorly known.
profile.dietFeeding: The Cocos Tyrannulet is primarily an insectivore. It likely takes small flying and surface-active insects from foliage and other vegetation, using short flights or quick movements from exposed perches. It forages in forest, along edges, and in more open vegetation, where insects are accessible. As with many small tyrant flycatchers, it may return repeatedly to favored perches while searching for prey.
profile.behavior: This active, vocal bird is commonly observed moving through vegetation and along forest edges. It makes short sallies to capture insects and may defend a small feeding or breeding territory. Observations on Cocos Island report strong vocal activity, particularly around forest edges and bays. Its behavior is generally unobtrusive, but its restricted range and endemic status make every population observation valuable.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is estimated at approximately 6,000–15,000 mature individuals and is currently considered stable, although its very small range leaves it vulnerable to rapid change.
conservation.threats: Potential threats include introduced rats and cats, which may prey on birds or nests, and introduced pigs, goats, and deer, which damage the forest understory, disturb soils, and hinder regeneration of native vegetation. Tourism-related disturbance may also affect localized habitat, although Cocos Island remains protected and largely forested.
conservation.howToHelp: Protecting Cocos Island’s native forest and maintaining effective control of introduced mammals are the most important conservation actions. Visitors should follow park rules, avoid disturbing birds and nesting areas, prevent the introduction of non-native species, and support monitoring and restoration programs for Cocos Island’s endemic wildlife.

profile.overview: The Mouse-colored Tyrannulet (Nesotriccus murinus) is a small, inconspicuous tyrant flycatcher of open tropical habitats. Its subdued grayish-brown plumage and active insect-catching behavior can make it easy to overlook among shrubs and woodland edges. The species has a broad distribution extending from Central America through much of northern and eastern South America. In Costa Rica it is a scarce or localized resident, mainly associated with the southeastern lowlands near the Panamanian border.
profile.classification: The Mouse-colored Tyrannulet belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the subfamily Elaeniinae. It is placed in the genus Nesotriccus. Some taxonomic treatments have recognized northern and southern forms separately, so names and limits may vary among field guides and checklists.
profile.identification: This is a small tyrannulet, about 10 to 11 cm long, with plain olive-gray to brown upperparts and pale grayish or whitish underparts. It has a broad but indistinct pale eyebrow, a fine pale eye ring, and relatively long wings and tail. The bill is short and narrow, typical of a small flycatcher. It can resemble other plain tyrannulets, especially the Southern Beardless-Tyrannulet, but its larger proportions, browner appearance, and characteristic calls can help separate it.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Costa Rica and Panama south through Colombia, Venezuela, the Guianas, much of Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, northern Argentina, and adjacent regions. In Costa Rica it is known mainly from the southeastern Pacific lowlands, especially around the Coto River and the Paso Canoas region near the Panamanian border, where it uses secondary vegetation, scrub, farmland with scattered trees, plantations, and forest edges. Elsewhere it occupies dry lowland scrub, tropical deciduous forest, gallery forest, and second growth, generally from lowlands to lower elevations.
profile.migrationStatus: Generally resident, with no regular long-distance migration known. In Costa Rica it is treated as a resident species, but records are localized and relatively uncommon, concentrated chiefly in the southeastern lowlands near the Panama border.
profile.breeding: Breeding information for the species is limited and varies across its extensive range. It is believed to nest in shrubs or small trees in open woodland, scrub, forest edges, and other semi-open habitats. The nest is a small cup, and both adults probably participate in territory defense and care of the young. Detailed, Costa Rica-specific information on nesting dates, nest structure, clutch size, and breeding success is not well documented.
profile.dietFeeding: The Mouse-colored Tyrannulet feeds mainly on small insects and other arthropods, with fruit possibly included at times. It usually forages actively from low to middle levels of vegetation, making short sallies from exposed perches to seize prey from the air or foliage. It favors edges, scattered trees, and shrubby growth where open spaces allow efficient aerial attacks while nearby vegetation provides cover and perches.
profile.behavior: This active but unobtrusive tyrannulet is usually encountered singly or in pairs. It moves quickly through shrubs and small trees, frequently flicking or shifting its position while searching for prey. Its calls are important for detection because its plumage is subdued and it often remains partly concealed. Like many small flycatchers, it is mainly diurnal and may defend a breeding territory during the nesting season.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not well quantified. It remains widespread, but available assessments indicate that some range and habitat measures may be declining; this has not resulted in a threatened-category listing.

profile.overview: The Yellow Tyrannulet (Capsiempis flaveola) is a very small, active tyrant flycatcher with bright yellow underparts and olive-green upperparts. It usually lives in dense, tangled vegetation rather than the interior of mature forest. The species has a broad but patchy distribution from Central America through northern and eastern South America. In Costa Rica, it is a resident of suitable lowland and foothill habitats on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes.
profile.classification: The Yellow Tyrannulet belongs to the order Passeriformes and family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers. It is the only species in the genus Capsiempis.
profile.identification: A tiny, slim flycatcher, the Yellow Tyrannulet has olive-green upperparts, a vivid yellow face and underparts, and darker wings and tail. The wings often show yellowish edging or bars, while the bill is short, narrow, and dark. It frequently flicks its wings and moves quickly through shrubs, bamboo, vines, and leafy tangles. Its combination of intense yellow plumage, small size, and preference for dense vegetation helps distinguish it from other Costa Rican tyrannulets.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southeastern Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama, with a separate, highly disjunct distribution across much of northern and eastern South America. In Costa Rica, it is found on both slopes, generally at low elevations: to about 600 meters on the Caribbean slope and about 1,200 meters on the Pacific slope. It favors humid lowland and foothill vegetation, forest clearings, streamside growth, bamboo stands, dense secondary forest, scrubby pastures, plantations, and mangroves.
profile.migrationStatus: The Yellow Tyrannulet is considered a resident species in Costa Rica. Individuals may make local movements in response to food and habitat conditions, but there is no reliable evidence that the Costa Rican population undertakes regular long-distance migration.
profile.breeding: The species breeds in dense vegetation within its tropical range, including thickets, forest edges, bamboo, and secondary growth. Like many small tyrant flycatchers, it builds a compact cup-like nest among vegetation, where it lays a small clutch. Detailed information on nesting dates and reproductive success in Costa Rica is limited, but breeding is likely associated with the local rainy season, when insect food is more abundant.
profile.dietFeeding: The Yellow Tyrannulet feeds mainly on small insects and other arthropods, including flies, beetles, and caterpillars. It forages actively in dense foliage, often making short sallies from low perches to capture prey from leaves or in the air. It commonly works through shrubs, vines, bamboo, and tangled vegetation, sometimes moving in pairs or small family groups.
profile.behavior: This species is restless and nimble, usually remaining within thick vegetation and calling frequently. It often perches briefly before moving to another branch and may flick its wings or tail while foraging. Yellow Tyrannulets are commonly encountered singly, in pairs, or in small groups. Their sharp calls can help locate them, because the birds are often difficult to see among leaves and vines.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly quantified, but the species has a broad distribution and is not currently considered globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Yellow-crowned Tyrannulet (Tyrannulus elatus) is a small, active flycatcher of humid tropical lowlands and foothills. It is recognized by its olive-green upperparts, pale underparts, dark wings, and a yellow crown patch that is often partly concealed. The species frequently searches for insects in foliage and is usually encountered singly or in pairs. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly in suitable humid forest and wooded habitats, especially in lowland regions.
profile.classification: The Yellow-crowned Tyrannulet belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae. It is the only species in the genus Tyrannulus.
profile.identification: This small tyrannulet has olive-green to grayish upperparts, pale yellowish or whitish underparts, and dark wings with lighter edging. Its most distinctive feature is the yellow crown, which may be difficult to see unless the bird raises its crown feathers. The bill is short and pointed, and the tail is relatively short. It is often identified by its rapid movements through foliage, soft calls, and habit of making short sallies after insects.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Yellow-crowned Tyrannulet occurs from Costa Rica and Panama south through much of northern and western South America, including Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, and parts of Brazil. In Costa Rica, it is a localized lowland and foothill species rather than a bird of the high mountains. It uses humid evergreen forest, forest edges, clearings with trees, plantations, gardens, and second-growth vegetation, generally where mature or scattered trees provide insect-rich foliage.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally considered resident in Costa Rica and across most of its range. Individuals may make local movements in response to food availability, but there is no well-established long-distance migration pattern.
profile.breeding: The species is believed to breed during the wet-season or locally variable breeding periods across its range. Like many small tyrant flycatchers, it builds a small cup-shaped nest, usually placed in vegetation above the ground, and both adults may participate in territorial defense and care of the young. Detailed breeding information is limited in some parts of its distribution, including Costa Rica, where nesting records are less frequently documented than observations of adults.
profile.dietFeeding: The Yellow-crowned Tyrannulet feeds mainly on small insects and other arthropods. It gleans prey from leaves and twigs and may make short flights from a perch to capture flying insects. It usually forages in the middle and upper levels of shrubs and trees, often moving actively through dense foliage. Fruit may occasionally supplement its diet, but insects appear to be its principal food.
profile.behavior: This species is an alert, active, and often inconspicuous flycatcher. It typically moves quickly through foliage, flicking its wings or tail and giving brief calls while maintaining contact with a mate or nearby individuals. It is usually seen alone or in pairs and may defend a small feeding territory. The yellow crown is frequently hidden, making patience and close observation useful for identification.

conservation.populationTrend: The species is not considered globally threatened, although its population may be affected locally by the loss and fragmentation of humid forest.

profile.overview: The Greenish Elaenia (Myiopagis viridicata) is a small, active tyrant flycatcher of tropical woodlands. It is generally olive-green above, paler below, and often shows two whitish wingbars and light edging on the wings. Despite its subdued appearance, it can be detected by its distinctive, repeated vocalizations. The species occupies a broad range from Mexico through Central America and much of South America, using forest, woodland, edges, and regenerating habitats.
profile.classification: The Greenish Elaenia belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family Tyrannidae and the elaenia genus Myiopagis. Several geographic forms are recognized across its large Neotropical range.
profile.identification: A small to medium-sized elaenia with olive-green upperparts, a grayish head, pale throat and breast, and a whitish to yellowish belly. Two pale wingbars and light feather edging are usually visible. The bill is short and fairly broad, and the head may appear slightly crested when the bird is alert. In Costa Rica, careful comparison with Yellow-bellied Elaenia and other small flycatchers is important; vocalizations are often especially useful for confirmation.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Greenish Elaenia ranges from Mexico through Central America, including Costa Rica, and extends across much of northern, western, and central South America. In Costa Rica it is a resident, occurring mainly along the Pacific slope and becoming less numerous around the Golfo Dulce region. It uses humid and dry forest, gallery forest, forest edges, mature second growth, taller scrub, and semi-open wooded areas. It is generally found from lowlands into foothills and locally to about 1,500 meters.
profile.migrationStatus: Most populations, including those in Costa Rica, are considered resident. Some southern South American populations undertake seasonal movements, but these do not represent the main pattern for Costa Rican birds.
profile.breeding: Breeding timing varies across the range. In much of Central America, including Costa Rica, breeding is generally associated with the early wet-season period, mainly from April through June. The species builds a small cup-shaped nest in vegetation, usually in a tree or shrub. Available information indicates that both adults participate in caring for the young, but detailed nesting information is less complete than for many better-studied flycatchers.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects and other small arthropods, supplemented by fruits, seeds, and occasionally insect eggs. It forages from the understory through the canopy, usually alone or in pairs. Typical feeding actions include hovering briefly to glean prey from leaves and making short sallies from exposed perches. It may also join mixed-species feeding flocks, especially where woodland birds concentrate around productive vegetation.
