profile.behavior: Greenish Elaenias are active but often inconspicuous, moving through leafy vegetation while giving frequent calls. They commonly perch quietly before making short flights to capture prey, and they may shift between forest edges, second growth, and interior woodland. Individuals are usually encountered singly or in pairs, although temporary associations with mixed-species flocks occur. Their vocal behavior is important for detection and can help distinguish them from similar-looking elaenias.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population trend is not precisely quantified, but the species remains widespread and is not regarded as a conservation concern at the global level.

profile.overview: The Yellow-bellied Elaenia (Elaenia flavogaster) is a small, active tyrant flycatcher of the American tropics. It is recognizable by its bushy crest, olive-green upperparts, pale wing bars, grayish head and breast, and yellowish belly. Unlike many flycatchers, it commonly uses gardens, farmland, scrub, forest edges, and other open habitats. It often perches conspicuously while making short flights to catch insects or take small fruits.
profile.classification: The Yellow-bellied Elaenia belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Elaenia. Its scientific name is Elaenia flavogaster.
profile.identification: This medium-small flycatcher has olive-green upperparts, a grayish head and throat, a whitish or pale eye ring, and two pale wing bars. The underparts are grayish on the breast and yellow on the belly and undertail coverts. Its bushy crest is a useful feature, although it may be held flat. The bill is broad and dark, and the wings and tail are relatively plain. Its emphatic, somewhat harsh calls are often easier to detect than the bird itself.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and eastern South America, with additional populations in parts of the Caribbean. In Costa Rica, it is a resident species found widely from the lowlands into the highlands, locally reaching about 1,850–2,200 meters. It is generally associated with secondary growth, scrub, open woodland, forest edges, clearings, gardens, plantations, parks, and other habitats with scattered trees. It avoids the interior of dense, continuous forest.
profile.migrationStatus: The Yellow-bellied Elaenia is generally resident in Costa Rica and does not undertake a regular long-distance migration there. Local or seasonal movements may occur, especially in response to food availability or rainfall, but Costa Rican birds are present throughout the year.
profile.breeding: The Yellow-bellied Elaenia usually nests in an open cup built from plant fibers and other fine materials, placed on a branch or in a small tree or shrub. Breeding pairs defend a territory and may nest in disturbed habitats as well as along forest edges. The female performs most incubation, while both adults participate in feeding the young. Nesting timing varies across its broad range and is linked to local rainfall and food conditions.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of insects and other small arthropods, supplemented by small fruits and occasionally seeds. It commonly waits from a perch and makes short sallies to seize flying insects or pluck items from foliage. In Costa Rica it frequently feeds in the middle levels of shrubs and trees, and it may visit fruiting plants in gardens, secondary vegetation, and forest margins.
profile.behavior: The Yellow-bellied Elaenia is alert, active, and usually encountered singly or in pairs rather than in large flocks. It often sits upright on an exposed perch, repeatedly calling and making brief flights through nearby vegetation. Individuals may defend territories throughout the year. Its tolerance of gardens, farms, and regenerating woodland allows it to live close to people, where its loud calls can reveal its presence before it is seen.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable.

profile.overview: The Lesser Elaenia (Elaenia chiriquensis) is a small, active flycatcher of tropical America. It is usually recognized by its modest size, plain olive-green upperparts, pale underparts, and subtle crest. The species often perches quietly in shrubs or low trees before making short flights to capture insects. In Costa Rica, it is associated mainly with warm, seasonally dry habitats and open woodland, where it can be overlooked because of its subdued appearance and soft vocalizations.
profile.classification: The Lesser Elaenia belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Elaenia. It is one of several closely related elaenias that can be difficult to separate in the field.
profile.identification: This small flycatcher has olive-green to grayish upperparts, two pale wing bars, pale edging on the flight feathers, and whitish to pale yellowish underparts. Its head has a short, often inconspicuous crest and a dark bill with a paler lower mandible. The Lesser Elaenia is smaller and generally less strongly marked than some similar elaenias. Identification is best confirmed using a combination of plumage, habitat, voice, size, and geographic location.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Lesser Elaenia occurs from Mexico and Central America south through much of tropical South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly in the warmer Pacific lowlands and seasonally dry northwest, including open woodland, forest edges, scrub, second growth, gallery vegetation, plantations, and other partly open habitats. It generally favors areas with scattered trees and dense shrubs rather than unbroken mature rainforest, and may also use wooded edges around farms and settlements.
profile.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Lesser Elaenia is generally considered a resident or locally occurring species, although its abundance may vary seasonally and some movements can occur. South American populations may undertake regional or longer-distance movements, so migration patterns differ across the species’ broad range.
profile.breeding: Breeding information varies across the species’ range. The Lesser Elaenia builds a small cup-shaped nest, usually placed in a shrub or low tree and made from fine plant fibers, grasses, and other soft materials. The female generally lays a small clutch of pale eggs with darker markings. In Costa Rica, breeding is expected to be associated mainly with the late dry season and rainy season in suitable lowland habitats, but local timing can vary with rainfall and food availability.
profile.dietFeeding: The Lesser Elaenia feeds mainly on insects and other small arthropods captured during short sallies from exposed perches. It also takes small fruits and berries, especially when insect prey is less abundant. It usually forages in shrubs, low and middle levels of vegetation, and woodland edges, moving actively among perches while occasionally flicking its wings or tail.
profile.behavior: This species is usually alert and active but can be inconspicuous. It often sits quietly on a partially exposed branch, then flies out to seize prey before returning to a perch. Lesser Elaenias may forage singly, in pairs, or in mixed-species flocks outside the breeding season. Their calls are useful for detection, because the plumage is relatively plain and can be confused with that of other small elaenias.

conservation.populationTrend: The species is widespread, and no reliable evidence indicates a rapid global population decline. Local populations may be affected by habitat change, but the overall trend is not clearly established.

profile.overview: The Mountain Elaenia (Elaenia frantzii) is a small, active tyrant flycatcher of the highlands of Central America and northern South America. It is associated especially with humid montane forest, cloud forest edges, secondary growth, and other partially open habitats. The species is generally plain-looking but has a subtle pale eye ring, two light wing bars, and a short crest. In Costa Rica it is a familiar resident or seasonal elevational migrant of the country's mountain ranges.
profile.classification: The Mountain Elaenia belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the elaenia genus Elaenia. It is a passerine bird.
profile.identification: This small flycatcher has olive-green to grayish upperparts, a gray head, a pale throat, and whitish to pale yellow underparts. Its bill is short and broad, with a dark upper mandible and a paler lower mandible. Two pale wing bars, pale feather edges, and a light eye ring are useful field marks. The crown may show a small crest when the bird is alert. It can resemble other elaenias, so voice, habitat, and elevation are helpful for confirmation.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Mountain Elaenia has a disjunct range from southern Mexico through Central America and from Colombia and Venezuela into the northern Andes. In Costa Rica, the nominate form occurs mainly in the highlands and mountain ranges, including suitable habitats in the Central and southern parts of the country. It uses humid montane forest, cloud-forest margins, secondary woodland, forest clearings, shrubby edges, and sometimes lightly modified areas. It is usually found from roughly 1,200 to 2,500 meters, with lower seasonal movements.
profile.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Mountain Elaenia is not a long-distance migrant but appears to make regular elevational movements. It breeds at higher elevations and may descend to lower mountain zones after breeding, especially from late summer through the nonbreeding season. The timing and extent of these movements vary and are not fully understood. Elsewhere in northern Central America it is considered largely resident.
profile.breeding: Most available breeding information comes from Costa Rica. Breeding generally occurs in the higher parts of the species' elevational range, with the season extending at least from early April through June. The species builds a small open cup nest, usually placed in vegetation above the ground, although exact nest-site details can vary. Pairs defend breeding territories and adults care for the young. Outside the breeding season, individuals may move downslope and appear less closely tied to particular territories.
profile.dietFeeding: The Mountain Elaenia eats insects, other small arthropods, and small fruits. Fruit may form a larger part of its diet than in many related elaenias. It usually forages alone in dense foliage at several levels of the forest, taking food by gleaning from leaves and twigs, briefly hovering, or making short sallies to capture insects. It may visit fruiting trees with other Mountain Elaenias and occasionally joins mixed-species feeding flocks.
profile.behavior: This species is an alert, active, and vocal forest-edge flycatcher. It often perches quietly within foliage before making short flights to collect insects or moving to another branch. Individuals may flick or raise the crest when attentive. Mountain Elaenias are commonly seen singly or in pairs, although several may gather at fruiting trees. Their behavior and presence in Costa Rica can change seasonally as birds move between higher breeding areas and lower elevations.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to be undergoing a major decline, although precise population data are limited.

profile.overview: The Torrent Tyrannulet (Serpophaga cinerea) is a small, active flycatcher closely associated with mountain streams. It perches on rocks, branches, and streamside vegetation before making short flights to catch insects. Its distinctive habitat, frequent tail-wagging, and preference for clear, fast-flowing water help separate it from other small tyrant flycatchers. The species has a discontinuous distribution in Central and South America, including Costa Rica, Panama, the Andes, and parts of Venezuela and Bolivia.
profile.classification: The Torrent Tyrannulet belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family Tyrannidae and the genus Serpophaga. Two subspecies are generally recognized, including the Central American form S. c. grisea.
profile.identification: This is a small, slim tyrannulet measuring about 9.5 centimeters long. Adults are gray overall, with darker wings and tail, a whitish throat and underparts, and a dark head that may show a partly concealed pale crown patch. The bill is short and the tail is relatively long. It is often recognized more readily by behavior and habitat than by plumage: it repeatedly wags or flicks its tail while perched beside rocky watercourses and makes quick sallies after flying insects.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Torrent Tyrannulet has a disjunct range. In Central America, the subspecies S. c. grisea occurs from the Cordillera de Tilarán in Costa Rica south through western Panama. In Costa Rica it is found mainly along rocky, fast-flowing mountain streams, especially at middle and upper elevations, generally around 500 meters and higher, although it can occur lower in some Caribbean-slope valleys. It uses forested stream margins, open riparian areas, and occasionally altered waterways or marshy habitats.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, individuals remain in suitable stream habitat throughout the year, with breeding records mainly from January through June. Local movements may occur when stream conditions or human activity alter habitat, but regular seasonal departure from Costa Rica is not established.
profile.breeding: Breeding has been recorded in Costa Rica mainly from January through June. The nest is a small cup made from plant fibers and other vegetation, often covered externally with moss and lined with soft down. It is typically attached to streamside vegetation, frequently on a branch overhanging the water, usually less than a meter above the stream. Most documented nests have come from Costa Rica, where the species breeds along suitable mountain waterways.
profile.dietFeeding: The Torrent Tyrannulet feeds mainly on arthropods, especially flying insects. It usually forages alone or in pairs from rocks, low branches, and vegetation beside streams. From a perch, it makes short flights to hawk insects in the air, then returns to the same or a nearby perch. It may also take prey from streamside foliage while hovering briefly and occasionally searches for food on gravel, paths, or other open ground.
profile.behavior: This species is energetic and strongly tied to running water. It spends much of its time near boulders and low vegetation along streams, often perching in exposed positions where it can watch for insects. Repeated tail-wagging and tail-flicking are characteristic. It may occur singly or in pairs and commonly makes short, direct flights across the water. Its dependence on noisy mountain streams can make its calls difficult to detect, even when the bird is nearby.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to be undergoing a major decline, although its specialized streamside habitat may make local populations sensitive to habitat degradation.

profile.overview: The White-fronted Tyrannulet (Acrochordopus zeledoni) is a small, little-known tyrant flycatcher of humid mountain forests in the Neotropics. It is usually encountered high in the forest, where it searches foliage for insects and takes small fruits. The species has a notably fragmented distribution, with separate populations in Central America, the Andes, northern Venezuela, and the tepui region of southern Venezuela. Its quiet, canopy-oriented habits can make it easy to overlook, even where it is locally established.
profile.classification: The White-fronted Tyrannulet belongs to the order Passeriformes and family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers. It is placed in the genus Acrochordopus; older references may use Phyllomyias zeledoni or Pogonotriccus zeledoni.
profile.identification: A small, predominantly olive-green and gray tyrannulet with a conspicuous whitish forehead and generally pale facial markings. The upperparts are olive, while the underparts are paler, often with a subdued yellowish or grayish wash. It has a short, pointed bill and a compact flycatcher shape. Identification is often difficult because it moves actively in foliage, stays near the canopy, and may be detected first by its sharp, high-pitched calls rather than by a prolonged view.
profile.rangeHabitat: The White-fronted Tyrannulet has a disjunct range extending from Costa Rica and western Panama through several isolated mountain regions of northern and southern Venezuela and along the eastern Andes from Colombia to Peru. In Costa Rica, the nominate subspecies occurs in the mountains, including the Cordillera de Tilarán and other humid highland areas, generally from foothill elevations to about 2,800 meters. It uses humid evergreen forest, forest edges, clearings with scattered trees, and mature secondary woodland, especially in the canopy and upper levels.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident, including in Costa Rica. There is no reliable evidence of regular long-distance migration, although local movements may occur in response to food availability or changing conditions.
profile.breeding: The breeding biology of the White-fronted Tyrannulet remains poorly documented. A nest recorded in Panama was a cup made largely of moss and placed on a horizontal branch in the canopy, about 12 meters above the ground. Both members of the pair reportedly helped construct it. The breeding season has not been fully defined; available observations include nesting activity or breeding evidence in August in Panama. Reliable information on clutch size, incubation, and parental care is limited.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet is incompletely known but includes arthropods and small berries. It usually forages alone or in mixed-species feeding flocks, mainly in the middle and upper forest levels. The bird gleans prey and fruit from foliage and branches, sometimes making short hovering movements to reach items. Its small bill and active behavior are typical of an insect-oriented canopy tyrannulet, but the relative importance of animal and plant food is not well established.
profile.behavior: The White-fronted Tyrannulet is an active, canopy-associated bird that is often encountered singly or with mixed feeding flocks. It moves rapidly through foliage and may make brief hovering flights while feeding. Vocal activity is greatest in the morning. Its song or main call has been described as a high, piercing note, sometimes repeated in a series or delivered as a descending sequence of several notes. Because it is local and inconspicuous, it is frequently overlooked during forest surveys.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is believed to be decreasing, although the rate and geographic pattern of decline are uncertain.

profile.overview: The Mistletoe Tyrannulet (Zimmerius parvus) is a very small tyrant flycatcher of Central America and northwestern South America. It is associated especially with mistletoe-bearing trees, whose berries are an important food. Although inconspicuous, it is widespread and can live in forest, woodland, plantations, gardens, and other partly modified habitats. The species was formerly included within the broader Paltry Tyrannulet complex but is now generally recognized as a separate species.
profile.classification: The Mistletoe Tyrannulet belongs to the order Passeriformes and family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers. Its scientific name is Zimmerius parvus.
profile.identification: This small, subtly marked tyrannulet has mainly grayish-green upperparts, pale underparts, a dull whitish eyebrow, a small bill, and yellow edging on the wing feathers. It may show a slightly olive or yellowish wash below. The bird often perches horizontally with its tail slightly cocked. It is easily overlooked because it usually stays in middle and upper vegetation, where it moves quickly among leaves and fruiting branches, often alone or in pairs.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Mistletoe Tyrannulet occurs from eastern Guatemala and Belize through Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama to extreme northwestern Colombia. In Costa Rica it is a widespread resident, recorded through much of the country, including humid Caribbean and Pacific regions and interior highlands. It occupies evergreen forest, forest edges, second-growth, plantations, shaded farmland, pastures with scattered trees, gardens, and other wooded habitats. It is especially associated with trees supporting mistletoes and may occur from lowlands to high elevations, locally approaching treeline.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident, including in Costa Rica, with no regular long-distance migration known. Local movements may follow food availability and fruiting mistletoes.
profile.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding activity has been reported mainly from about January through July, possibly extending into August. The female builds a small oval nest with a side entrance, using mosses and plant fibers bound with spider web and lined with soft seed down. The nest is usually attached to a mossy or lichen-covered mass hanging from a branch, commonly a few metres above the ground. Clutches generally contain two eggs; incubation and nestling periods are both relatively short.
profile.dietFeeding: Its diet includes mistletoe berries, other small fruits, insects, and spiders. It searches actively through the middle and upper levels of vegetation, often moving rapidly between perches. Arthropods are commonly gleaned from leaves and branches, while fruit may be taken directly from clusters or obtained during brief hovering flights. In some parts of its range, it also joins mixed-species feeding flocks.
profile.behavior: The Mistletoe Tyrannulet is usually seen singly or in pairs and is more often detected by its quick movements or sharp vocalizations than by prolonged views. It forages at several forest levels but commonly favors the mid-story and canopy. Its tail is often held slightly cocked while perched. The species may tolerate human-altered landscapes, particularly where mature trees, fruiting plants, and mistletoes remain available. It is believed to defend territories during breeding.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population size has not been quantified. It is believed to be decreasing, but the species remains widespread and relatively adaptable, including in Costa Rica.

profile.overview: The Bran-colored Flycatcher (Myiophobus fasciatus) is a small, mainly brown tyrant flycatcher of open woodland, forest edges, and shrubby second growth. It often perches quietly on low branches before making short flights to capture insects. The species has a broad distribution from Costa Rica and Panama through much of South America. In Costa Rica, it is a localized bird of southern intermontane and Pacific-slope regions rather than a widespread species throughout the country.
profile.classification: The Bran-colored Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, in the order Passeriformes. Its scientific name is Myiophobus fasciatus.
profile.identification: This small flycatcher is predominantly warm brown or bran-colored, with darker wings and tail. The breast and upper underparts are usually marked with fine streaking, while the wings show narrow pale or tan wingbars. It lacks a strong facial pattern and generally appears compact and unobtrusive. Individuals are often seen alone or in pairs on exposed low perches. Its calls and song vary geographically and may include clear whistles, rising trills, or short, somewhat husky phrases.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Bran-colored Flycatcher has a wide but discontinuous range extending from Costa Rica and Panama across much of northern, central, and eastern South America. In Costa Rica, the species is localized mainly in southern intermontane areas and the southern Pacific region, including parts of San José and Puntarenas Provinces, and is associated with elevations of roughly 700 to 1,500 meters. It uses lightly wooded habitats, forest edges, riverbanks, shrubby second growth, clearings, and other regenerating vegetation.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally considered a resident species in Costa Rica, with no regular long-distance migration documented there. Local movements may occur in response to seasonal conditions or habitat changes.
profile.breeding: The nest is a deep cup made from plant fibers and often bound with spider web; moss or feathers may also be included. It is usually placed in a fork of a low branch, sometimes in bamboo, only a few meters above the ground. The usual clutch contains two eggs, although one- and three-egg clutches occur. The female generally incubates the eggs for about 14 to 17 days, and young leave the nest approximately 13 to 17 days after hatching. Both parents feed the young.
profile.dietFeeding: The Bran-colored Flycatcher feeds primarily on insects and other small arthropods. It usually hunts from a low or moderately elevated perch, making short sallies to seize prey from the air, foliage, or nearby vegetation. Its preference for open woodland, shrubby edges, and regenerating growth provides suitable foraging sites. It may remain still for long periods between brief, direct feeding flights.
profile.behavior: This flycatcher is usually encountered alone or in pairs and is often more easily detected by its vocalizations than by movement. It tends to sit quietly on an exposed low perch, occasionally flicking its wings or tail before launching a short flight. Males may sing from open perches, particularly during the breeding period. The species commonly occupies disturbed or naturally regenerating habitats and can benefit from a mosaic of shrubs, scattered trees, and forest edges.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not precisely known, but it has been considered stable to increasing, with no evidence of a rapid overall decline.

profile.overview: The Tawny-chested Flycatcher (Aphanotriccus capitalis) is a small forest flycatcher of Central America. It is associated mainly with humid Caribbean-slope forests, where it often uses shaded edges, clearings, and dense secondary vegetation. The species is unobtrusive and usually detected by its calls or by brief sallies from a low perch to capture insects. In Costa Rica, it is a localized resident of suitable humid forest, especially in the Caribbean lowlands and adjacent foothills.
profile.classification: The species belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae. It is the only species in the genus Aphanotriccus.
profile.identification: The Tawny-chested Flycatcher is a small, compact flycatcher with a warm tawny or cinnamon-colored chest and underparts, contrasting with olive-brown upperparts. It has a relatively broad bill, a dark head, and pale wingbars that can be visible in good light. Its plumage may resemble other small forest flycatchers, so identification is best confirmed using habitat, behavior, vocalizations, and the combination of tawny underparts with its overall dark, subdued appearance.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Tawny-chested Flycatcher occurs in humid Caribbean-slope forests of Central America, from eastern Honduras and Nicaragua through Costa Rica and into western Panama. In Costa Rica, it is a local and generally uncommon resident, reported mainly from wet lowland forest and foothill habitats on the Caribbean side, including mature forest, forest margins, and dense second growth. It favors shaded vegetation with a well-developed understory and may occur near streams, openings, or lightly disturbed forest where cover remains dense.
profile.migrationStatus: It is considered essentially resident in Costa Rica and across its range. Individuals may make local movements in response to food availability or seasonal conditions, but it is not known as a regular long-distance migrant.
profile.breeding: Reliable details of its breeding biology are limited. Like other small tyrant flycatchers, it is expected to defend a territory and raise its young in humid forest vegetation, but published information on nest placement, clutch size, incubation, and nesting season is scarce. In Costa Rica, breeding is likely associated with the wet Caribbean forest zone, where suitable dense understory and insect-rich habitat are available.
profile.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on insects and other small arthropods. It typically forages from low or middle-level perches, making short sallies to catch prey from foliage or the air and then returning to a perch. Dense, shaded vegetation is important because it provides both hunting perches and the insect prey associated with humid forest habitats.
profile.behavior: The Tawny-chested Flycatcher is generally quiet and inconspicuous, often remaining inside dense vegetation rather than sitting in exposed locations. It watches from a perch and makes quick, short flights to capture prey. It may occur singly or in pairs and is more readily located by its vocalizations than by prolonged visual observation. Its preference for forest understory and shaded edges can make it difficult to detect.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is believed to be declining, primarily because of continuing loss and degradation of humid forest habitat, although the species remains distributed across several countries.
conservation.threats: Conversion of Caribbean lowland forest for agriculture, pasture, plantations, roads, and settlement can reduce and fragment habitat. Selective logging, removal of dense understory, and degradation of forest edges may also lower habitat quality. In Costa Rica, protection and connectivity of remaining wet lowland and foothill forests are important for maintaining local populations.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore humid Caribbean-slope forest, including forest corridors between larger reserves. Retain native understory and shaded vegetation, limit unnecessary clearing along streams and forest margins, and support land-use practices that conserve mature and regenerating forest. Bird monitoring in Costa Rica can help clarify local abundance, breeding distribution, and population changes.

profile.overview: The Tufted Flycatcher is a small, active tyrant flycatcher of cool mountain forests from Mexico through Central America to northern South America. It is named for the short crest that gives its head a tufted appearance. The species often perches upright on exposed twigs, making short flights to catch insects before returning to the same perch. In Costa Rica, it is a characteristic bird of the highlands and is frequently encountered in forest edges and other partly open mountain habitats.
profile.classification: The Tufted Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the large family of New World flycatchers. Its scientific name is Mitrephanes phaeocercus.
profile.identification: This flycatcher is about 13 centimeters long and has a noticeable pointed crest, dark gray head and upperparts, and warm cinnamon or rufous wings and tail. The underparts are usually pale gray on the throat and breast, becoming yellowish on the belly. Its bill is broad and dark, and the overall shape is compact. In Costa Rica, its combination of a small crest, rufous wing panels, and mountain-forest habitat helps distinguish it from other small flycatchers.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Tufted Flycatcher ranges from western and southern Mexico through Central America and into parts of northwestern South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly in the central and southern highlands, generally from middle elevations to the upper montane zone, including areas such as the Cordillera de Tilarán, Cordillera Central, and Cordillera de Talamanca. It uses humid montane and cloud forests, woodland edges, clearings, shade-grown coffee areas, plantations, and roadsides with scattered trees, usually at roughly 900 to 3,000 meters elevation.
profile.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Tufted Flycatcher is generally a resident or local elevational migrant rather than a long-distance migrant. Individuals may move upslope or downslope in response to seasonal conditions, food availability, and breeding activity. The species is present in suitable Costa Rican highland habitats throughout much of the year.
profile.breeding: Breeding takes place during the rainy or early wet-season period, although timing varies across the species' broad range. The nest is typically placed in a natural cavity, an old woodpecker hole, or a similar sheltered opening, and may also be situated in a bank or other protected structure. The female lays a small clutch of pale eggs marked with darker spots. Both adults are involved in feeding the young, which are supplied mainly with captured insects.
profile.dietFeeding: The Tufted Flycatcher feeds mainly on flying insects, including beetles, flies, moths, wasps, and other small arthropods. It usually hunts from a fairly exposed perch, making quick sallies into the air to seize prey and then returning to the same or a nearby perch. It also takes insects from vegetation and may occasionally eat small fruits or other plant material, especially when insect prey is less available.
profile.behavior: This species is alert and energetic, commonly sitting upright on exposed branches while flicking its wings or tail. It defends feeding and breeding territories with calls and short aerial pursuits. The Tufted Flycatcher often forages alone or in pairs but may join mixed-species feeding flocks in mountain forests. Its call is a sharp, high-pitched note, and its short, repeated flights from a regular perch make it relatively conspicuous in suitable habitat.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains common or fairly common in many appropriate highland areas, including parts of Costa Rica.

profile.overview: The Olive-sided Flycatcher (Contopus cooperi) is a large, strongly built North American flycatcher known for its distinctive “quick, three beers” song and habit of hunting from exposed treetops. It breeds mainly in boreal and montane coniferous forests, especially where forest openings, wetlands, streams, burns, or dead trees provide abundant flying insects. It undertakes a remarkably long migration to Central and South America. In Costa Rica, it is primarily encountered as a passage migrant rather than a regular breeding species.
profile.classification: The Olive-sided Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers. Its scientific name is Contopus cooperi.
profile.identification: This is a relatively large flycatcher with a broad, heavy-based bill, a dark olive-gray back, and a dark head. The sides of the breast and flanks are blackish or deep olive, contrasting with a conspicuous white patch down the center of the breast and white tufts on the lower back that may show beside the folded wings. The tail is broad and slightly notched. Its emphatic, three-part whistle is often the easiest way to detect it.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species breeds from Alaska across much of Canada and in parts of the western and northeastern United States. It migrates through Mexico and Central America to wintering areas in northern South America. In Costa Rica, the Olive-sided Flycatcher is mainly a migrant, with records during spring and fall passage; it may use second-growth woodland, forest edges, open forest, and other semi-open habitats with prominent perches. It is not generally considered a resident or breeding species there.
profile.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Birds pass through Costa Rica during migration, and the country is part of the species’ Central American route between North American breeding grounds and South American wintering areas. It is generally uncommon and seasonal in Costa Rica rather than a regular year-round resident.
profile.breeding: Breeding occurs primarily in open or edge habitats within boreal, montane, and western coniferous forests. Suitable sites often include dead or dying trees, stream margins, wetlands, bogs, recent burns, beaver ponds, or other natural openings that provide exposed hunting and singing perches. The nest is a small cup placed on a horizontal branch, usually well above the ground and often near the end of a branch. The species does not normally breed in Costa Rica.
profile.dietFeeding: The Olive-sided Flycatcher feeds mainly on flying insects captured in aerial sallies from a high, exposed perch. Its prey includes bees, wasps, flying ants, beetles, dragonflies, grasshoppers, moths, and other flies. It often returns to the same perch after each attack and favors forest openings, edges, wetlands, and waterways where insect concentrations are high. Small amounts of fruit may occasionally be eaten during migration or on the wintering grounds.
profile.behavior: This flycatcher is usually solitary and conspicuous when perched on the top of a dead tree or other prominent snag. It frequently scans from one favored lookout and launches upward or outward to catch insects before returning. The species is generally less associated with mixed-species feeding flocks than many smaller flycatchers. Its loud, distinctive song is commonly delivered from an exposed perch during the breeding season, while migrants may be quiet and difficult to detect.

conservation.populationTrend: The population has undergone a marked long-term decline across much of its range. Recent trends appear more stable in some areas, but the species remains vulnerable because of its relatively small population and dependence on suitable habitats across several countries and seasons.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include loss and degradation of mature forest and forest-edge habitat on the breeding and wintering grounds, especially in Central and South America. Fire suppression, removal of standing dead trees, salvage logging after fires, and changes to natural forest disturbance can reduce breeding habitat and foraging perches. Habitat loss along migration routes may also affect the species. Because Olive-sided Flycatchers pass through Costa Rica, protecting wooded stopover habitat there can support the wider migratory population.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect mature forests, forest edges, wetlands, and wooded riparian corridors used during migration and on the wintering grounds. Retain suitable standing dead trees where public safety allows, and avoid unnecessary removal of snags in natural forest areas. Support conservation of forests in Costa Rica and throughout the species’ breeding and wintering range. Bird monitoring and reporting of migration records can help clarify local timing, abundance, and habitat use.

profile.overview: The Ochraceous Pewee (Contopus ochraceus) is a small, distinctive tyrant flycatcher of the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is associated mainly with montane forest edges, clearings, and open areas near high-elevation woodland. The species is usually recognized by its warm ochraceous-brown plumage, relatively long wings, upright posture, and habit of making short sallies from exposed perches to catch flying insects.
profile.classification: The Ochraceous Pewee belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Contopus, which includes several pewees and related aerial insectivores. It is treated as a distinct species, Contopus ochraceus.
profile.identification: This is a small to medium-sized pewee with generally warm brown or ochraceous upperparts and paler underparts washed with buff or cinnamon tones. The wings are darker, with subtle pale edging or wing bars, and the bill is broad at the base, as in many flycatchers. It often sits upright on an exposed twig, fence, or dead branch. Its repeated short flights from a perch to seize insects are useful for identification.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Ochraceous Pewee has a restricted Central American range, occurring in the highlands of Costa Rica and extending into western Panama. In Costa Rica it is principally a montane and high-elevation species, where it may be found along forest borders, shrubby clearings, open woodland, roadsides, and other semi-open habitats near humid mountain forests. It generally favors cool upland environments and can occur in disturbed landscapes when suitable perches and nearby insect-rich vegetation remain available.
profile.migrationStatus: It is generally considered resident or largely sedentary within its mountain range. In Costa Rica, individuals normally remain in highland regions year-round, although local movements may occur with elevation, weather, food availability, or seasonal habitat conditions.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is limited compared with that of better-studied widespread flycatchers. Like related Contopus species, it is expected to form breeding territories in suitable montane habitat and to nest during the local wet-season period when insect prey is abundant. The nest is likely placed on or near a branch or other elevated support, but detailed information on nest sites, clutch size, incubation, and parental care is not well documented in widely available sources.
profile.dietFeeding: The Ochraceous Pewee feeds mainly on flying insects and other arthropods. It commonly uses a visible perch and makes quick aerial sallies to capture prey, then returns to the same or a nearby perch. This sit-and-wait strategy is typical of pewees and is especially effective along forest edges, clearings, and open mountain vegetation where insects pass through the air.
profile.behavior: This species is usually encountered alone or in pairs and often appears calm while perched upright and scanning for prey. Its short, direct flights from exposed perches are characteristic. It may defend a feeding or breeding territory with calls and aerial activity, but it is not generally known for large flocks or conspicuous long-distance movements. Dense cover, mist, and high-elevation conditions can make it difficult to detect despite its use of open perches.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not confidently quantified in widely available summaries. The species has a restricted highland distribution, so local habitat changes may be important even though it is not currently classified as globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Dark Pewee (Contopus lugubris) is a distinctive flycatcher of the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is associated with wet montane forests, especially forest edges, clearings, and nearby semi-open areas with tall trees. Usually seen alone outside the breeding period, it hunts from exposed perches and makes short flights to catch insects. Costa Rica contains most of the species’ range, making the country especially important for its global conservation.
profile.classification: The Dark Pewee belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Contopus. It is closely related to several other large pewees of the highlands of Central America.
profile.identification: This is a relatively large, dark pewee with sooty-gray upperparts and a noticeably crested crown. The wings and tail are blackish, with grayish feather edges and a weak wing bar. The throat is pale gray, while the remaining underparts are paler olive-gray, becoming somewhat yellowish on the lower belly. The sexes look alike. Juveniles are browner above and show warmer, rufous-buff edging on some wing feathers.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Dark Pewee is endemic to the Talamancan montane region, occurring in Costa Rica and extreme western Panama. In Costa Rica it is resident in the mountains from the Cordillera de Tilarán southward, including suitable areas of the Central Volcanic and Talamanca ranges. It generally occupies wet montane evergreen forest, forest margins, clearings, and adjacent semi-open habitats with tall trees, mostly from about 1,200 to 2,150 meters elevation.
profile.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and western Panama; it is not considered a long-distance migrant. Individuals may move locally between forest, edge, and nearby open habitats, but regular seasonal migration is not documented.
profile.breeding: The Dark Pewee builds a broad, thick-walled cup or saucer-shaped nest made mainly of mosses and lichens, with a lining of plant fibers. The nest is placed across a branch, usually several meters above the ground, reportedly about 5–18 meters high. The female builds the nest and lays two eggs. Incubation lasts approximately 15–16 days. Adults may defend the nest forcefully, even against larger birds.
profile.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on flying insects and other arthropods. It typically waits on a high, exposed perch and makes short sallies into the air to capture prey, often returning to the same lookout. Forest edges, clearings, and semi-open mountain habitats provide suitable hunting positions and may improve access to aerial insects.
profile.behavior: Dark Pewees are generally solitary outside the breeding season. They are conspicuous because they often use prominent perches and give a loud, repeated whip-like call. The song has been described as a repetitive, emphatic series of notes. Birds regularly return to favored perches after feeding flights, and breeding adults can become aggressive when defending a nest.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly documented in readily available sources, but the species is not currently assessed as globally threatened.

profile.overview: The Western Wood-Pewee is a small, migratory tyrant flycatcher of open forests and woodland edges. It breeds mainly across western North America and spends the nonbreeding season in tropical regions of the Americas. The species is usually inconspicuous when perched, but its repeated sallies from exposed branches and distinctive, rough descending call make it easier to detect. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon migrant and winter visitor, and identification should be confirmed carefully because it resembles the Eastern Wood-Pewee.
profile.classification: The Western Wood-Pewee belongs to the order Passeriformes and the flycatcher family Tyrannidae. Its scientific name is Contopus sordidulus.
profile.identification: Adults are plain grayish-brown above with whitish underparts, a smudgy gray breast band and sides, two pale wingbars, and little or no obvious eye-ring. The bill is mostly dark, often with a paler or yellowish base to the lower mandible. It has a fairly upright posture, long wings, and a straight-looking tail. It is extremely similar to the Eastern Wood-Pewee, so the rough, nasal, slightly descending call is often the most dependable field mark, especially in Costa Rica.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species breeds from Alaska and western Canada through the western United States and parts of northern Mexico. It migrates south through Mexico and Central America to wintering areas in northern and western South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly as an uncommon migrant or winter visitor rather than a regular breeder; records may be scattered because silent Contopus flycatchers are difficult to identify. It uses open woodland, forest edges, riparian trees, secondary woodland, plantations, and other places with prominent perches and open flight space.
profile.migrationStatus: A long-distance Neotropical migrant. In Costa Rica it is generally a scarce passage migrant and uncommon winter visitor, with occurrence concentrated during migration and the northern winter; it is not considered a regular breeding species there.
profile.breeding: Breeding occurs mainly in open coniferous, mixed, deciduous, and riparian woodland across western North America. The nest is a small, shallow cup built on a horizontal or slightly sloping tree branch, often several metres above the ground. It is made from grasses, plant fibers, lichens, bark strips, and spider web. The female usually lays a small clutch of pale eggs marked with darker spots. Costa Rica lies outside the species’ normal established breeding range.
profile.dietFeeding: Western Wood-Pewees feed chiefly on flying insects, including beetles, moths, flies, wasps, bees, and other small arthropods. They usually wait on an exposed branch, scan the surrounding air, and launch on a short, rapid flight to seize prey before returning to the same or a nearby perch. They may also take insects from vegetation and occasionally eat small fruits, particularly when flying insects are less available.
profile.behavior: This species is typically solitary or found singly, although migrants may occur in loose concentrations where food is abundant. It spends much of the day perched upright in the canopy or along woodland edges, repeatedly making short flycatching flights. Individuals often return to a favored perch and may flutter their wings on landing. The song is a characteristic rough, buzzy, descending call. It defends breeding territories and can become vocal around dawn, dusk, and during nest defense.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered to be declining, although trends vary among regions and monitoring programs. The decline has not placed the species in a globally threatened category.
conservation.threats: Loss and degradation of mature woodland and riparian habitat on breeding and wintering grounds are important concerns. Habitat conversion, forest fragmentation, reduced insect abundance, pesticide exposure, and changing climate conditions may also affect survival and breeding success. Because the species depends on flying insects, prolonged cold or drought during migration can reduce feeding opportunities.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore open woodland, riparian forest, and mature tropical forest throughout its range, including wintering habitat in Central America. Reduce unnecessary pesticide use and maintain native trees, dead branches, and insect-rich vegetation. Support bird monitoring and habitat conservation, and report well-documented Costa Rican sightings with photographs or recordings because the species is uncommon there and can be confused with the Eastern Wood-Pewee.

profile.overview: The Northern Tropical Pewee (Contopus bogotensis) is a small, inconspicuous tyrant flycatcher of the Neotropics. It often perches quietly on exposed twigs and makes short flights to catch flying insects before returning to the same or a nearby perch. The species was formerly treated as part of the broader Tropical Pewee complex, so published information may use the name Contopus cinereus for populations now recognized as Northern Tropical Pewee.
profile.classification: The Northern Tropical Pewee belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Contopus. It is closely related to other pewees and wood-pewees, and its taxonomic treatment has changed as regional populations have been reassessed.
profile.identification: This is a small, slim flycatcher with generally gray-brown upperparts, paler gray underparts, and darker wings and tail. The bill is dark, and the wing feathers may show subtle pale edging or narrow wingbars. Plumage can vary geographically and is usually not distinctive enough for confident identification by appearance alone. In Costa Rica, careful comparison with other Contopus flycatchers, along with voice, habitat, range, and behavior, is important.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Northern Tropical Pewee occurs from parts of southern Mexico and Central America south through northern South America, with additional populations in the Caribbean region depending on taxonomic treatment. In Costa Rica it is a recorded resident or regularly occurring species, especially associated with the Pacific lowlands and foothills, although records may be uneven because the bird is quiet and difficult to separate from related pewees. It uses open woodland, forest edges, secondary growth, clearings, and lightly wooded habitats.
profile.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the species is generally regarded as resident rather than a long-distance migrant. Individuals may make local or seasonal movements related to rainfall, food availability, and breeding conditions. Costa Rican records can also be affected by changing taxonomy and identification of the Tropical Pewee complex.
profile.breeding: The Northern Tropical Pewee is believed to breed within its tropical range, including Central America, but detailed, species-specific information is limited where it was formerly combined with the Tropical Pewee. Like related Contopus flycatchers, it is expected to defend a breeding territory, use exposed perches for hunting, and place a small nest in vegetation, often in a tree or shrub. Precise nesting dates and nest-site details for Costa Rica are not consistently documented.
profile.dietFeeding: It feeds mainly on flying insects and other small arthropods. The usual hunting method is perch-and-sally foraging: the bird waits on a visible branch, flies out to seize an insect in the air or from nearby foliage, and returns to a perch. It may forage alone and often favors forest margins, open woodland, shaded clearings, and other places where perches overlook insect-rich airspace.
profile.behavior: The Northern Tropical Pewee is usually solitary and unobtrusive. It often remains still for long periods, making brief, direct flights after passing insects. Its subdued plumage and quiet behavior can make it easy to overlook in Costa Rica. Vocalizations are particularly useful for detection and identification, especially where several small gray flycatchers occur together. Territorial singing and calling are expected to be most noticeable during the breeding season.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to meet the thresholds for a threatened category. A precise population estimate and trend for the species are not well established, particularly because of recent taxonomic separation from the broader Tropical Pewee complex.

profile.overview: The Eastern Wood-Pewee (Contopus virens) is a small New World flycatcher that breeds in eastern and central North America and migrates to Central and northern South America. It is recognized by its subdued olive-gray plumage, two pale wing bars, peaked crown, and distinctive, plaintive “pee-a-wee” song. It usually hunts from exposed perches in forest edges, woodland clearings, shade plantations, and other habitats with scattered trees.
profile.classification: The Eastern Wood-Pewee belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Contopus. It is closely related to the Western Wood-Pewee, but the two species have largely different breeding ranges and distinct calls.
profile.identification: This is a slim, medium-small flycatcher with an olive-gray to brownish upper body, a dusky head, pale throat, and whitish or pale gray underparts. Two noticeable pale wing bars contrast with the dark wings, and the bill is broad and dark with a pale lower base. The tail is fairly long and dark. Its upright posture and habit of returning to the same perch are useful field marks. The clear, descending “pee-a-wee” song is often easier to recognize than the bird itself.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Eastern Wood-Pewee breeds across much of eastern and central North America, using deciduous and mixed forests, woodland margins, parks, and forest openings. It migrates through Mexico and Central America to wintering areas in northern and western South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs as a seasonal migrant and winter visitor rather than a breeding species. It can be found in lowland and middle-elevation woodland, forest edges, open forest, gardens, and shaded agricultural landscapes, with numbers varying by season and location.
profile.migrationStatus: Migratory. Eastern Wood-Pewees pass through Costa Rica during spring and fall migration, and some remain there during the northern winter. Costa Rica is outside the species’ breeding range; records are most likely from approximately September through April, although individual timing varies.
profile.breeding: Breeding takes place mainly from late spring through summer in North America. The species usually nests in a horizontal fork or on a small branch beneath the forest canopy, often in deciduous or mixed woodland. The female builds a small cup nest from plant fibers, grasses, and other material, commonly securing it with spider silk and decorating it with lichens. A typical clutch contains two or three eggs, and both adults participate in feeding the nestlings.
profile.dietFeeding: The Eastern Wood-Pewee feeds mainly on flying insects, including moths, beetles, flies, wasps, bees, and other small arthropods. It usually hunts by sallying from a shaded perch, catching prey in the air, and returning to the same or a nearby perch. It may also take insects from vegetation and occasionally consume small fruits, especially when insects are less available.
profile.behavior: This species is usually quiet outside the breeding season and often sits motionless on an exposed branch while scanning for prey. Its repeated flycatching sallies are short and direct. During the breeding season, adults defend territories with their characteristic song and may make short display flights. Migrants and wintering birds can occur alone or loosely associated with other insect-eating birds, but they generally retain separate feeding spaces.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population trend is declining, largely because of reduced numbers across parts of its breeding range. The species remains widespread and relatively numerous.
conservation.threats: Potential concerns include loss and fragmentation of breeding and wintering forests, degradation of forest edges and shaded agricultural habitats, collisions during migration, and declines in flying insect abundance. Climate change may also alter migration timing, habitat conditions, and food availability.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore native woodland in both breeding and wintering regions, retain mature trees and forest edges, and support shaded, pesticide-reduced agricultural systems. Reducing window collisions during migration and contributing observations to bird-monitoring programs can also help improve understanding of population changes.

profile.overview: The Yellow-bellied Flycatcher (Empidonax flaviventris) is a small North American tyrant flycatcher that breeds in cool, wet boreal forests and winters in Mexico and Central America. It is compact and olive-green, with a conspicuous pale eye-ring, whitish wingbars, and yellowish underparts. Like other Empidonax flycatchers, it is often identified most reliably by its voice, habitat, and range. In Costa Rica it occurs as a nonbreeding migrant rather than a breeding resident.
profile.classification: The Yellow-bellied Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Empidonax. It is one of several closely similar small insect-eating flycatchers in this genus.
profile.identification: This small, compact flycatcher is about 13–15 cm long, with a relatively large head, short tail, and broad-based bill. The upperparts are yellowish olive, while the underparts are yellow-washed from the throat through the belly, although worn individuals may appear duller. A strong whitish eye-ring and two pale wingbars are important field marks. It often sits quietly in dense vegetation, makes quick head movements, and sallies out to catch insects. Voice is especially useful for separating it from similar Empidonax species.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species breeds across much of Canada and the northeastern and north-central United States, especially in wet coniferous forest, spruce-fir swamps, bogs, peatlands, and openings with mossy ground. During the nonbreeding season it moves through Mexico into Central America, using humid lowland and montane evergreen forest, dense second growth, forest edges, and shaded coffee plantations. In Costa Rica, it is a regular seasonal migrant and winter visitor, occurring in suitable forested habitats across the country, including foothill and middle-elevation sites; it does not normally breed there.
profile.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Birds reach Costa Rica mainly during the northern winter, generally from about September or October through April or May, and return north to breed in spring. Costa Rica is part of the species’ nonbreeding range, not its breeding range.
profile.breeding: Breeding takes place in wet northern forests, particularly spruce or fir stands associated with bogs, swamps, peatlands, and mossy ground. The female builds a small open cup, commonly placed low in vegetation or on a moss-covered stump, bank, or other support near the ground. The nest is made from moss, plant fibers, grasses, and other fine materials and is often well concealed. Both adults feed the nestlings, which are primarily supplied with insects.
profile.dietFeeding: The Yellow-bellied Flycatcher feeds mainly on flying and foliage-dwelling insects, including flies, mosquitoes, moths, beetles, ants, and other small arthropods. It usually forages from low or middle levels of dense vegetation. From a quiet perch, it makes short flights to seize prey in the air or from leaves, sometimes hovering briefly. During migration and winter it may also consume small berries or other fruit when available.
profile.behavior: This species is generally inconspicuous and spends much of its time perched quietly in dense forest understory. It frequently turns its head, flicks its tail, and makes short, purposeful sallies after insects, often returning to the same perch. It is more readily detected by its sharp call than by movement or song. Territorial singing is associated mainly with the breeding season; in Costa Rica, migrants are usually quiet or give brief call notes rather than sustained breeding song.

conservation.populationTrend: Available continent-wide monitoring and modeling indicate an overall stable to increasing population pattern, although trends can vary among regions and wintering areas.

profile.overview: The Acadian Flycatcher (Empidonax virescens) is a small North American tyrant flycatcher that breeds in mature, mostly deciduous forests and migrates to the Neotropics. It is olive-green above, whitish below, and often remains high in the shaded forest canopy. Its sharp, explosive “peet-sah” song is an important identification clue. In Costa Rica, it is a migrant rather than a breeding resident, occurring mainly during passage between North America and its wintering range farther south.
profile.classification: The Acadian Flycatcher belongs to the order Passeriformes and the tyrant flycatcher family Tyrannidae. It is one of several closely similar Empidonax flycatchers, which are often difficult to identify by appearance alone.
profile.identification: This small flycatcher has olive-green upperparts, a whitish throat and breast, two pale wing bars, a relatively large bill, and a long primary projection that can make the tail appear short. The eye-ring is usually faint and whitish, and the lower belly may show a slight yellow or olive wash. It is best separated from similar Empidonax species by a combination of structure, habitat, behavior, and especially its distinctive sharp, rising “peet-sah” song.
profile.rangeHabitat: The Acadian Flycatcher breeds mainly in the eastern and central United States and locally in southern Ontario. During the nonbreeding season it occurs from southern Mexico and Central America south through Colombia, western Ecuador, and northwestern Venezuela. In Costa Rica, it is a regular but generally uncommon migrant on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes, using humid forest, forest edges, shaded clearings, second-growth woodland, and other wooded habitats. It is not considered a resident breeder there.
profile.migrationStatus: Long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, it is recorded mainly during spring and autumn passage, approximately March to mid-May and mid-September to late November, with some individuals possibly remaining into the winter period. It moves between breeding grounds in North America and wintering areas in northern South America.
profile.breeding: Breeding takes place in mature, moist deciduous or mixed forests, especially along streams, ravines, floodplains, and other sites with a closed canopy and relatively open understory. The species usually places its small cup nest on a horizontal branch or fork in the lower or middle forest levels. The female generally lays a small clutch of pale eggs, and both adults defend a breeding territory. Pairs commonly return to the same general forest regions in successive years.
profile.dietFeeding: The Acadian Flycatcher feeds mainly on flying insects, including beetles, moths, butterflies, flies, wasps, and other small arthropods. It usually hunts from a shaded perch in the middle or upper levels of forest, making short sallies to capture prey in the air or picking insects from foliage. Small berries and other fruit may also be eaten, particularly when insect prey is less abundant during migration or winter.
profile.behavior: This species is usually solitary or found in pairs during the breeding season. It often sits quietly on a horizontal branch before making a quick, direct flight to seize an insect, then returns to a perch. Its behavior can be inconspicuous, but its emphatic song makes it easier to detect in breeding areas. In Costa Rica, migrants may forage quietly in forest understory, gaps, edges, and second-growth vegetation.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered broadly stable, although trends vary among regions. Some local and regional populations face greater concern where mature forest habitat has been reduced or fragmented.

profile.overview: The Alder Flycatcher is a small, long-distance migratory songbird of wet shrubby habitats. It breeds mainly across the boreal and northern temperate regions of Canada and the northern United States, then travels south for the nonbreeding season. Its olive-brown plumage is subtle, but its harsh, distinctive “free-beer” song is useful for identification on the breeding grounds. In Costa Rica, it is a seasonal migrant and nonbreeding visitor rather than a resident breeding species.
profile.classification: The Alder Flycatcher belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Empidonax. It is closely related to the Willow Flycatcher, and the two species are difficult to distinguish by appearance alone.
profile.identification: This is a small, plain olive-green flycatcher with a grayish head, whitish throat, pale or whitish lower breast, two light wingbars, and a fairly long tail. The bill is broad at the base, and the pale eye-ring is usually weak or incomplete. It closely resembles the Willow Flycatcher, especially during migration, so visual identification can be uncertain. On breeding grounds, the Alder Flycatcher is best confirmed by its distinctive raspy, two-parted “free-beer” song.
profile.rangeHabitat: Alder Flycatchers breed across much of boreal Canada, Alaska, and the northern United States, especially in wet thickets, alder and willow stands, bog margins, beaver ponds, marsh edges, and regenerating clearings. During the nonbreeding season they move through Mexico and Central America to northern South America, using shrubby edges, second growth, wetlands, and open woodland. In Costa Rica, the species occurs as a migrant and seasonal visitor, mainly in suitable lowland and foothill habitats; it does not breed there.
profile.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica it is encountered during passage and the nonbreeding season, with records generally less frequent and less conspicuous than those of some other migrant Empidonax flycatchers. It leaves North America in late summer and autumn and returns north in spring.
profile.breeding: Breeding occurs in northern North America, usually in wet or poorly drained habitats with dense low shrubs. The female commonly builds a small cup nest in a shrub or sapling, often near water. The clutch generally contains several pale eggs marked with darker spots. Both parents feed the nestlings, which are supplied mainly with insects. Alder Flycatchers may nest in loose concentrations where suitable wet thickets are abundant.
profile.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of flying insects and other arthropods, including flies, beetles, moths, bees, wasps, and small grasshoppers. The bird typically waits from an exposed perch in a shrub, then sallies out to capture prey in the air or picks insects from nearby foliage. Small fruits may also be eaten, particularly during migration or the nonbreeding season. In Costa Rica it forages in open vegetation, forest edges, and other structurally varied habitats.
profile.behavior: Alder Flycatchers are usually solitary or found in loose concentrations during migration. They spend much of their time quietly perched in shrubs, making short aerial flights to capture insects before returning to the same or a nearby perch. The species is more easily detected by voice on its breeding grounds than by sight. During migration, it may be difficult to separate from Willow Flycatcher and other small Empidonax flycatchers without careful views or vocal evidence.

conservation.populationTrend: Population trend estimates vary by region, but monitoring in parts of North America indicates declines, including substantial long-term reductions in some surveyed areas. The global assessment nevertheless does not currently classify the species as threatened.
conservation.threats: Loss and degradation of wet shrub habitats on the breeding grounds, including drainage, development, altered water regimes, and vegetation succession, may reduce nesting habitat. Habitat loss and degradation along migration routes and in the Central American nonbreeding range may also affect the species. Climate change could alter wetland conditions and the timing or availability of insect prey.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore wetlands, bog margins, alder and willow thickets, and naturally regenerating shrublands in both breeding and nonbreeding areas. Maintaining connected habitat corridors, reducing unnecessary clearing near wetlands, and supporting bird monitoring can improve knowledge of population changes. In Costa Rica, conserving lowland wetlands, riparian vegetation, and structurally diverse second-growth habitat benefits this migrant and many other Neotropical migratory birds.

profile.overview: The Willow Flycatcher is a small, long-distance migrant in the tyrant flycatcher family. It breeds mainly in North America and spends the nonbreeding season from the southwestern United States and Mexico through Central America. Like many Empidonax flycatchers, it is difficult to identify by appearance alone, but its distinctive “fitz-bew” song is useful. The species is associated with shrubby vegetation, especially along streams, wetlands, and other areas with dense low growth.
profile.classification: The Willow Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Empidonax. It was formerly grouped with the Alder Flycatcher as Traill’s Flycatcher, but the two are now recognized as separate species.
profile.identification: This is a small, fairly plain flycatcher with olive-brown upperparts, a grayish or olive-gray head, pale underparts, two whitish wing bars, and a noticeable pale lower wing bar or tertial edging. The bill is broad and relatively flat, with a pale or orange lower mandible. Plumage varies among subspecies and can look dull in worn birds. Willow and Alder Flycatchers are usually not safely separated by appearance; the Willow Flycatcher’s characteristic “fitz-bew” song is the best field clue.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species breeds across much of western and central North America, with some populations in the northeastern United States and Canada, and migrates south for winter. In Costa Rica it is a nonbreeding visitor, occurring mainly on the Pacific slope and especially in lowland areas, although individuals may also occur on the Caribbean slope. It uses brushy clearings, streamside thickets, second-growth scrub, woodland edges, plantations, and other semi-open habitats, often near standing or slow-moving water.
profile.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Willow Flycatchers arrive in Costa Rica mainly during the northern winter and depart northward in spring; the country is not a regular breeding area. The Pacific lowlands of Costa Rica are considered an important wintering region, including for some Southwestern Willow Flycatchers.
profile.breeding: Breeding takes place mainly in North America during spring and summer. The species usually nests in dense shrubs or small trees beside streams, ponds, marshes, and other wetlands, often where willows or similar vegetation provide concealment. The nest is an open cup placed in a fork or on a horizontal branch, commonly low above the ground. A typical clutch contains three or four eggs, and both habitat structure and water availability strongly influence nesting success.
profile.dietFeeding: Willow Flycatchers feed mainly on flying insects, including flies, wasps, bees, beetles, moths, and other arthropods. They usually hunt from a low or mid-level perch, making short sallies to capture prey in the air or picking insects from nearby vegetation. During migration and winter in Costa Rica, they forage in brushy habitats, riparian vegetation, forest edges, and semi-open woodland. Small fruits may occasionally supplement the diet.
profile.behavior: This species is often solitary and inconspicuous, remaining within dense vegetation while giving soft calls. It frequently perches upright and repeatedly returns to favored lookouts after short flights to catch insects. Males defend breeding territories with song, while wintering birds may maintain individual feeding territories and show site fidelity. Its song is a sharp, emphatic “fitz-bew,” and its call is a softer, less distinctive note.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is declining, although the species remains fairly common in much of its range. Trends differ among subspecies and regions, with the greatest concerns involving specialized southwestern populations.
conservation.threats: Major concerns include loss, alteration, and fragmentation of riparian wetlands and shrublands; river regulation; groundwater depletion; drought; wildfire; invasive vegetation changes; livestock grazing; and brood parasitism by Brown-headed Cowbirds. In Costa Rica, degradation and scarcity of suitable winter habitat in Pacific lowlands may affect survival during the nonbreeding season.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore streamside thickets, wetlands, mangroves, and other brushy lowland habitats used during migration and winter. Maintain native vegetation near water, reduce unnecessary clearing and intensive grazing, and support monitoring of wintering Willow Flycatchers in Costa Rica. Birders can contribute useful records through reputable citizen-science programs, especially when photographs, recordings, dates, and precise locations are included.

profile.overview: The White-throated Flycatcher (Empidonax albigularis) is a small tyrant flycatcher of Mexico and Central America. It is named for its conspicuous white throat, which contrasts with its brownish upperparts, pale yellowish underparts, and buff wing bars. The species usually occupies open or semi-open habitats rather than dense forest. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon and locally distributed bird, with records from highland valleys, foothills, wetlands, grasslands, and other brushy areas.
profile.classification: The White-throated Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Empidonax. It is closely related to other small, visually similar Empidonax flycatchers, which are often difficult to identify without careful attention to plumage, habitat, and voice.
profile.identification: This is a small, compact flycatcher with a brownish head and back, two pale buff wing bars, a whitish eye-ring, and yellowish to pale olive underparts. Its strongest field mark is the bright white throat, sharply contrasting with the darker upper breast. The bill is broad at the base, with a dark upper mandible and paler lower mandible. Identification can be difficult because several Empidonax species share similar shapes and wing markings; the call is often useful.
profile.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from Mexico south through Central America to Panama. In Costa Rica it is locally distributed, especially from about 500 to 1,500 meters along the western and southern slopes of Irazú and the Caribbean-facing slopes of the Guanacaste, Tilarán, and Central Volcanic ranges. It also occurs in intermontane valleys of the southern Pacific lowlands, with lower-elevation records from wetlands and grasslands. Typical habitat includes wet meadows, marsh edges, brushy fields, hedgerows, riparian thickets, clearings, and second-growth vegetation.
profile.migrationStatus: The White-throated Flycatcher is resident or seasonally elevational in Costa Rica rather than a regular long-distance migrant. Birds occur in the country's highlands year-round in some areas, while others may move to lower elevations outside the breeding season. Costa Rican lowland records are scattered and may include local elevational movements or migrants from farther north; the timing and extent of these movements are not fully understood.
profile.breeding: Breeding information is better documented in northern Central America than in Costa Rica, but the species is considered a breeding resident in parts of the Costa Rican highlands. It generally nests in open or semi-open areas near water, including riparian scrub, wet clearings, marsh margins, and young second growth. The nest is an open cup made from grasses and other plant fibers, usually placed low in a shrub or small tree. Breeding activity elsewhere in Central America is concentrated mainly from April through July or August.
profile.dietFeeding: The White-throated Flycatcher feeds mainly on insects and other small arthropods. It typically hunts from a low exposed perch, making short sallies to catch flying insects and sometimes returning to the same perch. It may also glean prey from leaves and stems. In Costa Rica, suitable feeding sites include marsh edges, grassy clearings, brushy pasture, hedgerows, and open woodland margins. Small fruits may occasionally supplement its primarily insect-based diet.
profile.behavior: This flycatcher is usually encountered singly or in pairs and often remains inconspicuous in dense grass or low shrubbery. It perches quietly before making short, quick flights after insects. When returning to a perch, it may flick or quiver its wings and tail, a useful behavioral clue. Males defend breeding territories with repeated calls. The species tends to favor edges and semi-open vegetation, where scattered perches provide clear views over nearby ground and vegetation.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is considered stable or not known to be declining at a rate that approaches a threatened category. Detailed population estimates are limited, especially for local populations in Costa Rica.
